0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “first book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus, likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final words are without hindrance. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Who wrote Acts, and when? The same author as Luke’s Gospel: both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by referring back to the first book (1:1). In several passages the story shifts to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–28:16), so the writer travelled with Paul, and the early church agreed that he was Luke, the beloved physician (Col 4:14; cf. Philem 24; 2 Tim 4:11). Some date Acts in the 80s. The more likely date is the early 60s: the book ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after two years (28:30), and says nothing of his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem, events Luke could hardly have left out had they already happened.

Should churches copy everything in Acts? Acts is history, the record of what God did as the church was founded. What it describes is not automatically a command. A pattern binds us when the rest of the New Testament teaches it, or when Luke shows it as God’s settled way: preaching Christ, baptizing believers, appointing elders, devotion to the apostles’ teaching and prayer. But the casting of lots (1:26), the sharing of all property (4:32), and the signs that marked the apostles (2:43; 5:12) belonged to that unrepeatable time.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
Acts is the second volume of Luke’s work, written for the same Theophilus as his Gospel. The Gospel told what Jesus “began” to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Jesus goes on doing by his Spirit through his church, as the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Rome in about thirty years. Chapter 1 is the hinge between the two volumes. For forty days the risen Jesus shows himself alive and teaches about the kingdom. He tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised baptism with the Holy Spirit. When they ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers that the timing is the Father’s business; their business is to receive power and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth, a sentence that maps out the whole book. Then he is taken up into heaven, and angels promise he will return in the same way.

The second half of the chapter shows the church waiting: about a hundred and twenty believers, including Jesus’ mother and his once-sceptical brothers, praying together in an upper room. Peter explains from the Psalms that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture and that his place must be filled, so that the Twelve, symbolising the renewed Israel, are complete before the Spirit comes. Two men who had been with Jesus from the beginning and witnessed the resurrection are nominated, the church prays, lots are cast, and Matthias is added to the apostles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke reminds Theophilus that his first book covered all that Jesus began to do and teach until he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. After his suffering Jesus gave them many convincing proofs that he was alive, appearing over forty days and speaking about God’s kingdom. While eating with them he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the Father’s promised gift: John baptised with water, but in a few days they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit. When they asked whether he was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel, he said it was not for them to know the times the Father has set, but they would receive power when the Spirit came on them, and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he was taken up before their eyes and a cloud hid him. As they stared into the sky, two men in white told them that this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but the exaltation of Jesus. He who died and rose now reigns at the right hand of the Father (Psalm 110:1), exercising all authority in heaven and on earth. The church does not act in the absence of its king; it acts under the authority of its enthroned king. The cloud that received him is the glory-cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had already described the scene from the other side: one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13-14). The Reformed churches have insisted that the ascension is essential to the gospel and not an epilogue to it: without it Christ does not send the Spirit (John 16:7), does not intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and does not carry our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations at either end are unchanged: to stand looking into heaven, absorbed in timetables the Father reserved to himself, or to rush at the work in a strength that was never promised. The command is the same as it was on the hillside — receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my earlier book, Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day he was taken up to heaven, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen.

Theophilus. “Friend of God” or “loved by God”. In Luke 1:3 he is “most excellent Theophilus”, a title for a Roman official or person of high rank. Probably a real person, perhaps Luke’s patron, who paid for the books to be copied. Some think the name stands for every reader who loves God.

The first book. Luke’s Gospel. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14), Paul’s companion, wrote both, more than a quarter of the New Testament.

Began to do and teach. The key word is “began”. Acts is the continuation of Jesus’ work, now from heaven, by his Spirit. Some have suggested renaming the book “the Acts of the risen Lord” or “the Acts of the Holy Spirit”.

Through the Holy Spirit. Even the risen Jesus gave his commands by the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is still at work in the world today, through his people. You are part of the continuation.
verseByVerse.note: “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus. “Began” implies that Acts records what Jesus continued to do through his Spirit and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After his suffering, he showed himself to them and gave many convincing proofs that he was alive. He appeared to them over a period of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.”

Many proofs. Tekmēria: a word for decisive evidence in Greek logic and law. He ate, talked, showed his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27).

Forty days. A number of preparation in Scripture: Moses on Sinai, Elijah’s journey, Jesus’ temptation. Pentecost comes ten days after the ascension.

The kingdom of God. Jesus’ constant subject. Acts begins and ends with it (28:31).

Eating with them. Or “staying with them”; the Greek word is uncertain. Either way, real, physical fellowship.

Wait. “Stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). The mission must not start in human strength.

On a Tuesday. Before you serve, pray. Waiting on God is not wasted time.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For John baptised with water, but in a few days you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

John’s promise. “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16). Fulfilled at Pentecost.

Baptised with the Spirit. Immersed, drenched, in the Spirit, as Joel prophesied: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

A second blessing? Pentecostals note that the apostles were already believers before Pentecost, and conclude that baptism in the Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, for all Christians. Verdict: the apostles lived through a unique turning point in history, from the old covenant to the new. Their experience was not a pattern for every believer. Since Pentecost, every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9; Acts 2:38).

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ, the Spirit lives in you. You do not have to seek a second experience to be a full Christian; ask instead to be filled continually (Ephesians 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they met together, they asked him, “Lord, are you at this time going to restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It is not for you to know the times or dates the Father has set by his own authority.”

Their question. Many Jews expected the Messiah to drive out the Romans and re-establish David’s kingdom. Even after the resurrection, the disciples were thinking politically.

Jesus’ answer. He does not deny that God will fulfil his promises to Israel. He refuses to give a timetable and redirects them to their mission.

What about Israel? Dispensationalists see here a promise of a future earthly kingdom for national Israel, postponed but certain. Others see the kingdom restored now, as the risen Messiah reigns and gathers Israel’s remnant and the nations. Verdict: Jesus redirects them to a kingdom that spreads through witness, beginning with Jerusalem. The promises to Israel are being fulfilled in Christ and his church, Jew and Gentile together, and Paul still expects a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26). But Christians should not try to fix dates.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone who claims to know the timetable of the end. Jesus said it is not for us to know. Our job is to witness.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

The outline of Acts. Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), the ends of the earth (13–28, ending in Rome, the centre of the empire).

Power. Dynamis: not for show but for witness.

Witnesses. Martyres: those who testify to what they have seen. The word later came to mean “martyrs”, because so many witnesses died for their testimony.

The end of the earth. Echoing Isaiah 49:6, where God tells his Servant, “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” Paul quotes it in Acts 13:47.

Samaria. Jews and Samaritans despised each other. The gospel would cross that barrier first.

On a Tuesday. Your Jerusalem is your home and street; your Samaria may be people you find hard to like; the ends of the earth may be reached by prayer and giving. Where are you a witness?
verseByVerse.note: This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the end of the earth (13–28).

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he said this, he was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid him from their sight. They were looking intently up into the sky as he was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them.

Lifted up. The ascension: Jesus’ bodily departure to the Father’s right hand (Luke 24:50–51; Ephesians 1:20).

The cloud. The cloud of God’s glorious presence, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:9), the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the transfiguration (Luke 9:34). And Daniel’s vision: “with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man” to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14).

Two men in white. Angels, as at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4).

What it does not mean. Not that heaven is literally somewhere above the clouds. The ascension was a visible sign of Jesus’ passing into God’s presence, into the realm we cannot see.

For worship. Christ is reigning now. The ascension means our human nature is seated on the throne of the universe.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence.

parallels.desc: two men in dazzling apparel

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven.”

Why stand looking? A gentle rebuke: do not gaze; get on with the mission.

This same Jesus. The return will be personal: the same Jesus, not a different figure.

In the same way. Bodily, visibly, with the clouds (Matthew 24:30; Revelation 1:7).

Has he already come? Full preterists teach that Christ’s second coming happened, spiritually, in AD 70 with the fall of Jerusalem. Verdict: this verse rules that out. He went visibly and bodily; he will come back visibly and bodily. The historic creeds confess: “he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.”

On a Tuesday. Live each day as someone who expects Jesus to come back, not staring at the sky, but busy with his work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, about a kilometre away, and went to the upstairs room where they were staying: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James. They all devoted themselves to prayer together, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among about a hundred and twenty believers. He said that the Scripture the Holy Spirit spoke through David had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus, though he had been one of them and shared in their ministry. Judas had bought a field with the money from his wickedness, and there he fell headlong, burst open and died; everyone in Jerusalem heard of it, and the field became known as Akeldama, Field of Blood. The Psalms say his place should be deserted and someone else should take his office. So one of the men who had been with them throughout Jesus’ ministry, from John’s baptism to the ascension, must become a witness with them to the resurrection. They proposed Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. They prayed that the Lord, who knows every heart, would show which one he had chosen, then cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was added to the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Apostolic College and Its Significance

The reconstitution of the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and represent the reconstituted people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30); an incomplete Twelve would be a broken sign at the moment the sign was about to be needed. The qualifications Peter states (v. 22) mark the apostolic circle as a closed and historically anchored group — the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. The New Testament does use apostle more widely of sent ones and church messengers, but no one alive can meet the terms stated here, which is why the church has no further foundational word to wait for. Judas, meanwhile, stands as the sober warning at the door of the book: he was numbered among them, sent out with them, and trusted with the money, and nearness to Jesus did not save him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no money, no standing and no strategy prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture rather than by argument, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church's preparation for anything God intends to do has not changed shape: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere. Barsabbas, qualified and passed over in front of everyone, was, so far as we know, still among them when the Spirit fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they went back to Jerusalem from the hill called the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day’s walk from the city. When they arrived, they went upstairs to the room where they were staying. Those present were Peter, John, James and Andrew; Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew; James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.

Olivet. The Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. Zechariah prophesied: “On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4).

A Sabbath day’s journey. The distance Jewish tradition allowed on the Sabbath: 2,000 cubits, about a kilometre.

The upper room. Perhaps the room of the Last Supper (Luke 22:12), possibly in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12).

The Eleven. Ordinary men: fishermen, a tax collector (Matthew), a Zealot (Simon, perhaps once a political revolutionary against Rome). Tax collector and Zealot together in one room: only Christ could do that.

On a Tuesday. Your church is likely made up of very different people. That is how Christ builds his church.
verseByVerse.note: A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed on the Sabbath, a little over half a mile. The list of eleven matches the Gospels’ lists; Judas the son of James is probably Thaddaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all joined together constantly in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the believers, a group numbering about a hundred and twenty.

With one accord. Homothymadon: of one mind. A favourite word of Luke for the early church (2:46; 4:24).

Devoting themselves to prayer. The church was born in a prayer meeting.

The women. Those who followed Jesus from Galilee and witnessed the resurrection (Luke 8:2–3; 24:10).

Mary. Her last appearance in Scripture: praying with the church, not prayed to. Honoured as the Lord’s mother, a believer among believers.

His brothers. Who did not believe during his ministry (John 7:5), and now pray with his followers. James had seen the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:7).

One hundred and twenty. A small start for a world mission.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “in prayer and supplication”) add “and supplication”. The earliest have only “prayer”.

On a Tuesday. Go to your church’s prayer meeting this week. It is where Acts begins.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry, are now among the believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Brothers and sisters,” he said, “the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke long ago through David about Judas, who served as guide for those who arrested Jesus. He was one of our number and shared in our ministry.”

Had to be fulfilled. Even Judas’s betrayal fell within God’s plan, though Judas was fully responsible (Luke 22:22).

The Spirit spoke by David. A clear statement of the inspiration of Scripture: the human author spoke, but the Spirit was the speaker (2 Peter 1:21).

One of us. The tragedy of Judas: an apostle who betrayed Christ. Privilege does not guarantee faith.

On a Tuesday. Even betrayals in the church are not outside God’s control.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(With the payment he received for his wickedness, Judas bought a field. There he fell headlong, his body burst open and all his intestines spilled out. Everyone in Jerusalem heard about this, so they called that field in their language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)

A parenthesis. Luke’s explanation for Greek readers, not part of Peter’s speech.

Two accounts. Matthew says Judas “went and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5) and the priests bought the potter’s field with the returned money (27:6–8). Luke says Judas acquired the field and fell headlong. Verdict: the accounts can be harmonised. The priests bought the field with Judas’s money, so in effect he bought it; he hanged himself, and his body later fell and burst, perhaps when the rope broke or the body decayed. The traditional site, in the Hinnom valley, is on a steep slope above rocks.

Akeldama. Aramaic for “field of blood”, the language of Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Money gained by betraying Christ buys only a graveyard.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; the two accounts are often harmonised as a hanging followed by a fall. Akeldama is Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For,” said Peter, “it is written in the Book of Psalms: ‘May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,’ and, ‘May another take his place of leadership.’”

Two psalms. Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8. Both are psalms of a righteous sufferer betrayed by friends. Jesus is the ultimate righteous sufferer, and Judas the ultimate betrayer.

Office. Episkopē: oversight, the word later used for the office of bishop or overseer.

On a Tuesday. The early Christians read the Psalms as speaking of Jesus. Read Psalm 69 and look for him.

parallels.desc: may their camp be a desolation
may another take his office

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore it is necessary to choose one of the men who have been with us the whole time the Lord Jesus was living among us, beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us. For one of these must become a witness with us of his resurrection.”

Qualifications. An apostle had to be an eyewitness of Jesus’ ministry and resurrection. This is why there can be no apostles in this sense today.

Why replace Judas? Twelve apostles for the twelve tribes: the renewed Israel (Luke 22:30). When James was killed later (12:2), he was not replaced, because he had not fallen away.

A witness to his resurrection. The heart of the apostles’ message.

On a Tuesday. The faith you hold rests on eyewitness testimony. Read the Gospels as testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they nominated two men: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias.

Two candidates. Both qualified. Neither is mentioned again in the New Testament, though tradition tells of their later ministries.

Three names. Joseph (Hebrew), Barsabbas (Aramaic, perhaps “son of the Sabbath”), Justus (Latin). A man at home in several cultures.

A textual note. One important Western manuscript (Codex Bezae) reads “Barnabas” instead of “Barsabbas”, probably a scribal confusion.

On a Tuesday. Joseph was not chosen. There is honour in being a faithful candidate whom God passes over.

parallels.desc: Judas called Barsabbas

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they prayed, “Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two you have chosen to take over this apostolic ministry, which Judas left to go where he belongs.”

You know the hearts. Kardiognōsta: heart-knower. Only God sees inside a person (1 Samuel 16:7).

Which you have chosen. They believed the choice was already the Lord’s. The apostle is chosen by the Lord, as the Twelve were (1:2).

His own place. A sombre phrase for Judas’s destiny.

On a Tuesday. When facing a decision about leadership in your church, begin with prayer that God will show whom he has chosen.

parallels.desc: God, who knows the heart

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, so he was added to the eleven apostles.

Casting lots. Marked stones were shaken in a container until one fell out. Used in Israel to discover God’s will: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The high priest’s Urim and Thummim worked in a similar way (Exodus 28:30).

Should Christians use lots today? This is the last time lots are used in the Bible. After Pentecost, decisions were made by the Spirit’s guidance through prayer, Scripture, counsel and the church’s judgement (15:28, “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”). Verdict: lots are not wrong in themselves, but Christians now have the Spirit and the completed Scriptures, and should seek wisdom rather than random signs.

Was choosing Matthias a mistake? Some (such as G. Campbell Morgan) argue the apostles acted hastily and that God’s real choice was Paul. Verdict: Luke gives no hint of disapproval; Matthias is counted among the Twelve (2:14; 6:2). Paul himself speaks of “the twelve” and of himself as a special case (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

For worship. Thank God that he chooses and equips his servants, then and now.
verseByVerse.note: Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after the Spirit is given.

parallels.desc: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is the most neglected event in the Christian calendar — and one of the most theologically freighted. It is not simply that Jesus left; it is that he was enthroned. Psalm 110:1 — “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” — is the most-quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament. The early church was obsessed with it because it explained everything: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is not waiting to begin his kingdom; his kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church. Every prayer prayed in his name, every sermon preached, every soul converted is an act of the reigning Christ extending his dominion.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples in Jerusalem, staring at the sky, confused about timing and kingdom, learning that faithfulness in the interval between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness. They had no map, no strategy document, no budget — only a promise and an upper room.

Now: We live in the same interval — between the first coming and the second, between the already and the not-yet. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, obsessing over the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. The command is unchanged: wait in prayer, go in the Spirit, witness to the ends of the earth. He is coming. In the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. <sup>2</sup>And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. <sup>3</sup>And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. <sup>4</sup>And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. <sup>5</sup>Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. <sup>6</sup>And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. <sup>7</sup>And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? <sup>8</sup>And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? <sup>9</sup>Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, <sup>10</sup>Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, <sup>11</sup>both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.” <sup>12</sup>And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” <sup>13</sup>But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. <sup>15</sup>For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. <sup>16</sup>But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: <sup>17</sup>‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream <sup>21</sup>And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’ <sup>22</sup>“Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know— <sup>23</sup>this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says the proceeds to all, as any had need. <sup>46</sup>And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Pentecost (Greek for “fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Israel thanked God for the wheat harvest by offering the first loaves of the new crop (Leviticus 23:15–21). By New Testament times some Jews also linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai, which Exodus places in the third month after the exodus. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims from across the Jewish world. On that day, ten days after the ascension, the Spirit came as Jesus promised: a sound like a rushing wind, flames resting on each believer, and the disciples speaking in the languages of the pilgrims, so that people from Parthia to Rome heard God’s mighty works in their own native tongues. At Babel, God confused human languages to scatter proud rebels; now he speaks in every language to gather a people for himself.

Some mocked, saying the disciples were drunk. Peter stood and preached the first Christian sermon. This, he said, is what Joel promised for the last days: the Spirit poured out on all kinds of people, and salvation for everyone who calls on the Lord’s name. Then he proclaimed Jesus: attested by miracles, handed over by God’s plan and killed by them through lawless men, but raised by God, as David foresaw in Psalm 16. Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and God has made him both Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, the crowd asked what to do. Repent and be baptised in Jesus’ name, Peter said, and you will receive forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. About three thousand did. The chapter ends with a portrait of the new community: devoted to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, sharing generously, meeting in the temple and in homes, praising God, and growing daily as the Lord added to their number.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the day of Pentecost the believers were all together in one place. Suddenly a sound like a violent wind came from heaven and filled the house where they were sitting. They saw what looked like tongues of fire that separated and settled on each of them, and all of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them. Devout Jews from every nation were staying in Jerusalem, and when they heard the sound a crowd gathered, bewildered, because each one heard the believers speaking in his own language. Amazed, they asked how these Galileans could be speaking in their native languages: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome, Jews and converts to Judaism, Cretans and Arabs. All heard God’s wonderful works declared in their own tongues. Amazed and perplexed, they asked what it meant, while others mocked and said the believers had drunk too much wine.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament had promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a handful of officeholders but on his whole people — Joel 2, Ezekiel 36–37 and Jeremiah 31 all say it, and Moses had wished for it out loud some fourteen centuries earlier (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day arriving. This governs how the event should be read. The Spirit's coming is not a private enrichment handed to a hundred and twenty people who happened to pray hard enough; it is a public, datable, once-for-all act in the history of salvation, standing alongside the birth, the cross and the empty tomb. Christ was born once, died once, rose once, and poured out his Spirit once. What is repeated afterwards is not the outpouring but the filling — and Luke will use that second word again of Peter and the company (4:8, 4:31), and later of Paul (13:9), which is a mercy, because it means what happened to them is not sealed inside one morning in the first century.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia — the first four names on Luke's list are exile addresses. Assyria deported the northern tribes and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and seven centuries later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street hearing the mighty works of God in the language of the country their forefathers were carried off to. Now: The same thing happens every time the Bible is put into a language that has never had it. The God who gave the church its first sermon in fifteen languages at once has never shown the slightest interest in making anyone learn a holy one first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place. Suddenly a sound like the blowing of a violent wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting.

Pentecost. The Feast of Weeks (Exodus 23:16; Leviticus 23:15–21), the harvest festival of firstfruits. At Passover Christ, the first sheaf, rose (1 Corinthians 15:20); at Pentecost the first great harvest of believers is gathered in.

Sinai. Later Jewish tradition linked Pentecost with the giving of the law. At Sinai there was fire, a great sound and God’s presence (Exodus 19:16–19). Now God gives not tablets of stone but his Spirit, writing the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3).

Wind. In Hebrew and Greek, “wind”, “breath” and “spirit” are the same word (ruach, pneuma). Ezekiel saw the breath of God bring dry bones to life (Ezekiel 37:9–14). Jesus compared the Spirit to the wind (John 3:8).

On a Tuesday. The church was born when God acted, not when the disciples organised. Pray for God to work in your church in ways only he can.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest. Wind and breath picture the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Weeks

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They saw what seemed to be tongues of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them.

Fire. A sign of God’s presence: the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of fire, Sinai (“the LORD had descended on it in fire”, Exodus 19:18). John the Baptist promised a baptism “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16).

On each one. Not just on the apostles: on every believer present. In the Old Testament God’s glory rested on the tabernacle and the temple; now it rests on each member of the new temple, the church.

Other tongues. Real languages they had not learned (vv. 6–11).

Speaking or hearing? Some suggest the miracle was in the hearing: the disciples spoke one language and the hearers understood in their own. Verdict: Luke says they “began to speak in other tongues”, so the miracle was in the speaking.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit was given to every believer. You too are a dwelling place of God.
verseByVerse.note: Fire often signals God’s presence.

parallels.desc: the LORD descended on it in fire

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were staying in Jerusalem God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven. When they heard this sound, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard their own language being spoken.

Dwelling. Some were pilgrims for the feast; others were Jews born abroad who had settled in Jerusalem. The Jewish dispersion (the Diaspora) stretched from Babylon to Spain.

Every nation. A foretaste of the gospel going to all nations (Matthew 28:19).

Bewildered. Synechythē: confounded, the same word used in the Greek of Genesis 11:7, 9 for the confusion of languages at Babel. Babel is reversed: there, languages divided a proud humanity; here, God speaks every language to unite a redeemed people.

On a Tuesday. God wants worship in every language. Support Bible translation, and welcome believers from other cultures in your church.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came as pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Utterly amazed, they asked, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? Then how is it that each of us hears them in our native language?”

Galileans. Northerners, considered uneducated, with a recognisable accent: “your accent betrays you” (Matthew 26:73). Not polyglots.

Native language. Literally “the dialect in which we were born”. God speaks to people in their heart language.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary people. Do not think you are too unqualified to speak about Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parthians, Medes and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome.

The list. A roll-call of the Jewish world, roughly from east to west. Parthia, Media and Elam lay beyond the Roman empire, in modern Iran; Jews had lived there since the exile. Mesopotamia is modern Iraq. Then the provinces of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), north Africa, and finally Rome.

Visitors from Rome. Perhaps some returned home and founded the church in Rome, which existed before Paul reached it (Romans 1:8).

On a Tuesday. Find on a map the places named here. Pray for Christians in those regions today, many of them persecuted.
verseByVerse.note: The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome): the whole Jewish world scattered among the nations.

parallels.desc: the table of nations
Babel, where languages were confused

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Both Jews and converts to Judaism, Cretans and Arabs: we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own languages!”

Proselytes. Gentiles who had converted fully to Judaism. Already a hint of the Gentile mission.

The mighty works of God. The content of tongues at Pentecost: praise for God’s saving acts in Christ. Tongues here were worship and witness, not private ecstasy.

For worship. Praise God for his mighty works: creation, the exodus, the cross, the resurrection, your own conversion.
verseByVerse.note: Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

parallels.desc: Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amazed and perplexed, they asked one another, “What does this mean?” Some, however, made fun of them and said, “They have had too much wine.”

What does this mean? Miracles raise questions; they need the word to explain them. Peter’s sermon follows.

New wine. Literally “sweet wine”. The mockers saw only noisy, excited men. Spiritual realities can look foolish to outsiders (1 Corinthians 2:14).

On a Tuesday. When people mock your faith, it may be the opening for an explanation, as it was for Peter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter stood up with the Eleven and addressed the crowd. These men are not drunk, he said; it is only nine in the morning. This is what the prophet Joel foretold: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all people; sons and daughters will prophesy, young men see visions and old men dream dreams, and even slaves, men and women, will receive the Spirit and prophesy. There will be wonders above and signs below, blood, fire and smoke; the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood before the great day of the Lord. And everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Peter then spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God had clearly approved by miracles, wonders and signs done among them, as they knew. This man was handed over according to God’s settled plan and foreknowledge, and they killed him by having lawless men nail him to a cross. But God raised him, freeing him from death’s agony, because death could not keep its hold on him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's argument from Psalm 16 is not proof-texting; it is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption. David died, was buried, and his tomb was a landmark a short walk from where Peter was standing. Therefore the words say more than David's own life could pay, and they are prophecy — and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. He does the same with Psalm 110: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which David hears the LORD speak to my Lord must be about somebody else. This is the way the risen Christ himself had taught them to read on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27, 44). The Reformed tradition has taken this sermon as the pattern for reading the whole Old Testament — not squeezing Christ out of texts that will not hold him, but recognising that the Scriptures were written by a Spirit who knew where the story was going and left the shape of it in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated — this Jesus whom you crucified — and he said it to their faces in the seventh week after they had done it. He did not soften the charge in order to get a hearing, and three thousand of them were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer never has anything to forgive him for. The reason this crowd asked what shall we do is that Peter had left them with something that needed doing. Preaching which manages to be about sin in general, committed by people in general, will produce interest, and will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter stood up with the Eleven, raised his voice and addressed the crowd: “Fellow Jews and all of you who live in Jerusalem, let me explain this to you; listen carefully to what I say. These people are not drunk, as you suppose. It is only nine in the morning!”

Peter. Seven weeks earlier he had denied Jesus to a servant girl. Now he preaches boldly to thousands. The difference is the Spirit.

With the eleven. The Twelve, restored with Matthias, stand together.

The third hour. About 9 a.m., the hour of morning prayer and sacrifice. Jews normally did not eat or drink until after morning prayers on a feast day. Peter’s first argument is common sense.

On a Tuesday. If you have failed Christ in the past, as Peter had, he can still use you boldly.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m. — far too early for drunkenness.

parallels.desc: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.”

This is that. The key to apostolic preaching: the events of Christ and the Spirit fulfil the Old Testament. Joel 2:28–32 is now happening.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament prophets looking for what has been fulfilled in Christ and the church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.’”

The last days. Peter changes Joel’s “afterward” to “in the last days”. The last days began with Christ’s first coming and continue until his return (Hebrews 1:2).

All flesh. Not only prophets, priests and kings, as in the Old Testament, but all God’s people: male and female, young and old, slave and free. Moses longed for this: “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29).

Prophesy. Here, in its broadest sense, declaring God’s mighty works (v. 11).

Visions and dreams. Part of Joel’s picture of the Spirit’s outpouring. God did guide through visions in Acts (9:10; 10:3; 16:9). Whether he does so regularly today is debated; all agree that dreams and visions must be tested by Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Every believer, including the elderly, the young, women, and those with no status, has the Spirit and something to say about God’s works.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!
Philip’s four daughters prophesied

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and billows of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and glorious day of the Lord.’”

Cosmic signs. The prophets used such images for God’s great acts of judgement and salvation (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7–8). They describe history-shaking events in the language of the heavens shaking.

Fulfilled when? Some see fulfilment at the cross, when darkness covered the land at noon (Luke 23:44–45). Others see a future fulfilment at Christ’s return. Verdict: both. The last days began at the cross and Pentecost and will end with the great day of the Lord. Peter includes these lines because the whole period is one: the Spirit has come, and the day is coming.

On a Tuesday. We live between Pentecost and the great day. Both should shape how we live.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: darkness at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’”

The goal. Salvation for everyone who calls on the Lord.

The Lord. In Joel, “the LORD” is Yahweh. Peter applies the verse to Jesus (v. 36, “God has made him both Lord and Christ”; v. 38). Paul does the same (Romans 10:13). From the first sermon, Jesus is identified with Israel’s God.

Everyone. No one is excluded who calls on him.

For worship. Call on the name of the Lord Jesus today, in prayer and praise.
verseByVerse.note: In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD; Peter applies the name to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fellow Israelites, listen to this: Jesus of Nazareth was a man accredited by God to you by miracles, wonders and signs, which God did among you through him, as you yourselves know. This man was handed over to you by God’s deliberate plan and foreknowledge; and you, with the help of lawless men, put him to death by nailing him to the cross.”

Attested. Jesus’ miracles were public knowledge: “as you yourselves know”.

God’s plan and human guilt. Both are true together. God planned the cross; those who crucified Jesus were fully responsible. This is how Scripture holds divine sovereignty and human responsibility (Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27–28). The Reformed call it compatibilism: God ordains all that happens, yet people act freely and are accountable for their choices.

Lawless men. The Romans, who did not have God’s law.

You crucified. Peter does not blame Jews as a race for all time; the guilt was shared by Jews and Gentiles, and by all of us whose sins put him there. The charge here is to the Jerusalem crowd, some of whom had shouted “Crucify him!” Christians must never use this verse to justify antisemitism.

On a Tuesday. Even the worst event in history was within God’s plan, and turned to salvation. Your hardest circumstances are not outside his purpose.
verseByVerse.note: Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But God raised him from the dead, freeing him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep its hold on him.”

God raised him. The divine reversal of the human verdict.

The pangs of death. Literally “birth pains”. Death was like labour pains, which ended in new life.

Not possible. Death could not hold the Holy One, the author of life (3:15).

For worship. Thank God that death could not hold Jesus, and will not hold you.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“David said about him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me. Because he is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will rest in hope.’”

Psalm 16:8–11. A psalm of trust in God in the face of death.

Concerning him. Peter reads the psalm as spoken by the Messiah. David wrote it, but its words fit Jesus better than David.

Hope. The flesh will rest in hope: hope of bodily resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Like the psalmist, set the Lord always before you. Then your heart can be glad even facing death.

parallels.desc: I have set the LORD always before me

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘Because you will not abandon me to the realm of the dead, you will not let your holy one see decay. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence.’”

Hades. The Greek for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead.

Not see corruption. The body of the Holy One would not decay. Jesus was raised on the third day, before decay set in.

Did Jesus descend into hell? The Apostles’ Creed says “he descended into hell”. Interpretations vary.

Roman Catholic and Orthodox tradition: Christ went to the realm of the dead to free the Old Testament saints (the “harrowing of hell”).

Calvin: it refers to Christ’s spiritual agony on the cross, enduring God’s wrath.

The Westminster tradition: he continued under the power of death until the third day (Larger Catechism 50).

Verdict: the verse says Christ’s soul was not abandoned in the realm of the dead; it does not describe a journey to preach there. The Westminster reading fits best: Jesus truly died, and his soul went where the souls of the dead go, but he was not left there.

For worship. The paths of life: Jesus has walked them through death and out the other side, and he leads us on them.
verseByVerse.note: Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fellow Israelites, I can tell you confidently that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is here to this day. But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that he would place one of his descendants on his throne.”

David’s tomb. A known landmark in Jerusalem. The Jewish historian Josephus says Herod tried to rob it. David’s body was still there: the psalm cannot be about David himself.

A prophet. David is called a prophet, for he spoke by the Spirit (2 Samuel 23:2).

The oath. God’s promise to David: “I will raise up your offspring after you … and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:12–13; Psalm 132:11).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ”. The earliest lack it; it seems to be an explanatory expansion.

On a Tuesday. The empty tomb of Jesus stands in contrast to the occupied tomb of David. Visit any grave and remember the difference.
verseByVerse.note: David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: the LORD swore to David a sure oath

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Seeing what was to come, he spoke of the resurrection of the Messiah: that he was not abandoned to the realm of the dead, nor did his body see decay. God has raised this Jesus to life, and we are all witnesses of it.”

He foresaw. David looked ahead to the Messiah. The prophets “searched and inquired carefully” about the sufferings and glories of Christ (1 Peter 1:10–11).

We are witnesses. Not a theory, but testimony. The 120 had seen him.

On a Tuesday. Peter’s argument is Scripture plus eyewitness testimony. That is still the basis of our faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Exalted to the right hand of God, he has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear. For David did not ascend to heaven, and yet he said, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand…’”

Exalted. The ascension placed Jesus at the place of supreme authority.

Poured out. The risen Jesus gives the Spirit. This shows his deity: only God can pour out God’s Spirit (Joel 2:28, “I will pour out my Spirit”).

The Trinity at Pentecost. The Father promises, the Son receives and pours out, the Spirit is given.

Psalm 110:1. David’s “Lord” is the Messiah, whom God invites to sit at his right hand. Jesus himself used this psalm to show that the Messiah was greater than David (Luke 20:41–44).

For worship. Every good work of the Spirit in your life comes from the exalted Christ. Thank him.

parallels.desc: “Sit at my right hand”

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘…until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’ Therefore let all Israel be assured of this: God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Messiah.”

Footstool. Ancient kings placed their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24).

Lord and Christ. The climax of the sermon. “Lord” is the title of God in the Greek Old Testament; “Christ” is the anointed King, the Messiah. Jesus is both.

Made him. Not that Jesus became divine at the resurrection, but that God publicly installed him in the position that was his by right (Romans 1:4).

Whom you crucified. A piercing ending. The one they killed is the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Is Jesus Lord of your money, relationships and work? “Lord” is not a title to admire but a rule to obey.
verseByVerse.note: “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God’s name; “Christ” means the Messiah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the people heard this, they were deeply moved and asked Peter and the other apostles what they should do. Peter replied that every one of them should repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for them and their children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord God will call. With many other words he warned them and pleaded with them to save themselves from this corrupt generation. Those who accepted his message were baptised, and about three thousand were added that day. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs the apostles performed. All the believers were together and shared everything; they sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. Every day they kept meeting together in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes, eating together with glad and sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the favour of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 gives the church four practices, and each is named with its definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. These are not four vague virtues but four definite things a visitor to Jerusalem that summer could have been taken to and shown. Reformed ecclesiology has read them as the permanent shape of church life. The apostles' teaching — which is now the New Testament — norms everything else, so that no experience, however vivid, is permitted to correct it. The fellowship is not sociability but a shared life the Spirit creates, and in this chapter it costs people money within three verses. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. And the prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation strong in all four will be healthy in almost any circumstances; a congregation that quietly lets one go will be impoverished in ways it may take a generation to notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was already equipped. The southern approach to the temple mount was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock, so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; dozens have been excavated and can still be walked into. The infrastructure of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it. Now: God is not in the habit of waiting for ideal conditions, and he has a long record of using whatever is already lying about — a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths, and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Peter replied, “Repent and be baptised, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Cut to the heart. Katenygēsan: pierced, stabbed. Conviction of sin is the Spirit’s work (John 16:8).

Repent. Metanoēsate: change your mind and direction; turn from sin to God.

Be baptised. The public sign of turning to Christ.

For the forgiveness of sins. Does baptism itself forgive sins? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Churches of Christ teach that it does. Verdict: forgiveness is received by repentance and faith (3:19; 10:43; 26:18), and baptism is its sign and seal. In 10:44–48 the Spirit comes on Cornelius before baptism. “For” (eis) can mean “with a view to”: repentance and baptism belong together as the response to the gospel, but the forgiveness rests on Christ.

In the name of Jesus. Oneness Pentecostals say baptism must use the name of Jesus only, not the Trinitarian formula. Verdict: “in the name of Jesus” means by his authority and into union with him, not a required formula. Jesus commanded baptism “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and the church has always used it.

The gift of the Spirit. Promised to all who repent. Not a later second blessing.

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ but have never been baptised, talk to your pastor. It is Christ’s command.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call.”

You and your children. The promise of the Spirit and forgiveness extends to the next generation. Paedobaptists see here the covenant principle that believers’ children belong to the covenant and should be baptised, as Israel’s children were circumcised. Credobaptists note that the promise is qualified: “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself”, and that it is received by repentance (v. 38), which infants cannot do. Verdict: the credobaptist reading is more natural, since the condition applies to the children as much as to the far off. But all agree that God’s promises are for families, and that parents should raise their children in hope.

All who are far off. Isaiah 57:19, “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near”. Paul uses it of the Gentiles (Ephesians 2:13, 17).

As many as the Lord calls. Salvation depends on God’s effectual call (Romans 8:30).

On a Tuesday. Pray for your children and grandchildren by name, that God would call them.
verseByVerse.note: “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many other words he warned them; and he pleaded with them, “Save yourselves from this corrupt generation.” Those who accepted his message were baptised, and about three thousand were added to their number that day.

Save yourselves. Not by your own power, but by responding to God’s offer. The phrase echoes Moses’ “crooked and twisted generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5).

Three thousand. When Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai, “about three thousand men of the people fell” (Exodus 32:28). At the new Sinai, three thousand were saved. “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

How were 3,000 baptised in one day? Jerusalem had many ritual immersion pools (mikvaot), including large ones near the temple, used by pilgrims. Archaeologists have found dozens.

On a Tuesday. God can save many at once, or one at a time. Keep praying for revival, and keep witnessing to individuals.
verseByVerse.note: Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai; now three thousand receive life.

parallels.desc: a crooked and twisted generation

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

Four marks of a healthy church.

The apostles’ teaching: now preserved in the New Testament. First on the list.

Fellowship: koinōnia, sharing life and goods.

The breaking of bread: shared meals, including the Lord’s Supper.

The prayers: literally “the prayers”, perhaps set times of prayer, as at the temple (3:1).

Devoted. Proskarterountes: persisting, continuing steadfastly. Not occasional attendance.

On a Tuesday. Check your Christian life against these four. Which is weakest?
verseByVerse.note: “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles. All the believers were together and had everything in common.

Awe. Phobos: holy fear. A sense of God’s presence.

Through the apostles. The signs were done especially by the apostles, confirming their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

All things in common. They treated possessions as available to all in need.

On a Tuesday. Hold your possessions with an open hand. They are God’s, lent to you for others too.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need.

Voluntary. Not compulsory communism. Property remained private: “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (5:4). People still had homes (v. 46; 12:12).

As any had need. Need-based giving. Many pilgrims who believed stayed in Jerusalem without income; the church cared for them.

Fulfilment. Moses had said, “there will be no poor among you” (Deuteronomy 15:4) if Israel obeyed. Luke notes in 4:34 that there was not a needy person among them.

Is this a model for today? Some groups (monastic orders, Hutterites, some communes) have taken it as a pattern for shared property. Others say it was a unique moment. Verdict: the principle, generous voluntary sharing so that no believer is in want, is binding; the exact form may vary. Later in Acts and the letters, believers kept property and gave generously (11:29; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

On a Tuesday. Is there someone in your church in financial need? Could you meet it quietly?
verseByVerse.note: Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of property.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day they continued to meet together in the temple courts. They broke bread in their homes and ate together with glad and sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the favour of all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.

The temple. The first Christians were Jews who kept worshipping at the temple, especially at Solomon’s Portico (3:11; 5:12). They did not see themselves as a new religion but as Israel’s faith fulfilled.

In their homes. Big gatherings and small. Both matter.

Glad and generous hearts. Joy and simplicity.

Favour with all. Their lives attracted the watching city.

The Lord added. Growth was God’s work, not their technique.
