You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter said, “Ananias, how is it that Satan has so filled your heart that you have lied to the Holy Spirit and kept for yourself some of the money you received for the land? Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was the money not at your disposal? What made you think of doing such a thing? You have not lied just to human beings but to God.”

The sin. Not keeping part of the money, which was his right, but pretending to give it all. Hypocrisy: wanting the reputation for generosity without paying the price.

Satan filled your heart. As with Judas (Luke 22:3). Satan attacks the church from inside as well as outside.

Your own. Proof that the sharing in Acts was voluntary. Property was private.

Lied to the Spirit, lied to God. Verse 3 says “to the Holy Spirit”; verse 4 says “to God”. The Spirit is God. And one can only lie to a person: the Spirit is not a force but a divine person (Psalm 139:7).

On a Tuesday. Do you want to be seen as more generous, more prayerful or more spiritual than you are? That is the sin of Ananias. Be honest.
verseByVerse.note: Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Ananias heard this, he fell down and died. And great fear seized all who heard what had happened. Then some young men came forward, wrapped up his body, and carried him out and buried him.

He died. Peter did not pronounce a curse; God acted. Like Nadab and Abihu, when “fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them” for offering unauthorised fire (Leviticus 10:2), or Uzzah touching the ark (2 Samuel 6:7).

Buried quickly. In the hot climate, burial usually happened the same day.

Was Ananias a true believer? Some say he was a believer disciplined by death, like those in Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:30–32); others say his hypocrisy showed he was never genuine. Verdict: we cannot know. Luke records the judgement, not his eternal state. The lesson is about the holiness of God in his church.

On a Tuesday. God does not usually strike hypocrites dead today, but that does not mean he takes it lightly. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).
verseByVerse.note: Burial usually took place the same day.

parallels.desc: Nadab and Abihu struck down

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. Peter asked her, “Tell me, is this the price you and Ananias got for the land?” “Yes,” she said, “that is the price.”

A chance to repent. Peter’s question gave her the opportunity to tell the truth.

She lied. Repeating the agreed story.

On a Tuesday. When someone gives you a chance to tell the truth, take it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to her, “How could you conspire to test the Spirit of the Lord? Listen! The feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.” At that moment she fell down at his feet and died. Then the young men came in and, finding her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband.

Test the Spirit. To see whether they could get away with it; to see whether God would notice.

At his feet. Where the money had been laid.

On a Tuesday. Hypocrisy in the church is more dangerous than opposition from outside.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD your God to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great fear seized the whole church and all who heard about these events.

The church. Ekklēsia: the first time Luke uses the word for the believers. In the Greek Old Testament it was used for the assembly of Israel. The church is God’s assembly.

Great fear. Holy awe at God’s presence and purity. A church that has lost the fear of God has lost something essential.

For worship. Come to God this week with joy and with reverence. Both belong together (Psalm 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Acts uses the word “church.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people. And all the believers used to meet together in Solomon’s Colonnade.

By the hands of the apostles. Again, the signs are linked to the apostles (2:43; 2 Corinthians 12:12).

Solomon’s Portico. A public space in the temple courts, big enough for thousands.

On a Tuesday. The early church met publicly and openly. Do not hide your faith.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one else dared join them, even though they were highly regarded by the people.

The rest. Probably outsiders, who respected the believers but were afraid after Ananias’s death to join casually. The church was attractive and holy.

On a Tuesday. A church should be both welcoming and serious about holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, more and more men and women believed in the Lord and were added to their number.

Multitudes. Holiness did not hinder growth.

Men and women. Luke regularly notes women believers (8:3, 12; 17:4, 12).

On a Tuesday. Pray that your church will grow by people truly believing in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a result, people brought the sick into the streets and laid them on beds and mats so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by. Crowds gathered also from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing their sick and those tormented by impure spirits, and all of them were healed.

Peter’s shadow. In the ancient world a person’s shadow was sometimes thought to carry their power. Luke records what people did, not necessarily that the shadow healed, though all were healed. Compare the woman who touched Jesus’ garment (Luke 8:44) and Paul’s handkerchiefs: “handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick” (Acts 19:12).

Relics and healing objects? Roman Catholic and Orthodox practice venerates relics of saints, and some Christians today send “prayer cloths”. Scripture records such things a few times (2 Kings 13:21, the bones of Elisha). Verdict: these were extraordinary works of God around the apostles, not a pattern for us. God heals by his own will, not through objects, and veneration of relics easily slides into superstition.

All healed. A time of extraordinary power, fulfilling Jesus’ promise that the apostles would do even greater works (John 14:12).

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick in your church, with faith in God, not in objects or people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest and his Sadducee allies, filled with jealousy, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out and told them to go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people all about this new life. At daybreak they did so. When the high priest convened the full council and sent for the prisoners, the officers found the jail securely locked with guards at the doors but no one inside. While the leaders were puzzling over this, someone reported that the men were standing in the temple teaching the people. The captain went with his officers and brought them, without force, fearing the crowd would stone them. The high priest reminded them of the strict order not to teach in this name, and accused them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and trying to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood. Peter and the apostles replied that they must obey God rather than human beings. The God of their ancestors raised Jesus, whom the leaders killed by hanging him on a cross; God exalted him to his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. The apostles are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to those who obey him. Furious, the council wanted to put them to death. But Gamaliel, a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law, had the men put outside and warned the council to be careful. Theudas had claimed to be somebody and gathered about four hundred men, but he was killed and his followers scattered; Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the time of the census and he too perished. So they should leave these men alone: if their plan is of human origin it will fail, but if it is from God they will not be able to stop them and may find themselves fighting against God. The council agreed, had the apostles flogged, ordered them not to speak in Jesus’ name, and let them go. The apostles left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name, and day after day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God Rather Than Men

Gamaliel's advice — if it is of man it will fail, if it is of God you cannot overthrow it — is often praised as tolerance. It is not Christian reasoning. It is pragmatic patience that never distinguishes truth from falsehood, only durable movements from short-lived ones, and it allows a man to avoid the one question in the room: did God raise Jesus? He is a providential restraint, not a theological authority. The apostles rest their case on something else entirely. Their principle is not defiance but a hierarchy of obedience: the state's authority is real and derived, and a delegated authority that forbids what God commands has run out of warrant at that point and no further. The same New Testament that records these words commands submission to governing authorities under Nero (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17). And the apostles supply the test that keeps the principle honest — they did not resist arrest, did not raise the crowd that was ready to riot for them, and did not flee. They took the flogging. Biblical civil disobedience characteristically accepts the penalty rather than looking for an escape clause.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the Name — led by the man who, only months earlier, had denied that he knew Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire. What changed was not his temperament.

Now: Suffering for the Name is not masochism and joy in it is not a duty to be manufactured in advance; it was given to those men on the way out of the building. Two things this passage is not: it is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person, since the suffering in view is dishonour incurred for Christ; and it is not a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes. The question is always whether God is being forbidden what he commands — and whether one is prepared to bear the cost of saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the high priest and all his associates, who were members of the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail.

Jealousy. The real motive. The apostles had popularity, power and the people’s respect, which the high priestly party wanted for themselves.

All the apostles. This time not just Peter and John.

On a Tuesday. Opposition to the gospel is often driven by jealousy and fear of losing control, more than by argument.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out. “Go, stand in the temple courts,” he said, “and tell the people all about this new life.”

An angel. Ironically, the Sadducees denied angels (23:8).

Go, stand, speak. The release was not for escape but for preaching.

This Life. A beautiful name for the gospel: the message of the life Jesus gives (John 10:10).

On a Tuesday. When God opens a door, it is usually to send you back into the place of witness.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At daybreak they entered the temple courts, as they had been told, and began to teach the people. When the high priest and his associates arrived, they called together the Sanhedrin, the full assembly of the elders of Israel, and sent to the jail for the apostles.

At daybreak. When the temple opened and people came for morning prayer.

The council and senate. A full, formal session.

On a Tuesday. Obey promptly when God speaks.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there. So they went back and reported, “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards standing at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.”

Locked and guarded. A miracle with humour: the authorities convene to try prisoners who are not there.

On a Tuesday. No human prison can hold back God’s word (2 Timothy 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On hearing this report, the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests were at a loss, wondering what this might lead to. Then someone came and said, “Look! The men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people.”

Perplexed. Their plans are frustrated.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes leaves opponents of the gospel baffled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that, the captain went with his officers and brought the apostles. They did not use force, because they feared that the people would stone them. The apostles were brought in and made to appear before the Sanhedrin.

Not by force. The apostles came willingly. They did not resist arrest.

Afraid of the people. Public support restrained the authorities, as with Jesus (Luke 22:2).

On a Tuesday. Christians may disobey a sinful command, but should not resist with violence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest questioned them. “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us guilty of this man’s blood.”

This name. Again the high priest will not say “Jesus”.

Filled Jerusalem. An unintended compliment.

This man’s blood. Ironically, at Jesus’ trial the crowd had said, “His blood be on us and on our children!” (Matthew 27:25).

A textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “Did not we straitly command you?”) read the opening as a question. The earliest read a statement. The sense is the same.

On a Tuesday. Fill your town with Christ’s teaching: in conversations, in service, in kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and the other apostles replied: “We must obey God rather than human beings! The God of our ancestors raised Jesus from the dead, whom you killed by hanging him on a cross.”

Must obey God. The principle of 4:19, now stated as a firm rule. See the discussion there.

Hanging on a tree. An allusion to Deuteronomy 21:23, “a hanged man is cursed by God”. The leaders thought the cross proved Jesus was cursed. In fact he bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

On a Tuesday. Where is the line for you between obeying authorities and obeying God? Think about it before you are tested.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God exalted him to his own right hand as Prince and Saviour, that he might bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

Leader and Saviour. Archēgos (pioneer, prince) and Sōtēr (saviour). Both titles were used of rulers and heroes. Jesus is the true one.

To give repentance. Repentance is a gift of the risen Christ, not something we produce ourselves (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25).

The Spirit as witness. Two witnesses: the apostles and the Spirit, who confirms the message in hearts and by signs (John 15:26–27).

Those who obey. Obeying the gospel by repentance and faith (2:38).

For worship. Thank Christ that even your repentance is his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this, they were furious and wanted to put them to death. But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, who was honoured by all the people, stood up in the Sanhedrin and ordered that the men be put outside for a little while.

Enraged. Literally “sawn through”, cut to the quick (compare 2:37, “cut to the heart”, in repentance).

Gamaliel. Gamaliel I, grandson of the great teacher Hillel, the most respected rabbi of his day, and Paul’s teacher (22:3). The Mishnah says that when he died, “the glory of the Torah ceased.”

A Pharisee. The Pharisees, unlike the Sadducees, believed in resurrection and had popular support. A Pharisee could restrain the Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. God can use people who are not believers to protect his people.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he addressed the Sanhedrin: “Men of Israel, consider carefully what you intend to do to these men. Some time ago Theudas appeared, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men rallied to him. He was killed, all his followers were dispersed, and it all came to nothing.”

Theudas. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions a Theudas who led a movement under the governor Fadus around AD 45, about ten years after Gamaliel’s speech.

A contradiction? Critics say Luke got the date wrong. Verdict: not necessarily. Theudas was a common name, and there were many rebel leaders after Herod the Great’s death in 4 BC. Gamaliel places this Theudas before Judas the Galilean (AD 6), so he is probably a different man. Josephus himself is not always precise in his dating. Luke’s accuracy elsewhere on titles and details is well established.

On a Tuesday. When someone says the Bible has a historical mistake, look more closely. Often the answer is in the details.
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and led a band of people in revolt. He too was killed, and all his followers were scattered. Therefore, in the present case I advise you: leave these men alone! Let them go! For if their purpose or activity is of human origin, it will fail.”

Judas the Galilean. He led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6 (Luke 2:1–2 refers to an earlier census), teaching that paying taxes to Caesar was slavery. Josephus calls his movement the “fourth philosophy”, the forerunner of the Zealots. His sons were later crucified by the Romans.

Leave them alone. Gamaliel’s principle: time will tell.

On a Tuesday. Movements built on human ambition rise and fall. Christ’s church has lasted two thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop these men; you will only find yourselves fighting against God.”

Fighting God. Theomachoi. A word used in Greek tragedy for those who foolishly fight the gods.

Is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some take it as a general rule: whatever succeeds is from God. Verdict: not as a universal test. Many false movements have lasted for centuries, and true churches have sometimes been crushed in certain places. Truth is tested by Scripture, not by success. But in this case Gamaliel’s caution was providential, and the church’s survival was indeed God’s doing.

On a Tuesday. Do not judge a church or ministry only by its size or success. Judge it by its faithfulness to God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His speech persuaded them. They called the apostles in and had them flogged. Then they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

Beaten. Probably the thirty-nine lashes of the synagogue (2 Corinthians 11:24; Deuteronomy 25:3): a brutal punishment that could kill.

Charged. The same order again, which they would ignore again.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Christians who are beaten for their faith today, in many countries.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing because they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. Day after day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Messiah.

Rejoicing. As Jesus taught: “Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you … Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5:11–12).

Counted worthy. Suffering for Christ is an honour, not a disgrace. “If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name” (1 Peter 4:16).

The Name. Simply “the Name”, as Jews spoke of God’s name with reverence.

Temple and house. Public preaching and private teaching. The pattern of Christian ministry (20:20).

For worship. Thank God for the courage of the apostles, and ask for courage when your turn comes to suffer, even in small ways, for the Name.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church only weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; a few verses later we are told that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The growing church faces a problem from within. It now contained two groups of Jewish believers: “Hebrews”, who spoke Aramaic and were rooted in the land, and “Hellenists”, Greek-speaking Jews, many born abroad, who had settled in Jerusalem. Many Hellenists were elderly couples who had come to Jerusalem to die near the temple, which left a large number of widows without family support. The church shared food daily with widows in need, and the Hellenists complained that their widows were being overlooked. Prejudice between language groups was threatening the unity of chapter 4.

The apostles do not ignore the problem or try to handle it themselves. They tell the church to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of the distribution, so that the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. All seven have Greek names, so the church entrusts the matter to the very group that complained. The apostles pray and lay hands on them, and the word of God spreads, even many priests becoming believers. Then Luke turns to one of the seven, Stephen, full of grace and power, who works wonders and debates with Greek-speaking Jews from the Synagogue of the Freedmen. When they cannot answer his wisdom, they bring false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law, and he is brought before the council, where those staring at him see that his face is like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the number of disciples grew, the Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained against the Aramaic-speaking ones that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food. So the Twelve gathered all the disciples and said it would not be right for them to neglect the ministry of God’s word to wait on tables. The believers should choose seven men from among them who were known to be full of the Spirit and wisdom, and the apostles would put them in charge of this task, while giving their own attention to prayer and the ministry of the word. The proposal pleased everyone. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch. They presented these men to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. So God’s word spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about vocation, not about dignity, and the passage guards against the misreading in the very next sentence: the men appointed to the tables must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower bar. The whole argument turns on a single Greek root that appears on both sides of it — the apostles will not abandon the service of the word in order to serve tables. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, one menial and one spiritual. They are two forms of one thing, and the only question is which form a particular man is called to. Nor are the Seven junior figures: Stephen is preaching within a paragraph and dead within a chapter, and Philip is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. What the passage protects is not the apostles' status but the church's food supply — a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked has already stopped believing what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows were very likely the kind of women Luke described in chapter 2 — Diaspora Jews, some of whom had come home to Jerusalem to end their days near the temple. Their husbands died, and the widows were left in a city where they had no land, no clan and no relatives, and could not follow the conversation at the distribution. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone. It is who is currently being looked past — the people whose absence nobody notices, because they were never in the middle of the room to begin with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days, when the number of disciples was increasing, the Greek-speaking Jews among them complained against the Aramaic-speaking community because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.

Increasing. Growth brings new problems.

Hellenists and Hebrews. Both were Jews and believers. The difference was language and culture: Hellenists spoke Greek, read the Greek Old Testament and had grown up in the cities of the Diaspora; Hebrews spoke Aramaic and were native to the land. Each group had its own synagogues in Jerusalem.

Widows. In Jewish society, widows without family were among the poorest. Many devout Jews from abroad came to Jerusalem in old age to die and be buried near the temple, so many Hellenist widows were alone. God himself “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18), and true religion is “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

Daily distribution. Jewish communities already had systems of poor relief, with a weekly fund and daily food. The church did the same.

Neglected. Perhaps unintentional, perhaps prejudice, perhaps language: the distributors may have known the Aramaic-speaking widows better.

On a Tuesday. In your church, who might be overlooked because they speak a different language, come from another culture or are not well connected? Notice them.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside the land; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic. Widows without family depended on the community’s daily food distribution.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Twelve gathered all the disciples together and said, “It would not be right for us to neglect the ministry of the word of God in order to wait on tables. Brothers and sisters, choose seven men from among you who are known to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will turn this responsibility over to them and will give our attention to prayer and the ministry of the word.”

Serve tables. Not beneath them: the apostles had served Jesus’ meals (Luke 9:16). But it was not their primary calling.

Prayer and the word. The priorities of church leaders who teach. A pastor who is too busy to pray and study will starve the church.

Good repute, Spirit, wisdom. Practical tasks need spiritual people. Compare Moses’ advice from Jethro: “look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe” (Exodus 18:21).

Pick out from among you. The congregation chooses; the apostles appoint. A shared process.

How should churches be governed? Episcopal churches (Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox) have bishops with authority to appoint; congregational churches give the final say to the members; presbyterian churches are led by elders, with congregations electing them. Verdict: this passage shows both the leaders’ authority and the people’s participation. Presbyterian and many congregational churches capture that balance, though the pattern is not rigidly fixed.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “full of the Holy Ghost”) add “Holy”. The earliest have “full of the Spirit”. The meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. Pastors: guard your time for prayer and the word. Church members: release your pastors for it by serving in practical ways yourselves.

parallels.desc: Jethro advises Moses to share the load

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This proposal pleased the whole group. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit; also Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism. They presented these men to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.

Greek names. All seven have Greek names. The church, wisely and generously, chose men from the group that had complained.

Stephen and Philip. Both soon became powerful preachers (chapter 7; 8:5–40). Their service was not limited to tables.

Nicolaus. A Gentile who had converted to Judaism, then become a Christian. The first Gentile-born leader in the church. (Some early writers linked him with the Nicolaitans of Revelation 2:6, but without good evidence.)

Laying on of hands. A sign of commissioning and identification, as Moses laid hands on Joshua: “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him” (Numbers 27:18). Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches regard ordination as a sacrament conferring grace. Verdict: the Reformed view: the laying on of hands publicly recognises and commissions those whom God has already gifted, with prayer for his blessing. The seven were already “full of the Spirit” before it.

Were they the first deacons? The word “deacon” (diakonos) is not used of them, though the verb “serve” (diakonein) is (v. 2). Many, since Irenaeus, have seen them as the first deacons. Verdict: they are at least the forerunners of the deacons of 1 Timothy 3:8–13: men set apart to care for the practical needs of the church, freeing the elders for the word.

On a Tuesday. If your church is choosing deacons, look first for character: good reputation, the Spirit, wisdom.
verseByVerse.note: All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. Laying on hands marked commissioning for a task.

parallels.desc: Moses lays hands on Joshua

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the word of God spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.

The word increased. One of Luke’s progress reports (also 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:31). Solving a problem well led to more growth.

Priests. There were thousands of ordinary priests in Judea, serving at the temple in rotation (Luke 1:8–9). Unlike the high priestly aristocracy, many were humble and devout. Some now believed in the true High Priest.

Obedient to the faith. Faith is obedience to the gospel’s call (Romans 1:5).

For worship. Thank God that he can turn a church crisis into growth.
verseByVerse.note: There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen, full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. Opposition arose from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, as it was called, Jews from Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia, who began to argue with him. But they could not stand up against his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke. So they secretly persuaded some men to say they had heard Stephen speak blasphemy against Moses and God. They stirred up the people, the elders and the teachers of the law, seized Stephen and brought him before the council. They produced false witnesses, who said that this man never stopped speaking against the holy place and the law, and that they had heard him say Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down. Everyone in the council looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest follows the shape of his master's with a precision Luke's first readers cannot have missed: suborned witnesses, a charge concerning the temple and the law, a council, a verdict of blasphemy. The accusation that Matthew and Mark record against Jesus (Matthew 26:61; Mark 14:58) is in fact the accusation Luke records against Stephen — the servant is handed the master's charge sheet. Reformed theology has read this as more than a coincidence of circumstance. Where the gospel genuinely threatens entrenched religious power it meets the same resistance in the same order, because the objection is never finally to the argument — the argument had already been lost at verse 10 — but to what conceding it would cost. What Stephen's case adds to the pattern is the sober detail that winning the argument and losing your life are entirely compatible, and that Luke plainly did not consider the second to be a reversal of the first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they changed the subject to blasphemy and found men who would swear to it. The gospel does not always win in the short term; sometimes the first thing it wins is a grave. Now: The promise attached to moments of that kind is more modest, and more useful, than it is usually made out to be. A believer put on the spot is promised a mouth, not a result — that he will not be left standing there with nothing to say. Whether he is believed, and what it costs him, are God's business.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.

Full of grace and power. Stephen is described as “full” four times: of the Spirit, wisdom, faith, grace and power (6:3, 5, 8; 7:55).

Not only an apostle. Stephen was not one of the Twelve, yet did signs. The signs were associated especially with the apostles and those they commissioned (6:6; 8:6, 18).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “full of faith and power”) read “faith” instead of “grace”, probably from verse 5. The earliest read “grace”.

On a Tuesday. A man appointed to serve tables became the church’s first martyr. Do not despise practical service; God can do great things through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opposition arose, however, from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, as it was called, Jews of Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia. These men began to argue with Stephen.

The Freedmen. Libertinoi, from Latin: descendants of Jews taken to Rome as slaves by Pompey in 63 BC and later freed. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built by one Theodotus, son of Vettenus, a priest and ruler of a synagogue, for “the reading of the law and teaching of the commandments”, with a guesthouse for visitors from abroad. Some think it may be this synagogue.

Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, Asia. North Africa, Egypt, south-east Turkey and west Turkey. All Greek-speaking Jews.

Cilicia. The home province of Saul of Tarsus (22:3). Saul may well have been among those who debated Stephen.

On a Tuesday. Opposition often comes from religious people who feel their traditions are threatened.
verseByVerse.note: The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps taken captive to Rome. Cilicia, in south-east Asia Minor, was Paul’s home province.

parallels.desc: Tarsus in Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke.

A promise kept. Jesus had said, “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict” (Luke 21:15).

On a Tuesday. When you face hard questions about your faith, prepare as well as you can, and trust the Spirit for the moment.

parallels.desc: a mouth and wisdom none can withstand

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they secretly persuaded some men to say, “We have heard Stephen speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God.” So they stirred up the people and the elders and the teachers of the law. They seized Stephen and brought him before the Sanhedrin.

Secretly instigated. When argument failed, they turned to slander. Exactly as with Jesus (Mark 14:55–59).

The people. For the first time the ordinary people turn against the church. Until now they had been favourable (2:47; 5:13).

On a Tuesday. When people cannot answer your arguments, they may attack your character. Make sure the accusations are false.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: false witnesses against Naboth

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They produced false witnesses, who testified, “This fellow never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down to us.”

False witnesses. A breach of the ninth commandment, in a trial about God’s law.

Half-truths. The charges twisted something real. Jesus had said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), speaking of his body, and his accusers turned it into “I will destroy this temple that is made with hands” (Mark 14:58). Stephen probably taught that Jesus fulfilled and replaced the temple and the ceremonial law, which his speech in chapter 7 will show.

The holy place. The temple was the heart of Jewish identity. To speak against it was dangerous.

On a Tuesday. The truth about Jesus will often be twisted. Keep explaining it clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

The face of an angel. Radiant, calm, perhaps shining with God’s glory, as Moses’ face shone after speaking with God (Exodus 34:29). Accused of speaking against Moses, Stephen looks like Moses.

Peace under accusation. Stephen was not anxious or angry. God’s presence was on him.

For worship. Pray for that kind of peace when you are falsely accused: God’s presence showing in your face.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

6.theology: Word and Deed, Order and Spirit. Acts 6 is the New Testament’s foundational text on church structure. It establishes that the body has different members with different callings; that no one person can or should do everything; that the criterion for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and that when ministry is rightly ordered, the Word — not the institution, not the ministers — is what grows. This is not a management manual; it is a theology of the church as the body of Christ, each member functioning according to its calling, all of it in service of the one mission: that the Word of God would run and be glorified.
6.examples:
Then: A rapidly growing Jerusalem church discovering that love without structure produces injustice — the widows being neglected are real women with real needs — and that structure without love produces dead religion. The seven are the church’s solution: Spirit-filled servants who bring both.

Now: Every growing church faces the tension of Acts 6: how do we care well for people without the leaders becoming so consumed with management that the Word is starved? The answer is not to choose between pastoral care and proclamation; it is to raise up men and women of Spirit and wisdom to share the load — and then to watch what God does with a church that is both devoted to the Word and devoted to its neighbours.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built a house for him. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts. Accused of speaking against the temple and the law, he answers by retelling Israel’s history, and two threads run through it. First, God has never been confined to one land or one building: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, met Moses in the desert at the burning bush, and was worshipped in a portable tent; Solomon built him a house, but, as the prophets said, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. Second, Israel has repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed aside, the people turned to idols in the wilderness and persecuted the prophets. The pattern ends where Stephen’s hearers stand: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One.

Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament and some Jewish traditions of his day, which explains a few details that differ from the Hebrew text, such as seventy-five rather than seventy members of Jacob’s family. His conclusion is a direct charge: they are stiff-necked and resist the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did. Enraged, the council rushes at him. Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees heaven open and Jesus, the Son of Man, standing at God’s right hand. They drag him out of the city and stone him, laying their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen dies as his Lord did, committing his spirit to Jesus and praying that this sin not be held against them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest asked whether the charges were true. Stephen began with Abraham: the God of glory appeared to him in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran, and told him to leave his country for a land God would show him. So Abraham moved to Haran and then, after his father’s death, to Canaan, though God gave him no inheritance there, not even a foot of ground, only a promise that his descendants would possess it, when as yet he had no child. God warned that his descendants would be foreigners, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but God would judge their oppressors and they would come out and worship him. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and the line ran through Isaac, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs. The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt, but God was with him, rescued him and gave him wisdom and favour with Pharaoh, who made him ruler over Egypt. In a famine Jacob sent the patriarchs to buy grain; on their second visit Joseph revealed himself, and he brought his whole family, seventy-five people, to Egypt. Jacob and the patriarchs died there and were buried in Shechem. As the time of the promise drew near, the people grew in Egypt until a new king arose who did not know Joseph. He oppressed them and forced them to abandon their babies. Moses was born then, a fine child, raised for three months in his father’s house and then adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. He was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt and was powerful in speech and action. At forty he visited his fellow Israelites, defended one who was being mistreated and killed the Egyptian, thinking his people would realise that God was using him to rescue them; but they did not. The next day he tried to reconcile two Israelites who were fighting, and the one in the wrong pushed him aside, asking who had made him ruler and judge, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian. Moses fled to Midian and had two sons there. After forty years an angel appeared to him in the flames of a burning bush near Mount Sinai. The Lord’s voice said he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled. God told him to take off his sandals, for the place was holy ground. God had seen his people’s oppression and heard their groaning, and was sending Moses to Egypt. This Moses, whom they rejected, God sent as ruler and deliverer through the angel in the bush. He led them out with wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. He told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from their own people. He was with the congregation in the wilderness, with the angel at Sinai and with their ancestors, and he received living words to pass on. But their ancestors refused to obey him; in their hearts they turned back to Egypt and asked Aaron to make them gods. They made a calf, sacrificed to it and celebrated what their hands had made. So God gave them over to worship the stars, as the prophet Amos says: they did not bring sacrifices to God in the wilderness but carried the shrine of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, and so God would send them into exile beyond Babylon. Their ancestors had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, made to the pattern Moses was shown, and brought it in with Joshua when they took the land, until the time of David. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling for him, but it was Solomon who built him a house. Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is his throne and earth his footstool; what house could anyone build for him, or where would his resting place be? Did his hand not make all these things?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Temple and the Transcendence of God

Stephen's climax — the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48) — is not an outsider's attack on the temple. It is the temple's own prophetic self-criticism, read back to the men who ran it. Solomon said it himself on the day he dedicated the building: the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27). Isaiah said it within sight of the same building. God had said it to David before a stone was laid, pointing out that since the exodus he had never once asked anybody for a house of cedar. The problem was never the temple; it was the reduction of God to a location — the belief that having the building in Jerusalem meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Reformed theology has read Stephen's argument as the permanent warning against every arrangement in which the sign is kept and the reality quietly replaced by it. And the warning has teeth precisely because Stephen is not against the sign: God designed the tent, God filled the temple, and God was the one who said he would not be confined to either.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Every institution Stephen's accusers trusted came after the God who made it. Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is not whether it values its building, its tradition or its structures — Stephen valued the tabernacle and said God designed it. It is whether it could lose them and still know where to find God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the high priest asked Stephen, “Are these charges true?”

The high priest. Probably still Caiaphas. A formal invitation to answer.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked to give an account of your faith, see it as an opportunity (1 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To this he replied: “Brothers and fathers, listen to me! The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Harran. ‘Leave your country and your people,’ God said, ‘and go to the land I will show you.’”

Brothers and fathers. Respectful: Stephen speaks as a fellow Jew.

The God of glory. The first words of the defence. Accused of blasphemy, Stephen begins with God’s glory.

In Mesopotamia. God appeared to Abraham outside the promised land, in Ur of the Chaldeans, before the move to Haran (Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7). Genesis 12:1 records the call in Haran; Stephen follows the tradition that God first called him in Ur. Both are true: God called him first in Ur and repeated the call in Haran.

The point. God’s presence is not limited to the holy land or the temple.

On a Tuesday. God can meet you anywhere: in a hospital ward, an office or a foreign city.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building, and that Israel repeatedly rejected his messengers.

parallels.desc: go to the land that I will show you

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Harran. After the death of his father, God sent him to this land where you are now living. He gave him no inheritance here, not even enough ground to set his foot on. But God promised him that he and his descendants after him would possess the land, even though at that time Abraham had no child.”

After his father died. A puzzle: Genesis 11:26 and 11:32 seem to imply Terah lived another sixty years after Abraham left. But Abraham may not have been Terah’s firstborn (11:26 lists the three sons together), and the Samaritan version of Genesis gives Terah 145 years, which fits Stephen. The Jewish writer Philo also says Abraham left after Terah’s death. Stephen follows a tradition known in his day.

Not a foot’s length. Abraham owned only a burial plot (Genesis 23). He lived by promise, not possession (Hebrews 11:8–10).

On a Tuesday. Like Abraham, you may live with promises you do not yet see fulfilled. Keep trusting.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God spoke to him in this way: ‘For four hundred years your descendants will be strangers in a country not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated. But I will punish the nation they serve as slaves,’ God said, ‘and afterwards they will come out of that country and worship me in this place.’”

Genesis 15:13–14. “Your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years.” A round number; Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years.

Worship me. The goal of the exodus was worship (Exodus 3:12).

On a Tuesday. God’s plans can take centuries. He is never late.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Then he gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision. And Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him eight days after his birth. Later Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs.”

The covenant. Circumcision came before the law and the temple (Genesis 17). Stephen honours it, answering the charge that he despised Moses’ customs.

The twelve patriarchs. The founders of the tribes.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his covenant from generation to generation. Pray for the next generation in your family.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles. He gave Joseph wisdom and enabled him to gain the goodwill of Pharaoh king of Egypt. So Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt and all his palace.”

The first rejected deliverer. Joseph’s brothers rejected him; God raised him up to save them. The pattern of Jesus.

God was with him. In a foreign land, as a slave and a prisoner. Not in the temple.

Joseph’s verdict. “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

On a Tuesday. If you have been betrayed by family, God can be with you in it and bring good from it.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Then a famine struck all Egypt and Canaan, bringing great suffering, and our ancestors could not find food. When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our forefathers on their first visit.”

Famine. God used the famine to bring Joseph’s family to him (Genesis 41–42).

On a Tuesday. Hard times may be the way God leads people to the one who can save them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“On their second visit, Joseph told his brothers who he was, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph’s family. After this, Joseph sent for his father Jacob and his whole family, seventy-five in all.”

The second visit. Joseph was recognised only the second time. Stephen may hint that Israel failed to recognise Jesus at his first coming.

Seventy-five. The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy; the Greek Old Testament says seventy-five, counting additional descendants of Joseph. Stephen, a Greek-speaking Jew, follows his Bible. Both counts are correct on their own terms.

On a Tuesday. Small details in Scripture often have simple explanations when we know the sources.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Then Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our ancestors died. Their bodies were brought back to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a sum of money.”

Buried in Shechem. Joseph’s bones were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Jacob was buried at Hebron, in the cave Abraham bought from Ephron (Genesis 50:13).

A compression. Abraham bought the cave at Hebron (Genesis 23); Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Stephen telescopes the two purchases into one summary, as ancient speakers often did when retelling history. Shechem was in Samaria, the land of the despised Samaritans: the patriarchs were buried there, not in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. When you read a summary of history in Scripture, remember it may compress events; read it alongside the fuller account.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As the time drew near for God to fulfil his promise to Abraham, the number of our people in Egypt had greatly increased. Then ‘a new king, to whom Joseph meant nothing, came to power in Egypt.’”

The time of the promise. God’s timing, set four hundred years earlier.

Who did not know Joseph. Exodus 1:8. Perhaps a new dynasty. Human memory fades; God’s does not.

On a Tuesday. Even when a new regime forgets God’s people, God remembers.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He dealt treacherously with our people and oppressed our ancestors by forcing them to throw out their newborn babies so that they would die. At that time Moses was born, and he was no ordinary child. For three months he was cared for by his family.”

Exposing infants. Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). Exposure of unwanted infants was common in the Greek and Roman world too; Christians became known for rescuing abandoned babies.

Beautiful in God’s sight. Literally “beautiful to God”. God had his eye on this child.

On a Tuesday. Every child is precious to God. Christians should defend the lives of the unborn and the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When he was placed outside, Pharaoh’s daughter took him and brought him up as her own son. Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action.”

Egyptian education. Egypt was the most advanced civilisation of its day, in writing, mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Jewish tradition (Philo, Josephus) elaborated Moses’ education.

Mighty in words. Moses later said he was “slow of speech” (Exodus 4:10); perhaps a fear, not a fact, or he had lost confidence after forty years in Midian.

On a Tuesday. God uses secular education. Learning is no enemy of faith, but it is not enough by itself.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his own people, the Israelites. He saw one of them being mistreated by an Egyptian, so he went to his defence and avenged him by killing the Egyptian.”

Forty. Jewish tradition divided Moses’ 120 years (Deuteronomy 34:7) into three forties: in Egypt, in Midian and in the wilderness.

Avenged him. Moses acted in zeal but in his own strength. God’s time had not come.

On a Tuesday. Zeal without God’s timing can do harm. Wait for him.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Moses thought that his own people would realise that God was using him to rescue them, but they did not. The next day Moses came upon two Israelites who were fighting. He tried to reconcile them by saying, ‘Men, you are brothers; why do you want to hurt each other?’”

They did not understand. The key line. Israel failed to recognise its deliverer, as it failed to recognise Jesus.

Peacemaker. Moses tried to reconcile brothers, as Jesus came to do.

On a Tuesday. If you try to make peace between people, do not be surprised if you are rejected. Jesus was.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But the man who was mistreating the other pushed Moses aside and said, ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’”
