Exodus 2:14. “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” Stephen will repeat the question in verse 35, with God’s answer.

Thrust him aside. The wrongdoer rejected the peacemaker.

On a Tuesday. People in the wrong often resent correction. Correct gently anyway.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When Moses heard this, he fled to Midian, where he settled as a foreigner and had two sons.”

Midian. East of the Gulf of Aqaba, in north-west Arabia. Again God’s servant is outside the land.

Two sons. Gershom, whose name sounds like the Hebrew for “a sojourner there”, and Eliezer (see Exodus 2:22; 18:3–4).

On a Tuesday. A season of exile or failure can be a season of preparation. Moses spent forty years as a shepherd before leading God’s flock.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“After forty years had passed, an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a burning bush in the desert near Mount Sinai. When he saw this, he was amazed at the sight. As he went over to get a closer look, he heard the Lord say…”

The burning bush. Exodus 3. A bush on fire but not consumed.

The angel and the Lord. The angel of the LORD often speaks as God himself (Exodus 3:2, 4). Many Christian interpreters have seen him as the Son of God before his incarnation.

In the wilderness. God met Moses far from any temple.

On a Tuesday. Be curious about God, as Moses was. Turn aside to look.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.’ Moses trembled with fear and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’”

Holy ground. “Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). The point for Stephen’s hearers: a desert bush was holy ground, because God was there. Holiness is God’s presence, not a building.

Trembling. The right response to God’s presence.

For worship. Wherever you meet God, your kitchen, your car, your sickbed, it is holy ground.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘I have indeed seen the oppression of my people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to set them free. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt.’”

Exodus 3:7–10. “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt.” God sees, hears, comes down and sends.

Come down. A foreshadowing of the incarnation: God coming down to save.

On a Tuesday. God sees your affliction and hears your groaning. He has come down in Christ.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“This is the same Moses they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ He was sent to be their ruler and deliverer by God himself, through the angel who appeared to him in the bush. He led them out of Egypt and performed wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and for forty years in the wilderness.”

This Moses. Repeated four times in verses 35–38, with emphasis: the rejected one is the one God sent.

Ruler and redeemer. Lytrōtēs, redeemer: a word never used of Moses in the Old Testament, chosen to point to Jesus.

Signs and wonders. As Jesus did (2:22).

On a Tuesday. The one people reject may be God’s chosen deliverer.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“This is the Moses who told the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your own people.’ He was in the assembly in the wilderness, with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our ancestors; and he received living words to pass on to us.”

A prophet like me. Deuteronomy 18:15, applied to Jesus (3:22).

The congregation. Ekklēsia, the word for “church”. Israel in the wilderness was the church of the Old Testament.

Living oracles. Stephen calls the law “living words”. He does not despise the law, as accused, but honours it.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “him shall ye hear” in verse 37, from Deuteronomy 18:15. The earliest lack it.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is living. Read it expecting him to speak.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But our ancestors refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. They told Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this fellow Moses who led us out of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!’”

Refused to obey. The accusation turns: it was Israel, not Stephen, who rejected Moses.

Turned to Egypt. They longed for slavery’s comforts (Numbers 11:5).

On a Tuesday. Are you tempted to go back to old comforts that once enslaved you?

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“That was the time they made an idol in the form of a calf. They brought sacrifices to it and revelled in what their own hands had made. But God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the sun, moon and stars. This agrees with what is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, people of Israel?’”

The golden calf. Exodus 32. “These are your gods, O Israel” (Exodus 32:4).

Works of their hands. The phrase is key: Stephen will say God does not live in houses “made by hands” (v. 48). The temple, too, can become a work of hands that people worship instead of God.

God gave them up. Judgement by handing people over to what they chose (Romans 1:24).

Amos 5:25. “Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?” A rhetorical question: their worship was not truly for God.

On a Tuesday. What have you made with your own hands that you are tempted to trust: a career, a reputation, a home?

parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘You have taken up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’”

Moloch and Rephan. Stephen quotes Amos 5:26–27 from the Greek. Moloch was the Canaanite god of child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21); Rephan was probably an astral god linked with the planet Saturn.

Beyond Babylon. Amos says “beyond Damascus”, speaking of the Assyrian exile. Stephen says “beyond Babylon”, extending the prophecy to the later Babylonian exile, which fulfilled it more fully.

A textual note. The god’s name appears in many spellings in the manuscripts: Rephan, Romphan, Remphan (KJV). The Hebrew of Amos has Kaiwan.

On a Tuesday. Idolatry leads to exile: being cut off from God’s presence. Turn back before it is too late.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Our ancestors had the tabernacle of the covenant law with them in the wilderness. It had been made as God directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen. After receiving the tabernacle, our ancestors under Joshua brought it with them when they took the land from the nations God drove out before them. It remained in the land until the time of David.”

The tent of witness. The tabernacle, which held the ark with the tablets of the law (the “testimony”). Portable: God travelled with his people.

According to the pattern. Exodus 25:9, 40. The tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly reality (Hebrews 8:5).

Joshua. In Greek, the same name as Jesus. A hint, perhaps: Joshua led them into the land; Jesus leads us into God’s rest (Hebrews 4:8).

On a Tuesday. God moves with his people. He is not tied to a building.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“David enjoyed God’s favour and asked that he might provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him.”

A dwelling place. Psalm 132:5. David wanted to build God a house; God promised to build David a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7).

A textual note. The best early manuscripts read “a dwelling place for the house of Jacob”; others read “for the God of Jacob” (ESV text). “House” is the harder and better-attested reading, and may mean a place for the people of Jacob to worship. The point is the same.

But Solomon built. “But” is significant: the temple was a concession, good but not the final word.

On a Tuesday. Church buildings are useful gifts, not God’s dwelling place in a special sense. The church is the people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“However, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says: ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me? says the Lord. Or where will my resting place be?’”

Not made with hands. In the Greek Old Testament, “made with hands” often describes idols. Stephen’s point is daring: the temple can become an idol.

Solomon knew it. At the temple’s dedication he prayed, “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

Isaiah 66:1. “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.”

Anti-temple? Some say Stephen rejected the temple altogether. Verdict: he rejected the idea that God was confined to it. Jesus is the true temple (John 2:21), and true worship is “in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–24, “the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father”).

On a Tuesday. You can worship God in a factory, a field or a flat as truly as in a cathedral.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘Has not my hand made all these things?’”

The Creator. The God who made everything cannot be contained by anything he made.

For worship. Praise the Creator, whose hand made the universe and who chose to dwell with us in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen turned the charge back on his accusers: they were stubborn, with hearts and ears uncircumcised, always resisting the Holy Spirit just as their ancestors did. Their ancestors persecuted every prophet and killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, and now they had betrayed and murdered him. They had received the law through angels and had not kept it. Hearing this, they were furious and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said he could see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. At this they covered their ears, shouted, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” With that he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it did not come to mean somebody killed for the faith until enough witnesses had been. Stephen is where the shift begins, and the shape of his death is the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Reformed theology has been careful about what this is and is not. It is not heroism and it is not an achievement that earns anything — Luke states plainly that Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit at the moment he looked up, which is to say that the courage and the vision and the forgiveness were all supplied to him. What this passage exhibits is not a strong man but a sustained one. And it should be added, because the church has periodically forgotten it, that martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for this. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: Nobody watching that morning could have identified what was actually happening. The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You stubborn people, with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You are just like your ancestors: you always resist the Holy Spirit!”

Stiff-necked. God’s own description of Israel at the golden calf (Exodus 33:5): an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

Uncircumcised in heart. They had the outward sign, but not the reality. “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16).

Resist the Spirit. As Israel did in the wilderness (Isaiah 63:10).

A sudden change. Some think Stephen saw the council’s anger and abandoned his speech for direct accusation.

Can the Spirit be resisted? Arminians cite this verse to show that God’s grace can be resisted. Reformed theology agrees that the Spirit’s outward call through the word can be and often is resisted; what cannot finally be resisted is his inward, effectual call by which he gives new life (John 6:37, 44). Verdict: both are true, and Stephen speaks of the first.

On a Tuesday. Is there something the Spirit has been pressing on you through God’s word that you keep resisting?
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Was there ever a prophet your ancestors did not persecute? They even killed those who predicted the coming of the Righteous One. And now you have betrayed and murdered him, you who have received the law that was given through angels but have not obeyed it.”

The prophets persecuted. Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned; Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two. Jesus: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets” (Matthew 23:37).

The Righteous One. Jesus, the climax of the line of rejected deliverers.

Delivered by angels. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at Sinai and mediated the law (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek; Galatians 3:19, “put in place through angels”; Hebrews 2:2).

Did not keep it. The final reversal: they accused Stephen of breaking the law; they themselves had broken it.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to honour dead prophets and persecute living ones. Listen to faithful voices God sends you now.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the members of the Sanhedrin heard this, they were furious and gnashed their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Gnashed their teeth. A sign of fury and hatred (Psalm 35:16; 37:12).

Full of the Spirit. The contrast: they are full of rage, he is full of the Spirit.

The glory of God. The speech began with “the God of glory” (v. 2) and ends with Stephen seeing it.

On a Tuesday. When people rage against you, look up.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

The Son of Man. The only time in the New Testament someone other than Jesus uses this title. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure who receives eternal dominion. At his own trial Jesus had told this council, “from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke 22:69). Stephen says it has happened.

Standing. Elsewhere Jesus is seated. Why standing?

To welcome his servant home.

As a witness or advocate, standing to plead Stephen’s case in the heavenly court while the earthly court condemns him.

As the judge rising to give sentence.

Verdict: probably as Stephen’s witness and advocate (Luke 12:8, “everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God”), and to welcome him. Stephen confessed Jesus; Jesus stands to confess him.

For worship. When you are rejected for Christ, picture him standing for you in heaven.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.

parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At this they covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile, the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Stopped their ears. They refused to hear what they took as blasphemy: a man exalted to God’s right hand.

A trial or a lynching? Under Roman rule the Sanhedrin was not normally allowed to carry out executions (John 18:31). This looks like mob violence, perhaps in a gap between Roman governors.

Outside the city. The law required executions outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). Jesus too suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12).

The witnesses. They threw the first stones: “The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death” (Deuteronomy 17:7). They took off their outer garments to throw.

Saul. The first mention of the man who would become the apostle Paul. “A young man”: perhaps around thirty. He never forgot this day (22:20).

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who persecute Christians today. Among them may be a future Paul.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

Like his Lord. Jesus prayed, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46) and “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Stephen prays the same prayers, now addressed to Jesus.

Prayer to Jesus. Stephen commits his spirit to Jesus as Jesus committed his to the Father. The first Christian martyr treated Jesus as God.

Forgiveness. He prays for his killers. Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul.

Fell asleep. The Christian way to speak of a believer’s death: violent, yet peaceful, and temporary.

For worship. Thank God for the martyrs of the church, from Stephen until today. Ask for grace to forgive those who wrong you.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Stephen’s death sets off the first great persecution, led by Saul, who goes from house to house dragging believers to prison. The church in Jerusalem is scattered, except the apostles, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. So the second stage of Jesus’ plan in 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria. The Samaritans were descendants of northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest; they accepted only the five books of Moses, worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and were despised by Jews, and the feeling was mutual (John 4:9). Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ there with signs, and many believe, including a famous magician named Simon. The apostles send Peter and John, and only when they pray and lay hands on the Samaritans do they receive the Spirit, a sign to everyone that Samaritans and Jews are one church. Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter sternly rebukes him.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where he meets a high official of the queen of Ethiopia, the kingdom of Meroë on the Nile far south of Egypt. The man is a eunuch who had come to worship in Jerusalem, and he is reading aloud from Isaiah 53 about the lamb led to the slaughter. Philip explains that the passage is about Jesus, and when they come to water the Ethiopian asks to be baptised. Philip is then taken away by the Spirit, and the Ethiopian goes home rejoicing, the gospel already heading towards the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered through Judea and Samaria. Devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. Saul set out to destroy the church, entering house after house and dragging men and women off to prison. Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. When the crowds heard Philip and saw his signs they all paid close attention: impure spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many paralysed and lame people were healed, so there was great joy in that city. A man named Simon had practised sorcery there for some time and amazed the Samaritans, claiming to be someone great; everyone, high and low, called him the great power of God, because he had astonished them with his magic for so long. But when they believed Philip’s good news of God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptised. Simon himself believed and was baptised, and followed Philip everywhere, astonished by the signs and miracles. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had simply been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John laid hands on them and they received the Spirit. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money to give him the same power. Peter told him to take his money to destruction with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift; he had no share in this ministry, because his heart was not right before God. He must repent and pray that the Lord would perhaps forgive him for such a thought, for Peter could see he was full of bitterness and captive to sin. Simon asked them to pray for him that none of this would happen to him. After testifying and proclaiming the Lord’s word, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology has read Acts 8 as the clearest narrative demonstration that God's purposes are not merely undamaged by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Saul approved of their killing him. On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. Godly men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him.

Saul approved. Syneudokōn: he heartily agreed. Later he confessed it (22:20).

Scattered. Diesparēsan, from which we get “diaspora”: sown like seed. Persecution scattered the seed of the gospel.

Except the apostles. Perhaps the persecution targeted especially the Greek-speaking believers associated with Stephen’s views on the temple.

Great lamentation. Grief is right. Christians mourn their dead, though not as those without hope.

On a Tuesday. When hardship scatters you, through a job loss or a move, ask where God wants you to sow the gospel in the new place.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off both men and women and put them in prison.

Ravaging. Elymaineto: used of wild animals tearing prey. Paul later admitted, “I persecuted this Way to the death” (22:4), and called himself the least of the apostles because of it (1 Corinthians 15:9).

House after house. The church met in homes, so the homes were raided.

Men and women. Women were persecuted equally.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who persecute Christians today, and for house churches facing raids in countries such as China and Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there.

Preaching. Euangelizomenoi: announcing the good news. Ordinary believers, not just apostles, spread the gospel.

Philip. The evangelist, one of the seven (6:5; 21:8), not the apostle Philip.

Samaria. Samaritans were descended from the northern Israelites and the foreign settlers brought in by the Assyrians after 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim. Jews and Samaritans despised each other: “Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9). Yet the Samaritans too expected a Messiah (John 4:25), whom they called the Taheb, “the Restorer”.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “the city of Samaria” (the capital, then called Sebaste) and “a city of Samaria”. The meaning is unaffected.

On a Tuesday. Who are your Samaritans, the people your community dislikes? The gospel is for them.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowds heard Philip and saw the signs he performed, they all paid close attention to what he said. For with loud shrieks, impure spirits came out of many, and many who were paralysed or lame were healed.

One accord. United attention.

Signs. Like those of Jesus and the apostles. Philip had been commissioned by the apostles (6:6).

On a Tuesday. The gospel brings freedom from spiritual bondage. Pray for those trapped in the occult.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was great joy in that city. Now for some time a man named Simon had practised sorcery in the city and amazed all the people of Samaria. He boasted that he was someone great.

Much joy. The fruit of the gospel (8:39; 13:52).

Simon. Later Christian writers (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) called him Simon Magus and saw him as the father of Gnostic heresy, claiming he went to Rome and was honoured as a god. These traditions mix fact and legend.

Magic. Mageuōn: sorcery, the practice of manipulating spiritual powers. Widespread in the ancient world (19:19).

On a Tuesday. Fascination with magic, astrology and the occult is still common. The gospel brings something far greater.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the people, both high and low, gave him their attention and exclaimed, “This man is rightly called the Great Power of God.” They followed him because he had amazed them for a long time with his sorcery.

The Great Power. Perhaps Simon claimed to be a divine being, an emanation of God.

Amazed. Simon amazed people; Philip’s miracles amazed Simon (v. 13).

On a Tuesday. Charismatic personalities can captivate whole communities. Test claims of spiritual power by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they believed Philip as he proclaimed the good news of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptised, both men and women. Simon himself believed and was baptised. And he followed Philip everywhere, astonished by the great signs and miracles he saw.

The kingdom and the name. Philip’s message: God’s reign has arrived in Jesus.

Men and women. Baptism followed belief. No infants are mentioned here.

Simon believed. Was his faith genuine? The rest of the story suggests not: Peter says his heart is not right with God and he is in the bond of iniquity (vv. 21–23). His “faith” was fascination with power. Jesus warned of those who say “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name” but whom he never knew (Matthew 7:22–23). Baptism does not guarantee new birth.

On a Tuesday. Being impressed by Christianity is not the same as trusting Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to Samaria. When they arrived, they prayed for the new believers there that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

Sent Peter and John. The apostles confirm the new work. John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village: “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” (Luke 9:54). Now he prays for the Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. God can change our prejudices. Whom did you once despise that you now pray for?
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the Holy Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had simply been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John placed their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

Not yet received. Unusual: elsewhere the Spirit is given at faith (2:38; 10:44; Romans 8:9). Why the delay?

Pentecostals see a pattern: conversion first, Spirit baptism later.

Roman Catholics see the origin of confirmation: the bishop’s laying on of hands confers the Spirit.

Some say the Samaritans’ faith was defective until the apostles came.

Most Reformed and evangelical interpreters see a unique moment in salvation history: the first time the gospel crossed the Jew–Samaritan divide.

Verdict: the last. God withheld the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritans would not form a rival church, and so that the Jerusalem apostles would see with their own eyes that God accepted Samaritans. It was a “Samaritan Pentecost”, as there will be a Gentile Pentecost in chapter 10. It was not meant as a pattern for all believers.

On a Tuesday. God cares about the unity of his church across ethnic and historic divides. So should we.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given at the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money and said, “Give me also this ability so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”

Simon saw. Something visible happened, perhaps tongues or prophecy.

Offered money. Simon saw spiritual power as a technique to acquire, like a trade secret magicians bought and sold. From his name comes “simony”, the medieval sin of buying church offices.

On a Tuesday. Watch out for any thinking that treats God’s gifts as products to purchase: paying for blessings, healing or position.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter answered: “May your money perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money! You have no part or share in this ministry, because your heart is not right before God.”

Perish with you. Literally “to destruction”. J. B. Phillips once translated it, “To hell with you and your money!” Peter is not cursing casually but declaring that Simon is on the road to ruin.

The gift of God. The Spirit is a gift, not for sale.

No part. Simon had no share in the kingdom. His baptism was empty.

On a Tuesday. No amount of money can buy God’s favour, and no amount of giving earns it.

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Repent of this wickedness and pray to the Lord in the hope that he may forgive you for having such a thought in your heart. For I see that you are full of bitterness and captive to sin.”

Repent. Even after so severe a rebuke, Peter offers hope.

If possible. Not doubt about God’s mercy, but about whether Simon will truly repent.

The gall of bitterness. Echoing Moses’ warning against “a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit” in Israel: someone who turns to other gods while thinking himself safe (Deuteronomy 29:18).

The bond of iniquity. Chained by sin. Simon was still a slave.

On a Tuesday. Bitterness poisons. If it is growing in you, bring it to God today.
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Simon answered, “Pray to the Lord for me so that nothing you have said may happen to me.” After they had further proclaimed the word of the Lord and testified about Jesus, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages.

Pray for me. Simon asks for prayer to avoid punishment, not for a new heart. Fear of consequences is not repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Many villages. Peter and John themselves now preach to Samaritans on their way home.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself: am I sorry for sin, or sorry for its consequences?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. On the way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a senior official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the man reading Isaiah and asked whether he understood it. He replied that he could not unless someone explained it, and invited Philip to sit with him. He was reading the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whom the prophet meant, himself or someone else. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. As they travelled they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what stood in the way of his being baptised. He ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are usually the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road, the desert road, that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, which means queen of the Ethiopians. This man had gone to Jerusalem to worship.

From a revival to a desert. Philip leaves a city-wide awakening for one man on a lonely road.

Gaza. The last town before the desert route to Egypt.

Ethiopia. Not modern Ethiopia, but the ancient kingdom of Kush or Meroë, on the Nile in what is now Sudan. To Greeks and Romans it was the edge of the known world. “Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 68:31).

Candace. A title, not a name: Kandake, the queen mother who ruled in Meroë.

A eunuch. Castrated men often served royal courts. Under the law a eunuch could not enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1), so this man, though he worshipped Israel’s God, was kept at a distance in the temple. But Isaiah promised eunuchs who keep God’s covenant, “I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:4–5). Now that promise is fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. God may send you away from a busy, fruitful place to meet one person. Be ready to go.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On his way home he was sitting in his chariot reading the book of Isaiah the prophet. The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.”

Reading Isaiah. A scroll was expensive; he had probably bought it in Jerusalem. People read aloud in the ancient world.

The Spirit said. The angel started Philip on the road; the Spirit guided him to the chariot.

On a Tuesday. God prepares people before we arrive. Pray for God to lead you to someone already searching.
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

Philip ran. Eager obedience.

Do you understand? A wordplay in Greek: ginōskeis ha anaginōskeis, “do you know what you are reading?”

Someone to guide. Scripture is clear in its central message, but God uses teachers to help us understand (Ephesians 4:11). Humility asks for help.

On a Tuesday. Offer to read the Bible with someone. Many want to understand but need a guide.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation he was deprived of justice. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth.”

Isaiah 53:7–8. The heart of the fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13–53:12), about a Servant who suffers silently for the sins of others and is then exalted.

The Greek version. The quotation follows the Greek Old Testament, which differs slightly from the Hebrew.

His generation. “Who can describe his descendants?” Perhaps: he died without children. Fitting words for a eunuch to read. But Isaiah 53:10 says “he shall see his offspring”: the Servant will have spiritual descendants, and the eunuch was about to become one.

On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 this week, slowly, thinking of Jesus.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eunuch asked Philip, “Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.

The great question. Jewish interpreters had various answers: the prophet himself, Israel as a nation, or the Messiah. Philip says: Jesus.

Beginning with this Scripture. Philip started where the man was. Jesus did the same on the Emmaus road: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

On a Tuesday. Start where people are, with their questions, and lead them to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they travelled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptised?”

What prevents me? Philip must have explained baptism. Perhaps the eunuch wondered whether, as a eunuch and a foreigner, he would be excluded again, as he had been from the temple. Nothing prevents him.

A textual note. Verse 37 (“And Philip said, ‘If you believe with all your heart, you may.’ And he replied, ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’”) is in the KJV but absent from the earliest and best manuscripts. It was probably added from early baptismal practice, where a confession of faith was required. Its content is true, but it was not part of what Luke wrote, which is why modern translations put it in a footnote.

On a Tuesday. No barrier of race, disability or past can keep anyone from Christ who believes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing.

Down into the water. Both went down into the water. This suggests immersion, the earliest practice, though the phrase could describe stepping into water for pouring. Baptists and many others see immersion as the clearest picture of burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4). Verdict: immersion is the most likely New Testament practice, though the validity of baptism does not depend on the amount of water.

Carried away. A miraculous removal, like the prophet Elijah: “the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where” (1 Kings 18:12).

Rejoicing. The eunuch went home alone, with no church nearby, but with Christ, Scripture and joy. Ethiopian Christians traditionally trace their faith to him.

A textual note. Some Western manuscripts expand: “the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch, and an angel of the Lord caught up Philip”. The shorter reading is original.

For worship. Thank God that the gospel reached the ends of the earth, and reached you.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip, however, appeared at Azotus and travelled about, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

Azotus. The old Philistine city of Ashdod, on the coast.

Caesarea. Caesarea Maritima, the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great. Philip settled there, and twenty years later Paul stayed in his home, where his four unmarried daughters prophesied (21:8–9).

All the towns. Philip kept preaching wherever he went.

On a Tuesday. Whatever town you are in this week, you can share the gospel there.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
The chapter tells the most important conversion in church history; Luke tells it three times in Acts (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18). Saul of Tarsus, a brilliant young Pharisee, is so zealous against “the Way”, as the Christian movement was called, that he obtains letters from the high priest to arrest believers in the synagogues of Damascus, about 135 miles to the north-east. Near the city a blinding light flashes from heaven and a voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” It is Jesus. Blind, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to lay hands on him, calling Saul his chosen instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and to suffer for it. Saul’s sight returns, he is filled with the Spirit and baptised, and at once he preaches in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

The persecutor becomes the persecuted. After some time, including a period in Arabia (Galatians 1:17), plots in Damascus force him to escape in a basket over the wall. In Jerusalem the believers are afraid of him until Barnabas vouches for him; when Greek-speaking Jews try to kill him, the church sends him home to Tarsus. The church enjoys a season of peace and growth. Luke then returns to Peter, who heals a paralysed man named Aeneas at Lydda and raises a beloved disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas) from death at Joppa, and stays there in the house of a tanner, setting the scene for chapter 10.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul, still breathing murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. As he neared Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asked who it was, and the reply came: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” His companions stood speechless; they heard the sound but saw no one. Saul got up, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days he was blind and did not eat or drink. In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias, whom the Lord called in a vision and sent to the house of Judas on Straight Street to ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying and had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come and lay hands on him to restore his sight. Ananias protested that he had heard how much harm this man had done to the Lord’s people in Jerusalem, and that he had come with authority to arrest everyone who called on the Lord’s name. But the Lord told him to go, for this man was his chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles, their kings and the people of Israel, and the Lord would show him how much he must suffer for his name. So Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul and called him brother, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Immediately something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes and he could see. He got up and was baptised, and after eating he regained his strength. He spent several days with the disciples in Damascus and at once began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. All who heard him were astonished, asking whether this was not the man who had caused havoc among those who call on this name in Jerusalem, and had come to take them as prisoners. Yet Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah. After many days the Jews conspired to kill him, watching the city gates day and night, but Saul learned of their plan, and his followers lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall. When he came to Jerusalem he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing he was really a disciple. Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and how he had preached fearlessly in Damascus in Jesus’ name. So Saul stayed with them, moving freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the Lord’s name. He talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they tried to kill him. When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed peace and was strengthened. Living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He was not wavering, not quietly troubled, not secretly drawn — he was riding to Damascus with an arrest warrant in his bag. Nothing in the account suggests any prior movement toward faith, and Paul himself, looking back, never once describes his conversion as a search that ended. He describes it as being laid hold of. Reformed theology has read it as the pattern rather than the exception: everybody who comes to Christ was, in one degree or another, going the other way when God stopped them, and the difference between Saul and a quieter case is a matter of speed and lighting rather than of mechanism. It is also the passage that makes despair about anybody unreasonable. The church's most violent enemy would go on to write a great part of its Scriptures, and not one person in Jerusalem could have guessed it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was told to go to the man who had done much evil to the saints in Jerusalem and who was carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He said what he thought about it, out loud, to God — and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the existence of people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies. That is not an argument anybody constructs. It is one a congregation either exhibits or does not.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples. He went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any there who belonged to the Way, whether men or women, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

Breathing threats. Persecution was his very breath.

Letters. The high priest had authority over Jewish communities in religious matters, and the Romans tolerated it. The letters would ask the synagogue leaders in Damascus to hand over Christian Jews.

Damascus. An ancient city in Syria, about 135 miles (220 km) north-east of Jerusalem, a week’s journey, with a large Jewish community. Believers had fled there.

The Way. An early name for the Christian movement (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14), perhaps from Jesus’ words, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Saul’s zeal. He later said, “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6). He thought he was serving God (John 16:2).

On a Tuesday. Zeal is not the same as being right. Sincere people can be sincerely wrong.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus lay about 135 miles north-east of Jerusalem and had a large Jewish community. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he neared Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”

A light from heaven. At midday, brighter than the sun (26:13). The glory of the risen Christ.

Saul, Saul. The doubled name, as God called Abraham, Jacob, Moses and Samuel (Genesis 22:11; 46:2; Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10).

Persecuting me. Not “my followers” but “me”. Christ is so united with his people that what is done to them is done to him (Matthew 25:40). Paul’s later teaching on the church as Christ’s body may have its roots in this moment.

Converted or called? Some scholars (Krister Stendahl) argue that Paul was not converted from one religion to another, but called, like a prophet, to a new task within Judaism. Verdict: both. Paul himself speaks of a prophetic call (Galatians 1:15–16; Jeremiah 1:5), but also of a radical turning from his old righteousness to Christ (Philippians 3:4–9). He was a sinner saved by grace (1 Timothy 1:13–16), and an apostle sent.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond the reach of Christ. Pray for the most hostile opponent of the gospel you know.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

Who are you, Lord? “Lord” may at first be a respectful address, but Saul knows he is facing a heavenly being.

I am Jesus. The shattering answer. The crucified man Saul hated is alive and Lord of glory. Everything Saul believed was overturned in a moment.

Go into the city. Christ uses an ordinary disciple to complete the work.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add here: “it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” These words were borrowed from Paul’s later accounts (26:14; 22:10) and are not in the earliest manuscripts of chapter 9.

On a Tuesday. Every Christian’s story has this moment, quiet or dramatic: discovering that Jesus is Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men travelling with Saul stood there speechless; they heard the sound but did not see anyone. Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus.
