Hearing but not seeing. In 22:9 Paul says his companions “did not understand the voice”. Not a contradiction. The Greek verb “hear” can mean “hear a sound” or “understand words”. They heard a noise but did not understand the words; only Saul did. Compare John 12:28–29, where a voice from heaven sounded to some like thunder.

Led by the hand. The proud persecutor, who came to lead prisoners, is led like a child.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes humbles us before he uses us.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three days he was blind, and did not eat or drink anything.

Three days. A period of darkness before light, like Jesus’ three days in the tomb. Saul’s old life was dying.

Fasting. Shock, repentance and prayer (v. 11).

On a Tuesday. If you are in a time of darkness after a great change, God is still at work.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. The Lord told him, “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying.”

Ananias. An ordinary disciple, “a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews” (22:12). Not the Ananias of chapter 5.

Here I am, Lord. Like Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10). Ready to listen.

Straight Street. The main east–west street of Damascus, still there today, called Via Recta by the Romans.

Tarsus. A major city in Cilicia, famous for its university and philosophers: “no obscure city” (21:39).

He is praying. The persecutor has become a man of prayer.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers at key moments. You may be someone’s Ananias.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.”

Two visions. God prepared both men. When God brings two people together for his purposes, he often works on both sides.

On a Tuesday. When you feel prompted to speak to someone about Christ, God may already be preparing them.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Lord,” Ananias answered, “I have heard many reports about this man and all the harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem. And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on your name.”

Ananias’s fear. Natural and honest. He tells the Lord what the Lord already knows.

Your saints. All believers are “holy ones”, set apart for God.

Call on your name. A definition of Christians: those who pray to Jesus as Lord (1 Corinthians 1:2).

On a Tuesday. It is fine to tell God honestly that you are afraid of what he asks. Then obey.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord said to Ananias, “Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.”

A chosen instrument. Skeuos eklogēs: a vessel of election. Saul did not choose Christ; Christ chose him. Paul later wrote that God “set me apart before I was born, and … called me by his grace” (Galatians 1:15). A clear example of God’s sovereign, effectual call: Saul was not seeking Christ but fighting him.

Gentiles, kings, Israel. A summary of Paul’s future ministry: to the nations, before rulers (Agrippa, Festus, Caesar), and to Jews.

How much he must suffer. The persecutor will be persecuted. Suffering was part of the calling (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).

On a Tuesday. If God has saved you, he has a purpose for you. Ask him what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptised.

Brother Saul. The first word Saul hears from a Christian is “brother”. The man he came to arrest welcomes him into the family.

Filled with the Spirit. Through a non-apostle. Paul’s apostleship came directly from Christ, not from the Twelve (Galatians 1:1, 12).

Scales. Luke the doctor describes it precisely. Physical and spiritual sight restored together.

Baptised. At once, as the outward sign of his new life (22:16, “Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name”).

On a Tuesday. Welcome new believers warmly, whatever their past. Call them “brother” and “sister”.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus. At once he began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

With the disciples. Saul joined the people he had come to destroy.

Immediately. No long delay before witness.

The Son of God. The only use of this title in Acts. Saul’s message from the beginning: Jesus is divine.

Arabia. At some point in this period Saul went to Arabia, the Nabataean kingdom south and east of Damascus, perhaps to preach or to reflect, before returning (Galatians 1:17, “I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus”). Luke does not mention it.

On a Tuesday. New Christians can witness straight away. Their story of change is powerful.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All those who heard him were astonished and asked, “Is not this the man who raised havoc in Jerusalem among those who call on this name? And has he not come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?” Yet Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah.

Amazed. The change was undeniable.

Proving. Symbibazōn: putting together, showing by comparing Scriptures. Saul used his training in the Old Testament to show that Jesus fulfilled it.

On a Tuesday. Use your gifts and training, now redeemed, for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After many days had gone by, there was a conspiracy among the Jews to kill him, but Saul learned of their plan. Day and night they kept close watch on the city gates in order to kill him.

Many days. Probably about three years, including the time in Arabia (Galatians 1:18).

The plot. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas of the Nabataeans was also guarding the city to arrest him (2 Corinthians 11:32). Saul had made enemies among Jews and Nabataean officials alike.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness can bring opposition quickly. Do not be surprised.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his followers took him by night and lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall.

His disciples. Saul already had followers who believed through him.

A basket. A large rope basket, used for goods. Paul later boasted of this humiliating escape as a sign of weakness (2 Corinthians 11:32–33, “I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall”).

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the wise course is to escape danger, not to stay and die. Jesus also withdrew at times (Luke 4:30).

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he really was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. He told them how Saul on his journey had seen the Lord and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had preached fearlessly in the name of Jesus.

Afraid. Understandable: they suspected a trick.

Barnabas. The “son of encouragement” (4:36) lives up to his name. He took a risk on Saul when no one else would. Paul says he saw only Peter and James on this visit, which lasted fifteen days (Galatians 1:18–19).

On a Tuesday. Is there a new believer, or someone with a bad reputation, whom you could take under your wing?
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Saul stayed with them and moved about freely in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord. He talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they tried to kill him.

Boldly. The same courage as the apostles (4:13, 31).

The Hellenists. The Greek-speaking Jews who had opposed Stephen (6:9). Saul had been one of them. Now he takes up Stephen’s argument, and they try to kill him as they killed Stephen.

On a Tuesday. God can make a former opponent of the gospel its most effective advocate.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

The brothers. The church protected Saul.

Tarsus. Saul’s home town. He spent several years there, probably preaching in Cilicia and Syria (Galatians 1:21), until Barnabas fetched him to Antioch (11:25–26). These are sometimes called Paul’s “silent years”, perhaps when he had the vision of 2 Corinthians 12:2.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes sends his servants into a quiet season before a great work. Do not despise yours.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace and was strengthened. Living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.

The church. Singular, spread across three regions. One church in many places.

Peace. The persecutor had become a preacher. Perhaps also because the Roman emperor Caligula’s attempt to put his statue in the temple (around AD 40) distracted the Jewish authorities.

Fear and comfort. Reverence for the Lord and the Spirit’s encouragement together. A healthy church has both.

Galilee. The only mention in Acts of churches in Galilee, where Jesus ministered.

For worship. Thank God for seasons of peace in your church. Use them for growth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and roll up his mat, and Aeneas got up at once. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas), always doing good and helping the poor. She became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples sent two men to urge Peter to come at once. When he arrived he was taken upstairs, where all the widows stood around him crying and showing him the robes and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, knelt and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up. He took her hand and helped her to her feet, then called the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them. That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people who lived in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, who was paralysed and had been bedridden for eight years.

Lydda. Modern Lod, near Tel Aviv’s airport, about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem. The church there probably began through believers scattered after Stephen’s death, or through Philip (8:40).

Aeneas. A Greek name (the hero of Virgil’s epic of Rome’s founding).

Eight years. A chronic, hopeless case.

On a Tuesday. Visit believers who are housebound. They are often forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Aeneas,” Peter said to him, “Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and roll up your mat.” Immediately Aeneas got up. All those who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

Jesus Christ heals you. Present tense: Jesus is healing you now. Peter is clear that it is not his power.

Make your bed. Or “get yourself something to eat”; the phrase is uncertain. Either way, a practical sign of restored strength.

Sharon. The fertile coastal plain from Joppa to Caesarea.

Turned to the Lord. The purpose of the miracle: not spectacle, but conversion.

On a Tuesday. When God answers prayer, tell others so that they too may turn to the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek her name is Dorcas). She was always doing good and helping the poor. About that time she became ill and died, and her body was washed and placed in an upstairs room.

Joppa. Modern Jaffa, the ancient port of Jerusalem. The port from which Jonah fled to avoid going to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3, “went down to Joppa”). Here Peter will be sent to the Gentiles.

Tabitha, Dorcas. Both mean “gazelle”, in Aramaic and Greek. The only woman in the New Testament explicitly called a “disciple” (mathētria).

Good works and charity. Like the woman of Proverbs: “She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy” (Proverbs 31:20).

Washed. Jewish burial preparation. She was clearly dead.

On a Tuesday. Tabitha’s ministry was making clothes for widows. Practical kindness is a great ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lydda was near Joppa; so when the disciples heard that Peter was in Lydda, they sent two men to him and urged him, “Please come at once!”

Near. About 11 miles, a few hours’ walk.

Please come. The disciples had faith that something could be done, though she was dead.

On a Tuesday. In a crisis, call for your church’s elders and pray (James 5:14).
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter went with them, and when he arrived he was taken upstairs to the room. All the widows stood around him, crying and showing him the robes and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them. Peter sent them all out of the room; then he got down on his knees and prayed. Turning towards the dead woman, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter she sat up.

The widows. The poor women she had clothed. Their grief and her garments are her memorial.

Put them outside. Exactly as Jesus did when he raised Jairus’s daughter, which Peter had witnessed (Mark 5:40).

Knelt and prayed. Peter had no power of his own.

Tabitha, arise. In Aramaic, Tabitha qumi, one letter different from Jesus’ words to Jairus’s daughter, Talitha cumi, “Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41). Peter does what he saw his Lord do.

On a Tuesday. Your good works may be remembered more than you know, by the people you helped.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took her by the hand and helped her to her feet. Then he called for the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive.

Gave her his hand. As Peter had raised the lame man (3:7).

Presented her alive. To the widows who loved her. A foretaste of the resurrection reunion.

What it does not mean. Tabitha was raised to mortal life and died again later. Resurrection to immortal life awaits the last day (1 Corinthians 15:52).

For worship. Thank God that death will not have the last word over those you love in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.

Many believed. Again the miracle leads to faith.

A tanner. Tanners worked with the hides of dead animals, which made them ritually unclean under Jewish law, and the smell of their trade meant they often lived on the edge of town. That Peter stayed with one shows he was already loosening his scruples, preparing for the vision of chapter 10, where God tells him not to call unclean what God has made clean.

On a Tuesday. Where you stay and with whom you eat can be a witness. Do not avoid people others consider unclean.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Luke tells it twice (again in chapter 11) and Peter retells it at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius is a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God, prayed at the Jewish hours of prayer and gave generously to Jewish causes, but had not become a Jew by circumcision. In a vision at three in the afternoon an angel tells him that God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he should send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

The next day at noon, on a flat rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law of Moses called unclean, and hears a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers: “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happens three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius’s messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them. Peter, who earlier would never have entered a Gentile’s house, goes to Caesarea, finds a house full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and declares that God shows no partiality. He preaches Jesus: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter’s Jewish companions are astonished. Peter asks who could refuse them water for baptism, and they are baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion at Caesarea, is told by an angel to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop at noon, sees a sheet full of animals the law called unclean and hears a voice telling him to eat; when he refuses, the voice says three times that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Cornelius’s messengers arrive, the Spirit tells Peter to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where he enters a Gentile home full of people waiting to hear him. Peter declares that God shows no favouritism and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He tells them about Jesus: anointed by the Spirit, doing good and healing, put to death on a cross, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of all, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all the Gentiles listening, to the astonishment of Peter’s Jewish companions, and Peter has them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was known as the Italian Regiment. He and all his family were devout and God-fearing; he gave generously to those in need and prayed to God regularly.

Caesarea. Caesarea Maritima, built by Herod the Great as a Roman-style city with a huge artificial harbour, theatre and temple to Augustus. The Roman governors of Judea lived there. An inscription naming Pontius Pilate was found in its theatre.

A centurion. Commander of about eighty men, a career soldier and a respected figure. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (Luke 7:2–10; 23:47; Acts 27:43).

The Italian Cohort. A unit originally raised in Italy. Inscriptions mention a “second Italian cohort” in Syria in this period.

Devout and God-fearing. A “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel, attended synagogue, kept some Jewish customs, but was not circumcised. Many such people were drawn to the gospel.

His household. His family, servants and perhaps soldiers.

On a Tuesday. Pray for soldiers, police and officials. God can reach people in every profession.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day at about three in the afternoon he had a vision. He distinctly saw an angel of God, who came to him and said, “Cornelius!” Cornelius stared at him in fear. “What is it, Lord?” he asked. The angel answered, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have come up as a memorial offering before God.”

The ninth hour. 3 p.m., the Jewish hour of afternoon prayer (3:1). Cornelius kept Jewish prayer times.

A memorial. Language of sacrifice: part of the grain offering burned on the altar was called a “memorial portion” (Leviticus 2:2). Cornelius’s prayers and alms rose to God like an offering.

Was Cornelius already saved? Some (inclusivists) argue that Cornelius shows God accepts devout people of other faiths before they hear of Christ. Verdict: no. Peter later reports the angel’s words: Peter would “declare to you a message by which you will be saved” (11:14). Cornelius was seeking God, and God answered by sending the gospel. His prayers were heard, not as earning salvation, but as the cry of a seeker God was drawing.

On a Tuesday. Pray for seekers you know: people interested in God but not yet trusting Christ. God hears their prayers and may send you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now send men to Joppa to bring back a man named Simon who is called Peter. He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.”

Why Peter? The angel could have explained the gospel himself. God has chosen to spread the gospel through human messengers (Romans 10:14).

By the sea. Tanners worked near water, and away from town because of the smell.

On a Tuesday. God has given the job of telling the gospel to people, not angels. That means you.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angel who spoke to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier who was one of his attendants. He told them everything that had happened and sent them to Joppa.

A devout soldier. Cornelius’s faith had spread to his men.

Immediate obedience. He acted at once.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks through his word, respond promptly.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
About noon the following day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray.

The sixth hour. Noon. Not an official Jewish hour of prayer, but devout Jews often prayed three times a day (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10).

The roof. Flat roofs were used for rest, work and prayer, private and cool.

Timing. God coordinated two visions in two places so that the messengers arrived as Peter finished.

On a Tuesday. Have a regular time and place to pray. God often meets us there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He became hungry and wanted something to eat, and while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners.

Hungry. God used Peter’s physical hunger to frame the vision.

A trance. Ekstasis: a state of heightened spiritual perception.

Four corners. Perhaps suggesting the four corners of the earth: all nations.

On a Tuesday. God can speak through ordinary moments, like hunger before lunch.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It contained all kinds of four-footed animals, as well as reptiles and birds. Then a voice told him, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.”

All kinds. Clean and unclean mixed together. The law of Moses divided animals into clean (which could be eaten) and unclean (which could not), “to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean” (Leviticus 11:47). The food laws marked Israel off from the nations.

Kill and eat. A shocking command for an observant Jew.

On a Tuesday. God may ask you to step outside your comfort zone for the sake of others.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Surely not, Lord!” Peter replied. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.”

By no means, Lord. A contradiction in terms: if he is Lord, the answer cannot be no. Peter had said the same before (Matthew 16:22; John 13:8).

Never. Peter had kept the food laws all his life, like Daniel, who “resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food” (Daniel 1:8), and Ezekiel, who protested, “I have never defiled myself” (Ezekiel 4:14).

Common. Koinos: ritually profane, unfit for God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Even devout Christians can resist what God is doing because it challenges long-held habits.
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice spoke to him a second time, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” This happened three times, and immediately the sheet was taken back to heaven.

God has made clean. The food laws are set aside. Jesus had already taught this: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Christians are free to eat any food (Romans 14:14; 1 Timothy 4:4).

The real meaning. Peter soon realises that the vision is about people, not just food (v. 28). The barrier between Jews and Gentiles is removed in Christ (Ephesians 2:14, “he himself is our peace, who has made us both one”).

Three times. As Peter had denied Jesus three times and been restored three times (John 21:15–17).

Does the Old Testament law still apply? The Reformed tradition distinguishes the moral law, which continues (summed up in the Ten Commandments), from the ceremonial law (sacrifices, food laws, purity rules) fulfilled in Christ, and the civil law of Israel as a nation (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). This chapter is a clear example of the ceremonial law being set aside.

On a Tuesday. Is there a group of people you regard as “unclean”, beyond God’s reach or unworthy of your company? God has made clean those he calls.

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was wondering about the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found out where Simon’s house was and stopped at the gate. They called out, asking if Simon who was known as Peter was staying there.

Perplexed. Peter does not understand at once. God explains through events.

At the gate. Gentiles would not enter a Jewish house uninvited.

On a Tuesday. When you do not understand what God is doing, keep watching. The meaning often comes with the next event.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Simon, three men are looking for you. So get up and go downstairs. Do not hesitate to go with them, for I have sent them.”

The Spirit said. The Spirit speaks as a person: “I have sent them”.

Without hesitation. Literally “without discriminating”, the same word Peter uses in 11:12. Do not make distinctions.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary: “three men”, “two men” (one important early manuscript), or simply “men”. The two servants and the soldier make three (v. 7).

On a Tuesday. When God makes his will clear, do not hesitate.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter went down and said to the men, “I am the one you are looking for. Why have you come?” The men replied, “We have come from Cornelius the centurion. He is a righteous and God-fearing man, who is respected by all the Jewish people. A holy angel told him to ask you to come to his house so that he could hear what you have to say.”

Well spoken of. Cornelius had a good reputation among Jews, like the centurion who built a synagogue (Luke 7:5).

To hear what you have to say. A man ready to listen.

On a Tuesday. A good reputation with outsiders opens doors for the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter invited the men into the house to be his guests. The next day Peter started out with them, and some of the believers from Joppa went along.

Guests. Peter, in a tanner’s house, offered hospitality to Gentiles. The barrier is already falling.

Some brothers. Six Jewish believers (11:12), witnesses of what would happen.

The journey. About 30 miles from Joppa to Caesarea, more than a day’s walk.

Jonah again. Jonah ran from Joppa to avoid preaching to Gentiles. Peter, whose father was also named Jonah (Matthew 16:17, “Simon Bar-Jonah”), goes from Joppa to preach to them.

On a Tuesday. Take other believers with you when you step into new ministry. They will be your witnesses and support.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The following day he arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.

Expecting. He was sure Peter would come.

Relatives and friends. Cornelius gathered everyone he could. A natural evangelist before he was even a believer.

On a Tuesday. Invite your family and friends to hear the gospel: at a church event, a carol service, a meal.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Peter entered the house, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in reverence. But Peter made him get up. “Stand up,” he said, “I am only a man myself.”

Worshipped. Prosekynēsen: bowed down. Romans bowed before superiors and gods.

I too am a man. Peter refuses worship, as Paul and Barnabas did at Lystra (14:14–15) and as the angel did to John: “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you” (Revelation 19:10).

Veneration of saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians distinguish worship given to God from honour (dulia) given to saints. Verdict: Peter refused even the bodily gesture of reverence. Christians should honour godly people, but bow to God alone.

On a Tuesday. If people put you on a pedestal, step down. Point them to God.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While talking with him, Peter went inside and found a large gathering of people. He said to them: “You are well aware that it is against our law for a Jew to associate with or visit a Gentile. But God has shown me that I should not call anyone impure or unclean.”

Not lawful. Not the written law of Moses, but Jewish custom and tradition, which treated Gentile homes as unclean. Pious Jews would not eat in a Gentile home (11:3; Galatians 2:12).

Any person. Peter has understood the vision: it was about people.

On a Tuesday. What social barriers keep you from people: class, race, religion, politics? God calls you across them.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So when I was sent for, I came without raising any objection. May I ask why you sent for me?”

Without objection. A changed Peter, in contrast to his “by no means” on the roof.

On a Tuesday. Ask people questions. Let them tell you what they are looking for.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius answered: “Three days ago I was in my house praying at this hour, at three in the afternoon. Suddenly a man in shining clothes stood before me and said, ‘Cornelius, God has heard your prayer and remembered your gifts to the poor.’”

Four days ago. Counting inclusively, as ancient people did.

Bright clothing. An angel, as at the tomb (Luke 24:4).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “I was fasting until this hour”) add “fasting”. The earliest mention only praying.

On a Tuesday. Keep praying. God hears and remembers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter. He is a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, who lives by the sea.’ So I sent for you immediately, and it was good of you to come. Now we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has commanded you to tell us.”

In the presence of God. Cornelius knew this was a holy moment.

All that you have been commanded. Eager to hear the whole message. A preacher’s dream audience.

On a Tuesday. Come to church on Sunday with Cornelius’s attitude: ready to hear everything God has to say.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter began to speak: “I now realise how true it is that God does not show favouritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.”

Now I understand. A new insight for Peter.

No partiality. God “is not partial and takes no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17). He does not prefer one race.

Acceptable. Dektos: welcome, eligible to come. Not that God-fearers are already saved by their good deeds, but that their nationality does not exclude them; the gospel is offered to them on the same terms as to Jews.

On a Tuesday. Check your heart for favouritism in church: towards the wealthy, the educated, your own culture (James 2:1–9).

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You know the message God sent to the people of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.”

Good news of peace. Echoing Isaiah 52:7, the messenger “who publishes peace”. Peace with God, and peace between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–17).

Lord of all. Not just of Jews. A striking claim to make to a Roman officer, whose emperor was called lord.

A textual note. The Greek of verses 36–38 is notoriously tangled, and manuscripts differ on small words. The meaning is clear.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is Lord of all: of your neighbour from another country and your boss alike.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You know what has happened throughout the province of Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism that John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and how he went around doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil, because God was with him.”

You know. Jesus’ ministry was public knowledge. Cornelius, living in Judea, had heard.

Anointed with the Spirit. At his baptism (Luke 3:22). Jesus said, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). “Christ” means “anointed one”.

Doing good. A beautiful summary of Jesus’ life.

The shape of Mark. Peter’s outline (Galilee, John’s baptism, healing, cross, resurrection) matches Mark’s Gospel, which early tradition says was based on Peter’s preaching.

On a Tuesday. Could your life be summed up as “went about doing good”?
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We are witnesses of everything he did in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They killed him by hanging him on a cross, but God raised him from the dead on the third day and caused him to be seen.”

Witnesses. The apostles saw it all.

On a tree. The cross, recalling Deuteronomy 21:23.

The third day. A precise detail of history.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is news about real events. Tell it as news.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He was not seen by all the people, but by witnesses whom God had already chosen: by us who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.”

Chosen witnesses. The risen Jesus did not appear to Pilate or the Sanhedrin, but to his followers, who then told the world.

Ate and drank. Proof of a bodily resurrection (Luke 24:41–43; John 21:13).

On a Tuesday. You believe on the testimony of people who ate with the risen Christ. That testimony is reliable.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one whom God appointed as judge of the living and the dead. All the prophets testify about him that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

Judge. Jesus will judge everyone, living and dead (17:31; John 5:22). The Apostles’ Creed: “from thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead.”

All the prophets. The whole Old Testament points to him.

Everyone who believes. Jew or Gentile. The condition is faith, not circumcision.

Forgiveness. Through his name, by trusting him.

On a Tuesday. The same Jesus is both judge and Saviour. Trust him now as Saviour, and you need not fear him as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on Gentiles.

While Peter was still speaking. God interrupts the sermon. No altar call, no laying on of hands, no baptism yet. The Spirit came as they believed the word (15:7–9).

The Gentile Pentecost. As at Pentecost (Jews) and Samaria (Samaritans), God gives a visible sign to show that Gentiles are fully accepted.

Before baptism. This is strong evidence against the idea that baptism itself confers the Spirit or regeneration.

Amazed. The Jewish believers had not expected Gentiles to receive the Spirit without becoming Jews first.

On a Tuesday. God saves people through his word. Keep speaking it.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. Then Peter said…

Tongues. As at Pentecost (2:4), a visible and audible sign. Peter later says it was “just as on us at the beginning” (11:15).

Extolling God. Praise, the content of the tongues.

On a Tuesday. The fruit of the Spirit’s coming is praise of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptised with water. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have.” So he ordered that they be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked Peter to stay with them for a few days.

Who can forbid? If God has given the reality, the church cannot withhold the sign.

Commanded them to be baptised. Baptism is still necessary, as obedience, even after the Spirit has been received. Peter may have let his companions do the baptising (compare 1 Corinthians 1:17).

Stayed some days. Peter ate and lodged with Gentiles, which he would have to defend in Jerusalem (11:3).

For worship. Thank God that the gospel came to the Gentiles. If you are not Jewish, Cornelius’s story is your story.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
News that Gentiles have received the word reaches Jerusalem, and when Peter returns, Jewish believers who insisted on circumcision criticise him: he went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them. Table fellowship meant full acceptance, and that was the offence. Peter tells the whole story step by step, with six witnesses, and ends with the decisive fact: God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Spirit he gave the apostles, so who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and praise God that he has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles.

Meanwhile, believers scattered after Stephen’s death reach Antioch in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, a great trading centre on the Orontes river, with a large Jewish community and a reputation for luxury and loose living. Some of them, from Cyprus and Cyrene, begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and many believe. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who is delighted by what he sees, and fetches Saul from Tarsus to help him; for a whole year they teach the new church, and it is at Antioch that the disciples are first called “Christians”. When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, which came in the reign of the emperor Claudius, the Antioch church sends relief to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul, a first sign of the Gentile churches caring for the mother church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles and believers in Judea heard that the Gentiles had received God’s word. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticised him for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter explained everything in order: the vision at Joppa of the sheet with animals, the voice telling him to eat, his refusal, the voice saying three times not to call unclean what God has made clean, and the arrival at that moment of three men from Caesarea. The Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation, and six brothers went with him into the man’s house. The man told them how an angel had told him to send for Peter, who would bring a message through which he and his household would be saved. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words that John baptised with water but they would be baptised with the Spirit. If God gave them the same gift he gave those who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? When they heard this they had no further objections and praised God, saying that God had granted even the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Reach and the Church's Lag

What this passage shows is not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter at the door were not bigots inventing a rule; they were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, for reasons he himself had given, which had been kept at enormous cost for centuries. Their difficulty was that the boundary had done its work and been retired, and nobody had told them. Reformed theology has taken the episode as the clearest case in Scripture of the Spirit going ahead of the church's understanding — and of how he settles such questions. Not by a decree, not by a text, and not by an apostolic ruling: by doing the thing in public, in front of witnesses who could be cross-examined, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct. The Jerusalem church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council several years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's answer to a hostile hearing was to narrate what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He produced no proof text and pulled no rank. Now: That is still the strongest thing available in a disputed matter, and the rarest. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is very hard to answer — and a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has said nothing anybody can test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles and the believers throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticised him.

The news spread. A Gentile household had received the word. It was the talk of the churches.

The circumcision party. Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses (15:1, 5; Galatians 2:12, “fearing the circumcision party”).

Criticised. Diekrinonto: disputed with him. Peter was not above questioning; leaders are accountable to the church.

On a Tuesday. When God does something new, expect some believers to object. Answer patiently.
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said, “You went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

The real issue. Not that Gentiles believed, but that Peter ate with them. Table fellowship meant full acceptance. Strict Jews would not eat with Gentiles, whose food might be unclean or offered to idols.

On a Tuesday. Whom you eat with says whom you accept. Is your table open?
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Starting from the beginning, Peter told them the whole story: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision. I saw something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to where I was.”

In order. Kathexēs: the word Luke uses of his own orderly account (Luke 1:3). Peter does not argue theology first; he tells what God did.

Luke repeats it. Ancient writers repeated stories to show their importance. This is the hinge of Acts.

On a Tuesday. When defending your faith or a decision, tell the story of what God did. Testimony is powerful.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I looked into it and saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles and birds. Then I heard a voice telling me, ‘Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.’”

Beasts of prey. A detail not in chapter 10: even predators, among the most unclean.

On a Tuesday. God’s grace reaches even the people we think most unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I replied, ‘Surely not, Lord! Nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ The voice spoke from heaven a second time, ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’”

Peter admits his resistance. He shares his critics’ instincts. He is not saying he was more enlightened; God overruled him.

On a Tuesday. Be honest about your own prejudices when talking with others about theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“This happened three times, and then it was all pulled up to heaven again.”

Three times. Emphatic: not a passing thought.

On a Tuesday. When God repeats a lesson, pay attention.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Right then three men who had been sent to me from Caesarea stopped at the house where I was staying. The Spirit told me to have no hesitation about going with them. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s house.”

The Spirit told me. Peter stresses that he acted under God’s direction.

Six brothers. With Peter, seven witnesses. In Egyptian and Roman law seven witnesses gave complete validation; in Jewish law, two or three were enough. Peter brings more than required.

On a Tuesday. When stepping into something new, take others with you to see and confirm it.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He told us how he had seen an angel appear in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter. He will bring you a message through which you and all your household will be saved.’”

Words by which you will be saved. Cornelius was not yet saved, for all his piety. Salvation came through the message about Christ (Romans 10:17, “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ”).

Your household. The promise extended to his family and servants, who also heard and believed (10:44).

On a Tuesday. Good people still need the gospel. Do not assume religious friends are already saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as he had come on us at the beginning. Then I remembered what the Lord had said: ‘John baptised with water, but you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit.’”

As I began. In 10:44 Peter was in the middle of his sermon. From his point of view, he had hardly begun.

As on us at the beginning. At Pentecost. The same gift.

The Lord’s word. Jesus’ promise (1:5). Peter interprets experience by Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Test spiritual experiences by the words of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So if God gave them the same gift he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to think that I could stand in God’s way?”

The same gift. No first and second class in the church.

When we believed. The Spirit was given when people believed, Jews and Gentiles alike.

Who was I? To refuse would be to fight God (5:39).

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, who are you to keep them at a distance?

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this, they had no further objections and praised God, saying, “So then, even to Gentiles God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Now those who had been scattered by the persecution that broke out when Stephen was killed travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, spreading the word only among Jews.

They fell silent. The critics were convinced, at least for now. The issue would return (chapter 15).

Granted repentance. Repentance is God’s gift (5:31; 2 Timothy 2:25). Even turning to God is a work of grace, given to Gentiles as to Jews. This is one of the texts behind the Reformed doctrine that faith and repentance are gifts.

That leads to life. Eternal life.

Phoenicia, Cyprus, Antioch. The coast of modern Lebanon, the island of Cyprus, and Antioch in Syria.

Only to Jews. At first, the scattered believers kept to Jewish audiences.

For worship. Thank God that he grants repentance, and that he granted it to you.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death travelled to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, telling the message only to Jews. But some from Cyprus and Cyrene went to Antioch and began speaking to Greeks as well, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus. The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. When news reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
