Arriving and seeing what God’s grace had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord. Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, found him and brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught great numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. During this time some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, Agabus, predicted through the Spirit that a severe famine would spread over the entire Roman world, which happened during the reign of Claudius. The disciples, each according to their ability, decided to provide help for the believers living in Judea, and sent their gift to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the model the New Testament actually gives us for a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with unnamed laymen doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was established by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first corporate act was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Reformed missiology has drawn the pattern out: rooted in the word, generous beyond its own borders, and willing to give away its best men — for within two chapters Antioch will send Barnabas and Saul off on the first missionary journey, which is to say it exported its two finest teachers and kept none of them. A church is not measured by what it gathers. It is measured by what it is prepared to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The single most important barrier in Christian history was crossed by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Luke knows their home towns and not their names, which tells you they were never anybody's leadership. Now: The work that turns out to have mattered most in any generation is very often done by people who will not appear in an account of it — who simply spoke to whoever was in front of them, because it did not occur to them to check first whether they were allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of them, however, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began to speak to Greeks also, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus.

Unnamed pioneers. The first deliberate mission to Gentiles was started by ordinary believers whose names we do not know.

Antioch. Antioch on the Orontes, capital of the Roman province of Syria, the third city of the empire, with perhaps a quarter of a million people. A cosmopolitan trading city, famous for its colonnaded main street, its luxury, and the pleasure grove of Daphne nearby, notorious for immorality. It had a large Jewish community.

Greeks or Hellenists? A textual note: some manuscripts read “Hellenists” (Greek-speaking Jews), others “Greeks” (Gentiles). The context requires a contrast with “Jews only” in verse 19, so the meaning is Gentiles, whichever word Luke used.

The Lord Jesus. To Gentiles, “Messiah” meant little; “Lord” was a title they understood.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a title to start something great for God. Ordinary believers began the Gentile mission.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord. News of this reached the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he arrived and saw what the grace of God had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts.

The hand of the Lord. God’s power at work (Isaiah 59:1).

Barnabas. A Cypriot himself, like some of the pioneers. The perfect choice: generous, encouraging.

He saw the grace of God. Grace can be seen, in changed lives.

Steadfast purpose. Literally “with purpose of heart”. A resolve to keep close to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Look for evidence of God’s grace in others, and tell them you see it.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.

A good man. Rare praise in the New Testament. Barnabas’s character drew people to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Character is a powerful witness. Pray to be “a good man” or “a good woman”, full of the Spirit and faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he found him, he brought him to Antioch. So for a whole year Barnabas and Saul met with the church and taught great numbers of people. The disciples were called Christians first at Antioch.

To look for Saul. Anazētēsai: to search hard. Barnabas knew whom the work needed, and was humble enough to bring in someone more gifted.

A whole year. Teaching new believers thoroughly. Solid foundations matter.

Christians. Christianoi: “Christ’s people”, “Christ-partisans”, a Latin-style ending like “Herodians”. Probably a nickname given by outsiders, perhaps mocking. Only three times in the New Testament (26:28; 1 Peter 4:16). The name shows that outsiders saw Christ at the centre of the movement, and that it was now distinct from Judaism.

On a Tuesday. Would your neighbours call you a Christian, “a Christ person”, from what they see?
verseByVerse.note: “Christians” means “Christ’s people” — probably a nickname given by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
During this time some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, named Agabus, stood up and through the Spirit predicted that a severe famine would spread over the entire Roman world. (This happened during the reign of Claudius.)

Prophets. The early church had recognised prophets (13:1; 15:32; 21:9–10).

Agabus. He appears again in 21:10–11, predicting Paul’s arrest.

A famine. The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54. Roman historians (Suetonius, Tacitus) record repeated food shortages in his reign. Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea around AD 45–47, when Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain from Egypt for Jerusalem’s starving people.

The whole world. The Roman world, a common way of speaking (Luke 2:1).

Predictive prophecy today? Agabus’s prophecy came true. Cessationists see such revelatory prophecy as part of the apostolic foundation; continuationists believe predictive prophecy may still occur. Verdict: held charitably. Any claimed prophecy today must be tested, and must never be treated as equal to Scripture.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes warns his people ahead of trouble so they can prepare to help others.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record severe famines in his reign, including in Judea.

parallels.desc: Agabus again

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples, as each one was able, decided to provide help for the brothers and sisters living in Judea. This they did, sending their gift to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.

Each according to ability. Proportional, voluntary giving (2 Corinthians 8:11–12).

Gentiles helping Jews. The first sign of the Gentile churches caring for the mother church, later the great collection (Romans 15:25–27).

The elders. The first mention of elders in the church at Jerusalem. Leadership was developing alongside the apostles (15:2, 4).

Which visit? Many think this “famine visit” is the one Paul describes in Galatians 2:1–10, when the Jerusalem leaders asked him to “remember the poor”. Others identify Galatians 2 with the council of Acts 15. The question affects the dating of Galatians but not its teaching.

For worship. Thank God for churches in other countries that have helped yours, and for the chance to help others.

parallels.desc: remember the poor

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. Acts 11:18 contains one of the clearest biblical statements of the Reformed doctrine of monergism in conversion: “God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards with salvation; it is itself a divine gift, granted by God to those he is drawing to himself. This does not eliminate human responsibility — the Gentiles in Cornelius’s house genuinely repented, genuinely believed, genuinely turned to Christ. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the grammar of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory. Antioch is not merely a sociological phenomenon — it is a theological one: God giving repentance to people who had no claim on him, because he is the God of all grace.
11.examples:
Then: Anonymous men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names are not recorded in Scripture, who crossed the ethnic boundary no one else had thought to cross, and started the church in Antioch. The hand of the Lord was with them. History turned on their obedience.

Now: The church at Antioch is the model of a healthy sending church: multi-ethnic, Spirit-filled, taught by gifted teachers, responsive to need (the famine collection), and willing to send its best people out on mission. Every local church must ask whether it looks more like the fearful circumcision party in Jerusalem or the glad, generous, outward-facing church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
A new persecution comes from the top. Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, had grown up in Rome as a friend of the imperial family; the emperors Caligula and Claudius gave him his grandfather’s whole kingdom, and from AD 41 to 44 he ruled Judea, courting Jewish favour by careful religious observance. To please the Jewish leaders he has James the brother of John executed with the sword, the first apostle to be martyred, and arrests Peter during the Passover festival, intending a public trial afterwards. Peter is chained between two soldiers, with sixteen guarding him in shifts, while the church prays earnestly. On the night before the trial an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards and through the iron city gate, which opens by itself.

Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many are praying. The servant girl Rhoda is so excited to hear his voice that she runs to tell the others without opening the door, and they tell her she is mad, or that it must be his angel. When they finally let him in, Peter tells them what happened, asks them to tell James, the Lord’s brother, and leaves for another place. Herod executes the guards. Then, at Caesarea, while the crowd hails his speech as the voice of a god, he is struck down by an angel and dies, eaten by worms, an event the Jewish historian Josephus also records. The tyrant dies, and the word of God keeps growing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About that time King Herod arrested some who belonged to the church, intending to persecute them. He had James, John’s brother, put to death with the sword. Seeing that this pleased the Jewish leaders, he arrested Peter too, during the Festival of Unleavened Bread. He put him in prison under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each, planning to bring him out for public trial after the Passover. So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was praying earnestly to God for him. The night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries at the entrance. Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, woke him and told him to get up quickly, and the chains fell off his wrists. The angel told him to put on his clothes, sandals and cloak and follow him. Peter followed, not knowing whether it was real or a vision. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself, and when they had walked the length of a street the angel left him. Then Peter came to himself and realised that the Lord had sent his angel to rescue him from Herod and from everything the Jewish people were hoping for. He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John called Mark, where many were praying. When he knocked at the outer gate, a servant named Rhoda came to answer; recognising Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she ran back without opening it and announced that Peter was at the door. They told her she was out of her mind, and when she insisted, they said it must be his angel. Peter kept knocking, and when they opened the door they were astonished. He motioned for silence, described how the Lord had brought him out of prison, asked them to tell James and the other believers, and then left for another place. In the morning there was great commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. Herod searched for him, cross-examined the guards and ordered their execution, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there. Herod had been quarrelling with the people of Tyre and Sidon; they sought an audience, secured the support of Blastus, the king’s trusted servant, and asked for peace, because they depended on the king’s country for their food. On the appointed day Herod, in his royal robes, sat on his throne and addressed the people. They shouted that this was the voice of a god, not a man. Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God continued to spread and flourish. Barnabas and Saul, having completed their mission, returned, taking with them John, also called Mark.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

This chapter is where a theology of prayer either becomes honest or becomes cruel. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; the church, we may be sure, had prayed for James too, and James was buried. Luke gives no reason, and the Reformed tradition has been right to refuse to supply one. Prayer is not a mechanism that produces outcomes in proportion to fervency — if it were, the only conclusion available about James would be an obscene one. What prayer is, is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God who answers according to his own purposes and does not explain them. And notice that Luke reports the failure of the church's expectation in the same breath as the success of its prayer: God answered a request offered by people who did not believe it would be answered, which settles for ever the question of whether the power lies in the praying or in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda's announcement was met with you are out of your mind from the very people who had been up all night asking for exactly this. Luke records it without a word of rebuke, and the deliverance stood. Now: A great many Christians pray for things while quietly not expecting them, and then feel like frauds. This chapter is unusually kind to that condition. The answer arrived and stood knocking at the gate while the intercessors argued about whether it could be him.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was about this time that King Herod arrested some who belonged to the church, intending to persecute them. He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword.

Herod Agrippa I. Grandson of Herod the Great. Raised in Rome with the imperial family, he became a close friend of Caligula and Claudius, who made him king over all his grandfather’s territory. He worked hard to win Jewish approval.

James. Son of Zebedee, one of the inner three with Peter and John. Jesus had told him he would drink his cup: “The cup that I drink you will drink” (Mark 10:39). The first apostle martyred. Luke gives him a single sentence.

The sword. Beheading: the Roman method of execution, used for political enemies.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness does not guarantee long life. James died young; John lived to old age. Both served Christ.
verseByVerse.note: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. James is the first of the Twelve to die for his faith.

parallels.desc: the cup that I drink you will drink

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw that this met with approval among the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This happened during the Festival of Unleavened Bread. After arresting him, he put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring him out for public trial after the Passover.

It pleased the Jews. The leaders, not every Jew. Herod was politically motivated.

Unleavened Bread. The week following Passover. The anniversary of Jesus’ own arrest and trial.

Four squads. Sixteen soldiers rotating through the four watches of the night. Peter had escaped before (5:19); Herod was taking no chances.

On a Tuesday. No security system can keep out God.
verseByVerse.note: Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the night watches.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was earnestly praying to God for him. The night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries stood guard at the entrance.

But. Herod’s power on one side, the church’s prayer on the other.

Earnestly. Ektenōs: fervently, stretched out. The word used of Jesus praying in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44).

Sleeping. On the night before his likely execution, Peter slept. “He gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2).

On a Tuesday. Pray earnestly for believers in prison today. And when you are anxious, ask God for Peter’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him up. “Quick, get up!” he said, and the chains fell off Peter’s wrists.

Struck him. Peter was so deeply asleep the angel had to hit him.

Chains fell off. No human help needed.

On a Tuesday. God can break chains, literal and spiritual. Pray for those bound by addiction or despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel said to him, “Put on your clothes and sandals.” And Peter did so. “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me,” the angel told him. Peter followed him out of the prison, but he had no idea that what the angel was doing was really happening; he thought he was seeing a vision.

Practical instructions. Get dressed, put on sandals. The miracle includes ordinary details.

A vision? Peter had had visions before (10:10). This one was real.

On a Tuesday. God’s rescues sometimes feel unreal. Follow anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city. It opened for them by itself, and they went through it. When they had walked the length of one street, suddenly the angel left him.

The guards. Perhaps asleep, perhaps blinded.

Of its own accord. Automatē, from which we get “automatic”.

The angel left. Once Peter could manage alone, the miracle stopped. God does not do for us what we can do ourselves.

On a Tuesday. Expect God to help where you cannot help yourself, and to leave you to act where you can.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter came to himself and said, “Now I know without a doubt that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s clutches and from everything the Jewish people were hoping would happen.” When this had dawned on him, he went to the house of Mary the mother of John, also called Mark, where many people had gathered and were praying.

Came to himself. Woke up fully.

Mary’s house. A large house with a gateway and a servant, big enough for many to gather. Perhaps the upper room of 1:13. Mary was a wealthy widow.

John Mark. Barnabas’s cousin (Colossians 4:10), who joined the first missionary journey and left it (13:13), was later restored, and wrote the Gospel of Mark.

Many were praying. In the middle of the night. The prayer meeting was still going on.

On a Tuesday. Open your home for prayer. Some of the greatest works of God begin in living rooms.
verseByVerse.note: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas. His mother’s house was large enough to hold a gathering.

parallels.desc: God sent his angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter knocked at the outer entrance, and a servant named Rhoda came to answer the door. When she recognised Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed she ran back without opening it and exclaimed, “Peter is at the door!”

Rhoda. “Rose”: a common name for a slave girl. Luke remembers her name.

Overjoyed. So happy she forgot to open the door. A touch of humour in the story.

On a Tuesday. Joy at answered prayer can make us forget practical things. Better that than not expecting answers at all.
verseByVerse.note: Rhoda means “rose.”

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You’re out of your mind,” they told her. When she kept insisting that it was so, they said, “It must be his angel.” But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astonished.

Out of your mind. They were praying for Peter’s release but did not believe it when it came. Their faith was weak, yet God answered. God answers prayer even when our faith is small.

His angel. Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel who could resemble them. Jesus said of children, “in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). Do individuals have guardian angels? Scripture says angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14), but does not clearly teach one angel per person. Verdict: angels do care for God’s people; whether each has a personal guardian is uncertain, and Calvin advised caution about it.

Kept knocking. The man who walked through an iron gate could not get through a house door.

On a Tuesday. Do you expect your prayers to be answered? Pray, and then watch for the knock at the door.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter motioned with his hand for them to be quiet and described how the Lord had brought him out of prison. “Tell James and the other brothers and sisters about this,” he said, and then he left for another place.

James. Not the apostle just killed, but the Lord’s brother, now the leading figure in the Jerusalem church (15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Author of the letter of James.

Another place. Luke does not say where, perhaps to protect people. Some Roman Catholic tradition says Peter went to Rome at this point and founded the church there. Verdict: there is no evidence for it. Peter was back in Jerusalem for the council (15:7), and later travelled to Antioch (Galatians 2:11) and perhaps Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:12). Strong early tradition places his death in Rome in the 60s.

On a Tuesday. Share answers to prayer with the wider church. It builds everyone’s faith.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning there was no small commotion among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter. After Herod had a thorough search made for him and did not find him, he cross-examined the guards and ordered that they be executed. Then Herod went from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

No small commotion. Luke’s understatement.

Executed. Under Roman practice, a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty (16:27; 27:42).

On a Tuesday. Tyrants destroy those around them. Pray for people who serve cruel bosses.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had been quarrelling with the people of Tyre and Sidon; they now joined together and sought an audience with him. After securing the support of Blastus, a trusted personal servant of the king, they asked for peace, because they depended on the king’s country for their food supply.

Tyre and Sidon. Phoenician port cities on the coast of modern Lebanon. They had always depended on Israel’s farmland for grain (1 Kings 5:11; Ezekiel 27:17). A trade dispute with Herod meant hunger.

Blastus. The king’s chamberlain. They probably bribed him.

On a Tuesday. Political power can be used to starve people. Pray for justice in trade and food supply.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the appointed day Herod, wearing his royal robes, sat on his throne and delivered a public address to the people. They shouted, “This is the voice of a god, not of a man.” Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died.

Josephus’s account. The Jewish historian describes the same event (AD 44) at a festival in Caesarea in honour of Caesar. Herod entered the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven entirely of silver, which shone in the rising sun. Flatterers cried out that he was a god. He did not rebuke them, and at once was seized with severe pain in his stomach, and died five days later.

The voice of a god. Ruler worship was common in the Roman world. Herod accepted divine honours, which a Jewish king should have refused.

Did not give God the glory. The sin of pride: “my glory I give to no other” (Isaiah 42:8). Contrast Peter refusing worship (10:26).

Eaten by worms. Luke the doctor gives a vivid description, perhaps of a parasitic infection. Herod the Great, his grandfather, also died a horrible death.

On a Tuesday. When people praise you, pass the glory on to God. “Pride goes before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18).
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God continued to spread and flourish. When Barnabas and Saul had finished their mission, they returned from Jerusalem, taking with them John, also called Mark.

But the word increased. The chapter began with Herod killing an apostle and imprisoning another. It ends with Herod dead and the word growing. The church outlives its persecutors.

Their service. The famine relief (11:29–30).

A textual note. The best manuscripts read “returned to Jerusalem”, which seems to contradict the context. Others read “from Jerusalem”. Perhaps the original means “returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem”. The sense is clear: they went back to Antioch with Mark.

For worship. Herod is dead; the word of God lives. Thank God that no ruler can stop his kingdom.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door a few streets from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The third stage of Acts 1:8, “to the end of the earth”, begins in earnest. The church at Antioch, led by a strikingly mixed group of prophets and teachers, is worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special work. With prayer and the laying on of hands they send them off, with John Mark as their assistant. They sail to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island, preach in synagogues from Salamis in the east to Paphos in the west, and there meet the Roman governor, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet, Elymas, who tries to turn him from the faith. Saul, from now on called by his Roman name Paul, rebukes Elymas, who is struck blind, and the proconsul believes.

They sail to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where Mark leaves them, and travel inland over the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony on the high plateau. In the synagogue Paul is invited to speak and gives the first of his sermons recorded in Acts: God chose Israel, brought them out of Egypt, gave them the land, judges and kings, and from David’s line has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. The people of Jerusalem condemned him, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is proclaimed and everyone who believes is freed from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathers. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas announce that they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. Opposition drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet, while the new disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he had called them. After more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on them and sent them off. Sent out by the Spirit, the two went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper. They travelled through the whole island to Paphos, where they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, an intelligent man, sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name was translated, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. Then Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, looked straight at Elymas and called him a child of the devil, an enemy of everything right, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the Lord’s right ways. The Lord’s hand was against him, and he would be blind for a time. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had been sent to build up that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting. A church's seriousness about mission is not measured by what it collects for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in verse 1 is the most cosmopolitan leadership team in the New Testament, and it was assembled by a persecution. Every man on it was in Antioch because something had gone wrong somewhere else. Now: Congregations tend to produce leaders who resemble each other, and to regard that as normal rather than as a symptom. Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what the room looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch) and Saul. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”

A diverse leadership. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus; Simeon “Niger” (Latin for “black”), perhaps African; Lucius from Cyrene in north Africa; Manaen, raised at court as a foster-brother of Herod Antipas, the ruler who killed John the Baptist; and Saul, a Pharisee from Tarsus. The church reflected the gospel’s reach.

Worshipping and fasting. The mission began in worship, not in a strategy meeting.

The Spirit said. Probably through one of the prophets. The Spirit speaks as a person, with his own will (“for me”, “I have called”).

Set apart. Their best leaders were sent away. A generous church gives its best for mission.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church to be willing to send its best people into mission, even if it costs.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off.

Laying on hands. Commissioning for a specific task, with the church’s blessing. Not making them apostles, which Christ had already done.

Sent them off. Literally “released them”. The church released them; the Spirit sent them (v. 4).

On a Tuesday. Pray and fast before big decisions in your church.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two of them, sent on their way by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. John was with them as their helper.

Seleucia. The port of Antioch, 16 miles west.

Cyprus. Barnabas’s home (4:36), famous for its copper (its name may come from the Greek word for copper). A large Jewish population.

Salamis. The main city in the east of the island.

Synagogues first. Paul’s regular method: start with Jews and God-fearers, who knew the Scriptures.

John. John Mark, as assistant (hypēretēs), perhaps handling practical arrangements, or teaching.

On a Tuesday. Start sharing the gospel with people who already know something of God.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They travelled through the whole island until they came to Paphos. There they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, an intelligent man, sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.

Paphos. The Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end, famous for its temple of Aphrodite, who was said to have been born from the sea nearby.

Proconsul. Luke uses the correct title: Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul. Luke’s precision with titles is one reason historians trust him.

Sergius Paulus. Inscriptions mention men of this family, including one Sergius Paulus who was a curator of the Tiber in Rome under Claudius, and family members in Pisidian Antioch, where Paul went next. Perhaps the proconsul suggested the destination.

Bar-Jesus. “Son of Joshua”, an ironic name for an enemy of Jesus. Roman officials often kept astrologers and seers.

On a Tuesday. Pray for intelligent, powerful people in your nation to want to hear God’s word.
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Elymas the sorcerer (for that is what his name means) opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith.

Elymas. Perhaps from an Arabic or Aramaic word for “wise man” or “sorcerer”.

Opposed. He feared losing his influence. Spiritual warfare is real (Ephesians 6:12).

On a Tuesday. When someone is near faith, expect opposition. Pray.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked straight at Elymas and said, “You are a child of the devil and an enemy of everything that is right! You are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery. Will you never stop perverting the right ways of the Lord?”

Saul, also called Paul. Not a new name at conversion. As a Roman citizen, he probably had both from birth: Saul, his Jewish name (after the king from his tribe of Benjamin), and Paulus, his Roman family name, meaning “small”. From here, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul. And from here Paul, not Barnabas, takes the lead.

Son of the devil. The “son of Jesus” is really a son of the devil (John 8:44).

Making crooked the straight paths. Echoing John the Baptist’s call to make the Lord’s paths straight (Luke 3:4–5).

On a Tuesday. There is a time for strong words against those who deliberately twist the truth to keep others from Christ. It is rare, and needs the Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now the hand of the Lord is against you. You are going to be blind for a time, not even able to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.

For a time. Temporary blindness, with mercy: a chance to repent, as Paul himself had been blinded and led by the hand on the Damascus road (9:8).

The proconsul believed. The first recorded conversion of a high Roman official.

The teaching. He was astonished not chiefly by the miracle but by the teaching.

On a Tuesday. Signs may get attention, but it is the teaching about the Lord that converts.

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The missionaries sail to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and go inland to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, Paul retells Israel’s story from the exodus to King David, and announces that from David’s line God has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. Jerusalem’s leaders condemned him, unknowingly fulfilling the prophets, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is offered: everyone who believes is set free from everything the law could not free them from. Many want to hear more, and the next Sabbath almost the whole city comes. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas declare that, since the word has been rejected, they now turn to the Gentiles, as Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations require. The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed for eternal life believe, and the word spreads, until opponents stir up the city’s leading people and expel the missionaries. They shake the dust from their feet and go on, leaving disciples full of joy and the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified — a courtroom word, the word for a judge declaring a man to be in the right. The law cannot issue that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends on Habakkuk's word to scoffers, be astounded and perish (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Paphos, Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them to return to Jerusalem. From Perga they went on to Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath they entered the synagogue and sat down.

Paul and his companions. Now Paul leads; Luke names him first.

Perga. On the south coast of modern Turkey.

Why did Mark leave? Luke does not say. Suggestions: homesickness, fear of the dangerous road inland, unhappiness that Paul had replaced his cousin Barnabas as leader, or doubts about the mission to Gentiles. Paul saw it as desertion (15:38). Later Mark was restored and became “very useful” to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11).

Pisidian Antioch. A Roman colony on the high plateau, about 3,600 feet above sea level and 100 miles inland over the Taurus mountains, notorious for bandits (2 Corinthians 11:26). Some think Paul fell ill with malaria in the lowlands of Pamphylia and went up to the healthier highlands, which would explain Galatians 4:13: “it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first”.

On a Tuesday. People who fail in ministry can be restored, as Mark was. Do not write anyone off.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the leaders of the synagogue sent word to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have a word of exhortation for the people, please speak.”

The synagogue service. It included the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–9), prayers, a reading from the Law, a reading from the Prophets, and a sermon, often by a visiting teacher.

A word of encouragement. The same phrase is used for the letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:22).

On a Tuesday. Christian worship grew out of the synagogue: reading Scripture, prayer and preaching. Keep them at the centre.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing up, Paul motioned with his hand and said: “Fellow Israelites and you Gentiles who worship God, listen to me! The God of the people of Israel chose our ancestors; he made the people prosper during their stay in Egypt; with mighty power he led them out of that country.”

Two audiences. Jews and God-fearing Gentiles.

God chose. Paul begins with God’s sovereign election of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).

Uplifted arm. Literally “with a high arm”, the language of the exodus (Exodus 6:6).

On a Tuesday. When sharing the gospel, start with God’s actions, not ours.
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For about forty years he endured their conduct in the wilderness. And he overthrew seven nations in Canaan, giving their land to his people as their inheritance.”

Put up with them. God’s patience with a grumbling people.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ by one letter: “put up with them” (etropophorēsen) or “cared for them like a nurse” (etrophophorēsen), echoing Deuteronomy 1:31, where God carried Israel as a father carries his son. Both are true of God.

Seven nations. Deuteronomy 7:1.

On a Tuesday. God has been patient with you too. Thank him.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All this took about 450 years. After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet.”

450 years. Probably the 400 years in Egypt, the 40 in the wilderness and some years of conquest, before the judges.

A textual note. In later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) the 450 years are attached to the period of the judges, which would conflict with 1 Kings 6:1. The earliest manuscripts place it before the judges, as the ESV does, which fits the chronology.

On a Tuesday. God works patiently over centuries.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Then the people asked for a king, and he gave them Saul son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled forty years. After removing Saul, he made David their king. God testified concerning him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart; he will do everything I want him to do.’”

Saul of Benjamin. Paul, also a Benjamite named Saul, mentions his namesake.

Forty years. The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly (1 Samuel 13:1 is uncertain in the Hebrew); Josephus also gives forty.

A man after my heart. Combining 1 Samuel 13:14 (“a man after his own heart”) and Psalm 89:20 (“I have found David, my servant”).

On a Tuesday. David was no perfect man, yet God called him a man after his heart. God looks for a heart turned to him.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“From this man’s descendants God has brought to Israel the Saviour Jesus, as he promised.”

The promise. To David, of an everlasting dynasty (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1).

A Saviour. The climax of the history: all of it was leading to Jesus.

For worship. Thank God that his promises across centuries met in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Before the coming of Jesus, John preached repentance and baptism to all the people of Israel. As John was completing his work, he said: ‘Who do you suppose I am? I am not the one you are looking for. But there is one coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.’”

John. Even in Asia Minor, people had heard of John the Baptist (19:3).

Not worthy. Untying sandals was a slave’s job. John put himself below a slave compared with Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fellow children of Abraham and you God-fearing Gentiles, it is to us that this message of salvation has been sent.”

To us. Paul includes himself and his hearers. The good news is for them.

On a Tuesday. The message of salvation is addressed to you personally.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise Jesus, yet in condemning him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every Sabbath. Though they found no proper ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him executed.”

Did not recognise him. Ignorance (3:17).

Fulfilled the prophets. The irony: the people who read the prophets every Sabbath fulfilled them by condemning the one the prophets described.

No guilt. Jesus was innocent (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

On a Tuesday. It is possible to read the Bible every week and miss Christ. Ask him to open your eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When they had carried out all that was written about him, they took him down from the cross and laid him in a tomb.”

All that was written. Every detail of the cross fulfilled Scripture.

The tree. The cross (5:30; 10:39).

A tomb. Joseph of Arimathea’s (Luke 23:50–53). A real burial, a real death.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was really dead and buried. That is why his resurrection matters.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he was seen by those who had travelled with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to our people.”

But God. The great reversal again.

Many days. Forty (1:3).

Witnesses. Paul refers to the original apostles, though he himself saw the risen Lord too (1 Corinthians 15:8).

On a Tuesday. Our faith rests on eyewitness testimony, preserved in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We tell you the good news: what God promised our ancestors he has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are my son; today I have become your father.’”

The good news. The promise is fulfilled.

Psalm 2:7. “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” Spoken at a king’s coronation. Paul applies it to the resurrection, when God publicly declared Jesus his Son and King (Romans 1:4, “declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead”).

Did Jesus become God’s Son at the resurrection? Adoptionists (an early heresy) taught that Jesus was a man adopted as God’s Son. Verdict: no. Jesus is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; Hebrews 1:2–3). The resurrection was his public installation as the Son in power, not the beginning of his Sonship.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “to us their children” and “to our children”. Some Western manuscripts call it “the first psalm”, since Psalms 1 and 2 were sometimes counted as one.

For worship. Worship Jesus as the eternal Son, crowned at the resurrection.

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God raised him from the dead so that he will never be subject to decay. As God has said, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.’ So it is also stated elsewhere: ‘You will not let your holy one see decay.’”

No more to return. Unlike Lazarus or Tabitha, who died again, Jesus rose to immortal life.

Isaiah 55:3. “My steadfast, sure love for David.” The promises to David are secured through the risen Christ, and offered to all who come (Isaiah 55:1).

Psalm 16:10. As in Peter’s sermon (2:27).

On a Tuesday. The blessings promised to David are yours in Christ: sure, and lasting.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now when David had served God’s purpose in his own generation, he fell asleep; he was buried with his ancestors and his body decayed. But the one whom God raised from the dead did not see decay.”

Served his generation. A beautiful epitaph. David did God’s will in his own time.

Saw corruption. David’s body decayed; the psalm must be about someone else.

On a Tuesday. Ask how you can serve God’s purpose in your generation, then rest in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, my friends, I want you to know that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. Through him everyone who believes is set free from every sin, a justification you were not able to obtain under the law of Moses.”

Forgiveness through this man. The heart of the gospel.

Freed. Literally “justified”: declared righteous. The first use of Paul’s great word in Acts.

Everyone who believes. The only condition.

What the law could not do. Does this mean the law justifies from some sins and Christ from the rest? Verdict: no. Paul means that the law could not justify from any sin, but Christ justifies from all. “By works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight” (Romans 3:20).

On a Tuesday. Whatever you have done, there is forgiveness through Jesus for everyone who believes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Take care that what the prophets have said does not happen to you: ‘Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish, for I am going to do something in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.’”

Habakkuk 1:5. “Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded.” God warned Judah that he was raising up the Babylonians as his instrument of judgement. Paul applies it: God’s astonishing work now is the gospel, and rejecting it is dangerous.

Scoffers. The Greek version reads “despisers”.

On a Tuesday. The gospel comes with a warning as well as an invitation. Do not shrug it off.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people invited them to speak further about these things on the next Sabbath. When the congregation was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and urged them to continue in the grace of God.

Interest. The sermon stirred real curiosity.

Proselytes. Gentiles who had become Jews.

Continue in grace. The Christian life begins and continues by grace.

On a Tuesday. Follow up with people who show interest. Talk with them after church.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy. They began to contradict what Paul was saying and heaped abuse on him.

The whole city. Gentiles came in large numbers to the synagogue.

Jealousy. The leaders resented Gentiles flocking to hear a message that welcomed them on equal terms, without circumcision.

Reviled. Literally “blasphemed”: abusive speech against Paul, and so against Christ.

On a Tuesday. Success in ministry can provoke jealousy, even among religious people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly: “We had to speak the word of God to you first. Since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles. For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’”

To you first. God’s plan: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

Judge yourselves unworthy. By rejecting the gospel, they passed sentence on themselves.

We turn to the Gentiles. A pattern repeated in Acts (18:6; 28:28). Paul kept going to synagogues in each new city, though.

Isaiah 49:6. “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” Spoken to the Servant, who is Christ (Luke 2:32), and now carried out through his apostles.

On a Tuesday. When some reject the gospel, take it to others. God’s plan is for all nations.
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and honoured the word of the Lord; and all who were appointed for eternal life believed. The word of the Lord spread through the whole region.

Glorifying the word. Joy and praise.

As many as were appointed. One of the clearest statements of election in Acts. Tetagmenoi is a perfect passive: “had been appointed, ordained, enrolled”. Those whom God had appointed to eternal life believed.

Christians differ. Some Arminian interpreters read the verb as middle, “as many as had disposed themselves to eternal life”, meaning those who were already inclined to believe. Verdict: the passive reading is the natural one; Luke uses the verb of appointment by authority (22:10; 28:23). Faith is the result of God’s appointment, not its cause (Romans 8:30, “those whom he predestined he also called”; John 6:37). Yet election never makes preaching unnecessary: those appointed came to believe through hearing Paul.

For worship. If you believe, it is because God appointed you to eternal life. Thank him, humbly.
