verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wanted to take him along on the journey, so he circumcised him because of the Jews who lived in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

Why circumcise Timothy, but not Titus? Paul refused to circumcise Titus, a Gentile, when false brothers demanded it as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Timothy, with a Jewish mother, would have been seen as a Jew who had abandoned the covenant, and his presence would have closed every synagogue door. Paul circumcised him not for salvation but for mission: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The principle. When a practice is demanded as necessary for salvation, refuse it. When it is a matter of freedom, use it in love for others.

On a Tuesday. Are there freedoms you could give up to remove a barrier for someone hearing the gospel?
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they travelled from town to town, they delivered the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the people to obey. So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.

The decisions. The decree of chapter 15.

Strengthened and increased. Clarity about the gospel led to growth.

On a Tuesday. Clear teaching on grace strengthens churches.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and his companions travelled throughout the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them to.

Asia. The Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its capital. Paul would preach there later (chapter 19).

Forbidden. How? Luke does not say: perhaps a prophecy, a circumstance, an illness, or an inner conviction.

The Spirit of Jesus. A rare phrase. The Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus, who directs his mission.

How does God guide today? Some Christians seek guidance through inner impressions, signs or visions. Verdict: God guides his people chiefly through his word, wise counsel and providence, the opening and closing of doors. He can guide in extraordinary ways, but we should not demand them. Paul himself did not wait in Antioch for a vision; he set out with a plan and let God redirect him. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “the Spirit suffered them not”) omit “of Jesus”. The earliest include it.

On a Tuesday. When your plans are blocked, do not despair. God may be redirecting you to something better.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.

Troas. Alexandria Troas, a Roman colony and port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy. The gateway to Europe.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God leads you to the edge before he shows the next step.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” After Paul had seen the vision, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

A man of Macedonia. Some have suggested it was Luke himself, perhaps a Macedonian; we cannot know.

Macedonia. The Roman province of northern Greece, homeland of Alexander the Great. The gospel’s first step into Europe.

We. Here the first of the “we” passages begins (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16). Luke the author has joined the team, and writes as an eyewitness.

Concluding. Symbibazontes: putting it together. The team discussed the vision and reached a shared conclusion. Guidance involved reasoning as well as revelation.

On a Tuesday. Discuss important decisions with trusted believers. Guidance is often confirmed together.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Troas we put out to sea and sailed straight for Samothrace, and the next day on to Neapolis. From there we travelled to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days.

A direct voyage. A favourable wind: two days. The reverse journey later took five (20:6).

Samothrace. A mountainous island, halfway across.

Neapolis. “New City”, modern Kavala, Philippi’s port, on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road across Macedonia.

Philippi. Named after Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander. In 42 BC Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, Caesar’s assassins, there, and Rome settled veterans in the city; Octavian (Augustus) settled more after 31 BC. As a Roman colony it had Roman law, Latin as its official language, and citizens proud of being Roman (16:21; Philippians 3:20).

A textual note. The phrase “a leading city of the district” is uncertain in the Greek; manuscripts differ, and some scholars propose “a city of the first district of Macedonia”, since Macedonia was divided into four districts. The meaning is not affected.

On a Tuesday. God sends the gospel to places of power and pride, too.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there.

No synagogue. Jewish tradition required ten Jewish men to form a synagogue. Philippi apparently did not have them, so Jews and God-fearers met outside by the river Gangites, perhaps for ritual washing.

Women. Paul sat down with a group of women, which many rabbis would not have done. The European church began with women at prayer.

On a Tuesday. Go where people already gather to seek God, and join them.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and the members of her household were baptised, she invited us to her home. “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” she said, “come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us.

Lydia. Perhaps her name (“the Lydian woman”) came from her home region of Lydia, where Thyatira lay.

Thyatira. In the province of Asia, famous for its purple dye. Inscriptions there mention a guild of dyers. Purple dye, made from shellfish or from the madder root, was very expensive; purple cloth was worn by the wealthy and by officials. Lydia was a businesswoman of means, with a household and a house large enough for guests.

A worshipper of God. A God-fearing Gentile.

The Lord opened her heart. Conversion is God’s work. She listened; but it was the Lord who opened her heart to respond. “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). This is effectual calling.

Her household. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as evidence for baptising infants. Credobaptists reply that nothing is said about children, Lydia may have been unmarried or widowed, and her household probably meant servants or workers who also heard. Verdict: the text does not settle it; elsewhere in Acts baptism follows hearing and believing.

Hospitality. Her first act as a believer was to open her home. It became the first church in Europe (v. 40).

On a Tuesday. Pray for God to open the hearts of people you speak to. And use your home for his work.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A slave girl whose fortune-telling earned money for her owners follows the missionaries for days, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God, until Paul casts the spirit out of her in Jesus’ name. Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them as Jews of promoting un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens every door and loosens every chain. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul, falls before them and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and speak the word to his whole household. He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and they rejoice together over a meal. In the morning Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the alarmed magistrates come in person to escort them out. After encouraging the believers at Lydia’s house, they leave.
verseByVerse.theology:
Midnight Praise and the Ministry of Suffering

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight — after being stripped and beaten with rods — and the other prisoners listen. The praise is not despite the suffering but in it: the same Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship. Reformed theology sees in this midnight scene the confirmation of what Paul will later write: 'we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance' (Romans 5:3). The songs at midnight are the most powerful proclamation the prisoners that night will ever hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked 'What must I do to be saved?' — the question of Pentecost (2:37) repeated in a Philippian prison. The answer is the same: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' Now: The gospel's answer to the question of salvation is always the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once when we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a female slave who had a spirit by which she predicted the future. She earned a great deal of money for her owners by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling you the way to be saved.”

A python spirit. The Greek says she had “a spirit, a python”. The python was the serpent associated with the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, where the priestess, the Pythia, gave prophecies in a trance. The Greek writer Plutarch says ventriloquist fortune-tellers were called “pythons”.

Exploited. A slave girl owned and used for profit. Her owners made money from her bondage.

Servants of the Most High God. True words. In the pagan world, “the Most High God” could mean Zeus, and “salvation” could mean physical safety. Demons sometimes spoke truth about Jesus (Mark 1:24), but their testimony confused people and was not wanted.

On a Tuesday. Not every spiritual voice that says the right words is from God. Test the source.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python” — linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She kept this up for many days. Finally Paul became so troubled that he turned round and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” At that moment the spirit left her.

Greatly annoyed. Perhaps troubled for the girl, or by the confusion she caused.

In the name of Jesus Christ. Paul’s authority came from Jesus, as Jesus cast out demons with a word.

That very hour. Instant deliverance.

What happened to her? Luke does not say. Perhaps she joined the church at Lydia’s house.

On a Tuesday. Pray for people trapped in occult practices, and for those exploited for profit, such as victims of trafficking.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When her owners realised that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to face the authorities. They brought them before the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews, and are throwing our city into an uproar.”

Their hope of gain. The real motive. The same Greek word “went out” is used of the spirit leaving and of their profit leaving.

The marketplace. The forum, where the magistrates sat. Its remains can be seen at Philippi today.

The magistrates. Stratēgoi: the two chief magistrates of a Roman colony (duoviri), who liked to call themselves praetors. Luke uses the local title.

Being Jews. Antisemitism: the emperor Claudius had recently expelled Jews from Rome (18:2). Luke (a Gentile, and likely Timothy, half-Greek) are not accused.

On a Tuesday. When the gospel threatens someone’s income, expect fierce opposition. Ask whether any of your income depends on exploiting others.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“They are advocating customs unlawful for us Romans to accept or practise.”

Customs. Roman law allowed Judaism as a legal religion, but forbade proselytising Roman citizens into foreign cults.

Us Romans. Colonists’ pride. Paul later wrote to this church, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

On a Tuesday. Christians may be accused of being un-national, un-British or un-American. Our first citizenship is in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered them to be stripped and beaten with rods. After they had been severely flogged, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was commanded to guard them carefully.

Beaten with rods. By the lictors, officers who carried bundles of rods (the fasces) as a symbol of the magistrates’ authority. Paul remembers: “Three times I was beaten with rods” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and later recalled how they had been “shamefully treated at Philippi” (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

No trial. Mob justice.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Christians beaten for their faith today.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he received these orders, he put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.

The inner prison. The darkest, most secure cell.

Stocks. Wooden blocks clamping the feet, sometimes spread wide to cause pain. With backs raw from the beating, they could not lie down.

On a Tuesday. When you feel locked in, remember Paul and Silas in the inner cell. God was there too.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose.

Singing at midnight. In pain, in the dark, in stocks, they sang. “At night his song is with me” (Psalm 42:8). Paul later wrote to this church: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4).

The prisoners listening. Worship in suffering is a witness.

An earthquake. The region is prone to earthquakes; the timing was God’s. Chains fastened to walls could come loose as the walls shook.

On a Tuesday. When life is darkest, try praying and singing to God. Others may be listening.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself because he thought the prisoners had escaped. But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!”

Suicide. A Roman guard who lost prisoners faced their penalty (12:19). Suicide seemed more honourable than execution. Philippi was the city where Brutus and Cassius had killed themselves after their defeat.

Do not harm yourself. Paul cared about the man who had locked him in the stocks.

We are all here. Remarkably, no one escaped. Perhaps the prisoners were awed by the singing and the earthquake.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone in despair, speak to them as Paul did. Life is precious. In the UK you can call Samaritans on 116 123; in the US, 988.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. He then brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

Trembling. Fear of God after the earthquake and the singing.

What must I do to be saved? The greatest question anyone can ask. Did he mean spiritual salvation? He had heard the slave girl’s cry about “the way of salvation” (v. 17), and probably the prisoners’ hymns.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks a question like this, be ready to answer simply.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

Believe. The simplest statement of the gospel: trust Jesus as Lord. Not “do” anything, but believe. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

And your household. Not that his family would be saved by his faith, but that the same offer was for them on the same terms (v. 32, 34): each must believe.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “Christ”: “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ”. The earliest have “the Lord Jesus”.

For worship. Thank God that the way of salvation is this simple: believe in the Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptised.

Spoke the word. The whole household heard the gospel explained.

Washed their wounds. The first fruit of faith: kindness to those he had hurt. He washed them; they baptised him.

Immediately. No delay. In Acts, baptism followed faith quickly.

His household. Again, paedobaptists see a household baptism including any children; credobaptists note that the word was spoken to all, and all rejoiced in believing (v. 34). Verdict: the household heard and believed, then was baptised; the text supports believer’s baptism, while not settling every question.

On a Tuesday. A real conversion changes how you treat people. Is there someone you need to make amends to?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God, he and his whole household.

A meal. Hospitality, perhaps the first Lord’s Supper in his home.

Rejoiced. Joy is a mark of salvation.

Believed in God. A Gentile who had worshipped Rome’s gods now believed in the true God.

On a Tuesday. Share a meal with new believers. It builds fellowship.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was daylight, the magistrates sent their officers to the jailer with the order: “Release those men.” The jailer told Paul, “The magistrates have ordered that you and Silas be released. Now you can leave. Go in peace.”

The police. The lictors, the rod-bearers who had beaten them.

Release them. Perhaps the magistrates thought the beating was enough, or the earthquake frightened them.

On a Tuesday. God can change the minds of rulers overnight.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul said to the officers: “They beat us publicly without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. And now do they want to get rid of us quietly? No! Let them come themselves and escort us out.”

Roman citizens. Roman law (the Valerian and Porcian laws) forbade beating a citizen, and certainly without trial. Cicero described the outrage of a citizen being flogged in public while crying out “I am a Roman citizen.”

Why not say so earlier? Perhaps he did, but was not heard in the uproar. Or he chose to suffer, then used his rights later to protect the young church.

Using legal rights. Christians may and sometimes should use their legal rights, especially to protect others. Paul did so again (22:25; 25:11).

On a Tuesday. If you or other Christians are treated unjustly, it is right to use lawful means to seek justice, especially for the sake of the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers reported this to the magistrates, and when they heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were alarmed. They came to appease them and escorted them from the prison, requesting them to leave the city.

Afraid. The magistrates could lose their office, or worse, for abusing citizens.

Apologised. A public vindication that would protect the church.

On a Tuesday. Justice protects the weak. Pray for just rulers.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house, where they met with the brothers and sisters and encouraged them. Then they left.

Lydia’s house. The first church in Europe.

The church at Philippi. A businesswoman, a freed slave girl perhaps, a Roman jailer: rich and poor, women and men. It became Paul’s most generous partner (Philippians 4:15–16), and he wrote it his warmest letter.

Encouraged them. The missionaries, beaten and bruised, comforted the believers.

Luke stays. The “we” stops here and resumes at Philippi in 20:5; Luke may have stayed behind to lead the church.

For worship. Thank God for the church at Philippi, and pray for the church in Greece today.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual Calling and the Opened Heart. Acts 16:14 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of what the Reformed tradition calls effectual calling: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” The Word is preached by Paul; the heart is opened by the Lord. Both acts are real and necessary. Without Paul’s preaching, Lydia has no content to respond to. Without the Lord’s opening of her heart, Paul’s words remain external noise. The Spirit works through the Word, but the Spirit’s work is the decisive one — the inward illumination that turns external proclamation into saving faith. This is why prayer for the lost must accompany every act of evangelism: we can preach; only God can open hearts.
16.examples:
Then: A purple-goods merchant, a slave girl, a Roman jailer — three people who could not have been more different in status, ethnicity, or circumstance — all met by one gospel in one city. The Philippian church is born from this unlikely trio, and Paul will write his most joyful letter to it from a prison cell a dozen years later.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts today. The Spirit who directed Paul away from Asia and toward Macedonia still directs his church. The closed doors are guidance; the midnight songs are witness; the simplest answer is still the truest: believe in the Lord Jesus. The gospel has not grown more complicated. We have.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Athens is the intellectual capital of the ancient world — full of philosophers, full of altars, full of the cleverest people alive and the most comprehensively wrong ideas about God. Paul’s spirit is provoked by the idolatry; he cannot stay quiet. He reasons in the synagogue, he argues in the marketplace, and then he is brought to the Areopagus — the great court of Athenian intellectual life — to explain himself.

The sermon Paul preaches is unlike any other in Acts. He does not begin with the Hebrew Scriptures — his audience does not know them. He begins where they are: the altar to the Unknown God. He finds in their own religious instinct the reaching-out for the God they do not know, and he announces that God: the Creator of all things, Lord of heaven and earth, Giver of life and breath, the one in whom they live and move and have their being — and the one who has set a day of judgment and given proof of it by raising a man from the dead.

The resurrection stops the sermon. Some mock. Some defer. Some believe. The response to the gospel in Athens is the same as in every other city — except that here the mockers are the loudest response. Athens is not a triumph. It is a faithful proclamation in hard soil, with a handful of converts, and Paul moves on to Corinth. The gospel is not always received well. It is always to be proclaimed truly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two towns, fifty miles apart, and two ways of receiving the same sermon. Luke sets them side by side on purpose, and the difference between them is not intelligence or advantage but what each did with a Bible.

Thessalonica (vv. 1–9). Paul goes to the synagogue, as his custom was, and for three Sabbaths reasons from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and that this Jesus is he (vv. 1–3). Some Jews are persuaded, along with a great many God-fearing Greeks and a number of leading women (v. 4). The response is a hired mob and a raid on the house of Jason, who had taken the missionaries in (v. 5). Failing to find them, the crowd drags Jason before the politarchs with a charge that is truer than it knows — these men who have turned the world upside down have come here also — and a second charge that is politically lethal: they say there is another king, Jesus (vv. 6–7). The magistrates, alarmed for their city's standing, take a bond from Jason and let him go (vv. 8–9), which may be why Paul was kept from returning for some years.

Berea (vv. 10–12). Sent out by night, they go straight to another synagogue — the method does not change, only the address. And here Luke gives the church one of its permanent standards. These Jews were more noble: they received the word with all eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Eagerness without testing is credulity; testing without eagerness is mere suspicion. They did both, and many believed, together with a number of Greek women of high standing and men.

And then it follows him (vv. 13–15). Men come the fifty miles from Thessalonica specifically to stir up the crowds. Paul is sent away to the coast while Silas and Timothy stay behind to hold the work — the mission does not depend on the presence of the apostle. His escort takes him all the way to Athens and goes home with a message: come as quickly as you can. Which leaves Paul, for the only extended stretch in Acts, entirely on his own in the most impressive city in the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean Standard for Scripture Engagement

The Bereans 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.' Reformed theology has always prized this as the model of how the gospel should be received: not credulity (accepting whatever the preacher says without examination) and not skepticism (dismissing the gospel without engagement), but eager reception combined with rigorous scriptural testing. The Berean standard is the Protestant hermeneutical ideal: sola Scriptura applied in the actual practice of hearing and evaluating proclamation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'These men who have turned the world upside down' — the Thessalonian accusation is the most accurate description of the gospel's social effect in Acts. Now: The gospel still turns every human order that opposes the kingdom upside down. The question for the church is not whether the gospel is socially disruptive but whether it is disrupting the right things — the powers of sin, death, and injustice — rather than merely producing comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica.

Two towns named and passed through in half a verse. They are a day's journey apart on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia, which ran from the Adriatic across to Byzantium, and the distance from Philippi to Thessalonica is about a hundred miles. Paul walked it with a back that had been opened by rods a few days earlier.

Luke does not say they preached in either place, and the reason is probably in the next clause: where there was a synagogue of the Jews. Thessalonica had one and the smaller towns evidently did not. He is not wandering; he is going to the next place with a congregation of people who already have the Scriptures.

And Paul went in, as was his custom. Read that against what had just happened to him. The last time he entered a public building in this province he came out of the city stripped and flogged. His custom did not change.

Then the detail that has caused more argument than any other in the chapter: on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures.

It is usually read as meaning Paul was in Thessalonica for three weeks, and that cannot be right, because his own letters to that church will not allow it. He tells them he worked night and day with his hands so as not to burden anyone (1 Thess. 2:9) — which takes longer than a fortnight to be worth mentioning. He reminds the Philippians that they sent him help in Thessalonica once and again (Phil. 4:16), and Philippi is a hundred miles away, so that is at least two round trips by messenger. And he describes the congregation as people who turned to God from idols (1 Thess. 1:9) — which is not a description of synagogue Jews.

The answer is in what Luke actually wrote. He says three Sabbaths in the synagogue. That is the length of the synagogue phase, not the length of the mission. When the synagogue closed to him, as it did in city after city, Paul went on working in the town among Gentiles for a good while longer, and it is those Gentiles who make up the church he writes to.

It is a small harmonisation and it is worth doing carefully, because this is exactly the sort of place where a reader is told there is a contradiction in the Bible. There is not one here. There is a summary and a letter, and they fit — once you notice which three weeks Luke is counting.

He reasoned with them. The word is dialegomai, from which we get dialogue: he argued, back and forth, taking questions. This was not a monologue delivered at people. For three Sabbaths a room full of men who knew the Scriptures put their objections to him and he answered them, out of the same book they were holding.

(On what a synagogue was, see 6:9; on how its service of Scripture-reading and teaching ran — the very platform Paul uses here, 'reasoning with them from the Scriptures' — see 13:15.) Note the deliberate pattern: Paul goes 'as was his custom' to the synagogue first in each new city, taking the gospel 'to the Jew first and also to the Greek' (Rom. 1:16) — beginning with those who already hold the Scriptures and await Israel's God, and showing them that the Christ they hoped for is Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead.

Two verbs, and both are pictures.

Explaining is dianoigo — to open up, to prise apart. Luke likes this word and keeps it for remarkable company. It is what Jesus did on the Emmaus road, when he opened to them the Scriptures and their hearts burned (Luke 24:32); it is what he did that evening when he opened their minds to understand them (Luke 24:45); and it is what the Lord did to Lydia in the last chapter, when he opened her heart to pay attention (16:14). Opening a book, opening a mind, opening a heart — and in three of the four cases the one doing the opening is the Lord himself. Paul opens the Scriptures; only God opens the person.

Proving is paratithemi, the word for setting food on a table in front of somebody. It is what the jailer did at Philippi when he set food before them (16:34). So the picture of Paul in that synagogue is a man taking the text apart and laying it out where people can reach it. He is not performing over their heads. He is serving.

Now the content, and it is the whole quarrel between the church and the synagogue in one sentence: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer.

Nothing in first-century Jewish expectation prepared anyone for that. The Messiah was the son of David who would come in power, break the oppressor and reign; a crucified Messiah was not a disappointing version of the hope, it was a contradiction of it. Paul knew precisely how that sounded, and wrote it down: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:23).

So where did he prove it from? He does not tell us here, but the trail is not hard to follow, because the risen Christ had already walked two disciples through the same argument, and asked the same question in almost the same words: Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). The texts are the ones the apostles use everywhere — the servant who was pierced for our transgressions and numbered with the transgressors, and who then shall see his offspring, he shall prolong his days (Isa. 53); the sufferer of Psalm 22, whose hands and feet are pierced and his garments divided, and whose psalm ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD; the one whose body will not see corruption (Ps. 16); the Anointed One who is cut off (Dan. 9:26); the pierced one they will look upon and mourn (Zech. 12:10).

The suffering was never an accident that theology had to be rearranged around. It was in the book the whole time, and had been read aloud in that synagogue for generations.

And saying, This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ. Notice the shape of the argument, because it is two steps and most people collapse them. First, from the Scriptures: this is what the Christ must be like. Second, from history: and here is the man who matches. Paul does not begin with Jesus and search for texts to fit him. He establishes the pattern first and then produces the person.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women.

Count the three groups, because the proportions are the story. Of the Jews, some. Of the God-fearing Greeks, a great many. Of the leading women, not a few. The synagogue produced a handful; the Gentiles attached to the synagogue came in crowds.

That imbalance is what lights the fuse. These God-fearers were the synagogue's own fruit — Gentiles it had taught, at cost, over years — and they are walking out of it behind two visitors after three weeks.

But the Jews were jealous. The same word, and the same mechanism, as at Pisidian Antioch, where it is worked out at 13:45. What is new here is the method.

Taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob. Luke's word is agoraioi — market men, the idlers who hung about the public square with nothing to do. Every ancient city had them, and they could be had cheaply by anyone who wanted a crowd assembled in a hurry. This is not a spontaneous outbreak of civic feeling. It is a demonstration that somebody put together, out of men who neither knew nor cared what the argument was about.

It is worth naming plainly, because it recurs in every century. The opposition to the gospel here did not come from the town. It was manufactured, by respectable people who would not have thrown a stone themselves, using men whose only interest was the day's pay. The noise in the street was real. The movement behind it was a handful of people with a grievance.

And attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.

Here is the sentence to sit with. They wanted Paul and Silas, and Paul and Silas were not there. So the mob went through the house of the man who had taken them in.

Jason has done nothing except offer a spare room. He is a local. When the missionaries move on — and they will move on tonight — he stays, with his door broken, his name on a charge sheet, and his money posted as a bond. Luke tells us nothing else about him, unless he is the Jason Paul later greets as a kinsman in Romans 16:21, which would mean he came through it and was still standing years later.

This is the part of the cost of the gospel that gets least attention, because the people who bear it do not write the letters. The visiting preacher is beaten and moves on. The local believer who housed him has to go on living in the town afterwards, among the neighbours who watched. If you have ever quietly paid for somebody else's ministry — in your family, your workplace, your street — Jason is in Scripture for you, and Luke thought his name was worth keeping.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also.

It is the most famous compliment ever paid to the church by its enemies, and it is usually quoted more cheerfully than Luke meant it. The verb is anastatoo, and it is not a gentle word: to unsettle, to throw into disorder, to drive out of house and home. Luke uses it once more in this book, of an Egyptian who stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins into the wilderness (21:38). The charge is not that these men are exciting. It is that they are insurgents.

And notice the geography inside the sentence: have come here also. News of Philippi and Pisidia has arrived ahead of them. Whatever this is, it is not local.

Then the accusation that could actually kill: they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.

You have to know what Thessalonica was to feel the weight of that. It was a free city — self-governing, exempt from a Roman garrison, allowed to keep its own assembly and its own magistrates, whom Luke calls by their correct and unusual local title, politarchs. That freedom was a gift from Rome and could be taken back. A city that harboured men who proclaimed a rival king would not stay free for a week.

So the charge is aimed with real skill. It is also, in the sense intended, false. Paul was not organising a revolt; he had spent three weeks in a synagogue arguing about Isaiah, and his settled instruction to Christians was to pay their taxes and honour the authorities.

And yet — and this is the thing the accusers grasped better than most modern Christians do — it was not simply untrue either. Paul really was going round the empire announcing that a man had been raised from the dead and made Lord, that every knee would bow to him, and that a day of judgment had been fixed with him as judge. He wrote to this very church, within a few months, about waiting for God's Son from heaven and about the Lord descending with a cry of command (1 Thess. 1:10; 4:16). If Caesar's men had read that letter they would have recognised their own vocabulary being used about somebody else.

The mob was wrong about the method and right about the collision. There is a rival king, and his claim is total, and no political arrangement in the world is finally neutral about him.

Which puts a question to a Christian in a comfortable country. The charge here is that the gospel had visibly rearranged something — households, loyalties, a marketplace, a synagogue — enough for the authorities to notice. It is worth asking what, in your life, the gospel has actually turned over. If the honest answer is that it has fitted in tidily beside everything else and disturbed nothing, that is not evidence that you are peaceable. It may be evidence that nothing much has arrived.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things.

Notice who is disturbed, and in what order. The crowd first, then the magistrates — agitated, thrown into confusion. Nobody in this verse is calm.

But the two groups are frightened of different things, and it is worth separating them.

The crowd has just been told there is another king. Most of them had no idea who Jesus was an hour ago; what they have now is a rumour of sedition in their own town, shouted by men who sound as if they know.

The politarchs are frightened of Rome. Thessalonica held its freedom — its own assembly, its own magistrates, no garrison — at Rome's pleasure, and a city that could not keep order was a city that would have order imposed on it. A few years later, the town clerk at Ephesus says the quiet part out loud when a riot has broken out there: we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today (19:40). These men are not weighing a theological claim. They are calculating what a report to the provincial governor would cost them.

Which explains what they do next, and it is worth having the pattern, because it repeats through the whole book and through most of history. The authorities never actually rule on the truth of the matter. Gallio will refuse to hear it (18:15). Felix will keep Paul two years and decide nothing (24:27). Festus will find no charge and send him to Rome anyway. Here the magistrates take a payment and make the problem go away.

There is a lesson in it for anyone who expects public vindication of the faith from the people in charge. Institutions are not usually in the business of deciding whether something is true. They are in the business of keeping things quiet — and a church that pins its hopes on being officially found innocent will wait a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go.

This is one of the most consequential sentences in Acts and it reads like an administrative footnote.

A security is a bond. Jason and the others put up money, and they forfeit it if the condition is broken. And the condition, in a case brought on a charge of proclaiming another king, can only have been one thing: that the trouble would not recur, which in practice meant that the men who caused it would not come back.

So Jason has bought Paul's freedom to leave with his own money, and the price is that Paul cannot return. Every visit would put Jason's property, and probably Jason, at risk.

Now read what Paul writes to this church a few months later, from Corinth, and see whether it does not fit exactly: we wanted to come to you — I, Paul, again and again — but Satan hindered us (1 Thess. 2:18). And earlier in the same paragraph, we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face (2:17).

We are not told what the hindrance was and should not pretend to certainty. But a bond lodged with the magistrates of a free city, which would cost a friend everything if Paul walked back through the gate, is the most natural candidate anyone has proposed. And if that is right, then the thing Paul calls Satan's work is a piece of ordinary municipal paperwork, and he was kept from a church he loved for years by a legal instrument nobody could appeal.

It is worth holding on to. Not every obstacle to God's work is dramatic. Some of it is a form, a rule, a signature, a condition attached in an office by men who were only trying to get home. Paul does not treat that as a lesser kind of opposition, and he does not pretend it did not hurt.

The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea.

By night — as at Damascus, when Paul was let down the wall in a basket (9:25). Then fifty miles, off the main highway, into a smaller place with no great importance.

And when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. Straight in. Not a period of recovery, not a change of tactics after two cities in a row had ended in violence. The same building, the same book, the same argument. They changed the address and nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica.

The word is eugenesteroi — better born, of finer stock. It is a class word, and Luke uses it about a synagogue in a country town fifty miles off the main road, by comparison with the synagogue of the provincial capital. He is redefining the term under everybody's nose. Nobility here has nothing to do with birth or address. It is measured by what a man does when he is handed something new that he did not ask for.

And Luke tells us exactly what they did, in two halves that have to be kept together.

They received the word with all eagerness — that is the first half, and it is not the cautious half. They were not braced against it. They wanted it, and received it gladly, before they had checked it.

Examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so — that is the second, and the verb is a legal one: to sift evidence, to conduct a judicial examination. And daily, which means this went on well past the Sabbath. Men who had a living to earn went home from a synagogue meeting, opened the scrolls, and worked through Isaiah and the Psalms to see whether a visitor had told them the truth.

Take either half on its own and you get something the Bible does not commend. Eagerness without examination is how people are swept into every enthusiasm that has ever damaged a church; a congregation that receives everything gladly will receive the next thing gladly too. Examination without eagerness is the other disease, and it is the more respectable one — the hearer who arrives armed, whose Bible is open to catch the preacher out, and who has not been moved by anything in twenty years. Luke praises the men who did both at once, which is much harder than either.

Then verse 12, and the result is worth stating because it settles an argument people still have: Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men.

Therefore. Luke puts a causal word in the sentence. The daily examination did not produce a congregation of sceptics who could never be satisfied; it produced faith, and more of it than the eager, unexamining city up the road had managed. Rigour was not the enemy of belief here. It was the road to it.

And notice the same two groups as in Thessalonica — Jews, and Greek women of standing, and men with them. The gospel is doing in Berea what it did there, without the riot.

Note well what you should take from this: the Bereans tested even the apostle Paul against Scripture, and were called 'noble' for it. No teacher, however gifted, learned, or authoritative, stands above the Bible; the Word is the final court, and every sermon and every book must be checked against it (the principle later named sola Scriptura, Scripture alone as the final rule). This is not suspicion but discernment: 'test everything; hold fast what is good' (1 Thess. 5:21; 1 John 4:1). The Berean way is to receive the Word eagerly and to search the Scriptures daily to see whether these things are so — never one without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds.

Fifty miles. On foot or by mule, over two or three days, for no purpose except to break up a meeting in a town they did not live in.

Acts has shown this once before — men who followed Paul from Antioch and Iconium to Lystra and got him stoned (14:19) — and the observation made there holds here: hatred will spend an effort that indifference never will. What is worth adding is what they actually did on arrival. They did not preach against him. Luke's two verbs are agitating and stirring up the crowds — the same trade as at Thessalonica, working on people who had no stake in the question until somebody gave them one.

And notice the target. Not the synagogue, where the argument would have to be conducted from the Scriptures and where the Bereans had been examining them daily and were not going to be hurried. The crowds. When a case cannot be won in the room where the evidence is, it gets taken outside to the people who have not seen any.

Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there.

Two things, and the second is easy to miss and is the more important.

First, immediately. The Berean Christians — converts of a few weeks — read the situation and moved Paul out before it developed. These are the people who had been carefully examining the Scriptures every day, and when the moment came they acted at once. Deliberate people are not necessarily slow people.

Second, Silas and Timothy stay. Paul is the one they are hunting, so Paul goes; the other two remain in a town that has just been stirred up against them, to hold and settle a young church.

That is the arrangement Paul used everywhere and it says something about how he understood his own importance. The work at Berea did not require him. It required somebody, and two somebodies stayed. A man who believed the mission stood or fell on his own presence could not have left, and would have been wrong.

It is worth asking, of anything you are responsible for, whether it could survive your absence — and whether you have arranged it so that it could. Paul had.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed.

The escort goes home, and Paul is left standing in Athens on his own.

That is unusual enough to be worth stopping on. Paul almost never worked alone. He had Barnabas, then Silas, then Timothy and Luke; he sent people ahead and kept people with him; his letters are full of names. This is the one extended stretch in Acts where he is by himself, and Luke marks it twice — here, and again at the start of the next paragraph, while Paul was waiting for them at Athens.

And we know how he felt about it, because he tells the Thessalonians. Writing a few months later, he says that when he could bear it no longer he sent Timothy to them, and that this meant we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone (1 Thess. 3:1). It is his own word — alone — and he uses it about the most celebrated city in the world.

Put the position together. He has been run out of Philippi with his back opened, run out of Thessalonica by night, and run out of Berea within weeks. He is in a city where he knows nobody. He has no synagogue standing yet, no lodging arranged that Luke mentions, and no colleague. He has sent a message asking for company as fast as it can be managed — as soon as possible, which is a phrase with feeling in it.

This is worth having, because there is a picture of Paul that makes him a kind of machine — indestructible, self-sufficient, always three steps ahead. Scripture will not support it. The same man who sang at midnight in a Philippian cell sends an urgent message from Athens asking his friends to hurry.

And the loneliness was not a failure of faith or a gap in his usefulness; the Areopagus address was preached out of it. Whatever you may have been told, being alone and finding it hard is not a sign that something has gone wrong in your Christian life. It is a thing that happened to the apostle Paul, in writing, and he did not apologise for minding.

One more detail. Luke says the escort brought him as far as Athens. These unnamed Bereans, converts of a few weeks, travelled several hundred miles to see him safely there and then walked home. Nobody records their names. They are in the New Testament as those who conducted Paul, and without them the next scene does not happen.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Athens was past its political prime and still the intellectual capital of the world — the city of Socrates and Plato, of the Stoics and the Epicureans, and a place so crowded with statues and shrines that visitors remarked on it. Paul arrives alone, waiting for his colleagues, and Luke says his spirit was provoked by what he saw (v. 16).

Getting a hearing (vv. 17–21). He works two rooms at once — the synagogue on the Sabbath, and the marketplace every day with whoever was there. Philosophers pick him up. Some call him a babbler, a scavenger of second-hand ideas; others think he is peddling foreign divinities, which is the very charge on which Athens had executed Socrates. So they bring him before the Areopagus, the ancient council that decided which gods and teachings the city would entertain.

The address (vv. 22–31). It is the most carefully built sermon in Acts and the fullest one preached to an audience with no Bible and no monotheism. Paul starts where they are — an altar to an unknown god — and works outward: God made the world and does not live in temples or need anything from human hands (vv. 24–25); he made every nation from one man and fixed their times and their borders so that they should seek him (vv. 26–27); he is close enough that their own poets have half-said it (v. 28). Therefore an image of gold or stone is an absurdity (v. 29). And therefore the times of ignorance are over: God commands all people everywhere to repent, because a day is fixed, a judge appointed, and the proof given by raising him from the dead (vv. 30–31).

The response (vv. 32–34). At the resurrection the room breaks into three: some mocked, some deferred, some believed. Luke names two of the converts — Dionysius, a member of the council itself, and a woman called Damaris — and mentions others with them. It is a small harvest by the standards of Thessalonica or Corinth, and Luke records it without apology or excuse.
verseByVerse.theology:
Natural Theology and Its Limits

Paul's Areopagus address is the New Testament's most extended engagement with natural theology — the knowledge of God available through creation. He acknowledges that God has not left himself without witness (14:17), that all nations are made from one blood and live in God-given boundaries (17:26), that the divine nature is reflected in creation sufficiently to leave humanity without excuse (Romans 1:20). But natural theology has limits: it can establish God's existence and general character; it cannot reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The movement from 'the God who made everything' to 'the man he has appointed' requires the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection; some said 'we will hear you again'; some believed. The three responses to the Areopagus address are the three responses to every gospel proclamation: dismissal, deferral, and faith. Now: The gospel continues to divide its hearers along these same three lines. The church's task is not to ensure the first response never comes but to preach in such a way that the third response is genuinely available to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.

The word for provoked is paroxyneto, and it is worth noticing where we last met that root. It is the noun paroxysmos that Luke used two chapters ago for the sharp disagreement that broke up Paul and Barnabas (15:39). The same capacity for strong, sharp feeling that ended a friendship is what the idols of Athens now provoke in him.

Luke does not comment on that, and it would be a mistake to make him either excuse the quarrel or condemn the zeal. But it is honest to see that this is one man's temperament — a man who felt things fiercely, and whose fierceness cost him something at Antioch and drove him into the marketplace at Athens. Our strongest characteristics do not come in two versions, one for use in church and one for private life.

Then what provoked him: the city was full of idols. Luke's word appears nowhere earlier in Greek literature and may be his own coinage — something like idol-infested, the way you would describe a house full of vermin. Ancient visitors remarked on how crowded the city was with statues and shrines.

And here is the thing to feel. Every one of those idols was a masterpiece. This was the greatest concentration of sculpture in the history of the world, on the Acropolis and in the streets below it, and any educated visitor came to admire it. Paul was an educated visitor. He walked through the finest art the human race had yet produced and what he felt was grief and anger, because he was not looking at the workmanship. He was looking at what it was for.

That is a very exposed place to stand, and it is worth being honest about it, because most of us do not feel this and are not sure we ought to. The thing that moved Paul was not the immorality of Athens or its arrogance. It was that the glory belonging to God was being handed to objects, beautifully.

Now watch what he did with the feeling, because this is the part that instructs: So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

Not despair, and not denunciation. He did not withdraw from the city and he did not stand in the street shouting at it. He went and talked to people — and note the two venues, because they are quite different rooms. In the synagogue, on the Sabbath, with people who had the Scriptures. In the marketplace, every day, with whoever happened to be about: shoppers, loafers, philosophers, slaves sent on errands.

The word is the same in both places — he reasoned, argued, took questions. He did not have one message for the religious and another for the street. He had one message and two doorways, and he used whichever was open on the day.

The provocation, in other words, was converted into conversation. That is what to do with the thing that grieves you about the place you live: not a post, not a private lament, not a decision to keep away from it. Go and talk to somebody who is in it.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him.

These were the two live schools in Athens, and it is worth knowing what each believed, because Paul's address is built to walk between them.

The Epicureans held that the gods exist but are entirely uninterested in us — serene, remote, and not to be feared. The world is atoms falling; there is no providence, no design, and death is simply the end, which is the good news of the system, because it means there is nothing waiting. The aim of life is tranquillity — pleasure understood as the absence of pain and fear.

The Stoics held nearly the opposite. The divine is a rational principle running through everything, and everything is therefore ordered; the aim of life is to align yourself with that order and accept it, cultivating virtue and enduring what comes without complaint. God is not remote; God is diffused, and in some sense is the universe.

Keep both in mind and you will see Paul's sermon doing very precise work. Against the Epicureans he will say that God made the world, fixed the times and the boundaries, is near, and has appointed a day of judgment. Against the Stoics he will say that God is personal, distinct from what he has made, and not to be identified with it. He agrees with each of them about something and disagrees with both about God.

Then the reception, and Luke preserves two reactions.

What does this babbler wish to say? The word is spermologos, a seed-picker. It began as a name for a bird hopping about pecking up scraps, passed into slang for the men who scavenged the market floor for what fell off the carts, and ended as an insult for someone who retails other people's ideas without understanding them. It is the sneer of the professional at the amateur, and it is worth noticing that this is the first thing the finest minds in the world said about the apostle to the Gentiles.

He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities. That sentence has a shadow over it that any educated Athenian would have felt at once. Introducing new divinities was the charge on which Athens had tried and executed Socrates, four and a half centuries earlier, in this city, before this council. Luke's readers know it, and he does not need to say so.

Luke then explains why they said it: because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. It is quite possible they misheard him. Jesus and Anastasis — the Greek word for resurrection — sound to a pagan ear like a pair of names, a god and his consort, which would explain the plural divinities exactly. If so, the cleverest men in Athens listened to the gospel and concluded that Paul was recommending two new gods, one of them called Resurrection.

And what was 'the Areopagus'? It is the 'Mars' Hill' of the older English Bibles. It was both a literal rocky outcrop northwest of the Acropolis and, more importantly here, the name of the venerable council that had long met there — Athens's most respected body of elders, its supreme court in matters of religion, morals, and education. By Paul's day the council likely convened down in the marketplace rather than on the hill itself, but it kept the old name. So to be 'brought to the Areopagus' was to be summoned before the cultural and intellectual gatekeepers of the most sophisticated city in the world, to give account of this 'new teaching' — not a formal trial so much as an examination by those who oversaw what ideas and gods Athens would entertain. It is the gospel getting its hearing before the philosophers, at the very summit of human wisdom — and Paul, far from being intimidated, will preach Christ and the resurrection straight into it (vv. 22–31).
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.

It is a courteous sentence and it is also a summons, and both things are true at once.

Strange is the word for foreign, alien, belonging somewhere else. They are not saying the message is offensive; they are saying it does not fit any of the shelves they own. That is an honest report. A crucified Jewish workman raised bodily from the dead and appointed judge of the world does not correspond to anything in Greek philosophy or Greek religion, and the philosophers were quite right to find it foreign.

We wish to know therefore what these things mean. Taken at face value that is exactly what a preacher wants to hear. And Paul takes it at face value — he does not complain about their motives, or demand a better attitude before he will speak. He gets the request and he preaches.

But hold it against the sentence Luke puts immediately after it, because he has arranged these two verses deliberately. They say we wish to know; and Luke's very next remark is that the Athenians spent their time on nothing except telling or hearing something new. He lets their request stand, and then quietly tells you what it was usually worth.

That is not cynicism, and it does not mean nobody in the room was serious — two of them are named, and others counted with them, as converts by the end of the chapter. It means Luke knows the difference between an appetite for the interesting and a willingness to be changed, and he expects his reader to know it too.

It is a distinction worth turning on ourselves, because we live in the most information-rich moment in history and it has made the confusion easier, not harder. It is entirely possible to consume a great deal about God — sermons, books, commentary — with genuine interest, and for the interest itself to be the thing that stands in for obedience. We wish to know therefore what these things mean can be the beginning of faith, or it can be a way of keeping a subject permanently under discussion so that it never has to be settled.

The test is simple enough and you can run it tonight. When you last understood something from Scripture that you had not understood before, what did you do about it?

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new.

Luke steps out of the narrative to tell us about a city, and it is the only aside of its kind in the book. He does it because everything that happens in the next fifteen verses depends on it.

The Greek is sharper than the English. It is not something new but something newer — a comparative. Newer than what? Than the last new thing. The appetite is not for novelty as such but for the next one, which means it can never be satisfied, only fed.

And note the verb: they spent their time in nothing else. It was a way of passing a life. Athens had been a great city and was no longer one; the politics had gone to Rome and the money had gone to Corinth, and what remained was its reputation and its conversation. A place with a magnificent past can become very good at discussing things.
