When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.

Luke's compression here is severe, and the two little direction words carry the meaning. You always go up to Jerusalem and down from it, whatever the map says, because it is the holy city. So went up and greeted the church, with no city named, means Jerusalem — several days' travel inland from the port, for a visit Luke covers in a handful of words.

And then Antioch, which is where the whole thing started. The church that fasted and prayed and laid hands on Barnabas and Saul in 13:2 gets its men back for the second time. He has now been round the Aegean, planted churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth, left Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, and written the first of his letters, and he comes home and reports to the congregation that sent him.

That is worth noticing about a man with as much authority as any Christian has ever had. He had seen the risen Christ, he had been given the gospel by revelation, and he still travelled several hundred miles at the end of every journey to stand in front of an ordinary local church and tell them what had happened.

The second missionary journey ends here. It began with a quarrel about John Mark and it ends in the same room, with the mission enormously enlarged and neither Barnabas nor Mark anywhere in sight.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third missionary journey opens in a single participle — Paul back on the roads of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (v. 23) — and then Luke turns aside from him altogether for five verses to tell us about somebody else entirely.

A gifted man with a gap (vv. 24–25). Apollos arrives at Ephesus from Alexandria: a Jew, eloquent, powerful in the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, boiling over in spirit, and teaching accurately the things concerning Jesus. Everything in that list is a commendation. And then one clause undoes none of it and changes everything — though he knew only the baptism of John. His information stopped somewhere around the Jordan. He was preaching a true message with an end missing.

Two tentmakers take him aside (v. 26). Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue and do not correct him in it. They take him home and explain the way of God more accurately — the most gifted speaker in the eastern Mediterranean instructed privately by a couple who worked with their hands, and Luke names the wife first.

And then he is sent (vv. 27–28). When he wants to cross to Achaia the brothers write ahead to commend him, and in Corinth he is a considerable force: he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, and refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. The man Priscilla and Aquila finished off in private went on to water the field Paul had planted — and to become, without wanting to, the name of a faction in Corinth that Paul had to write a letter about.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping short of the full apostolic message — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

That is the whole of the beginning of the third missionary journey. One verse. No commissioning service, no vision, no laying on of hands — before the first journey Luke gave us a whole scene in the church at Antioch, and here Paul simply leaves and starts walking.

And where does he go? Back over the same ground. Galatia and Phrygia are the towns of the first journey — Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch — the places where he was stoned and expelled, and which he had already revisited twice. This is the third time he has come back along those roads.

Nothing about that is new territory or new converts. It is maintenance, and the verb Luke chooses says so: strengthening, making firm what is already standing. He used the same word when Paul went back through those towns the first time (14:22) and when he set out on the second journey (15:41). Three journeys, and every one of them begins the same way, with an apostle propping up small congregations he has already planted.

Notice too the word all. Not the promising ones, not the strategic ones. All the disciples, in one place after another, going from one place to the next — a phrase suggesting an unhurried, methodical circuit rather than a dash through.

There is a temptation, in Christian work as in anything else, to believe that the real thing is the founding and everything afterwards is administration. Luke does not present it that way. Paul spent an enormous proportion of his life going back — and the letters, which are the reason we know anything about him, are simply this same activity conducted by post when he could not go in person.

If your own service to God consists largely of turning up again for the same people, who are not obviously further on than they were last year, you are doing the thing this verse describes, and it is what the apostle to the Gentiles did with his time.
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus.

Alexandria is worth pausing on, because it explains the man. It was the second city of the empire, the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library, and it held the largest and most cultured Jewish community outside Judea. The Old Testament had been translated into Greek there. Philo, the most celebrated Jewish thinker of the age, was writing there in Apollos's own lifetime. A Jew educated in Alexandria was educated as well as anyone then living.

And Luke piles up the commendations, five of them, before he raises any difficulty.

An eloquent man — and, it seems, a learned one.

Competent in the Scriptures — the word is dynatos, powerful. Not merely well-informed: strong in them, able to use them.

Being fervent in spirit — literally boiling. Paul uses the identical phrase when telling the Romans how a Christian ought to be (Rom. 12:11).

He spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus. Accurately. Luke is not damning him with faint praise and then correcting him; what Apollos said about Jesus was true.

So here is a man who is learned, powerful in the Bible, on fire, and doctrinally accurate — and Luke's next clause is though he knew only the baptism of John.

Hold those two things together, because the combination is the point of the whole paragraph and it is unusual in Scripture. There is nothing wrong with Apollos. He is not a false teacher, not a self-promoter, not lukewarm, not careless. He is excellent, and he is incomplete, and the two are not in tension. His problem is not his character, or his zeal, or his handling of the text. It is simply that the news had not all reached him yet.

That is a category we are not very good at. We tend to sort teachers into sound and unsound, and Apollos will not go in either box.

What does 'he knew only the baptism of John' mean? John the Baptist's baptism was a preparatory one — 'a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: 'I baptize you with water... but he who is coming after me... will baptize you with the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the 'getting ready' baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos 'knew only John's baptism,' then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point — he knew and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went — but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His faith was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart — he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre in Alexandria before the fuller news reached him.

(He is the cousin of the Ephesian 'disciples' of 19:1–7, who also knew only John's baptism — though note the difference: Apollos, already fervent in the Spirit and teaching accurately, is simply taught 'more accurately' by Priscilla and Aquila (v. 26) and is never re-baptized, whereas those men, who had not even heard the Spirit was given, are baptized into Jesus and receive the Spirit; see on 19:1–2.) And the lovely lessons here: even a brilliant, eloquent, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn — and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple (Priscilla named first). None of us has arrived; we keep growing. And the way to help someone whose understanding is incomplete is Priscilla and Aquila's way: not to attack him publicly, but to 'take him aside' and explain the way of God more accurately — gently, privately, helpfully.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

Everything about that sentence repays slow reading.

They took him aside. Not up. Not out. Aside — privately, away from the congregation he had been addressing. They heard a brilliant man preaching something short of the truth in a public meeting, and they did not stand up.

Consider the alternatives they declined. They could have corrected him from the floor, which would have been humiliating and would probably have hardened him. They could have warned people about him afterwards, which is the modern method and requires no courage at all. They could have said nothing, on the grounds that he was clearly gifted and it was not their place — two tentmakers against an Alexandrian scholar.

Instead they took him aside. Luke's word for what they did is not rebuked or refuted but explained — set it out for him — and the comparative is careful too: more accurately. Not accurately, as though he had been wrong. More accurately, because he had been right as far as he went.

That is the whole art of helping somebody whose understanding is incomplete, and there are two errors it avoids. One is the refusal to say anything, which leaves a man preaching half a gospel out of a misplaced deference. The other is public correction, which is far more satisfying and almost always makes the person defend the position he was about to abandon. If you have ever needed to say something difficult to a Christian you respect, this verse is the method: privately, personally, over a meal, beginning with what is right.

And notice who is doing it. A husband and wife, in partnership, teaching a man in their own home — and Luke names Priscilla first — as the New Testament does four times out of the six that the couple appear. In the ancient world that order is unusual enough to be deliberate, and the most natural explanation is that she took the lead in this.

It is fair to say plainly that Christians disagree about what follows from that for the question of women teaching, and that the disagreement is between people who take the whole Bible seriously. The historic reading of 1 Timothy 2:12 (see there) is the better one, that the authoritative teaching of the gathered church belongs to qualified men. What the text itself gives is a private setting, a married couple acting together, and Luke's evident approval — and any position on the wider question has to be able to hold this verse comfortably and gladly, because Luke plainly regarded what Priscilla did as one of the most useful things anybody did in this chapter.

Egalitarian Christians point to Priscilla, named first, together with Phoebe, Junia and the prophesying daughters of Philip (21:9), as evidence that women taught men in the early church. The more likely reading is that this was private instruction by a couple, who took him aside, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Tim 2:12). Women may and should explain the faith in many settings, and Priscilla is honoured for it.

Consider, finally, what it cost Apollos. He was the most gifted speaker in the room, and he sat down with two tentmakers and let them teach him. Everything he became afterwards — the power in Corinth, the letter Paul wrote urging him to go back there — runs through that evening. The gifted man's greatest asset here is not his eloquence. It is that he could be taught.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him.

A letter of commendation — the ordinary machinery by which the early church moved people around a hostile world where nobody could check anybody's credentials. A stranger arriving in a city with a letter from believers who knew him could be received at once. Paul refers to the practice repeatedly, and once, to this very church, with some feeling: are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you? (2 Cor. 3:1).

So the Ephesian church put its name behind a man who, weeks earlier, had been preaching an incomplete gospel in their synagogue. They did not send a warning ahead of him. They sent an endorsement.

When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed.

Note where the grace sits in that sentence. Not he greatly helped, by grace, but those who through grace had believed. Luke has slipped in, in a passing clause about somebody's travel arrangements, the whole doctrine of how anybody comes to faith. Their believing was through grace. It is the same thing said of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened (16:14), and of the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch (13:48).

For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.

The same work Paul had done in that city (v. 5), now done by somebody else, and done powerfully. Apollos was better at it than Paul, at least as a speaker; the Corinthians certainly thought so, and some of them said so in terms that were less than kind about Paul's own delivery (2 Cor. 10:10).

And here is the thing worth ending on, because it is a test almost nobody passes. Apollos went to Corinth — Paul's own church, planted at the cost of eighteen months and a trial — and was such a success that a faction formed round his name. Paul had to write about it: each one of you says, I follow Paul, or I follow Apollos (1 Cor. 1:12).

Watch how Paul handles a younger, more eloquent man who has become a rival brand in the church he founded. He refuses the rivalry entirely: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything (1 Cor. 3:6–7). And later, writing about the same city, he says he strongly urged Apollos to go back there (1 Cor. 16:12). He was pushing him toward the congregation that preferred him.

The chain in these five verses is worth tracing: Priscilla and Aquila, who had worked beside Paul, taught Apollos, Apollos strengthened the Corinthians. Not one link in it was jealous of the next.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is Paul’s most sustained ministry in any single city: three months in the synagogue, then two years in the hall of Tyrannus — reasoning daily, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord. Not all of Ephesus came to hear Paul; the word went out through those who heard and carried it. Two years. Daily. All of Asia. This is what sustained, patient, Word-centred ministry produces.

The power of the word in Ephesus is confirmed by two vivid episodes. The sons of Sceva attempt to use the name of Jesus as a formula — and the evil spirit recognises the difference between the name wielded by authority and the name borrowed without relationship: “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognise, but who are you?” The name of Jesus is not magic; it is the delegated authority of the living Lord, available only to those who are his. And the new believers burn their magic books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — in a public bonfire of repentance that is one of the most vivid pictures of genuine conversion in the New Testament.

Then the riot. Demetrius the silversmith has done the economic analysis: if people stop worshipping Artemis, the shrine-making trade is finished. His complaint is one of the most honest in Acts: it is not primarily about theology but about money. The Word of God is economically disruptive. When people stop giving themselves to idols, the industries built on those idols suffer. The gospel always costs someone something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ephesus is the high-water mark of Paul's working life. He had been forbidden to preach in this province at the start of the second journey (16:6) and had passed through the city in a hurry and declined an invitation to stay (18:20). Now he comes back and gives it three years, longer than he gave anywhere else, and Luke's verdict on the whole episode is one sentence: the word of the Lord kept increasing and prevailing mightily.

Twelve men and a missing ending (vv. 1–7). Paul finds disciples who have never heard there is a Holy Spirit. Their information had stopped at John the Baptist — the same gap Apollos had, and the same city. They are taught, baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus, and the Spirit comes.

Three months and two years (vv. 8–10). The synagogue for three months, then daily lectures in a rented hall — probably in the dead hours of the afternoon when the city slept — for two years, until all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord. Paul never visited most of those towns. Colossae, Laodicea and the seven churches of Revelation belong to this room.

The collision with magic (vv. 11–20). Ephesus was famous across the empire for its magic. God does extraordinary things through Paul; seven men try to use the name of Jesus as a formula and are beaten out of a house naked; and the city's own magicians burn their books in public at a cost of fifty thousand pieces of silver. The gospel does not negotiate with the magic trade — it bankrupts it.

The riot (vv. 21–41). Paul sets his face toward Jerusalem and Rome. Then Demetrius, a silversmith, calls a meeting of the guild and makes the most honest speech about opposition to the gospel in the whole New Testament: from this business we have our wealth. A city of a quarter of a million people goes into the theatre and shouts for two hours, most of them not knowing why they had come. It is ended not by an apostle but by the town clerk, on the grounds that Rome would take a dim view — and his speech clears the missionaries of any offence at law.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples.

He had promised to come back if God willed (18:21), and he has. And note the road he took — the inland country, the high road across the Anatolian plateau rather than the easy valley route, a journey of several hundred miles on foot.

What he finds when he arrives is a small puzzle, and Luke sets it up carefully.

Some disciples. That is Luke's ordinary word for Christians; he uses it dozens of times in this book. So the first impression is that Paul has walked into a group of the Ephesian church. And then his first recorded question to them turns out to be a strange one to ask of Christians.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?

Something prompted that. Luke does not say what — no doubt these men had said or failed to say something — but it is worth noticing that Paul was watching. He had been in the city a matter of days and had already registered that something was missing.

And the question itself assumes a great deal. It takes for granted that receiving the Spirit is what happens to a person who believes, and that it is the sort of thing you would know about. Paul is not asking whether they have had a further experience; he is asking whether the ordinary thing has happened.

And they said, No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.

Not we have not received him. They had not heard he existed.

That answer settles what these men are. Whatever they were, they were not people who had been converted and were waiting for something more; they were men whose information had run out before the story reached its end. Somebody had told them about repentance and a coming Messiah, and nobody had come back to tell them what happened at Pentecost.

And it is a sobering thing to find in a city with a church in it. These twelve had been in Ephesus, sincere and out of date, and the gap was found because one man asked one question. It is worth asking, of the people in your own congregation whom everybody assumes are fine, whether anybody has ever asked them anything.

This passage is the cousin of Acts 8, and is read the same several ways (see there). These men knew 'only the baptism of John' and had not even heard the Spirit was given (v. 2) — so the Reformed reading sees them not as ordinary Christians awaiting a second blessing, but as disciples still standing at the old, pre-Pentecost stage of John the Baptist, who on hearing of Jesus believe fully, are baptized into him, and receive the Spirit — their deficiency being in the gospel they had yet to hear, not a missing 'stage two' for already-complete believers. (Pentecostal brothers read it, with Acts 8, as evidence of a Spirit-baptism subsequent to conversion.) Note that Paul's question, 'did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?', naturally ties the receiving of the Spirit to believing, not to a later experience — which is how the letters speak of it (Eph. 1:13; Rom. 8:9). Said, as ever, with respect for those who differ.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, Into what then were you baptized?

Notice what Paul does with a wrong answer. He does not correct them, and he does not dismiss them. He asks a second question, and the second question is the diagnostic one: what were you baptised into?

That is worth having as a method. He is not trying to establish whether they are in or out. He is trying to find out where the gap is, and he does it by tracing the thing back to its source — what were you told, and by whom, and how far did it go? A great deal of unhelpful conversation between Christians would be avoided if the second question came before the verdict.

They said, Into John's baptism.

So now the shape of their situation is clear, and it is a strange one. These men are not pagans. They are not half-hearted. They had submitted to a baptism of repentance, turned from their sins, and were waiting for the one John had promised. By the standards of the Old Testament they were exemplary. Their problem was that they were living twenty years behind the news.

And Paul said, John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.

Look at how compact that is. Paul explains John's baptism by explaining what John said while he administered it — that it was never a destination. The whole point of the rite was to point past itself to a person who had not yet arrived. A man who stopped at John's baptism had not misunderstood John; he had simply never been told the sequel.

And then the last three words carry everything: that is, Jesus. Paul closes a twenty-year gap in a clause. The one you were told to wait for has come, and here is his name.

There is a particular kindness in this scene that is worth naming. Paul does not tell these men that their repentance was worthless or that their years of waiting were wasted. He tells them that what they had was real and unfinished. That is a rare and difficult combination to hold about anybody's spiritual history — including your own, if you look back on years of sincere religion before you understood the gospel. Those years were not a mistake. They were John's baptism, and this verse is where somebody tells you the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

Twelve men who had already been baptised are baptised again. It is the only occurrence of anything like it in the New Testament, and it needs stating plainly what it is and what it is not.

It is not a second Christian baptism. These men had never received one. What they had undergone was John's rite, which belonged to the era before the cross, and Paul has just explained that it was preparatory by John's own account of it. So this is not a re-baptism at all; it is their first, and the New Testament nowhere else has anybody baptised twice.

And notice how fast it is. On hearing this — no interval, no course of instruction, no probation. Luke's pattern all through the book is that baptism follows immediately upon believing: three thousand on the day of Pentecost, the eunuch at the roadside, Lydia and her household the same morning, the jailer in the middle of the night. There is no example in Acts of a believer waiting.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. That phrase is the whole difference between the two baptisms. John's was into a hope. This one is into a person, and into everything that belongs to him. To be baptised into someone's name in that world was to be transferred into his ownership and his protection — which is why the same men who had been standing on the far side of the Jordan waiting are now, in one act, publicly attached to a named Lord.

Does this license rebaptism today? These twelve had received only John’s baptism, before Christ’s death and resurrection and the coming of the Spirit; this was not a repeat of Christian baptism but their first. Those who believe that baptism belongs to believers may baptize someone who was baptized as an infant, since they regard that as not yet believer’s baptism; others regard any baptism in the triune name as valid. But someone baptized as a believer is not to be baptized again.

And does in the name of the Lord Jesus conflict with the Trinitarian formula of Matthew 28:19? No. Luke describes whose name and authority the person comes under, not the words spoken; the Oneness teaching that only Jesus’ name may be used reads a formula into a description.

And it is worth asking why Luke bothers to record so small an episode. Twelve obscure men in a large city, whose names we do not have and who are never mentioned again. He records it because the gospel had reached Ephesus in an incomplete form and God did not leave it there. Somebody had preached a half-message and sailed on. Apollos had done the same. And in both cases the correction came — privately, patiently, and without anybody being humiliated.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all.

This is the fourth and last time in Acts that the Spirit comes with this kind of public sign, and the four occasions repay being seen together, because the pattern in them is not what people usually take from this verse.

Jerusalem at Pentecost, Jews (ch. 2). Samaria, the half-Jews of the old northern kingdom, through Peter and John (ch. 8). Caesarea, Gentiles, in Cornelius's house (ch. 10). And now Ephesus, men left over from the old order. Each time, the Spirit falls visibly at a frontier — the first time the gospel crosses into a new group of people — and each time there is an apostle present to see it happen. After this chapter it does not occur again in Acts, and the letters never instruct any church to expect it.

That is the shape of the evidence, and it is the reason careful readers have been slow to build a doctrine of a standard second experience out of these verses. What Luke is documenting is not the normal Christian life but the joining up of a divided world: Jew, Samaritan, Gentile and John's leftover disciples, all publicly given the same Spirit, with apostolic witnesses to certify it.

It should be said, and gladly, that many godly Christians read these passages differently and expect the same experience today. The disagreement is a family one and it is not about whether the Spirit is given — every side agrees he is, and agrees that a Christian without the Spirit is a contradiction (Rom. 8:9).

Now the number, which Luke gives almost as an afterthought: about twelve men in all.

Twelve. In a city of perhaps a quarter of a million people, the church at Ephesus begins as a dozen men who had been following an out-of-date sermon. Within three years all Asia will have heard the word of the Lord, and within a decade this church will receive the letter to the Ephesians and, later still, the first of the letters to the seven churches in Revelation.

What were these tongues and prophecy, and are they for today? They marked these disciples, who had stood at the edge of the new covenant, as fully part of the church. Many Christians believe such gifts continue. The more likely reading is that tongues and prophecy belonged to the foundational age as signs of the Spirit’s coming, and ceased with it. Nothing here makes tongues the evidence of the Spirit for every believer.

And Luke says about twelve, which is the sort of thing a man writes when he is reporting rather than constructing. He did not need the number to be twelve. It simply was, roughly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly.

Three months. Set that beside the rest of the book — three Sabbaths at Thessalonica, two Sabbaths at Pisidian Antioch before the trouble started — and it is the longest run he ever had in a synagogue anywhere. Ephesus gave him a hearing for a quarter of a year.

Then it ends, and Luke describes the ending precisely: when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation.

Three stages, and they are worth separating because they are how this generally goes. First they became stubborn — the word means hardened, set, the same word used of Pharaoh's heart. Then they continued in unbelief, which is the settled state that hardening produces. And then they began speaking evil of the Way before the congregation — not private disagreement but public disparagement, aimed at the people who were still listening.

It is the third stage that moves him. Paul had put up with the first two for three months. What he will not do is go on providing a platform where the thing is being poisoned for everybody else in the room.

He withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus.

Notice that he does not leave Ephesus. In Pisidian Antioch he was expelled from the district; in Thessalonica he was smuggled out at night. Here he simply moves down the street and carries on, and he takes the converts with him — which is the first time in Acts we see a congregation formally separating from a synagogue and setting up elsewhere. The Christian assembly in Ephesus gets its own meeting-place on the day Paul moves into the hall of Tyrannus.

And the room is worth a word. A scholē was a hall where a teacher held discourses — a public lecture room, entirely secular, with no religious associations at all. Shut out of the sacred space, Paul took the gospel into the ancient equivalent of a rented conference room, open to anyone who wandered in off the street, and stayed there for two years.

What is Paul doing when he 'persuades them about the kingdom of God'? In plain terms, he is making the case for King Jesus. The 'kingdom of God' is God's kingly rule, and the great news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, now reigns and will one day return to reign in full. So to 'persuade about the kingdom' is to show people from the Scriptures who Jesus is and to urge them to bow to him as Lord — and so enter his kingdom, which a person does the moment he repents and trusts the King. (For what 'the kingdom of God' means, and why the phrase fills the Gospels but is rarer in the letters, see on 8:12; for the 'already, but not yet' of it — we are brought into it now, yet await its full coming — see on 14:22.)

And notice how he does it: 'reasoning and persuading.' He did not merely announce; he argued (the word means to discuss, to dialogue) and sought to convince, patiently, from the Scriptures, for three whole months. The faith is reasonable and invites the mind; commending Christ can mean kindly, patiently making the case and answering objections over time, not just a single quick pitch. You need not be a clever debater — but you can take heart that to 'persuade about the kingdom' is, at bottom, simply to help people see and trust the King.
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.

Take the second half of that sentence seriously, because it is an extraordinary claim and Luke makes it flatly.

Asia was a Roman province of some five hundred cities and towns, running down the western seaboard of what is now Turkey and inland for a hundred miles. And Luke says that in two years all its residents heard the word of the Lord.

Paul did not travel to them. That is the thing to grasp. So far as Acts records, he stayed in Ephesus the whole time, in one room, teaching daily. He never went to Colossae — he tells the Colossians they have not seen his face (Col. 2:1). He almost certainly never went to Laodicea or Hierapolis. Of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, he is only recorded as visiting one.

So how did the province hear? Because Ephesus was the funnel. It was the greatest port on that coast and the terminus of the road system from the interior; everybody in western Asia came through it — traders, pilgrims to the temple, officials, students, people selling goods. They came, some of them wandered into a lecture hall in the dead of the afternoon, and they went home.

Epaphras is the visible example. Paul tells the Colossians that they learned the gospel from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant (Col. 1:7) — a man of Colossae who evidently heard it in Ephesus and carried it a hundred miles inland to his own town, where a church was founded that Paul never saw.

That is the strategy, and it is worth naming because it is not the one we would expect from Paul. The most travelled man in the New Testament reached an entire province by staying still and teaching the same material every day for two years to whoever happened to be in the room.

And it is a considerable comfort for anybody whose service to God is fixed in one place. You do not know who is in the room, or where they are going afterwards. The letters to Colossae and Laodicea, and several of the churches Christ addresses by name in Revelation, trace back to a rented hall and a man who did not travel.

A little more on this 'hall of Tyrannus.' The word is scholē — our 'school' — a lecture hall where a teacher or rhetorician would hold his discourses and discussions. 'Tyrannus' (the name means 'ruler' or 'tyrant') was either the owner of the building or the lecturer who normally taught there; we know nothing more of him, save that his hall outlived his name by housing the gospel. As some early manuscripts add, Paul used it 'from the fifth hour to the tenth' — roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, the afternoon siesta when the hall stood empty and most people rested. Picture it: Paul at his tent-making bench in the cool early hours (20:34), then teaching through the sweltering midday while the city slept, and his hearers giving up their own rest to come and learn — labour and sacrifice on both sides. And note the move: shut out of the synagogue (sacred space), Paul carried the gospel straight into a public lecture hall (secular space), the open marketplace of ideas, where any Jew or Greek could wander in. The encouragement is plain: the gospel needs no grand temple. A rented room, used in the leftover hours of the day, by a man who also worked a trade, became the hub from which 'all Asia' — Colossae, Laodicea, the cities of Revelation — heard the word of the Lord. Ordinary, borrowed, off-peak means, and a whole province reached.
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul.

Luke's phrase is odd enough to be deliberate — literally, God was doing miracles not of the ordinary kind. Coming from the man who has already recorded the lame walking, the dead raised and prison doors opened, that is quite a qualification. He is telling us that even by the standards of this book, what happened at Ephesus was unusual.

So that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.

The two items are very probably workman's cloths: the sweat-rag a labourer tied round his head, and the apron a craftsman wore at the bench. These are not priestly vestments or relics. They are the working clothes of a man who made tents in that city for two years, taken away from his bench while he was using them.

Now, this passage has been put to a great deal of use it will not bear, and it is worth being exact about what Luke does and does not say.

He does not say Paul distributed them, or blessed them, or charged for them, or recommended the practice. He does not say a word about how it worked. The grammar puts God as the subject — God was doing these things — and the cloths in a purely passive role. Somebody in Ephesus took Paul's sweat-rag to a sick relative, and God, who was not obliged to do anything of the kind, healed them.

And the setting explains why God stooped to it. Ephesus was the centre of the magical arts in the empire; the city's name was literally attached to the trade, and written charms were known across the Mediterranean as Ephesian letters. This was a population that believed absolutely in power conveyed through objects — amulets, scraps of parchment, knotted cords, things you carried. God met that city where its convictions were, and then spent the next eight verses demonstrating the difference between his power and magic: the sons of Sceva try to work the name of Jesus as a formula and are thrown out of a house naked, and the magicians burn their books.

Should we expect miracles like these today? Luke calls them extraordinary, and they confirmed Paul as an apostle (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:3–4). God is still free to heal in answer to prayer, but Scripture gives no promise that such miracles will accompany ministry today, and nothing here supports selling healing cloths.

So the cloths are not a technique, and it should be said plainly that selling prayer cloths, anointed handkerchiefs and the rest to sick and desperate people is precisely the trade this chapter destroys. The Ephesians who understood this passage correctly did not start a business in it. They lit a bonfire.
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.

Listen to the formula, because the whole disaster is contained in it. Not by Jesus. By the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.

They cannot name him on their own account. They have to route the name through somebody else's relationship with him, the way you might quote an authority you have never met — the Jesus that man talks about, the one who seems to work for him. It is second-hand, and they say so in the act of trying it.

And that is the exact position of a great many religious people, then and now. They have watched Christianity function in somebody's life — a parent, a spouse, a friend whose faith is obviously real — and they would like the results. What they are reaching for is not Christ but the effect he evidently has on other people. The formula in this verse is the most honest confession of that ever recorded, and these men did not know they were making it.

Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.

Two details, and both are strange. No Jewish high priest called Sceva appears in any record we have, and the name is Latin. One explanation is that the man was claiming a title he did not hold, because a high-priestly pedigree was the best possible credential in the exorcism trade — the family that had access to the divine name. If so, then the fraud runs all the way down: a bogus priest's sons using a borrowed name they had no share in.

And there were seven of them. This was a family firm.

A word on these 'Jewish exorcists.' Exorcists were people who tried to drive evil spirits out of the afflicted — and in the ancient world it was a common, and often paid, trade, a kind of spiritual technician or magician-for-hire. They worked by technique: incantations and spells, secret formulas, herbs and charms, and above all the reciting of powerful names believed to compel the spirits to obey. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, precisely because they could invoke the name of the one true God and the sacred names of Scripture, which were thought to carry unusual power over the dark world (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). The point to grasp is that it was all about harnessing power by the right words, not about knowing God — they treated a holy name as a magic word.

That is exactly their fatal mistake here. Seeing Paul cast out demons in Jesus' name, the sons of Sceva simply added 'the Jesus whom Paul proclaims' to their list of power-words, as one more spell to try — and it ended in disaster (vv. 15–16), the evil spirit answering, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' before the man fell on them and beat them. The lesson is sharp and freeing: the name of Jesus is not a magic formula anyone can wield. It carries authority only on the lips of those who truly belong to him by faith. Real power over the powers of darkness is not a technique to be mastered but a gift that flows from being united to Christ — you cannot borrow Jesus' authority while keeping Jesus himself at arm's length.
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the evil spirit answered them, Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?

It is one of the most chilling sentences in the New Testament, and in Greek it uses two different verbs. The first is the word for knowing a person — Jesus I know. The second is the word for recognising, being acquainted with, having someone on file — Paul I recognize. And then the third clause has no verb of knowing at all: but who are you?

So there are three tiers in the demon's answer. There is the Lord, whom hell knows exactly. There is his servant, who is known in that world because he has been doing damage in it for two years — Paul had a reputation on the other side. And there are these seven men, who are nobody.

Sit with the middle tier for a moment, because it is a startling thing to be told. Paul was known in hell. His name had come up. Whatever we make of that, it puts a question to anyone who has ever wondered whether a quiet Christian life registers anywhere: this passage assumes that the powers of darkness keep track of people who are actually doing something.

And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

Luke piles up the verbs — leaped, mastered, overpowered — and the detail is almost comic in its humiliation. Seven men, professional exorcists, and one possessed man puts the lot of them into the street with their clothes torn off.

And this is the only exorcism in Acts that fails, which is why Luke records it. He has shown the name of Jesus casting out spirits repeatedly. Here he shows what happens when the same words are used by men who do not belong to the person they name.

The lesson is not that the demonic is dangerous to meddle with, true though that is. It is that Christianity is not a technology. There is no formula, no words that work, no transferable method — and this is a mercy, because a faith that worked by technique would be available to the manipulative and the cruel. The authority of Jesus is inseparable from Jesus, and cannot be detached and used by somebody who has not submitted to him.

But Jesus told his disciples not to stop a man casting out demons in his name (Mark 9:38–40), and warned of some who cast out demons in his name yet never knew him (Matt 7:22–23). The sons of Sceva were different: they used Jesus’ name as a borrowed spell, by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims, with no faith of their own, and the demon knew it.

Which means the question in this verse is one worth letting land: if the powers of darkness were asked about you, would the answer be I recognise him, or who are you?

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled.

Consider what actually got the city's attention. Not the extraordinary miracles of verse 11 — Ephesus was full of wonder-workers and one more would have been absorbed. What went round the city was a story about the name of Jesus refusing to work for people who had no right to it.

That is the opposite of what we would have arranged. A humiliating public failure involving the name of Christ turned out to be the most effective evangelism in the chapter, because it told a city of magicians something they could not have learned from a success: this name is not a commodity.

And note the two things that followed, in Luke's order.

Fear fell upon them all. Not admiration. Fear — the recognition that they were dealing with something real and not manageable. Ephesus had spent centuries trying to handle the invisible world by technique, and had just discovered a power that could not be handled at all.

And the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Made great. The name that had just been misused was, by the misuse, magnified.

Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices.

Now the sting, and it is aimed at the church rather than the city. These are believers — people already converted, already baptised, sitting in Paul's lecture hall — and they had been keeping something. Divulging — disclosing what was hidden; in the magical trade the spells were secret by definition, and their power was thought to depend on the secrecy.

So there were Christians in Ephesus who had been holding on to their charms. Not out of rebellion, most likely, but out of the ordinary human instinct to keep one door open — to trust Christ and also to keep the amulet, in case.

It took a violent incident in somebody else's house to bring it out.

Which is worth taking personally, because the modern version is not amulets. It is the habit you have never mentioned to anybody, the arrangement you have not brought into the light, the thing you would not want read out. These people had been genuinely converted and were genuinely holding something back, and the two states coexisted for a while without anyone noticing. Luke's word for the cure is not repented. It is divulged — they said it out loud, to somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all.

Every word of that is costly.

Their books. These were not printed volumes but rolls of spells, charms and formulae, laboriously copied by hand — the working capital of the trade and, in Ephesus, the most valuable religious property in the empire. Written charms from that city were famous enough across the Mediterranean to be known simply as Ephesian letters. A magician's scrolls were his livelihood, his reputation, and his protection.

Brought them together. They fetched them. Nobody raided the houses; the owners went home and came back carrying them.

And burned them in the sight of all. Publicly, where the city could watch, which is the one method that leaves no way back. A man who quietly disposes of something can quietly replace it. A man who burns it in the square in front of his neighbours has ended a career.

And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver.

Somebody added it up. That is a very human detail, and it is Luke at his most reportorial: while the fire was burning, people were working out what it was worth. A silver drachma was roughly a day's wage for a labourer, so fifty thousand of them is something in the order of a hundred and thirty years of a working man's income, going up in smoke in an afternoon.

Now the thing worth noticing, because it is the point. They could have sold them. There was a ready market — every one of those scrolls had a buyer somewhere in Asia, and the proceeds could have gone to the poor, or to the church, or to Paul's support. It would have been the responsible course, and somebody in the crowd almost certainly said so.

They burned them instead, because selling them would have meant putting back into circulation the exact thing they had been delivered from. Repentance that is careful to recoup its losses has not quite finished. There is a kind of obedience that costs you nothing because you found a way to make the disposal profitable, and there is the kind in this verse.

And then Luke's verdict, laid immediately alongside the bonfire: So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. The so is doing real work. The word prevailed in Ephesus at the point where Christians destroyed their own property in public.

Two small phrases worth a word. 'The word of the Lord' is Luke's regular name for the gospel message — the Christian message about and from the Lord Jesus, his own word carrying his own authority (much like 'the word of Christ,' explained at Col. 3:16). It is, in short, the gospel as God's living, authoritative word.

'Increased' does not mean the gospel grew larger in content, but that it spread, multiplied, and triumphed — more and more people heard and believed, and the message gained ground and overcame opposition ('prevailed mightily' — here, over the magic arts whose books had just gone up in smoke). But why does Luke put it so oddly, making the word itself the thing that grows, rather than simply saying 'more people believed'? On purpose — it is one of his favourite ways of speaking (6:7, 'the word of God continued to increase'; 12:24, 'the word of God increased and multiplied'; 13:49). Two reasons. First, he is deliberately picturing the gospel as a living seed: the very word for 'increase' (auxanō, 'grow') is the language of living, fruitful things, the word of Jesus' parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29; the seed is the word, Luke 8:11). The gospel is planted in the world and grows like wheat, and believers are its fruit.

Should Christians do the same today? Items that are themselves tools of the occult, divination or idolatry should be destroyed, not sold or passed on, since that would put them into other hands. The point is a clean break, at cost, with what once ruled us.

Second, and more pointedly, by making the word the actor Luke takes the credit off the preachers and puts it on God: it is not Paul's cleverness or the church's strategy that conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God's own power (Rom. 1:16; Isa. 55:11, 'my word... shall not return empty'). So the 'strange' phrasing is really a confession of faith: watch the word, not the men — and take heart, for that same living word is still growing and prevailing in the world today.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, After I have been there, I must also see Rome.

This is the hinge of the second half of the book, and everything from here to the last verse of Acts is the working out of the sentence.

Look at the route: Macedonia, Achaia, Jerusalem, Rome. Now look at what actually happens. He goes through Macedonia and Achaia (ch. 20). He reaches Jerusalem and is arrested in the temple (ch. 21). And he gets to Rome — years later, after hearings before governors and a king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a snakebite, in chains at the empire's expense (ch. 28).

Every stage of that plan is fulfilled and not one of them in the manner he intended. He meant to visit Rome; he arrived as a prisoner. It is worth holding those two facts together whenever this verse is read as a model of Spirit-led planning, because the plan was right, and God kept it, and the keeping of it cost Paul his liberty.

And the little word must — I must also see Rome — is Luke's word for divine necessity, the same one that stood over the cross. It is not ambition. Paul had wanted to see Rome for years and says so to the Romans themselves (Rom. 1:11–13; 15:23–24), but what he expresses here is obligation, not preference. And the Lord confirms it in as many words four chapters later, standing beside him the night after the riot in Jerusalem: as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome (23:11).

And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.

Two things in that. The first is the method, which by now is settled: he sends people ahead. Timothy has been doing this for years. Erastus appears here for the only time in Acts, and may be the man Paul calls the city treasurer of Corinth in the letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:23) — a paving stone found at Corinth records an Erastus who laid it at his own expense in return for the office of aedile. A senior municipal official is being used as a messenger boy.

The second is the last clause: he himself stayed in Asia for a while. Having decided to go, he did not go. He stayed on and finished. The riot in the next paragraph happens to a man who had already made up his mind to leave and had not yet left, which is exactly the moment at which most of us are least useful and most inclined to coast.

('Resolved in the Spirit' is slightly ambiguous — 'in his own spirit' (he made up his mind) or 'in the Holy Spirit' (under the Spirit's leading). Given how the Spirit steers Paul throughout, and that the Lord later confirms this very plan — 'you must testify also in Rome,' 23:11 — the Spirit-guided sense fits well.)

But the practical question: how may a believer know his decisions are Spirit-guided today? First, let the anxiety down. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering because of their unique founding role (see on 8:26); God's ordinary way is quieter, and he has not promised you a voice in your head for every choice. So how does the Spirit lead? Chiefly through the Word. Spirit and Scripture always go together: he guides by lighting up the Bible he inspired ('a lamp to my feet,' Ps. 119:105; 'equipped for every good work,' 2 Tim. 3:16–17). Most of God's will is already plainly revealed — be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, serve — so the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life. Then through a renewed mind and sanctified wisdom. For what Scripture does not directly settle (which job, where to live), the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but maturing it: 'be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God' (Rom. 12:2); and 'if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously' (James 1:5). Add prayer (Prov. 3:5–6), godly counsel (Prov. 15:22), and the providence of opened and closed doors. Inner promptings and a sense of 'peace' may play a part (Phil. 2:13), but never trusted alone; they must be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jer. 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

And the most freeing thing of all: the clearest mark of being 'led by the Spirit' is not a feeling about one decision but the shape of a life. 'For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God' (Rom. 8:14) — led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God's children; and 'the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience...' (Gal. 5:22–23). So a choice made in love, humility, holiness, and faith, by a person walking closely with God, is a Spirit-led choice, even if no special feeling attends it; while one driven by pride, lust, greed, or self-will is not, however 'peaceful' it feels. So your checklist is simple: Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed for wisdom and sought counsel? Is my heart surrendered, ready to do even the hard thing? Does it flow from love and holiness, or from the flesh? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome — he is sovereign over your steps ('the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps,' Prov. 16:9), big enough to guide a surrendered, Word-shaped heart, and kind enough to redeem even our wrong turns (Rom. 8:28). A Christian walking with God need not fear 'missing God's will'; the pressure is off, for the Guide is faithful.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way.

Luke's understatement is dry and deliberate — no little disturbance means a riot that filled a theatre with twenty-five thousand people. He uses the same trick about the silversmith's income two lines later: Demetrius brought no little business to the craftsmen.

Putting the same phrase on both is not an accident. The size of the disturbance and the size of the profits are being measured against each other, and Luke expects you to notice which caused which.

For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.

Here is the mechanism. Ephesus lived on its temple. Pilgrims came from across the empire to one of the seven wonders of the world, and — exactly as at any shrine since — they bought something to take home. Silver models of the goddess in her niche were the premium souvenir, and Demetrius made them.

So the man who starts the riot is not a priest, not a philosopher, not a theologian. He is a manufacturer with a warehouse, and the thing that has gone wrong is his order book.

And notice how honest Luke is willing to let him be. In the next verse Demetrius will say the quiet part aloud to his own guild — from this business we have our wealth — and only afterwards reach for the goddess. Luke could have written this as a clash of religions. He writes it as a trade dispute with a religious vocabulary, which is what it was.

'The Way' — here is one of the earliest names the Christian movement went by (Luke uses it repeatedly: 9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Why 'the Way'? Three roots run together. First and deepest, Jesus said, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me' (John 14:6) — so to follow the Way is to follow him, the one road home to God. Second, it echoes the Old Testament, where the life of faith is pictured as a road one walks: 'the way of the LORD,' 'the Way of Holiness' (Isa. 35:8; 40:3). Third, it captures that Christianity is not merely a creed to hold but a way of life to walk — a whole road travelled after Jesus (recall 'as you received Christ... so walk in him,' Col. 2:6). It is a humble, vivid name: the faith is a path you travel with the Lord who is himself the Way, not just a box you tick.

And 'Artemis' (the Romans' Diana) was the great goddess of Ephesus — not quite the classical Greek huntress, but a distinctive local mother- and fertility-goddess, patroness and protectress of the city. Her temple at Ephesus, the Artemision, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — vast, magnificent, and the heart of a huge pilgrimage and tourist economy. Demetrius and his guild made and sold silver models of the shrine, devotional souvenirs for the pilgrims, a very lucrative trade. So the gospel here collides with a formidable triple alliance — a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess's 'temple-keeper,' 19:35), and big money. When people turned from idols to Christ, the idol-souvenir business suffered, and that — not theology — is what lit the riot (19:27). The gospel had already burned the magic books (19:19); now it threatens the idol trade. Wherever Christ truly advances, the kingdoms of money and idolatry feel the tremor.
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth.

He called a meeting. Not of priests, not of the temple authorities, but of the guild — his own silversmiths plus the workmen in similar trades, which is a wider net: the men who supplied the silver, the ones who made the cases, the shops that sold them. Demetrius has understood that his grievance is an industry's grievance and has organised accordingly.

And then he opens with the sentence that makes this the most candid speech about opposition to the gospel anywhere in Scripture.

Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth.

No preamble about the goddess. No theology. The very first thing out of his mouth, to a room of men he can be honest with, is the money — and the reason he can say it is that he is talking to shareholders rather than to the public. He will produce Artemis in a moment, when he needs a crowd.

Watch the order carefully, because it is the anatomy of a great deal of resistance to Christ. First, in private, the interest: our wealth. Then, in public, the principle: the honour of the goddess and the dignity of our city. The interest is the engine and the principle is the paintwork, and Luke has arranged the speech so that we hear the private version first.

It would be comfortable to leave that with first-century idol manufacturers. It should not be left there. The mechanism is entirely ordinary and it operates in people who are not conscious of it: when the gospel threatens something we are getting — an income, a position, a habit, a relationship on terms we like — the objection that forms in us almost never presents itself as this would cost me. It presents itself as a reasonable difficulty with the Christian faith.

So there is a question worth putting to your own objections, and to those of people you are talking to, gently and mostly in silence: what would this person have to give up if it were true? It is not a way of dismissing anybody's argument, because an argument has to be answered on its merits whoever makes it. But Demetrius is in Scripture to tell us that the stated reason and the real reason are often two different things, and that the man himself may not have noticed.

Notice too that he is not lying about anything. Everything Demetrius says in this speech is factually true, including the parts about Paul. He is simply choosing which true thing to say to which audience.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people.

This is a hostile witness, which makes it the best evidence in the chapter. Demetrius has no interest in flattering the mission and every interest in exaggerating the threat — but he is speaking to men who can check him, about a market they all trade in, and what he reports is that the effect is measurable across the province.

Set it beside Luke's own claim in verse 10, that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord. That could be read as an evangelist's enthusiasm. Here is the same claim from the accounts department of the idol trade, and it agrees.

Saying that gods made with hands are not gods.

That is Paul's preaching summarised by an opponent, and it is accurate. It is also, word for word, the argument of the Hebrew prophets — Isaiah's magnificent mockery of the man who cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half (Isa. 44:14–20), and Jeremiah's scarecrow in a cucumber field (Jer. 10:5).
