And the irony is that Demetrius is the one man in Ephesus who cannot honestly disagree, because he makes them. He knows exactly what a silver shrine of Artemis is, having watched one being hammered out that morning.

And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.

Now the escalation, and it is a masterpiece of its kind. He begins with the trade — which is what he actually cares about — and lets it occupy one clause. Then he moves to the temple, then to the goddess herself, then to her standing before Asia and the world, and by the end of the sentence a fall in souvenir sales has become a threat to the cosmic order.

It is how such speeches are always built. The personal loss goes first and briefly, so that it can be said honestly and then left behind, and everything after it is about something nobody could be accused of self-interest for defending.

But notice what he has accidentally said about the gospel, because it is truer than he knows. His fear is that Artemis will be counted as nothing. That is precisely what the gospel does to an idol — not attack it, not disprove it, but reduce it to what it always was. Paul's own letter to this city puts it in the language of a demolished currency: the Ephesians had once been having no hope and without God in the world (Eph. 2:12), and the temple whose greatness Demetrius is defending was burned, rebuilt, plundered and finally lost so completely that its site had to be dug out of a marsh in the nineteenth century.

She was counted as nothing. It took rather longer than a riot.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!

A guild meeting about profits ends with religious chanting, and the transition takes no time at all. Demetrius has done his work: the men who came in worried about their order books go out shouting for their goddess, and the two things have fused so completely that nobody in the room could now separate them.

That fusion is the most dangerous thing in the chapter, and it is not confined to Ephesus. It is entirely possible to defend an interest with real religious passion and be quite sincere in the passion. The feeling is not manufactured; these men were genuinely enraged. But it had been aroused by a threat to something else, and it is the sincerity that makes it so hard to see.

So the city was filled with the confusion.

The word is one Luke likes for civic disorder — the noise, the running, the rumour outrunning the fact. It has spread beyond the guild in minutes.

And they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.

The theatre at Ephesus is still there, cut into the side of Mount Pion and looking down the marble street to the harbour, and it seated somewhere around twenty-five thousand people. That is where a mob went when it wanted to be a public meeting.

And they could not find Paul, so they took two of his colleagues instead.

Gaius and Aristarchus are named, and it is worth stopping on them, because they are the men in this story who paid. Aristarchus turns up again and again afterwards: he is with Paul on the journey to Jerusalem (20:4), he is on the ship to Rome (27:2), and he is in prison with Paul at the end, called my fellow prisoner (Col. 4:10; cf. Philem. 24). He met the apostle, was dragged into a theatre by a mob within a few years, and stayed with him to the chains.

Nobody in Ephesus was shouting about Gaius and Aristarchus. They were seized because they were near Paul, which is the ordinary experience of everyone who works closely with a person in the front line — the family, the colleagues, the host who lent the house. Jason had it in Thessalonica. These two have it here.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him.

Of course he wished to. Twenty-five thousand people in one place, most of them listening to nothing in particular, and his two friends on the floor of the theatre — it is the largest audience he would ever have had, and he wanted to go and preach to it.

And the Ephesian Christians physically stopped him. Luke's verb is plain: they would not let him. Somebody stood in a doorway and refused to move.

That is worth having, because Paul is the apostle, and these are converts of two or three years. They overruled him, and Luke records it without a hint that they were wrong. There is a kind of courage that needs restraining, and a man who cannot be restrained by the people around him is not brave but unaccountable. Paul submitted.

And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.

Now this is one of the more surprising sentences in Acts, and Luke drops it in as though it needed no explanation.

The Asiarchs were the leading men of the province — wealthy aristocrats elected to preside over the provincial council and the games, and closely associated with the imperial cult, the worship of Rome and the emperor. They were, in other words, the official religious establishment of the province.

And Luke says they were Paul's friends.

He does not say they were converted; there is no suggestion of that. But some of the most powerful men in Asia — men whose public duties included the promotion of a religion Paul preached against — had come to know a Jewish tentmaker well enough to send urgent private messages when they judged his life to be in danger.

Two years of daily teaching in a public lecture hall will do that. He had not been shouting at the city from a distance; he had been in a lecture hall, daily, available to anyone who walked in, and some of the men who walked in were the men who ran the province.

It is worth noticing what that means about the way he had conducted himself. He had preached that gods made with hands are not gods, in the city of Artemis, for two years, hard enough to bankrupt an industry. And the officers of the rival religion liked him enough to try to save his life. Those two things are meant to be held together, and most of us manage only one of them.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.

Luke was not in that theatre — he is not in the narrative at this point — so somebody told him this afterwards, and what they remembered was the noise and the bewilderment. It is the observation of a man who had been in the crowd and had turned round and asked his neighbour what was going on.

Notice the word Luke uses for the gathering: ekklesia. It is the ordinary Greek term for a citizens' assembly, and the town clerk uses it in its technical sense in verse 39 — the regular assembly, the lawful one. It is also the word the New Testament uses everywhere for the church.

So Luke has an ekklesia in this chapter which is a mob: gathered by a grievance, chanting a slogan, most of its members unable to say why they are present. He does not comment. He has spent the book describing another kind of assembly in the same city — a dozen men, then a lecture hall, then a province — and here is what the word means when the world uses it.

Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward.

The Jewish community pushes a spokesman to the front, and the reason is not hard to guess. Ephesus was rioting against people who said that gods made with hands are not gods, and that had been the Jewish position in that city for generations. They were in real danger of being lynched for somebody else's preaching, and Alexander was sent out to say so.

There is something bleak in it. The synagogue that had thrown Paul out two years earlier now finds that the city cannot tell the difference between them, and has to stand up in front of twenty-five thousand people to explain that it is not with him.

And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.

He got as far as the gesture. Luke gives him the orator's raised hand — the same movement he records of Paul at Pisidian Antioch and on the barracks steps — and then the next verse says what happened to the speech.

'Most of them did not know why they had come together' — it is indeed a touch of sad comedy, and Luke surely means us to feel the irony: a whole city roaring itself hoarse for two hours (v. 34) over a god, and most of the rioters cannot even say why they are there. But Scripture has a sober teaching that this little scene puts on display. The Bible takes a dim and realistic view of the mob: 'You shall not fall in with the many to do evil' (Exod. 23:2); crowds are fickle and passion-driven, the same Jerusalem voices crying 'Hosanna!' one week and 'Crucify him!' the next (Matt. 21:9; 27:22). And deeper still, this is what idolatry does to a mind. When men exchange the true God for idols, Paul says, 'they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools' (Rom. 1:21–22; Eph. 4:17–18). The psalmist is even more pointed: those who make idols 'become like them' — as deaf, blind, and senseless as the mute images they worship (Ps. 115:8). A senseless god makes for senseless worshippers; the confused babble of the Ephesian theatre is simply idolatry's darkened mind made audible.

Set against it is the gospel, for 'God is not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33). The riot is a little Babel — the proud city's voices dissolving into noise, as at the tower where God confused the tongues of the self-exalting (Gen. 11:7–9) — while the gospel is the Babel-reversing word that brings light, sanity, and order (think of Pentecost, Acts 2, undoing the confusion of tongues). It is the Word that gives a man back his right mind, as the delivered demoniac sat 'clothed and in his right mind' (Mark 5:15). For you it is a mirror held up to the world: so much of its frenzy — the crowds roaring for causes, fashions, and outrages — is people swept along without truly knowing why, defending empty things. The Scripture's counsel is plain: do not be carried by the herd, but let the truth of God steady and clear your mind (Rom. 12:2). The gospel does not merely save the soul; it brings the muddled head home to sanity and peace.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!

He never said a word. The crowd worked out what he was and shouted him down before he could begin, and then went on shouting.

For about two hours. Luke, or whoever told him, was keeping track of the time, which is exactly what you do when you are stuck somewhere and nothing is happening. Twenty-five thousand people chanting five words for two hours, in the open air, in a stone bowl built to carry sound.

And with one voice — the one thing in the day that was unanimous. Verse 32 said most of them did not know why they had come. They did not need to know. A slogan does not require you to have a reason; it requires you to have a side, and it will supply the feeling of certainty at no cost.

That is what a chant is for, and it is worth recognising because the modern forms are everywhere and they are not confined to the irreligious. Two hours of Great is Artemis settles nothing, proves nothing, and answers nobody — Demetrius's complaint is not addressed, Paul's argument is not refuted, Alexander is not heard. But for two hours the theatre was full of people who felt entirely sure.

And notice what the slogan actually asserts: not that Artemis is true, but that she is ours. Great is Artemis of the Ephesians — the possessive is the whole force of it. This is civic pride wearing a goddess. Take away the temple and Ephesus is just another port; the greatness being defended in that theatre is the city's, and the goddess is the flag it is carried under.

Which is why the noise proves the opposite of what it intends. Nobody chants for two hours about something that is not in doubt. The volume in that theatre is the sound of a religion that has begun to feel the ground move — and it had. Within a couple of centuries the temple was a ruin, and the letter written to the Christians of this city is still read every week somewhere in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd...

One man walks out in front of twenty-five thousand people who have been chanting for two hours, and quiets them.

The town clerk was not a minor official. In a Greek city of that period he was the senior executive officer — the man who drafted the decrees, ran the assembly, and above all was answerable to the Roman authorities for the conduct of the city. His name went on the correspondence. If Ephesus got into trouble with Rome, he was the one who would have to explain it.

Which is why he is the one person in the theatre with a strong personal reason to end this, and it shows in every line of what he says.

Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky?

He begins by agreeing with them, and this is the shrewdest thing in the speech. He does not tell an inflamed crowd that it is wrong. He tells them that they are so obviously right that the shouting is unnecessary.

Temple keeper — neokoros — was an official title Ephesus held and put on its coins, and he uses it deliberately: your status is not in question, it is on the currency in your pocket.

Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.

And there is the turn. If your position is unassailable, then this behaviour is beneath it. Panic is an admission; a city that is certain of its goddess does not need to roar for two hours in a theatre.

It is worth noticing that Luke, who is a Christian writing for Christians, reports this speech at length and with evident approval, although its argument is entirely pagan — Artemis is great, her stone fell from heaven, calm down. He is not endorsing the theology. He is showing his readers that the riot was ended by an ordinary civic official doing his job properly, and that the church in Ephesus was preserved that afternoon by nothing more spiritual than a competent bureaucrat who did not want trouble.

'The sacred stone that fell from the sky' — one Greek word, diopetes, 'fallen from Zeus/heaven.' It was probably a meteorite. In the ancient world, before anyone understood such things, a stone that fell flaming out of the sky seemed an obvious gift from the gods — heaven-sent, holy, undeniable proof of the deity; several pagan cults treasured such 'fallen-from-heaven' stones. The Ephesians believed their goddess (or her very image) was bound up with one, and the town clerk waves it as his clinching argument: everyone knows Artemis is real and we are her guardians, so settle down. The quiet irony is sharp: they revered the falling rock and the goddess, while missing the true God who actually made the heavens and flung the stone — worshipping 'the creature rather than the Creator' (Rom. 1:25). A meteorite is a wonder, but it points to its Maker, not to a goddess; 'every good gift... is from above, coming down from the Father of lights' (James 1:17).
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess.

This is a formal finding, delivered in public by the senior officer of the city, and it is worth weighing as evidence.

Two charges are named and both are dismissed. Sacrilegious — the charge covered the plundering of shrines, a serious crime everywhere in the ancient world. Blasphemers of our goddess means public abuse of Artemis.

So the town clerk of Ephesus, who has no interest in defending Christianity, states in front of the whole city that in two years of preaching that gods made with hands are not gods, Paul and his companions had not once robbed a shrine or insulted the goddess by name.

Think about how difficult that is. Paul had emptied the magic trade, damaged the souvenir industry across the province, and persuaded a great many people to abandon the city's religion — and he had done it without vandalism and without mockery. He argued that the idols were nothing. He did not throw anything at them.

That is a standard the church has frequently failed since, and the failure is usually defended as boldness. There is a way of opposing what is false that gives the opposition a grievance to point at, and it is generally the lazy way, because insulting a thing is much quicker than dismantling it. Paul's two years produced a bonfire lit by the magicians themselves, and not one prosecutable act.

If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.

And now the clerk turns the whole thing back on the man who started it. Demetrius called this meeting. If he has a case, there is a court sitting and a governor to hear it — so bring it. Of course he does not, because he had no case at law and knew it, which is precisely why he had gone to the guild and the theatre instead.

A grievance that will not go to the proper place for a hearing is usually a grievance that would not survive one.

('Proconsul' is explained at 18:12: the Senate-appointed governor of a province like Asia, who held supreme civil and judicial authority — in modern terms, roughly a regional governor who is also the province's chief judge. The clerk's point is simply that lawful channels exist: 'the courts are open, and there are proconsuls' — so let Demetrius take any real grievance to the proper authorities rather than whipping up a riot. There is a quiet wisdom here too: the gospel does not fear due process, and the Christian's way is to seek justice through lawful order, not mob passion.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly.

The word is ekklesia again, and this time it carries its precise civic meaning: the lawful assembly, the constitutional one that met on fixed days with a published agenda and a procedure. The clerk is drawing the line between that and what is in front of him, which is a crowd.

It is a small point of vocabulary and it does a lot of work in this chapter. The same word covers a legitimate gathering that decides things properly and a mob that has been shouting a slogan for two hours, and the difference is not the number of people or the strength of their feeling. It is whether there is a process by which anybody could be shown to be wrong.

For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.

Here is the real argument, and he has kept it until last.

Ephesus was a free city with privileges granted by Rome, and Rome was famously unsentimental about civil disorder in the provinces. An unexplained assembly of twenty-five thousand people was exactly the sort of thing that got charters reviewed and troops stationed. The clerk is telling his fellow citizens that they have spent the afternoon handing the proconsul a reason to take their liberties away.

And note the phrase no cause that we can give. He does not say the cause is weak. He says there is nothing they could put in writing. Somebody would have to draft the report, and that somebody is him, and there is no sentence he could compose that would not read as an admission.

So the riot that was called to defend the greatness of Artemis ends with the city's chief officer explaining that it cannot be explained.

What none of them can see is the shape of what has just happened. A silversmith raised a mob to protect an industry; a mob that mostly did not know why it was there shouted for two hours; and the outcome was a public declaration, from the highest civic authority in the city, that the Christians had broken no law and that any complaint against them must go to a proper court. Demetrius set out to stop the gospel and obtained for it the nearest thing to a licence that Ephesus could issue.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

That is how the greatest riot in the book of Acts ends. Not with an earthquake, not with a sermon, not with anyone being converted. A municipal officer finishes his remarks and sends everybody home, and the crowd goes.

Luke could have written this chapter very differently. He had material for it: extraordinary miracles, a violent deliverance, a bonfire of fifty thousand pieces of silver. And he ends the whole Ephesian ministry with a man closing a meeting.

That restraint is worth noticing, because it is how God most often works and it is not how we most often tell the story. Paul was not in the theatre. No apostle spoke. Nothing happened that anybody would call supernatural. The church at Ephesus was preserved that afternoon by the professional instincts of an official who wanted to keep his city out of trouble with Rome — and by the friendship of some provincial aristocrats, and by a few disciples who stood in a doorway and would not let Paul out.

Ordinary means, all of them. And every one of them was the hand of God, and not one of the people involved knew it.

There is a habit of mind that only counts God as present when something inexplicable happens, and it leaves most of a life looking empty. This verse is the corrective. The same God who threw open the prison at Philippi with an earthquake protected his people at Ephesus with a competent civil servant, and Luke gives both episodes the same weight.

And so the three years at Ephesus close. Twelve men who had never heard of the Holy Spirit; three months in a synagogue and two years in a rented hall; a province evangelised by people whose names we do not know, going home; the magic trade bankrupted by its own practitioners; a riot that ended in a legal finding of innocence. Paul will say goodbye to the elders of this church in the next chapter and tell them he will not see their faces again, and to this congregation will be written the letter that begins with God choosing his people before the foundation of the world.

Luke's own summary of all of it was given at verse 20, and he does not improve on it: so the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth more than a century’s wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
The farewell at Miletus is one of the most moving passages in Acts, and the only speech Paul addresses to Christians. It is a pastor’s testament — the account of a ministry offered to its people before the man who gave it disappears from their sight. Paul did not shrink. He did not select the comfortable texts and leave the hard ones. He declared the whole counsel of God — repentance and faith, warning and promise, the cross and the coming judgment — to Jews and Greeks, in public and house to house, with tears, for three years. This is the standard.

And now he commends them to two things: God, and the word of his grace. Not to his successors. Not to an institution. Not to a programme. To God and his Word — the two sources of power that will outlast every pastor and sustain every flock. The Word that built them up will continue to build them up. The God who saved them will continue to keep them. Paul is going to Jerusalem with chains waiting; the Ephesian elders are going home to fierce wolves. Both are in the same hands.

They kneel on the beach and pray together, and then they weep — sorrowing most of all because they will not see his face again. The affection between shepherd and flock is total and mutual. This is what three years of tears and teaching and house-to-house ministry produces: a bond that no departure can finally break, because it is a bond forged in the gospel and sealed in the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Sixteen verses to cover the best part of a year, and Luke moves so fast that it is easy to miss what is inside them. Two of Paul's greatest letters were written during this stretch, and Luke mentions neither.

Macedonia and Greece (vv. 1–3). Paul leaves Ephesus after the riot — though he had decided to go before it (19:21) — travels through Macedonia giving much encouragement, and spends three winter months in Greece. Behind that one line lie the anguish and relief recorded in 2 Corinthians, and behind the three months lies the letter to the Romans. Then a plot forces him to change route.

The delegates (vv. 4–5). Seven men are named, from three provinces — Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe, Asia. They are very probably the churches' appointed representatives for the collection Paul had been gathering for years, and they are travelling with him because large sums of other people's money should never be carried by one man alone.

Troas (vv. 6–12). Luke rejoins the party — the we returns after some seven years — and the narrative slows right down for one Sunday night. The church gathers to break bread; Paul talks until midnight; the room is hot and crowded and full of lamps; a young man in a window sinks into sleep and falls three floors and is picked up dead. Paul goes down, takes him in his arms, and gives him back alive — then goes upstairs, eats, and carries on talking until dawn.

Down the coast (vv. 13–16). Paul sends the ship round and walks the twenty miles to Assos alone, and Luke does not tell us why. Then Mitylene, Chios, Samos, Miletus — and a deliberate decision to sail past Ephesus rather than be detained there, because he is trying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — perhaps choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia.

Two things worth getting straight before anything else.

First, the riot did not drive him out. He had resolved to leave for Macedonia before Demetrius ever called his guild together (19:21) — Luke recorded the decision several verses earlier. So this is not a man fleeing; it is a man who had already packed and who stayed on to see the trouble through before going.

Second, look at the order of the two verbs: he sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell. He did not slip away. The city had just spent an afternoon shouting for two hours about a goddess whose trade he had ruined, and the Christians of Ephesus were the ones who would still be living there after his ship sailed. So he gathered them and put heart into them, and then left.

That word encouraging — and its noun in the next verse, much encouragement — is one of the most characteristic things about Paul, and it is worth noticing how often it turns up on the way out of somewhere. Strengthening people you are leaving behind is a very different discipline from inspiring people you are about to lead, and it has almost no reward in it.

When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.

Now read that sentence knowing what it covers, because Luke has compressed the most turbulent months of Paul's life into a single sentence.

Somewhere in this journey Paul went to Troas expecting to meet Titus with news from Corinth, and Titus was not there — and he tells us what that did to him: my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there, so I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia (2 Cor. 2:12–13). He had an open door for the gospel and could not use it, because he was too anxious. And when he did reach Macedonia it did not immediately improve: we were afflicted at every turn — fighting without and fear within (2 Cor. 7:5).

Then Titus arrived with good news, and out of that relief Paul wrote 2 Corinthians — the most personal and least guarded of all his letters, in which he defends his ministry, admits his despair, and gives us the thorn in the flesh.

Luke says: he came to Greece.

That gap between the two accounts is worth keeping. Luke is writing history and gives us the route; Paul, in his letters, gives us what the route cost. And it is a fair warning against reading anybody's outward record — including the tidy ones in Scripture — as though it told you what was going on inside the person walking it.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There he spent three months.

Greece here means Corinth, and the three months are the winter, when the sea lanes closed and nobody sailed. Paul is stuck in one city with time on his hands.

And this is when he wrote the letter to the Romans.

Luke does not mention it, but the evidence inside the letter is as clear as such things get. Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae (Rom. 16:1) — Corinth's eastern port. He sends greetings from Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church (Rom. 16:23), and Gaius was one of the two men Paul baptised at Corinth (1 Cor. 1:14). He mentions Erastus, the city treasurer — and a paving stone at Corinth still records an Erastus who laid it at his own expense. And he says he is on his way to Jerusalem with the collection from Macedonia and Achaia (Rom. 15:25–26), which is exactly where the next verse of Acts finds him.

So the greatest letter ever written — the one that converted Augustine, detonated Luther, and has shaped Christian thought for twenty centuries — was composed in a rented room in a port town during a three-month wait for the weather, by a man who could not travel. Luke gives it five words: there he spent three months.

It is worth sitting with that. The most productive quarter of Paul's life, measured by what survived it, was a period of enforced inactivity. He was not doing what he wanted to be doing. The season looks, from the outside and probably from the inside, like a delay.

And when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.

Luke gives no details of the plot, but it is not hard to imagine. A pilgrim ship sailing for Syria before Passover would be crowded with Jews going up to the feast; a man could be knifed at sea and put over the side, and Paul was carrying a very large sum of money. Somebody found out about the booking.

So he goes the long way round — back up through Macedonia on foot, hundreds of extra miles, weeks of delay. And notice what the detour produced, since Luke lets us watch: it is on this altered route that he spends the week at Troas, raises Eutychus, and gives the farewell at Miletus that is the theological centre of this half of the book. None of it happens if the ship sails.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus.

Luke rarely gives a list like this, and when he does it is because the list itself is the point. Seven men, named with their home towns, from three Roman provinces: Macedonia, Galatia and Asia — much of the mission field of all three journeys, walking together in one party.

And they are almost certainly there because of money.

For years Paul had been gathering a relief fund from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He gives instructions about it to Corinth (1 Cor. 16:1–4), devotes two whole chapters to it (2 Cor. 8–9), and tells the Romans he is on his way to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints (Rom. 15:25–26). These seven were very probably the churches' representatives, travelling with the collection.

Now read what Paul says about why they are coming, because it is one of the most practical sentences he ever wrote: We aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man (2 Cor. 8:21). He would not carry other people's money alone. Not because he might steal it, but because somebody might one day say he had, and the gospel would wear the accusation.

It is a plain standard and the church has suffered enormously wherever it has been ignored: never let one person handle the money, never let the arrangement depend on trusting a good man, and set it up so that the accusation cannot be made in the first place. Paul, an apostle who had seen the risen Christ, submitted himself to an audit committee of seven.

And keep two of the names, because they matter later. Tychicus will carry the letters to Ephesus and Colossae for Paul from prison (Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7). And Trophimus, an Ephesian, is the man some Jews will claim to have seen with Paul in the temple — the accusation, entirely false, that gets him arrested and eventually sends him to Rome in chains (21:29).

Is this Gaius of Derbe the same as the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29, or the Gaius of Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14? Gaius was a very common name, and Luke gives these two different homelands. They were probably different men.

He is standing here in a list of travelling companions, and he is the reason for everything that happens in the last eight chapters of the book.
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread.

The pronoun has changed again, and this time it has been a long wait. Luke's we last appeared at Philippi in chapter 16, when Paul and Silas were dragged before the magistrates and Luke was not — and then the narrative went back to they and stayed there for four chapters and something like seven years.

Now, at Philippi, it becomes we again.

The natural conclusion is that Luke had stayed there the whole time. He had been left in the city where Lydia was converted and the jailer's household baptised, and while Paul was in Thessalonica and Athens and Corinth and Ephesus, Luke was in Philippi. Nobody wrote about it. There is no chapter on what he did.

And it is worth noticing that the church at Philippi is the one Paul singles out as the only congregation that supported him when he left Macedonia, sending money more than once (Phil. 4:15–16), and the one he writes to with more warmth than any other. Somebody had been there, quietly, for years.

If your own service has consisted of staying somewhere while other people went and did things, this is the verse where the man who wrote a quarter of the New Testament comes back into the story after seven years of exactly that.

After the days of Unleavened Bread. They waited for Passover week to finish before sailing. Paul kept the Jewish calendar and Luke notes it without comment; the question of how a Christian relates to those observances is worked out at 18:18 and does not need going over here.

And in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days.

Five days for a crossing that had taken two on the outward voyage (16:11) — the wind was against them. And then seven days at Troas, which is a long stop for a man in a hurry to reach Jerusalem.

He is very probably waiting for the Sunday.

And that is worth stopping on, because the Sunday gathering is the only thing Luke mentions to account for a week's delay in a journey he was racing to finish. Paul had refused to enter Ephesus because he could not spare the days (v. 16), and he sat in Troas for seven of them.

What he was waiting for was the church's gathering. He would not pass through a town where there were believers without meeting them, and he would not ask them to reschedule — he waited for the day they already met. The apostle worked round the congregation's diary rather than the other way about.
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread.

This is the plainest narrative description we have of a Christian church meeting, and almost everything about our own Sundays is in it.

The first day of the week. Not the Sabbath. These are people among whom Jews and Gentiles worshipped together, in a world where the seventh day was the recognised holy day and the first day was an ordinary working day — Sunday was not a holiday anywhere in the empire for another three centuries. So they met either very early or, as here, at night, because they had jobs. And they did it on the first day because that was the day the tomb was found empty.

Nobody in the New Testament argues for this or commands it. It has simply already happened, in a church a long way from Jerusalem, within about twenty-five years of the resurrection.

To break bread. Luke's phrase covers both a shared meal and the Lord's Supper, and in the early church the two were not separated. The gathering was around a table.

Paul talked with them. And the verb here is worth having, because it is not the word for preaching. It is dialegomai — to discuss, to reason back and forth, the same word used of him in the synagogue and in the hall of Tyrannus. This was not a monologue delivered at a congregation. There were questions.

Intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight.

He was leaving in the morning and knew he would not be back, and so he kept going. Anyone who has sat up too late with somebody they will not see again understands exactly what is happening in that clause. It is not indiscipline. It is a man trying to get everything said.

There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.

Why mention the lamps? Luke is not decorating. Consider what many oil lamps do to a crowded upper room on a warm night in the eastern Mediterranean: they burn the oxygen, they throw out heat, and they fill the air with smoke and fumes.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that it is. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), so that no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5); but Christians from the beginning gathered on the first day, the day of the resurrection, and it is a wise and apostolic custom.

Was this the Lord’s Supper? Most likely yes, eaten within a shared meal (cf. 2:42, 46; 1 Cor 11:20–26). The New Testament does not fix how often the Supper should be observed; this passage suggests it was the reason for the weekly gathering, and many churches celebrate it weekly for that reason. And if Luke counts the day from sunset, as Jews did, the gathering was on Saturday evening; if from midnight, as Romans did, Sunday evening. Paul planned to leave on the next day, which fits either.

It is the reason a young man was sitting in an open window at midnight, and the reason he could not keep his eyes open. Luke has told us the cause of the accident one verse before it happens, and he has done it so quietly that most readers take it for scene-setting.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer.

His name means Fortunate, which was a common name for a slave, and given what is about to happen to him it is either the best or the worst joke in Acts. Luke keeps it either way.

He is a young man — Luke calls him the youth in verse 12, very possibly still a boy — and he is in the window because the room is hot and airless and full of lamp smoke, and because a boy sits where there is room, which at a crowded meeting is the ledge.

And then Luke's two stages, medically observed: he sank into a deep sleep, and then was overcome by sleep. He went under gradually and then completely. Anybody who has fought sleep in a warm room knows both stages, and knows that the second one is not a decision.

Which is worth saying plainly, because this story is regularly told as a joke against the boy or against long sermons, and Luke tells it against nobody. There is no rebuke here. Paul does not scold him when he revives, and Luke does not moralise. A tired child at midnight in a hot room fell asleep, and it is entirely understandable, and it nearly killed him.

He fell down from the third story and was taken up dead.

Not as though dead, not for dead. Luke, who was a doctor and who was in that room, says he was picked up dead.

It is worth pausing on how the writer of this book handles that. He had every opportunity to soften it — to say the boy was stunned, or gravely hurt — and the softening would have made the story less exposed to challenge. He says the child was dead, in a house full of witnesses, in a document addressed to a named reader who could have asked them.

And notice where it happened. Not at a healing meeting. Not while Paul was preaching about the resurrection to unbelievers. In the middle of an ordinary church gathering, the worst thing that can happen to a family happened, and the church was in the room when it did.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.

The first thing he does is go down the stairs. The second is get on the ground. The third is pick the boy up and hold him.

That posture is not an accident, and any Jew in the courtyard would have recognised it. Elijah stretched himself upon the widow's dead son three times and cried to the LORD, and the child revived (1 Kgs 17:21–22). Elisha lay upon the Shunammite's dead boy, mouth to mouth and hands to hands, and the child's flesh grew warm (2 Kgs 4:34). Paul is doing what the prophets did, and Luke describes it in their language.

Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him. He speaks to the crowd, not to the boy — the sentence is for the people standing round in the dark with a dead child on the ground. And he says it in the present tense, as an assurance about what is now the case rather than a prediction.

And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.

Now read that with the previous verse still in your hand, because the ordinariness of it is astonishing. A boy has just been raised from the dead in the courtyard. And they go back upstairs and have the Lord's Supper, and then Paul carries on talking until the sun comes up.

No meeting is called about it. Nobody suggests that this changes the plan. The miracle does not become the subject of the rest of the night; the bread is broken and the conversation resumes, and Luke gives the raising of the dead one verse and the talking until daybreak the same.

That proportion is the point, and it runs against every instinct we have about how such an evening ought to be reported. The extraordinary thing was not treated as the important thing. The church at Troas had one night with the apostle, and what they did with it — after the interruption — was eat together and keep asking him questions until it was light.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted.

They took him away. Presumably home, to whoever had been waiting up, and Luke does not tell us anything about that scene and it is the one most of us would want. Somebody had to be told what had happened and then told how it ended.

Alive. They carried out of that house a living boy.

And were not a little comforted.

Luke's understatement is one of his settled habits — the same turn of phrase runs through this book for a riot, a storm and a fortune — and it is worth noticing what it does. He could have written that they rejoiced greatly. Instead he uses a form that makes the reader supply the feeling, which is generally how the deepest relief is actually described by people who have been through it.

And the word he chooses for what they received is paraklesis — comfort, encouragement, the thing that comes alongside and holds a person up. It is the same root as the word used twice in verse 1 and 2 of this chapter, of what Paul had been doing to the churches all the way through Macedonia.

He had been going from town to town encouraging people. On this night, in this house, God did it, and Luke uses the same word for both.

One more thing, because the church has been carrying its own dead ever since. This is not a promise that the boy in your house will be given back; Luke has already recorded James executed in ten words and no rescue (12:2), and he expects you to hold both. What this night shows is not a rule about outcomes. It is what the apostle did when the worst had happened: he went down the stairs and got on the floor and put his arms round the child.

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land.

Luke is careful to tell us this was arranged in advance and was Paul's own decision, and then he does not tell us the reason. It is one of the more tantalising silences in the book.

Here are the facts. The ship had to round Cape Lectum, a long sail; the road across the neck of land was about twenty miles and shorter. Paul had been awake all night. He sent his companions — including Luke — round by sea and walked it alone.

Why, we are not told, and the honest thing is to say so. It is often suggested that he wanted the day to pray, and that is entirely plausible for a man heading toward imprisonment who has just told a church he will not see them again. It is also possible he simply could not face company after the night at Troas, or that he had business on the road. Luke knew and did not write it down.

What the verse does establish is that Paul deliberately arranged several hours by himself, at the cost of a twenty-mile walk on no sleep, at a point when time was short and he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem.

That is worth registering about a man whose life we mostly see as relentless public activity. He was almost never alone; the letters are full of names, and this whole chapter is a crowd. And when he wanted some hours to himself he did not find them by cancelling anything. He found them by taking the harder route to the same place.

And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.

He was there when they arrived. Whatever the walk was for, it did not delay the ship.

And then the names begin — Assos, Mitylene, and in the next verse Chios, Samos, Miletus. Luke is writing down the ports of call in order, day by day, which is what a man does when he is keeping a log. This is not a summary written years later from memory. Somebody on that ship was making notes.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus.

Three days, three anchorages, each recorded. Coastal ships in that world sailed by daylight and put in at night, and Luke gives us the itinerary the way a passenger keeping a diary would.

For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia.

Now that is a striking sentence when you know what Ephesus was to him. Three years of his life. The church he had worked hardest for and the one whose elders he is about to weep over. His ship goes past the harbour mouth and does not turn in.

And the reason Luke gives is not danger — nobody suggests he was afraid of the silversmiths. It is that he could not afford the time. He knew perfectly well what would happen if he set foot in that city: the whole congregation would come, and there would be meals and questions and people needing to be seen, and a day would become a fortnight. Love has a way of detaining people, and he had a deadline.

So he sends thirty miles up the coast for the elders instead, and meets them in a port where the ship is loading and nobody can keep him. It is a deliberate arrangement by a man who knew that if he went home he would not get away.

For he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.

Two reasons stand behind the hurry, and both are worth having. He was carrying the collection, and Pentecost was one of the three pilgrim feasts, so the city would be full of Jews from every province — the largest possible gathering to receive a gift from Gentile churches to Jewish believers, which was the whole point of the collection. And there is the plain fact that Pentecost was the day the Spirit fell.

Note also the words if possible. He is doing everything he can and he does not claim to know whether it will come off. That is a small and healthy thing to see in a man who is elsewhere so certain about his direction: absolute clarity about the destination, and no pretence of certainty about the timetable.

Is this hurry to reach Jerusalem 'on the day of Pentecost' a proof text that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part, yes — but read it carefully. It does show that Paul, himself a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast. Yet his haste was very likely as much missional as ceremonial: Pentecost packed Jerusalem with diaspora pilgrims (a prime moment to bear witness, as at the first Pentecost, Acts 2), and Paul was carrying the relief collection from the Gentile churches, which he wanted to deliver to the saints (24:17; Rom. 15:25–26). So the verse shows him honouring the festival and the Jerusalem gathering — not that he kept it as a binding law required for righteousness. (Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.)

And how does that square with Romans 7, where Paul says we 'have died to the law' (7:4–6)? It squares perfectly, once we see what 'died to the law' means. Paul is not saying the believer is now lawless, or that God's righteous will has been abolished — in the very same chapter he calls the law 'holy and righteous and good' (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master — the regime that could only accuse and curse us — so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit, not by the old written code. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost, then, is no contradiction at all:

He is not under the law as a way of being justified (his justification is in Christ alone), so he is free to keep the feast — not to earn standing, but as heritage, devotion, and a bridge to his people. The fuller framework — the threefold division of the law, and the careful line between keeping a custom freely and keeping it as a requirement — is laid out at 18:18 (Paul's vow). The test there governs here too: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty. Paul hurried to Pentecost as a free man in Christ, not as a slave under law — and that is the whole difference.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the only speech in Acts addressed entirely to Christians. Every other address in the book is aimed at a synagogue, a pagan crowd, a council or a governor; this one is to the leadership of a church, delivered by a man who does not expect to see them again, and taken down by somebody who was sitting there. It is the closest we ever get to hearing Paul talk the way he writes in his letters.

Retrospect (vv. 18–21). He calls them as witnesses — you yourselves know — and characterises three years of the most fruitful ministry in the book with three words nobody would choose: serving, humility, and tears. He did not shrink from anything profitable, taught in public and house to house, and preached repentance and faith to Jew and Greek alike.

Prospect (vv. 22–27). He is going to Jerusalem under compulsion, told by the Spirit in every city that chains are waiting, and not told what else. His life is not precious to him if only he may finish his course. Then the sentence that undoes them: they will not see his face again. He is innocent of the blood of all, because he did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God.

Charge (vv. 28–31). Watch yourselves first, then all the flock, which the Holy Spirit made you overseers of and which God bought with his own blood. Wolves will come in from outside; worse, men will arise from among your own selves, speaking twisted things, to draw disciples after themselves. So stay awake — remembering three years of night-and-day warning, with tears.

Handover and farewell (vv. 32–38). He commends them to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build them up and give them the inheritance — and leaves them nothing else: no successor, no structure, no chain of command. He holds up his working hands, reminds them that he funded the team and the poor from his own trade, and quotes a saying of Jesus that appears in no Gospel: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Then he kneels on the shore and prays, and they weep and kiss him and walk him to the ship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the letter to Ephesus in Revelation (2:1–7) shows a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him.

Work out what that message cost, because Luke does not.

Miletus is about thirty miles from Ephesus by road. A messenger has to be found and sent; he walks or rides a day; the elders have to be gathered from wherever they are, drop whatever they are doing, and walk a day back. So Paul's ship sat at Miletus for the best part of three days waiting for them — which is a considerable sacrifice from a man who has just refused to enter Ephesus because he had no time.

He would not spare a day for the city. He spent three on the elders.

That is not inconsistency; it is priority. The congregation would have detained him indefinitely and he could not have said the things he is about to say to a crowded room. What he needed was the leadership, alone, for one afternoon — because everything he is about to tell them is about what happens after he is gone, and it is for the men who will have to do it.

The elders of the church. Plural, as always in the New Testament, and one church. There were by now believers all over that city and probably several house congregations, and Luke calls them the church in the singular and their leaders elders in the plural. The pattern of a team of elders over one city church is set out at 14:23 and does not need going over again.

What follows is the only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians. Every other address in this book is evangelistic or a legal defence — synagogues, philosophers, governors, mobs. This one is to the church, and it is the closest thing we have to Paul talking the way he talks in his letters, recorded by a man who was sitting there.

One more thing about the summons itself. He sent for the elders — and then, in verse 28, he tells those same men that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, and instructs them to shepherd the flock. Three words for one group of men in one afternoon.

So whatever distinctions later centuries built between elder, bishop and pastor, they are not in this room. Paul calls the same men by all three names inside eleven verses, and Luke records it without a flicker of awkwardness.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia.

He opens by putting himself on trial and calling them as witnesses.

You yourselves know — he will use that phrase, or something like it, four times in this short speech. He is not telling them what his ministry was like. He is asking them to confirm it, and they were there for all three years, and some of them had watched him at the bench and in the lecture hall and in their own houses.

A man can only speak like this if the record will bear it. It is the opposite of a testimonial, which is what you produce when the people who actually know you are not in the room.

Serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.

Four things in a life's work, and not one of them is what a man would choose for himself.

Serving — the word is the one for a slave's work, not a leader's. Paul begins the summary of his apostolic career by describing himself as somebody else's property.

With all humility. In the Greek world lowliness was not a virtue — it was the disposition of the servile, and Greek moralists commonly counted it a fault. Christianity took a quality the world despised and made it the first thing an apostle says about his ministry.

And with tears. He will mention them twice more before he finishes (vv. 31, and the elders' own at v. 37). This is a man who wept over people, repeatedly, over years, and who thought it worth recording as one of the three defining features of his work.

That is worth weighing against how we would summarise a successful ministry. Paul had planted churches across a continent, written letters that would outlast the empire, raised the dead and been befriended by some of the rulers of Asia. Asked to characterise the three years, he says: I was a servant, I was of no account, and I cried a great deal.

And with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews. The last of these is the only one that came from outside, and he names it without heat — no adjectives, no complaint, just the fact that there had been plots and they had cost him something. The man who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Rom. 9:3) is describing what those same people had done to him, and there is not a word of bitterness in it.

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable.

The verb is a vivid one — to draw back, to furl a sail, to shrink away from something out of fear. It is what a man does when he sees where a conversation is going and decides not to go there.

And Paul chooses the negative form deliberately, both here and again at verse 27. He does not say I told you everything. He says I did not shrink — which admits, in passing, that there was something to shrink from. He felt the pull. He knew which subjects would cost him a hearing, or a friendship, or a household's welcome, and he is telling these men that he went ahead anyway.

That is the honest shape of it, and it is a good deal more useful than a claim to have found it easy. Every person who has ever had to say a hard thing to somebody they love knows the exact moment described by that verb.

And teaching you in public and from house to house.

Both, and the second is the expensive one. Public teaching is efficient: one preparation, many hearers, and you can be tired afterwards without anybody noticing. House to house means the same truth delivered again and again to small groups of people in their own rooms, where they can interrupt, and where you have to know their names.

Paul taught daily in the lecture hall for two years, and he also went round the houses. Whatever else the Ephesian ministry was, it was not conducted from a platform.

Testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Here is the content of three years, compressed into two nouns, and they are not interchangeable.

Repentance toward God — a turning round, and note the direction: toward God, not toward better behaviour. Repentance in Scripture is not primarily regret about actions but a change of allegiance, and it is aimed at a person.

Faith in our Lord Jesus Christ — the trusting, and it too is aimed at a person rather than a doctrine.

The two belong together and neither survives alone. Repentance without faith is remorse, which has killed people. Faith without repentance is agreement, which has comforted a great many people who never changed direction. Paul preached both to everybody — both to Jews and to Greeks, the religious and the pagan, the man who thought he was already right with God and the man who had never considered the question. Neither group needed less than the other.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.

Read those two clauses together, because the combination is unusual and it settles a question that troubles readers a chapter later.

He is constrained by the Spirit — bound, under compulsion — to go. And the same Spirit has been telling him, in city after city, what is waiting at the other end. So the Spirit is not sparing him the information. He is being sent, and he is being told what it will cost, and both of those are the work of the same Person.

Notice what he is not told: not knowing what will happen to me there. He has the direction and the general shape of the outcome, and no details at all. That is almost always the arrangement in Scripture, and it is worth registering, because we tend to imagine that guidance means being shown the plan. Abraham was told to go to a land that God would show him, which is not the same as being shown it.

Now the question this raises, and it should be faced here because it arrives shortly. In the next chapter, disciples at Tyre tell Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem (21:4), and Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and prophesies his arrest, and everyone present begs him not to go (21:11–12). So was Paul disobeying the Spirit by pressing on?

This verse is the answer, and it is the reason Luke put it here. What the Spirit revealed, consistently and in every city, was the suffering. What the disciples added was the conclusion — therefore do not go — and that was love talking, not prophecy. They had the message right and drew from it the inference any of us would draw about somebody we loved. Agabus, notably, does not tell him not to go; he says what will happen, and it is the bystanders who beg.

A true word from God about coming trouble is not automatically an instruction to avoid it. That distinction is worth keeping, because it is the difference between godly counsel and a warning wrongly applied — and the people who got it wrong at Tyre were sincere, Spirit-filled Christians who cared about him.

And there is comfort in the arrangement itself. Paul walked toward Jerusalem knowing there was a cell at the end of the road, and he knew because God had told him repeatedly. He was not tricked into it. Whatever else obedience cost him, it did not cost him the truth about what he was walking into.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus.

This is the sentence the whole speech turns on, and it should not be read as bravado. Paul is not saying his life is worthless, or that he is indifferent to it; he says it is not precious to myself — that he has stopped treating his own survival as the thing to be protected.

And notice that it is a comparison, not a denial: if only I may finish. There is something he values more, and the whole force of the sentence is in the ranking.

My course. The word is dromos, a runner's track, the distance a man is set to cover — the same word he used of John the Baptist finishing his course at 13:25, where what it means to finish badly and still finish is worked out. Here he uses it of himself, and he will use the picture once more, at the very end, from a Roman prison with his execution close: I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Tim. 4:7).

So the same image appears at the beginning of his ministry, applied to somebody else, and at the end, applied to himself, and here in the middle where the outcome is still open. A course is a fixed distance. The question is never how far you have got compared with anybody else; it is whether the ground assigned to you has been covered.

And the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus. Received — it was handed to him. He did not devise it, apply for it, or grow into it; it was given on a road to Damascus by a voice, to a man who had been travelling in the opposite direction.
