And there is an irony here that Luke leaves lying in the open. Tertullus's advice was taken. Felix did examine Paul — repeatedly, over two years, sending for him often (v. 26). What he found out was not sedition. He got a sermon on righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, and it frightened him out of the room.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so.

The delegation adds its voice. Everyone agrees. And that is the whole of their contribution to the proceedings: agreement.

It is worth holding these two things apart, because a courtroom is one of the few places that insists on the distinction and ordinary life almost never does. Consensus is not evidence. Not one of the men affirming this was in the temple court when Paul was seized. The people who were there — the Jews from Asia who started the riot by pointing at him and shouting — are not in this room, and Paul is about to say so with some force (v. 19).

So what Felix is being offered is a chorus. A number of respectable men, including the high priest, all saying that yes, it is so. No one who saw anything. No one who can be questioned about what he saw.

Luke's word for what they do is a legal one — they joined in the attack, piling on to the accusation. It has the flavour of a crowd rather than a witness list.

Run the test on the way things actually reach you. Almost everything you believe about people you have not met arrived exactly like this: not from someone who saw it, but from several people who all say the same thing. And the fact that they say the same thing feels like corroboration, when very often it only means they all heard it from the same place.

The defining feature of gossip is not that it is false. Sometimes it is not. The defining feature is that the person who actually saw it is never in the room — and that nobody notices, because so many people are nodding.

And there is one more layer, which is the saddest in the verse. These men are not lying in the way a criminal lies. Most of them almost certainly believe every word. They have been told by people they trust that Paul is an apostate who defiles the temple, and they have arrived at a conclusion the way most of us arrive at most of ours — by inheriting it from a source we never audited.

Sincerity is not innocence. A man can be entirely honest and entirely wrong, and do enormous damage while behaving well throughout. Paul knew that better than anyone in the room: he had once held these exact convictions, with a clear conscience, on the way to Damascus with warrants in his bag.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the governor had nodded to him to speak…

No advocate stands up for Paul. He has no Tertullus. A nod from the bench, and a prisoner in chains begins to speak for himself.

Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense.

Set that beside the speech that has just finished, because the contrast is the point, and Paul has clearly made a decision about it.

He does not flatter. There is not one word here about peace, or foresight, or reforms, or Felix's benevolence. What he offers instead is a single sentence of genuine courtesy that happens to be entirely true: you have been judging this nation for a long time. That was a fact — five years or so, longer than most — and it was relevant, because it meant Felix could actually assess a Jewish religious dispute rather than being baffled by it.

So Paul is respectful and Paul is honest, and he shows that these are not in competition. He does not sneer at the court, and he does not buy it. There is a way to address a powerful and corrupt man that neither grovels nor postures, and it consists mostly of refusing to say anything untrue.

Then there is the word cheerfully — euthymos, in good spirits, with a settled heart. Consider who is saying it. This is his third hearing in under a fortnight. He has been beaten by a mob, chained, nearly flogged, ambushed by a murder plot, moved sixty miles under armed guard at night, and he is standing in a Gentile hall listening to the high priest of Israel pay a man to call him a plague. And he is in good spirits.

That is not temperament. A week ago the Lord stood by him in the dark and said take courage, and told him he would testify at Rome (23:11). A man who knows the assignment holds can afford to be cheerful in a courtroom, because the courtroom is not the thing that decides.

You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem.

And now the facts, and Paul starts with arithmetic, because arithmetic can be checked.

Twelve days. Count them off the record: the arrival and the welcome from the brothers, the meeting with James and the elders the following day, the four men and the purification rites, the arrest in the temple towards the end of the seven days, the night in the barracks, the council, the night march to Antipatris, the arrival at Caesarea, and five days waiting for the prosecution to arrive.

Now set that number against the charge. Tertullus has accused him of stirring up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. Paul's answer is that he has been in the country a week and a half, and that the governor's own staff can confirm every day of it.

How is it not more than twelve days? Paul is counting the days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship, the days in which he could have stirred up trouble. Some count from his arrival to his arrest and transfer, others to this hearing, counting the five days in Caesarea; either way, his point is that he had too little time in the city to have done what they claim.

Notice, too, the last words: he went up to worship. Not to organise, not to agitate, not to lead a movement. He came to keep a feast and to bring money to the poor, and both of those are checkable as well.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

Paul takes the charge apart with a list of places. Not in the temple. Not in the synagogues. Not anywhere in the city. He names every venue in which an agitator would have to have been seen agitating, and challenges them to produce one person who saw it.

Then the sentence that is the hinge of the whole defence: neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

Under Roman procedure that was decisive. The burden lay on the accuser, and an accuser who brought a charge he could not sustain was not merely disbelieved; he could himself be liable for it. Paul is not asking for mercy or for the benefit of the doubt. He is pointing at an empty table and asking the court to notice that nothing has been put on it.

There is something bracing in the plainness of it. Paul does not begin with theology. He begins with: bring the evidence. Christianity has never asked to be exempted from that question, and it should never want to be. The faith is a set of claims about things that happened in public — a man executed under a named governor, a tomb found empty, witnesses who could be interrogated and were. Paul's own summary of the resurrection appearances says that most of the five hundred were still alive and could be asked (1 Cor. 15:6). That is not the language of a religion that wants to be taken on trust.

But the honest edge of this cuts both ways, and it is worth saying plainly. Paul can demand proof because there is nothing to find. A Christian accused of something he has actually done may not hide behind procedure — and the church has done exactly that, more than once, and brought the name of Christ into disrepute doing it. The right to say prove it belongs only to the man who could survive the investigation.

Which is why the small verse that comes a few lines later matters so much: I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man (v. 16). That is what makes verse 13 sayable. Paul's defence in this court rests on a life lived so that a subpoena would be boring.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers…

Here the defence stops being legal and becomes testimony, and Paul signals the change with one deliberate word. I confess — homologo, the verb for openly acknowledging what you believe, the word the New Testament uses for confessing Christ before men. He has spent four verses saying you cannot prove that. Now he says: but here is what I will happily admit to, and I will say it louder than you did.

Watch what he concedes and what he refuses. The Way, which they call a sect. He will not accept their word — hairesis, a faction, a splinter group. He will not deny the reality behind it either. Yes, this is the Way, and yes, I belong to it, and no, it is not a breakaway.

Then the claim itself, and it is enormous: I worship the God of our fathers. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Not a new god. Not an import from Greece. Not a revision. Paul is standing in a Roman court telling the high priest of Israel that the man in chains is the one worshipping Israel's God properly.

Believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets. Everything. Not the parts that suit him. This is a direct answer to the rumour that started all the trouble back in chapter 21 — that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. His answer is that he believes more of the book than his accusers do, not less, and that the difference between them is not that he has subtracted anything but that he has seen it arrive.

That is the sentence to hold on to whenever someone suggests Christianity is a departure from the Old Testament. Paul's position is not that the Law and the Prophets have been superseded. It is that they have been kept.

Having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.

And here Paul does something that ought to make the reader sit forward, because he is not only defending himself. He is laying a fuse.

Note first the generosity: which these men themselves accept. He grants his accusers their orthodoxy. His accusers themselves hold the resurrection hope; so does he; on this they are together, and he says so in open court rather than scoring the point.

Then note what he adds, because it is the one phrase nobody asked for. Of both the just and the unjust.

This is the only place in Acts where Paul spells out that the resurrection is not only for the righteous. It is Daniel's vision — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Dan. 12:2) — and it is the Lord's own teaching: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29).

Now ask why Paul says it here, in a defence speech, to a Roman governor who has asked him no question about eschatology.

Because Felix is listening. And ten verses from now, when Felix sends for him privately and asks to hear about faith in Christ Jesus, Paul will reason with him about the coming judgment — and Felix will be terrified. The charge was laid in open court, in front of everyone, dressed as a point of Jewish doctrine. It goes off later, in a private room, in the governor's own conscience.

There is a test in that phrase for anybody, and it is not complicated. Most people, asked whether they believe in life after death, will say something warm. Very few have taken in the second half of the sentence. The resurrection is not a reward reserved for the deserving; it is universal. Everyone gets their body back. The question the Bible puts is never will you rise? but what will you rise to?

And consider the God whose hope this is. He has been the God of our fathers for two thousand years by the time Paul says it in that hall, and he has not changed his mind, or lost the thread, or grown tired of the promise. He spoke to Abraham about a family and to Daniel about the dust waking, and he kept every word of it, and the keeping of it was a grave outside Jerusalem that could not hold what was put in it. The God of the fathers is the God of the empty tomb. The hope of Israel and the risen Christ are not two things, and no court in the world had jurisdiction over either.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man.

The word behind take pains is askeo. It is the athlete's word: to train, to work at something by discipline and repetition, the root that gives us ascetic. Paul is not describing a placid disposition. He is describing a practice.

That is worth pressing, because a clear conscience is usually imagined as something you either have or do not, like a good night's sleep. Paul treats it as something you build, daily, the way a runner builds a season — by keeping the accounts short. He does not let things accumulate. When something goes wrong with God he deals with it; when something goes wrong with a person he deals with that too, and he says toward both God and man because he knows perfectly well that people try to settle the first while leaving the second standing.

You met this claim in the previous chapter, in a different room, and it got him hit in the mouth: Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day (23:1). He has not retreated from it. He says it again, in front of the men who were there.

And it is the quiet foundation under the whole defence. Paul can invite investigation, name every venue, and challenge the court to produce a witness, because he has spent more than twenty years making sure there would be nothing to find. A man who trains at this can afford to be examined.

Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings.

This is a remarkable half-verse, and most readers go straight past it.

Paul is talking about the collection — the relief fund he had been gathering for years from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia and Galatia for the poor believers in Judea. It dominates his letters. He gives it two whole chapters in 2 Corinthians, organises it in 1 Corinthians 16, and tells the Romans that it is the reason he is going to Jerusalem at all (Rom. 15:25–28). It was the great project of his later ministry: hard currency carried across the empire by a committee of Gentile Christians, to prove that the church was one body and not two.

And in the whole book of Acts, this is the only time it is mentioned — in a single clause, in a courtroom, in a list of things Paul did in Jerusalem.

Luke's silence about it is its own lesson in how differently a thing can look from inside and outside. For Paul this was years of correspondence, delicate negotiation, and personal risk. For Luke it is a subordinate clause. Much of the work that costs a Christian most is recorded nowhere, summarised by somebody else in half a line, and known in full only to God.

There is a bitter irony in it too. He came to bring money to the poor, and it is the reason he is standing in the dock. And the mention of alms in open court may well have been the moment a thought entered Felix's head, because two verses from the end of the chapter we are told what the governor was really hoping for: that money would be given him by Paul (v. 26).

Paul's generosity toward the poor of Jerusalem bought him two years in a cell, because a corrupt man heard the word alms and concluded there must be a fund.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult.

Every word of that is a charge being dismantled. They accused him of profaning the temple: he was purified, ritually clean, in the middle of the very rites that prove it. They accused him of stirring up riots: there was no crowd and no tumult until his accusers created one.

The prosecution's own picture of the scene has been quietly reversed. Paul was standing quietly in a holy place, having completed a purification he paid for out of his own pocket, when men who had come from Asia pointed at him and started shouting.

But some Jews from Asia—

And then the sentence breaks off. Luke leaves the dash in. Paul, mid-flow, stops and changes direction, and what he says next is the sharpest legal thrust of the whole speech.

They ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.

Here is the hole in the case, and Paul walks the governor straight to the edge of it. The men who actually saw the alleged offence — the Jews from Asia who recognised him, who assumed he had brought Trophimus past the barrier, who seized him and raised the shout (21:27–29) — are not in the room. They have not come the sixty miles. They are the only eyewitnesses in existence, and the prosecution has arrived without them.

Under Roman law that was not a small gap. An accuser was expected to appear and prosecute; abandoning a charge you had raised was itself an offence. Paul is saying, in effect: the people who made this accusation have dropped it, and the men standing here in their place did not see anything.

Notice the fairness in his phrasing, too — should they have anything against me. He does not claim they are lying. He says: if they have a case, let them come and make it. That is the confidence of a man who would rather be examined than excused.

And that is the test worth taking away. Almost every reputation ever damaged has been damaged by an accusation whose original source never appeared. Somebody said something to somebody, and it travelled, and by the time it reached you it had four confirmations and no author. Paul's question is the only one that matters and the one almost nobody asks: where is the person who actually saw it, and why are they not here?
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council…

Having disposed of the absent witnesses, Paul turns to the men who are present. Very well — you were there at the Sanhedrin a week ago. You are the ones with first-hand knowledge of that hearing. Tell the governor what crime you established.

It is a dare, and it is safe, because he knows exactly what happened at that meeting: it collapsed into a brawl between Pharisees and Sadducees and never reached a finding at all. He is inviting them to describe their own most recent failure to the judge.

Other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.

And with that, Paul does something worth stopping over, because it settles a question the reader may still be carrying from the last chapter.

When he shouted that line in the council, it looked to many people like a manoeuvre — a clever man splitting his enemies by throwing a doctrinal bone between two factions who could be relied on to fight over it. Was it a trick?

Here is the answer. A week later, in a Roman court, in front of a governor who cannot be split and a delegation who cannot be provoked, with nothing whatever to gain from repeating it — he repeats it. He not only stands by the sentence; he offers it to the court as the single accurate summary of the entire case.

A trick is something you use once and quietly drop. Paul will say this again before Agrippa and Festus (26:6–8), and finally to the Jewish leaders of Rome at the very end of the book: it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain (28:20). It was never a tactic. It was the truth, and it happened to be a truth that broke the room.

And notice what he has now done to the charge sheet. Tertullus brought his counts: sedition, sect-leading, temple desecration. Paul has answered every one and reduced the case to one sentence about whether the dead are raised.

He has, in effect, told a Roman governor: the entire proceeding is a religious dispute about the resurrection, and you have no jurisdiction over that. He is right, and Felix knows he is right, which is exactly why the next thing that happens is not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off.

Luke's aside is easy to skim and it is the key to the man. The phrase is a comparative — akribesteron, more accurately — and it means Felix understood the Christian movement better than the people arguing in front of him.

That is not a guess on Luke's part. Felix had governed Judea for years. The church had been in Caesarea since Cornelius, and Philip the evangelist lived there with his four daughters (21:8). His own wife was a Jewish princess. This governor knew who the Nazarenes were, knew they were not a band of insurrectionists, and could see that the prosecution had produced no evidence for anything.

So Felix knew. And Felix did nothing.

He does not convict Paul, because he cannot. He does not release Paul, because that would cost him with the Jewish leadership. He finds a third option, and it is one of the most recognisable moves in human affairs: he asks for more information.

When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.

It sounds like diligence. It is a formula. There is no record that Lysias ever came down, no indication that Felix ever sent for him, and no sign in the following two years that the tribune's testimony was ever thought necessary again. The adjournment was not a step towards a verdict; it was a substitute for one.

This is the sin of this chapter, and it does not look like a sin at all. Felix is not cruel to Paul. He is scrupulously reasonable. He simply declines to act on what he already knows, and he dresses the refusal in procedure — and because the procedure is real, nobody can accuse him of anything.

Most of us are far more likely to fail this way than any other. Not by deciding against the truth, but by finding a legitimate reason to postpone deciding for it. There is always one more person to consult, one more consideration outstanding, one more sensible reason why now is not the moment. Felix invented nothing; he just never got round to it, on purpose, for two years.

Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs.

The terms are unusually generous. The word for liberty is anesis — a loosening, a relaxation of the conditions. Paul is not in a dungeon. He is in the governor's own palace complex under guard, permitted visitors, and his friends may come and go and bring him whatever he needs.

And it is worth pausing on what that arrangement made possible. For the next two years Paul is in one place, in a Roman provincial capital, with time and with free access to his companions. Luke is with him, and Luke has a Gospel to research and a second volume to write, in a country full of people who had been there — Philip, in the same city, who had known the church since chapter 6; Caesarea's own believers; anyone who could reach the coast.

Scripture does not tell us that this is where the research was done, and it would be wrong to state it as fact. But the two years are not blank, and the God who gave a discouraged prisoner a comfortable cell with an open door and a doctor for company was doing something, even while the governor was doing nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish.

Luke names her, and the name carries a history that makes the next two verses almost unbearable.

Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I — the king who executed James with the sword and was struck down at Caesarea for accepting the shout that he was a god (12:1–23). It happened in this city. She was six. Her brother is Agrippa II and her sister Bernice, and both of them will walk into this same palace in the next chapter to hear this same prisoner. Her great-grandfather was Herod the Great, who ordered the children of Bethlehem killed.

She is about twenty years old, and she is a Jew, and she is on her second marriage. She had been given to King Azizus of Emesa. Josephus records that Felix, wanting her, employed a Cypriot magician (the manuscripts give his name as Simon or Atomos) to work on her until she left her husband and married the governor instead.

So here they sit: a Roman official whose court was for sale, and a young Jewish princess living with him in a marriage her own law did not recognise. And they send for the prisoner, because they would like to hear him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.

It is a request for an interesting evening. What they get is verse 25.

And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment…

Three subjects. Look at who is in the room, and then look at them again, because this is the most precisely aimed sermon in the book of Acts.

Righteousness — dikaiosyne, which is both the character God requires and the justice a judge is supposed to dispense. Preached to a magistrate who was at that very moment hoping the defendant would offer him a bribe (v. 26).

Self-control — enkrateia, mastery of one's own appetites. Preached to a man with the woman he had taken from another man sitting at his side.

The coming judgment — krima to mellon. Preached to the most powerful man in the province, who had spent his life as the one who judges and had never seriously considered being judged.

Paul is a prisoner. Felix can hold him for two years without charge, and does. And Paul looks at the man who owns his freedom, and at the marriage everyone at court had agreed not to mention, and preaches righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come.

He was asked to explain faith in Christ Jesus, and this is how he did it. That is worth noticing, because it is not how most of us would have gone about it with a governor. Paul did not begin with comfort or with benefits. He began where the New Testament habitually begins with the comfortable and the powerful: with the standard, the failure to meet it, and the day it will be assessed. There is no good news in a pardon until there is bad news in a verdict.

Felix was alarmed.

The Greek says he became emphobos — filled with fear. This is not irritation, and it is not intellectual disagreement. The governor of Judea, sitting in his own palace with his own soldiers outside the door, listening to a man in chains, became frightened.

Nothing in the room had changed. No sign was given, no miracle done. A prisoner talked, and the word of God found the conscience of a man who had buried it, and he could not sit still under it.

The most dangerous word in Felix's reply is 'later': 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.' He was alarmed — genuinely under conviction — yet he postponed, and so far as Scripture records, the convenient season never came (he left Paul in prison two years, still angling for a bribe, vv. 26–27). Here is a solemn lesson for every hearer: conviction delayed is conviction deadened, and the 'convenient season' for repentance almost never arrives on its own. The Bible's word is always now: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts' (Heb. 3:15); 'now is the day of salvation' (2 Cor. 6:2). To say 'later' to Christ is the most natural thing in the world, and one of the most perilous.
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him.

Luke gives the real reason, and it is squalid. The governor was angling for a bribe.

It was illegal, and it was routine, and Felix had reason to think it possible: he had heard Paul mention in open court that he had come to Jerusalem bringing alms for his nation (v. 17). A man who can carry a relief fund across the empire can presumably find a purse for a governor. Somewhere behind this is a calculation that Paul's friends would pay to end it.

They never did, and Paul never offered, and that silence is worth a moment. A payment would have been the easy and obvious thing — arguably even a reasonable thing, since the imprisonment was unjust and everyone knew it. Two years of a man's life and the whole Gentile mission were on the other side of the scale. He did not do it. There are things a servant of Christ cannot buy his way out of without ceasing to be one.

So he sent for him often and conversed with him.

And here is the most frightening sentence in the chapter. Felix heard the gospel repeatedly. Not once. Over two years, again and again, from the best explainer of it who ever lived, in private, with every opportunity to ask whatever he wanted.

Very few people in the New Testament had that. And it did him no good at all, because he was never listening for the answer; he was listening for an opening.

That is the anatomy of a hardening heart, and it is not what people expect. Felix did not reject the gospel once and walk away. He kept coming back. He remained interested, and curious, and even entertained — and each conversation left him slightly less capable of the fear he had felt the first time. Familiarity with holy things is not the same as being changed by them, and it insulates far more people than open hostility ever has. It is possible to attend church for forty years the way Felix attended these conversations.

When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

Two years. Luke gives it a clause.

Stop and measure it against what the Lord said. In the barracks at Jerusalem, at the lowest point of Paul's life, the risen Christ stood over him and said take courage… you must testify also in Rome (23:11). Two days later Paul was in Caesarea. And then nothing happened for seven hundred and thirty days.

No trial. No verdict. No release. No visible movement of any kind toward Rome. The most fruitful missionary in history, in the prime of his working life, with churches all round the Aegean needing him and a promise from the Lord Jesus in his pocket, sat in a provincial palace on the wrong coast while a corrupt official waited for an envelope that never came.

This is why the two years are in the Bible. They are here for everyone who has been given a word from God and then handed a long stretch of nothing.

Because the honest question is not whether God keeps his promises. It is what those promises feel like from inside the waiting, when the calendar turns over twice and the door has not opened and there is no evidence that anything is being done. Paul did not know he had two years. He only knew he had today, and then another one.

And the promise had not weakened by a syllable. It was as strong on the last morning as on the first night. Delay is not decay. God is not slower than his word, and a promise sitting apparently idle is not a promise going stale — it is a promise being carried by someone who does not need to hurry and never forgets. What looked from the cell like two years of silence was two years of the Lord of history arranging a governor's recall, a successor's ambition, an appeal to Caesar, and a ship.

Felix's last recorded act is his most characteristic: desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. On his way out of office, with nothing to gain and no case to answer, he chose one final time to keep an innocent man in custody as a parting gift to people he had spent some seven years mistreating.

It did not work. Josephus records that the Jewish community of Caesarea sent a delegation to Rome to accuse him of his conduct anyway, and that he escaped punishment only through his brother's influence at court.

He sold his integrity, and he did not even get the price.
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A new governor arrives, and the case that Felix left to rot is reopened within seventy-two hours — by the prosecution, not by the court.

The ambush renewed (vv. 1–5). Three days into the job Festus goes up to Jerusalem, and the chief priests are waiting with a request dressed as a courtesy: send Paul to us. Two years have passed and the plan has not changed; there is still an ambush on the road. Festus says no, for the right reason and probably not for the right motive — the venue is Caesarea, so come to Caesarea.

The hearing (vv. 6–8). The prosecution brings many serious charges and proves none. Paul's answer is three denials and a full stop: nothing against the law, nothing against the temple, nothing against Caesar. A man defending himself elaborates; a man telling the truth can afford to be short.

The favour and the appeal (vv. 9–12). Then Festus asks the question that changes the rest of the book — wishing to do the Jews a favor, the very phrase Luke used of Felix (24:27). Paul sees it, refuses it, and plays the last card a Roman citizen holds: I appeal to Caesar. It is not panic and it is not despair; it is a man with a promise about Rome taking the one road that leads there.

The briefing (vv. 13–22). Agrippa II arrives — the last Herod in Scripture, from a family that has murdered the Baptist, mocked Christ, and executed an apostle — and over several days Festus lays the case out. His account is true in every clause and shaped in his own favour, exactly as Lysias's letter was (23:27). And in the middle of it he states the whole Christian faith without knowing it: the dispute is about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.

Agrippa has been wanting to hear this man. A Herod said that once before, about Jesus, and got silence (Luke 23:8–9). This one will be given the finest sermon of the age.
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

Paul's appeal to Caesar settles a question Christians still raise: may a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had a promise from the risen Christ that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a statutory right to get there. Faith in the promise did not make the appeal unnecessary; it made the appeal obvious. The same man who was told every soul aboard the ship would survive still warned that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31).

Providence does not bypass means. It employs them, and it is content to employ thoroughly unspiritual ones — a citizenship registry, a governor's ambition, an emperor's court, and a bureaucrat's need to fill in a form correctly. God ordains the end and he ordains the road, and the road here runs through Roman administrative procedure.

Two guards. First, the lawfulness of the means does not sanctify the motives of those who supply them: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did, and Luke uses the identical phrase so the reader will not miss it. Second, God's certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime and Paul stays in chains. Scripture never asks anyone to pretend that the second fact is softened by the first. They are simply both true, and the Christian lives in the overlap.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment — a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. He had identified the hinge of the entire religion. He could have passed an examination on it. And it never crossed his mind that if it were true it might concern him personally; it was a fact about somebody else's people.

Now: This is the particular danger of a life spent near the things of God. Anyone raised in a believing home, or twenty years in a pew, or halfway through a theology course, can state the resurrection more accurately than Festus did. The question the governor puts to such a reader is not whether the doctrine is held correctly. It is whether it has ever once been allowed to be about him. Say the sentence out loud — a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive — and notice honestly whether anything in you moves. Festus said it in passing and moved on.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.

Three days. The new governor lands, and inside seventy-two hours he is on the road to Jerusalem.

That tells you what he had been told about the posting. Porcius Festus was taking over from a man who had been recalled to Rome to answer for his conduct, in a province that would be in open revolt within six years. He does not spend a fortnight settling in. He goes straight to the city that matters and introduces himself to the people who can make his term ungovernable.

And they are ready for him.

And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him.

Stop and measure that against the calendar, because it is the most striking thing in the verse.

Two years have passed. Two full years since the riot in the temple, since the forty men swore their oath, since Felix first heard the case and did nothing. Governments have changed. The high priest who ordered Paul struck has himself been deposed. Everyone involved has had seven hundred days of other business.

And Paul is still the first item on the agenda. Not one of several matters raised with the incoming governor — the thing they came to say.

Set the two facts side by side, because Luke has: for Paul, two years of nothing whatever happening. For his enemies, two years of unbroken attention. The same stretch of time in which the prisoner saw no progress at all was, on the other side of the wall, a period of sustained and patient diligence.

That is worth knowing about opposition, and it is not comfortable. Hatred keeps its appointments. It does not need fresh provocation to stay warm, it survives changes of personnel, and it will still be there when the new man arrives. Most of us cannot sustain a good intention for a fortnight; a grudge will run for years on nothing at all.

The verb Luke uses for what they do to Festus means to press, to urge with insistence. They are not filing a complaint. They are lobbying, on day three, before the man has unpacked.

Is 'chief priest' the same as 'high priest'? Not quite. The high priest (singular) was the one supreme religious officer of Israel — the single man who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement (such as Caiaphas, or Ananias at Paul's hearing before Felix). The chief priests (plural) were the wider circle of leading priests, the priestly aristocracy who ran the temple: the serving high priest, former high priests (who kept the title and influence even after Rome deposed them — hence Annas is still called 'high priest' in Luke 3:2), the heads of the few wealthy high-priestly families from whom high priests were chosen, and senior temple officers like the captain of the temple and the treasurers.

So the high priest sits at the very top, and the chief priests are the powerful establishment gathered around and beneath him (mostly Sadducees — see 5:17). It is this priestly ruling class that appears again and again in the Gospels and Acts as the ringleaders against Jesus and his apostles.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.

The word is charis — a favour, a kindness. It is the ordinary currency of Roman public life: you do this for me now, and I am in your debt, and one day you will find that useful. They are not making a legal argument. They are opening an account with the new governor.

And Luke, who has been letting the scene play out straight, cuts in with the truth in a subordinate clause: because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.

Notice what he has done to us as readers. Festus does not know this. He is a competent official listening to a reasonable-sounding request from the religious leadership of the province, and there is nothing on the face of it to refuse. We know it is a murder plot. We watch him weigh a request whose real content is hidden from him and visible to us.

That is the second time this trap has been laid. Two years ago more than forty men bound themselves under a curse to eat nothing until Paul was dead, and asked the council to request exactly this — a transfer to Jerusalem, with an ambush on the road (23:12–15). It failed because a boy overheard it.

Whether these are the same men, Luke does not say. What he does say is that the plan is unchanged. Two years of failure has not produced a rethink, only a fresh attempt on a fresh governor. The oath-takers presumably ate long ago; the intention outlived the oath.

And there is something worth facing in that. It is easy to picture the people who wanted Paul dead as monsters, and they are not. They are religious men, respected men, who over two years have quietly kept a murder on the agenda and learned to think of it as the defence of God's honour. Nobody arrives there in one step. You arrive by a series of small permissions, each one granted to yourself on the grounds that the cause is good.

Which raises the only question this verse really asks. Is there anything you have been carrying against someone for two years — not acting on, simply carrying, keeping current, refreshing whenever the subject comes up? These men would have said they were defending the temple. It is remarkable what a settled hatred will agree to call itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly.

He says no. And he says it for entirely the wrong reason, which is the point.

Festus is not protecting Paul. He has never met Paul. What he is protecting is his own jurisdiction: the prisoner is in Roman custody in the provincial capital, the governor's court sits there, and a new administrator does not begin his term by handing a prisoner over to a local council that has asked for him as a personal favour. That is not mercy. It is a man declining to be managed in his first week.

Let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.

The offer is fair and it is also inconvenient. If they want this case heard, they must travel — sixty miles, down from the holy city to the Gentile administrative capital, to argue in a Roman hall on Roman terms. He will hear them. He will not come to them.

And with that, the ambush is dead. Not discovered, not defeated — simply bypassed, because the road Paul was to be killed on is now a road he will not travel.

Count how often this has happened. A tribune's fear after binding a Roman citizen (22:29). A boy who happened to overhear something. A Roman rule about where a case must be heard. Three times now Paul's life has been saved by ordinary institutional machinery operated by men with no interest in him at all, and not once has anyone in the story known they were doing it.

This is the doctrine of providence at its least romantic and most reassuring. God is not confined to working through people who are willing. He works through procedure, through self-interest, through a bureaucrat defending his own patch. The men of authority will make the journey because a governor stood on protocol, and the killers on the Jerusalem road will wait for a prisoner who is not coming.

There is a caution attached, and Scripture is honest about it. Providence protecting Paul here is the same providence that did not protect Stephen, or James, whom Herod killed with the sword while Peter walked out of prison past the guards. God's care is real and it is not a guarantee of safety. What it guarantees is that nothing will cut short the work he has assigned — and Paul had been told, in a barracks in Jerusalem, that the work included Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days…

Pause on that odd little phrase, because it is a small mark of a truthful book. Eight or ten days. Luke does not know exactly, and he says so. A writer inventing a narrative rounds the number and moves on; a writer working from testimony writes down what he was told, including the vagueness. The New Testament is full of these unhelpful details, and they are one of the quiet reasons to trust it.

And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought.

The bema — the raised judgment seat. Festus is prompt, and he is formal. Everything is being done properly.

When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove.

Luke's verb is periestesan — they stood around him, encircling him. It is a physical detail and a deliberate one. This is a courtroom, and the accusers have arranged themselves round the defendant the way the mob did in the temple court. The setting has changed; the posture has not.

Then the phrase that has become the refrain of these chapters: many and serious charges… that they could not prove.

Look at the strategy in those words, because it is one of the oldest there is and it has never stopped working. They cannot establish a single count. So they bring many, and they make each one grave. The hope is not that any particular charge will survive examination. The hope is that the sheer accumulation will do what no individual accusation can — that twenty unproven things will feel, to a listening judge, heavier than one unproven thing.

And it very often does, because that is not how the mind naturally works. We are built to treat volume as evidence. Twenty complaints about a man sound like a pattern even when not one of them can be substantiated, and the reasonable-sounding conclusion — there is no smoke without fire — is precisely the error the courtroom exists to prevent.

This is worth taking personally, because it is how nearly every damaged reputation is actually built. Rarely by one provable offence. Almost always by an accumulation of unprovable ones, each too small to challenge, none ever tested, all of them together forming an impression that no one can source and no one can refute.

Roman law had an answer to it, and the answer is the whole of Paul's defence: they could not prove it. Say what you can establish, or say nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.

One sentence. It is the shortest defence Paul makes in the whole book, and after two years and four hearings the brevity is itself an argument: there is nothing new to answer, so he will not pretend there is.

But it is not casual. Look at the three headings, because they are exhaustive.

The law of the Jews — the charge that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses, which started the riot in chapter 21 and was never true.

The temple — the charge that he brought a Gentile past the barrier, which has been shrinking steadily since it was first shouted: from he did it, to he tried, to nothing anyone will testify to.

Caesar — and this one nobody in the room had formally raised today.

That third heading is the interesting one, and Paul puts it there deliberately. Tertullus had called him a plague who stirred up riots throughout the world, which is sedition in all but name, and Paul knows that the charge which matters in a Roman court is the political one. So he does not wait to be accused of it. He names it himself and denies it flatly, in front of the man whose entire job is to keep this province quiet.

There is a lesson in the shape of the answer. Paul does not argue that the charges are unkind, or that his accusers are hypocrites, or that he has been badly treated — all of which were true and none of which is relevant. He addresses the actual counts, in the actual categories the court recognises, and he stops.

A man with a clear conscience can afford to be brief. He is not managing an impression; he is answering a question.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul…

Luke has used that phrase before, word for word. The last governor left office desiring to do the Jews a favor, and left Paul in prison to do it (24:27).

Now the new man. Festus is everything Felix was not — energetic, prompt, procedurally clean, on the road within three days, on the tribunal the morning after his return. He is, by any ordinary measure, a better official. And within two weeks Luke files him under the same sentence.

That is a bleak and accurate observation about power, and it is worth stating plainly: the problem was never Felix's laziness. The problem is that a man whose position depends on the goodwill of people who want an innocent man dead will find a way to give them something, and he will not experience it as corruption. He will experience it as being reasonable.

And notice how mild the form of it is. Festus does not order Paul to Jerusalem — that would be indefensible. He asks. Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me? Before me, he says: it will still be my court, my authority, my verdict. What he is proposing is a change of venue that sounds like a courtesy and would in fact put Paul on a road where men are waiting to kill him.

Festus does not know about the ambush. But he does know he is offering to move a prisoner into the reach of people who have been demanding him for two years, and he is doing it because it would be convenient.

I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried.

Paul's answer is legally exact and it closes the door. A provincial governor's court was not an alternative to Caesar's authority; it was Caesar's authority, delegated. Paul is saying: I am already in the correct court. There is no higher Jewish jurisdiction over a Roman citizen charged with offences against Rome, and moving me to Jerusalem would not be a procedural adjustment — it would be an abandonment of the very jurisdiction you are exercising.

To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

And then he says it to the governor's face.

The phrase is stronger in Greek than it looks in English — you know perfectly well, you know better than that. Paul is not appealing to Festus's sense of justice. He is telling a Roman governor, in open court, in front of the men who want him dead, that the governor is aware of the truth and is manoeuvring anyway.

He said the same thing of Felix in effect, and Luke told us Felix had a rather accurate knowledge of the Way (24:22). Two governors in two years, both of whom knew, and neither of whom did anything with the knowing.

That is the danger this whole section quietly circles. Not ignorance. Knowledge held without consequence — the settled human capacity to see clearly what is right and to route around it, politely, for reasons that will sound perfectly sensible when you explain them later.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death.

Before the appeal, the offer — and the order of the two matters enormously.

Paul does not begin by claiming his rights. He begins by submitting his neck. If I have done something capital, execute me; I am not asking for a way out. Only then, having conceded that the court has the right to kill him if the charge stands, does he point out that no charge stands.

That is not a debating tactic. It is the difference between a man defending himself and a man defending the truth. He is not trying to survive; he is trying to stop an injustice, and he says so by putting his life on the table before he says anything else.

But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.

The Latin was provocatio ad Caesarem, and it was one of the oldest and most jealously guarded rights a Roman citizen had: the right to have his case lifted out of a provincial court and heard by the emperor himself.

Understand what it did, because it explains the rest of the book. The moment the words were spoken, the governor lost the case. He could no longer convict; he could no longer acquit; he could no longer release. His only remaining duty was to forward the prisoner to Rome with a written statement of the charges. This is why Agrippa will remark, at the end of the next chapter, that this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:32).

Which raises the obvious question: did Paul make a mistake?

No. And the reason is not legal but theological, and it was settled two years earlier in a dark barracks in Jerusalem, when the Lord stood by him and said you must testify also in Rome (23:11). Paul is not gambling. He is holding a promise, and he has just been handed the only legal mechanism in the Roman world that guarantees delivery.

Note also who the Caesar is. This is around AD 59, and the emperor is Nero — at that point still in the early years that Roman writers themselves regarded as good government, before the fire, before the persecution in which Paul would die. Paul appeals to an emperor who has not yet become the monster he became. He goes to Rome under the protection of the man who will eventually kill him.

Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”

The Greek fronts the name both times, and so does the ESV: To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go. It is a formula, and it is final, and Festus means nothing by it beyond the discharge of a legal duty after a short consultation with his advisers.

And it is the promise of the risen Christ, ratified by a pagan magistrate who has no idea what he is saying.

Two years earlier the Lord Jesus told a beaten and discouraged man that he would testify at Rome. Nothing had moved since. And now the word comes back to him out of the mouth of a Roman governor, in a legal formula, with the full weight of the empire behind it: to Caesar you shall go. Heaven's purpose and Rome's procedure say the identical sentence, and only one of the two speakers knows what is happening.

This is how the Lord governs the world. Not usually by suspending it — by running it. He does not need to overrule the courts; he holds the whole apparatus, the statutes and the precedents and the consultations of the council, and it delivers his servant to the city he named. The kings of the earth take counsel together and their counsel is his instrument. He who sits in the heavens is not anxious about a provincial docket, and every decree signed against his people has, so far, only ever moved the gospel further down the road.

Worth pointing out: it is entirely right for a Christian to use his lawful legal rights. Paul, an apostle, does so without a flicker of guilt — here he appeals to Caesar; earlier he invoked his Roman citizenship to stop an illegal flogging (22:25–29) and refused a quiet, hushed-up release (16:37). Being a believer does not mean being a doormat who refuses all legal recourse and lets injustice simply roll over him.

And this is no contradiction of 'turn the other cheek.' That command forbids personal revenge (Matt. 5:39; Rom. 12:19, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord') — not the lawful appeal to the civil authority God himself has ordained to do justice ('the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer,' Rom. 13:4). Paul forgave his persecutors personally and used the courts; the two sit together.

But does this fit with Paul’s warning against going to court (1 Cor 6:1–8)? There Paul forbids believers to sue one another before unbelievers. Here Paul is a believer accused by unbelievers, appealing to a Roman court for justice. Christians may use the courts and civil rights to defend themselves and others; they should not take a brother to court.

So a Christian may rightly defend himself, appeal, invoke his protections, and seek justice through proper channels — these are good gifts of God's ordering of society, and using them can even serve the gospel (Paul's appeal carried him to Rome to preach, 23:11; 28:31). Two cautions keep it Christ-shaped: do it without bitterness or vengeance, for justice and not for getting even; and remember it is a freedom, not always a duty — sometimes love will gladly lay down a right for a higher good (1 Cor. 9:12, 15; 6:7, 'why not rather suffer wrong?'). Free to use them; free, for love's sake, to give them up.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus.

A king walks into the story, and for Luke's first readers the name alone would have carried a chill. This is the last Herod in the Bible, and it is worth laying the family out, because nobody should have to keep four Herods straight from memory.

Herod the Great tried to kill Jesus in the cradle and murdered the infants of Bethlehem to do it (Matt. 2:16). Herod Antipas, his son, beheaded John the Baptist to save face at a birthday party (Mark 6:26–27), and when Jesus was finally sent to him on the morning of the crucifixion he treated him with contempt, dressed him in fine clothing as a joke, and sent him back (Luke 23:11). Herod Agrippa I, the grandson, killed James the brother of John with the sword, arrested Peter intending the same, accepted the shout that his voice was the voice of a god, and was struck down and eaten by worms (Acts 12:2, 12:23). And now Herod Agrippa II, the great-grandson — the last of the line, and the last member of this family the New Testament will ever mention.

Four generations. The family has had the gospel brought to its door in every one of them, and in four generations not one Herod has ever done anything with it but destroy it, mock it, exploit it, or find it interesting.

That is a sober thing to sit with. Nearness to the gospel is not the same as receiving it, and it does not accumulate down a bloodline. There are families in every church where the third generation is further from Christ than the first, and the reason is almost never that the truth was unavailable. It was thoroughly available to every Herod who ever lived. Access is not the scarce commodity. Willingness is.

Agrippa II is, however, exactly the right man for Festus to consult, and not merely because he is a king. Rome had given him a peculiar portfolio: custody of the temple treasury, the keeping of the high priest's vestments, and the right to appoint and depose the high priest himself. He was the Roman-appointed manager of Jewish religion. If anyone in the province could tell a baffled governor what the dispute about Paul actually was, it was this man.

Bernice is his sister. She had been married to her uncle, was widowed young, and thereafter lived in her brother's household — an arrangement that produced a persistent rumour of incest, reported by Josephus and openly mocked in Rome. She would later become the mistress of Titus, the general who burned Jerusalem and became emperor. Luke names her without comment and lets the reader supply what he knows.

There is a man left prisoner by Felix.

Look at how Festus opens. Two years of a man's life — two years of a Roman citizen held without charge by a governor angling for a bribe — compressed into one dismissive clause. And note the verb: left. Not held, not detained, not committed for trial. Left. The way you leave a coat behind in a house you have moved out of.

That is how the machinery of the world tends to describe the people it has forgotten. It is not usually malice. It is that nobody's file is anybody's priority. Which is worth remembering the next time your own situation feels like an oversight rather than a plan: Paul was a line item in a handover briefing, and he was exactly where the Lord had told him he would be.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense.

Festus is telling Agrippa the story of his own week, and he tells it well. He is not lying. Every clause is true.

He simply leaves out that the priests had asked for a transfer to Jerusalem as a favour (v. 3), and when he mentions his own offer of a Jerusalem trial (v. 20) he recasts it as bewilderment — though it is the precise thing that would have handed him over to his accusers and gutted the principle he is now quoting so proudly. He states the rule; he omits the moment he was ready to bend it.

This is the second time in three chapters that Luke has printed a Roman official's own account of events the reader has just watched. Claudius Lysias did the same in his letter, rearranging one clause so that his rescue of Paul looked principled rather than accidental (23:27). Neither man invents a fact. Both arrange the true facts into a flattering shape, and Luke sets the arrangement down beside the events without a syllable of comment, because he is writing for a reader who has the transcript.

But do not miss what Festus is actually citing, because it is genuinely magnificent and it is the reason Paul is still breathing. Roman practice held that a man could not be condemned unheard, and that accuser and accused must stand face to face. Festus's own word for give up is the verb for granting a favour: no one was to be handed over as a favour. It is not a Christian principle in origin. It is a pagan empire's inherited sense of what a fair hearing requires, and it saved the apostle's life at least three times.

Now hold the two halves of this chapter together, because the contrast is the point and it is uncomfortable.

The chief priests and elders of Israel — the men entrusted with the law of God, who had the Scriptures, who knew that a matter is established by two or three witnesses and that a judge must not take a bribe or show partiality — asked for a sentence of condemnation on a man they had not allowed to speak, and asked for it as a favour, and were planning an ambush on the road.

The pagan governor said no, because it was not the custom.

Rome's custom behaved better than Israel's law, and it was not because Rome was righteous. It was because the men holding the law had stopped letting it govern them. That is always how it happens. The law does not fail; the men who hold it quietly decide that this once, in this case, for this outcome, the procedure can be set aside — and they discover afterwards that they have become the sort of people a pagan has to restrain.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.

Festus wants the king to notice his efficiency, and he has earned the right to mention it. On any reading he is a better administrator than the man he replaced.

Set the two governors side by side. Felix heard Paul's case, was genuinely frightened by what he heard, sent for him repeatedly hoping money would change hands, and then — Luke's most devastating sentence about him — desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison for two years (24:26–27). Festus arrived and had the case on the tribunal within a fortnight.

So the improvement is real, and it is worth saying that competence in office is a good thing and not a small one. A prompt hearing is a mercy to the man waiting for it. Two years of a governor's indecision cost Paul two years.

And yet.

Everything Festus claims here is true, and it did not stop him doing the one thing that would have killed Paul. He was prompt, procedurally correct, personally uncorrupt as far as we know — and eight verses ago he asked whether the prisoner would care to be tried in the city where men were waiting to kill him, because it would please the people he had to work with.

That is the thing to take away, and it applies well beyond Roman provincial administration. Speed is not integrity. Competence is not righteousness. It is entirely possible to be efficient, punctual, organised, blameless in every procedure that can be audited — and to make the one decision that matters on the basis of who you need to keep happy. The failure never shows up in the part of the record that gets inspected.

Festus's account of himself is accurate. It is his instincts under pressure that are the problem, and no honest man can read that without wondering about his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.

Stop here. This is one of the great sentences in the book, and it is great because of who says it and what he thinks he is saying.

A Roman governor, briefing a client king, summarises the entire Christian faith in a subordinate clause — and files it under local religious trivia.

Take it phrase by phrase, because every one of them is doing something.

No charge of such evils as I supposed. Festus had come into the hearing expecting sedition, fraud, violence — the ordinary business of a troublesome province. He got none of it. He is telling Agrippa, in effect, that the prosecution had nothing. That is one more official finding of no crime.

A certain Jesus. The Greek is tinos Iesou — some Jesus, a Jesus, one Jesus or other. It is the phrasing you use for a name you have no reason to remember. The governor of Judea, sitting a few days' journey from the hill where it happened, roughly thirty years after it happened, cannot be troubled to establish who the man was. The name at which every knee will one day bow is, to Festus, a detail in a religious quarrel he is trying to get out of.

Who was dead. Notice that this is not in dispute. Nobody in the room, on either side, questions that Jesus of Nazareth was executed and buried. The death of Christ is common ground between the apostle and the men trying to kill him.

But whom Paul asserted to be alive. The verb is ephasken, and the tense matters: Paul kept on asserting it. Not a statement made once under examination — a claim he would not stop making, the thing he had said in Damascus and Antioch and Philippi and Athens and Corinth and Ephesus and would say in Rome until they cut his head off.

And here is what should stop the reader cold: Festus has got it exactly right.

He has not misunderstood the case. He has stated it more precisely than most sermons manage. Christianity is, at bottom, a dispute about whether a particular dead man is alive. Paul said as much himself, in writing, to people who were trying to spiritualise it: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Cor. 15:17). Take that one clause out and there is nothing left worth arguing about. Festus, who believed none of it, put his finger on the hinge.

Which means it is entirely possible to state the gospel accurately and remain completely untouched by it. Festus could have passed an examination on the content. He could summarise the claim, identify the parties, and explain what was at stake — and it never once occurred to him that if the claim were true, it would concern him personally. It was a fact about somebody else's religion.

That is the test, and it is sharper than it looks, because the people most at risk from it are the ones who have been in church longest. Could you state what Christians believe about the resurrection more accurately than Festus did? Almost certainly. And when you last said it out loud, did it cost you anything, or change anything, or move anything in you at all?

Consider the one they were discussing. A certain Jesus — who was dead. He was dead: the centurion certified it, the spear settled it, the tomb received him, and the world went back to work. And he is alive. Not remembered, not revered, not living on in the hearts of his followers — alive, in a body, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, holding the keys of Death and Hades, and reigning until every enemy is under his feet. The empire that crucified him has been rubble for fifteen centuries. Festus is dust. Agrippa is dust. Bernice is dust. Nero is dust. And the certain Jesus whose name the governor could not be bothered to learn is on the throne of the universe tonight, and every one of those men has since met him and knows his name now.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being at a loss how to investigate these questions…

The word is aporoumenos — from a root meaning no way through, no passage, no road. Festus is not being falsely modest. He is a competent Roman lawyer standing in front of a question his training does not equip him to open: whether a crucified Galilean is alive.

And the honesty is almost attractive. He is not pretending. He does not bluster or invent a category. He says plainly that he was out of his depth.

But watch what a man at a loss actually does, because this is the part worth learning.

Being at a loss, he did not adjourn, or take advice, or send to Rome for a ruling. He turned to the prisoner and proposed the one course that would have ended his life — a trial in Jerusalem, in the city where the ambush was still waiting, before the men who had already asked him to hand the case over as a favour.
