Confusion is not neutral. That is the lesson, and it is a hard one. When a man genuinely does not know what to do, he does not stop; he falls back on whatever pressure is strongest in the room. Festus's honest bewilderment did not produce caution. It produced a proposal that happened to please the people he needed on his side. He would have called that pragmatism. Luke has already told us what it was: wishing to do the Jews a favor (v. 9).

So the test is not whether you know what to do. Often you will not. The test is what you reach for when you do not know — and for most of us the honest answer is that we reach for whatever will cause the least friction with the people whose opinion we most need. That is exactly what Festus did, and it nearly killed the apostle to the Gentiles.

But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.

Festus reports the appeal as an inconvenience he has had to accommodate. He does not know he is describing the mechanism of a promise. Two years earlier, in a barracks cell in Jerusalem, the Lord had stood by Paul in the dark and told him he must testify at Rome (23:11). This sentence, in a governor's briefing, is that promise moving one more stage down the road — and the man saying it thinks he is explaining a procedural difficulty.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I would like to hear the man myself.

The Greek is an imperfect — eboulomen — and it carries a history: I have been wanting to. This is not a passing whim. Agrippa has been meaning to hear Paul for some time.

And a reader of Luke's first volume will feel the floor shift, because a Herod has said this before.

Of Herod Antipas, when reports of Jesus reached the palace, Luke wrote: and he sought to see him (Luke 9:9). He kept seeking, for months. And on the morning of the crucifixion he finally got his wish — Pilate sent Jesus across to him — and Luke says he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer (Luke 23:8–9).

The most terrible silence in the Gospels. A Herod finally gets his audience with the Son of God, asks his questions, and receives nothing at all. Curiosity had had its years to become something else and had refused, and when the moment came there was nothing left to say to him.

Now the last Herod says the same sentence about the same message, and the outcome is different: Tomorrow, said he, you will hear him. Agrippa will get his hearing, and Paul will not be silent. He will give the longest and most personal defence in the book, tailored precisely to this man — King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe (26:27) — and it will bring him closer than any other ruler in Acts comes, close enough to say the words in a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?

That is mercy. Antipas mocked, and got silence. Agrippa is merely curious, and God sends him the finest preacher of the age with a message shaped for his exact history and knowledge.

But be careful with the comfort in that, because the next chapter records what Agrippa did with it, and the answer is nothing. He heard the whole thing, agreed it was harmless, remarked to Festus that the man could have been released, and went home a king.

Curiosity about Christ is a real gift and it is not conversion. There are people who enjoy the subject, follow the arguments, would happily sit through the sermon and discuss it intelligently afterwards, and have never once been to Christ for mercy. Agrippa wanted to hear the man. He got exactly what he asked for, and it was not what he needed, because he never asked for what he needed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Five verses of stagecraft, and Luke stages them deliberately.

The room (vv. 23–24). Agrippa and Bernice enter with great pomp — phantasia, the word behind our fantasy, meaning a display put on to be looked at. With them: the military tribunes of the garrison and the prominent men of Caesarea. The whole visible power of the province is in one hall. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in — one passive verb, and a set of chains he will mention himself the next day (26:29). Festus opens by telling the assembly that the Jewish people have been demanding this man's death.

The empty file (vv. 25–26). And in the same breath he says he found nothing deserving it. Which leaves the governor in an absurd position, and he admits it: he is shipping a prisoner to the imperial court with nothing to write in the covering letter. The word he uses for the emperor is kyrios, my lord — the ordinary courtesy of the empire, and the exact word the man in chains reserves for somebody else. Two lordships named in one sentence, and only one of them visible to the man speaking.

The last line (v. 27). It seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him. He knows it is unreasonable. He says so in front of the king and the tribunes and the leading men of the city, and then he does it anyway.

So the chapter closes on a bureaucrat's complaint about paperwork — which is precisely what will produce chapter 26, the fullest account of the risen Christ that any Roman official ever heard.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus told his disciples that they would be dragged before kings and governors for his name's sake, and then said something startling about it: this will be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). Not your ordeal — your opportunity. Acts 25 is that promise arriving in a form nobody would have designed. The hostility of the Sanhedrin, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king, and an administrative problem with a covering letter combine to assemble the entire ruling class of a Roman province in one room and sit them down in front of a preacher.

Note who did the assembling. Not the church, which had no power to convene such a gathering and no money to hire the hall. The opposition built the platform, paid for it, filled it with the most important people available, and then handed the prisoner the floor.

The Reformed instinct here is neither triumphalism nor passivity. God is not obliged to use worldly power, and he frequently works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he does use the machinery of the age, he does not ask its permission and he does not need its cooperation to be willing. Festus wanted a charge sheet. What he arranged was an evangelistic meeting for the aristocracy of Judea.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. The king had the title, Bernice had the jewels, the tribunes had the swords, the leading men had the money, and Festus had the authority to decide what happened next. Paul had a chain and the floor. Within a day the man with the chain had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to deflect him with a joke.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and the principle does not require it. It shows up in smaller rooms — the meeting where you are plainly the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the eccentric position, the conversation where everyone else has the confidence and the vocabulary and the standing. The instinct is to wait for a better platform, one where you are taken more seriously. Paul never got a better platform than the one his enemies built for him, and he did not ask for one. He used the floor he was given, in the clothes he was wearing, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp…

Luke's word for the pomp is phantasia. It is the root behind our word fantasy, and it means a showing, a display, an appearance put on to be looked at. He could have chosen any word for grandeur. He picked the one that means it is all surface.

Fill in the room, because Luke expects the reader to see it. A king and his sister in full Herodian state. The military tribunes of the Caesarean garrison in dress uniform. The prominent men of the city — the magistrates, the money, the people who mattered in the provincial capital. The governor of Judea presiding. This is the entire visible power structure of the province assembled in one hall.

Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.

One passive verb. He does not enter; he is brought. And he is in chains — he says so himself the next day, in the most gracious sentence in Acts, when he tells this room he wishes every one of them were as he is except for these chains (26:29).

So: all the display on one side of the room, and a short, worn, shackled man on the other.

And within twenty-four hours the prisoner will be the only person present who can say why he is there. Festus has just admitted he cannot. Agrippa has come to find out. The tribunes and the leading citizens are spectators at a hearing whose subject nobody in authority understands. The one man in the room who knows exactly what is going on is the one in irons.

You see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

Festus is overstating — the whole Jewish people is the language of a man dramatising his own difficulty, and thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem would have said otherwise. But look at what he has just entered into the record in front of the province's assembled nobility. The demand was for a man's death. And the governor is about to say, in the next breath, that he found no ground for it whatever.

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death… But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him.

Take the absurdity plainly first, because Luke means it to be felt. A Roman governor is putting a prisoner on a ship to the imperial court, and he cannot say what the man is accused of. He has held hearings. He has heard the prosecution. He has consulted the local expert. And the file is empty, because there is nothing to put in it.

Every authority that has examined Paul has found no crime — Gallio at Corinth on an earlier charge (18:14–15), Lysias in his letter (23:29), Festus at the hearing (25:18), and Festus again now — and Agrippa will add his voice tomorrow: this man could have been set free (26:32). Luke never once tells the reader what to conclude. He simply files the verdicts.

Then there is the phrase that a Christian reader should not walk past: my lord.

The Greek is kyrios. Festus uses it of Nero as naturally as breathing — it was becoming the ordinary courtesy for the emperor, and within a generation Domitian would demand to be addressed as dominus et deus, lord and god. In this room, on this afternoon, kyrios means the man on the throne in Rome.

And standing in front of him in chains is a man for whom that word means somebody else entirely. Paul had written to Corinth that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 8:6), and to Philippi that God has given him the name that is above every name, so that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil. 2:9–11). He is being shipped to Caesar's court for the specific purpose of saying so.

Two lordships are named in a single sentence, and the governor can only see one of them.

Consider the other. Nero was lord of the world, and he held it for fourteen years, and he died by his own hand at thirty with the senate declaring him a public enemy. Jesus Christ was lord of nothing anyone could see — no throne, no legion, no province, a borrowed tomb — and he is Lord tonight, and will be Lord when the last empire has gone the way of that one. The title Festus gives Nero in passing is a courtesy. The title Paul gives to Jesus in a set of chains is a fact, and the whole creation is running down toward the day when every tongue in it, including the governor's and the king's and the emperor's, says so out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.

The chapter ends on a bureaucrat's complaint about paperwork, and Luke could not have chosen a better last line.

Festus means it narrowly: the covering letter needs a charge, and he has not got one. But say the sentence again and hear what it actually concedes. It is unreasonable to send a prisoner without indicating the charges — and he is sending him. He knows the thing is unreasonable. He says so, out loud, in front of the king and the tribunes and the leading men of Caesarea, and then he does it anyway.

Every authority that has touched this case has now said the same thing in its own words, and not one of them has released him. That is the honest shape of it, and it is worth refusing the tidy version: Paul is innocent, everyone with the power to judge knows he is innocent, and none of them sets him free. The system did not malfunction. It worked exactly as designed, and it still could not do the right thing, because at every stage there was somebody who needed a favour.

And yet.

Two years earlier the Lord had stood beside him in the dark and said you must testify also in Rome (23:11). Here is what that promise looks like from ground level, at the end of chapter 25: a governor who cannot fill in a form. Not an angel, not an earthquake, not an acquittal. A procedural embarrassment in a provincial capital, which will put Paul on a ship at imperial expense and carry him to the one city he had been promised.

Both things are true at the same time, and the Christian life is mostly lived in the overlap. This is a real injustice, and it is not being pretended away; and it is also the exact mechanism of a promise, and it is not being frustrated for a moment.

Festus wanted something to write. Tomorrow he will get chapter 26 — the fullest account of the risen Christ that any Roman official ever heard — because a man needed to fill in a form correctly.

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the last defence Paul makes in Acts and the fullest, and it is the only one he is allowed to finish — almost. Four previous hearings gave him a mob, a brawl, a governor angling for a bribe, and a governor out of his depth. Here at last is a hearer who knows the Hebrew Scriptures, and Paul calls himself a fortunate man for it.

The request (vv. 1–3). A prisoner in irons makes the orator's gesture and asks one thing of the king: listen to me patiently — makrothumos, the long-tempered patience Scripture usually ascribes to God. What follows will not be a legal defence and Paul knows it; it needs time, and impatience is the commonest way of never dealing with Christ at all.

The credentials (vv. 4–8). His life is public record, and the prosecution will not testify because the evidence helps him. He belonged to the strictest party there was, and he says I have lived as a Pharisee without a word of disowning it — he never thought of following Jesus as leaving Israel. Then he turns to the whole room with one question: why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? If God made everything from nothing, one grave is not the hard part. The resistance was never really about power.

The persecutor (vv. 9–11). He volunteers the worst of himself to the most important man who will ever hear him: prisons, votes cast for executions in the plural, torture to force believers to curse the name — the very test Rome itself would later adopt. And the phrase in raging fury is built on the root mainomai, which Festus will throw at Paul in v. 24. Paul has already located the madness in this story, and it was not on the Damascus road.

The road (vv. 12–18). Midday, a light brighter than the Syrian sun, and a voice speaking Aramaic — the glorified Christ still speaks like a man from Nazareth. Unique to this telling is the goad: you cannot kick against something you have never felt, so the persecution had been costing the persecutor all along. Then the commission, the fullest in Scripture — opened eyes, darkness to light, Satan's dominion to God, forgiveness, a place among the sanctified — which is the Servant's own task from Isaiah 42, handed to Saul of Tarsus.

The obedience (vv. 19–23). Twenty-five years, two continents, five floggings, a stoning and three shipwrecks, summarised as I was not disobedient. He was kept by help that came from outside (epikouria, reinforcements), he preached the same gospel to small and great, and he added nothing to Moses and the prophets: a suffering Christ, the first to rise and stay risen, light for Jews and Gentiles alike.

The interruption and the appeal (vv. 24–29). Festus shouts that too many books have unhinged him — the oldest way of not answering an argument is to diagnose it. Paul answers with sophrosyne, the exact antonym, and with the claim that carries Christian apologetics still: this has not been done in a corner. Then he turns to Agrippa and closes every exit — do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe — and the king escapes into a joke about becoming a Christian. Paul refuses the exit, prays aloud for his judges in open court, and wishes them everything he has except for these chains.

The verdict (vv. 30–32). Nobody answers him. The king rises, and the standing is the answer. In the corridor they agree he has done nothing deserving death — one more such finding — and Agrippa delivers the line that closes the chapter: this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. Legally true. But the appeal was not a blunder; it was the road to a promise made in the dark two years earlier.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The theological spine of this speech is that Christianity is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the one question that would settle it — do you believe the prophets? The charge is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room and his accusers have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isa. 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Dan. 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isa. 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish settlement; that is precisely what his opponents wanted, and precisely what he would not give them.

Underneath it lies the doctrine this whole chapter is a case study in: grace that is entirely from God's side. Nothing in Paul's account belongs to Paul. He was not seeking, dissatisfied, or badly taught; he was convinced, exactingly trained, and in a raging fury, riding hard in the opposite direction — and he was stopped, blinded, named, and commissioned. He did not find Christ. Christ appeared to him. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness in the same breath. Repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20). The works are never the root; they are the fruit, exactly as Paul argued at length elsewhere (Eph. 2:8–10). A sovereign work of grace produces a visibly different life, and a life with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the finest presentation of the gospel any ruler in the New Testament ever received, delivered by the ablest preacher of the age, in his own theological vocabulary, by a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not argue with it. He did not refute a single point. He made a joke, stood up, walked out, and remarked in the corridor that the prisoner had done nothing wrong.

Now: Notice how the refusal was actually shaped, because almost nobody declines Christ the way we imagine. There was no debate, no crisis, no considered rejection. There was wit, and then there was standing up, and the standing up was the answer. That is how it usually goes — a subject changed with a light remark, an evening that ran late, a genuine intention to come back to it. If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa had none worth stating. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way five or six times, and whether anything is actually going to be different about the sixth. Paul's one request at the start of the speech was that the king would not become impatient before he had finished. It is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have permission to speak for yourself.

Paul has been waiting more than two years for this sentence.

Count what he has been given up to now. A mob on a staircase that heard him out until one word and then tried to tear him apart. A council that dissolved into a brawl before evidence was called. A governor who understood the case well enough to be frightened by it and sent for him repeatedly hoping for a bribe. A second governor who admitted he was out of his depth and proposed the one venue that would have killed him. Four hearings, and not one of them was a hearing.

Now a king with a working knowledge of the Hebrew Scriptures says: speak.

Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense.

It is the orator's gesture, the formal opening of a set speech, and Luke expects us to see it. But remember what is on that hand. Paul will mention it himself before the afternoon is out — except for these chains (v. 29). A prisoner in irons makes the gesture of a free rhetorician in front of the assembled nobility of the province, and nobody stops him.

I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today.

The word is makarios — the word of the Beatitudes, blessed, happy, well off. It is not the ordinary courtroom flattery, and it is worth pausing on, because Paul is on trial for his life and has just called himself a fortunate man.

Why? Not because Agrippa is powerful; Paul has stood in front of more powerful men without saying this. Because Agrippa can follow the argument. Here at last is someone who knows what a prophet is, who knows what Israel has been waiting for, who will not hear the word resurrection as a piece of provincial nonsense. Paul is not counting his chances of acquittal. He is counting his chances of being understood about Jesus Christ.

That is worth holding up against our own instinctive arithmetic. Most of us measure a day by what it cost us and what it returned. Paul has been in custody for two years, is being tried on a charge nobody can name, and is going to be shipped to Nero — and his verdict on the afternoon is that he is a fortunate man, because someone competent is finally going to hear about Christ. If that reordering seems extreme, it is only because it is complete.

Who were Agrippa and Bernice? Herod Agrippa II, great-grandson of Herod the Great, ruled territories north and east of Galilee and had the Roman right to appoint the high priest, so Festus wanted his advice on a Jewish matter. Bernice was his sister. Festus had recently replaced Felix as governor.

One note for the reader, since the phrase recurs: the accusations of the Jews. Luke's shorthand throughout Acts means the Jerusalem leadership who brought the case — not the Jewish people as such, and certainly not Jews as a race. The man speaking is himself a Jew, defending himself as a Pharisee, arguing from the Hebrew prophets, and about to say that his one grief is that his own nation has not seen it. This book has been misread down the centuries to justify appalling things. It does not say them.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.

Paul names the qualification precisely: customs and controversies. Agrippa knows the practices, and — more useful still — he knows the arguments. He knows that Pharisees and Sadducees have been at odds over the resurrection for generations. He knows what messianic expectation is and why it matters. He has appointed high priests. He is, in the exact sense, competent to hear this case.

And so Paul makes a request that tells you what kind of speech is coming: I beg you to listen to me patiently.

The word is makrothumos — long-tempered. It is the word the New Testament normally translates as patient or longsuffering, and it is used most often of God himself, who is slow to anger and endures with people for a very long time. Paul asks the king for a small share of that quality: do not become irritated with me before I have finished.

It is an honest request, because what follows is not a legal defence and Paul knows it. He will barely address the charges. He will instead tell a king the story of how the risen Jesus stopped him on a road, and then argue from Moses and the prophets that this is precisely what Israel's Scriptures had promised. That takes time. It cannot be done in a soundbite, and it cannot be done at all if the hearer has already decided how long he is prepared to give it.

Which is a quietly searching thing, because impatience is the most common and least examined reason people never deal with Christ. Not hostility — hostility at least engages. Impatience. The subject is granted about ninety seconds, and ninety seconds is not enough for anything that matters, and so the verdict is reached on a case that was never actually heard.

Paul is not asking Agrippa to agree. He is asking him to stay in the room long enough for the argument to be made. It is the only thing he asks of him, and it is the thing most people will not give.

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
My manner of life from my youth… is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify…

Paul opens his case with the public record, and the phrasing is deliberately awkward for his accusers.

His life was not lived privately. He was raised in Jerusalem, trained under the most famous rabbi of the age, and made his reputation in front of witnesses who are still alive. Anyone in the Sanhedrin could confirm every word of it. That is the force of the conditional: if they are willing to testify. The prosecution has the evidence and will not produce it, because the evidence helps the defendant.

They cannot say Paul left Judaism because he never understood it. He understood it better than they did.

According to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.

The word is akribestaten — the superlative of akribes, meaning exact, precise, no margin of error. It is the same root Paul used on the barracks steps when he said he was educated according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers (22:3). He is not claiming to have been religious in a general way. He is claiming to have belonged to the most exacting school available, and to have belonged to it thoroughly.

Notice too that he does not disown it. He said the same to the council — I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees (23:6) — and years after his conversion he still wrote it down in a letter as a plain fact about himself (Phil. 3:5). Paul never regarded following Jesus as leaving Israel. He regarded it as Israel's hope arriving.

And here is why the biography matters more than it looks. There is a comfortable explanation for conversion that every generation reaches for: he did not really know what he was giving up. He was badly taught. He was unhappy. He was young. Something was missing.

None of it is available here, and Paul is closing the exits one by one. He had the best training in the nation. He had status, momentum, and the approval of the men who mattered. He was not drifting and he was not searching — he was riding a career, hard, in the opposite direction, and he was winning.

Whatever happened to him on that road, it was not the collapse of a man who had run out of alternatives. It was the interruption of a man who had none of the usual reasons to be interrupted.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers… And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!

Paul puts the whole absurdity of his position into one sentence, and it is worth letting it land before the exposition begins.

He is standing in chains, prosecuted by the leadership of his own nation, on a charge that comes down to this: he believes what Israel has been praying for. Not a rival hope. Not an import. The promise made by God to the fathers — the thing the twelve tribes have been reaching toward, in synagogue after synagogue, morning and evening, for centuries.

Note the detail he chooses: as they earnestly worship night and day. He is not scoring points off his accusers' piety. He grants it, warmly and completely. These are devout people. The prayers are real. The waiting has been real for a very long time.

And that is exactly what makes the charge so strange, and so sad. The accusation, laid out plainly, is that Paul has found what Israel has been asking for, and is being tried by Israel for finding it.

It is the oldest and most human of failures, and it is not confined to first-century Jerusalem. A thing can be prayed for so long that the praying becomes the settled shape of life, and the arrival of the answer feels less like fulfilment than like disruption. Paul is not accusing them of wanting the wrong thing. He is telling a king that they got it, and did not recognise it, because it came in a form that cost them something.

This 'hope... the promise made to the fathers' gathers up the great threads of Israel's expectation that run all through Acts, each of which Paul insists is fulfilled in Jesus. For the reader who wants to follow them: the resurrection hope is the heart of it — Paul says again and again that this is what he is really on trial for (23:6; 24:15, 21; 26:8; and see how it split Athens, 17:32); the coming of the promised Messiah, 'what God promised to the fathers' now fulfilled in Jesus (13:23, 32–33; the Abrahamic promise, 3:25–26); and the redemption of Israel, 'the hope of Israel' for which Paul wears his very chain (28:20; the disciples' own question about restoring the kingdom, 1:6–7, and the present-and-future kingdom discussed at 20:25). All three are finally one hope, and Paul's whole defence is that Israel's centuries-long longing has found its Yes in the risen Christ.

And the hope itself is rooted in the Old Testament of the twelve tribes who 'earnestly worship night and day' (v. 7). The resurrection was promised there — 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' (Dan. 12:2; cf. Job 19:25–27; Isa. 26:19) — and by Paul's day it was woven into daily Jewish prayer: the second blessing of the Amidah still praises God as the One 'who revives the dead,' and the Mishnah counted denying the resurrection a grave error (Sanhedrin 10:1).

The Messiah's coming is the 'promise to the fathers' itself — Abraham's offspring in whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 22:18) and David's everlasting throne (2 Sam. 7:12–16), sung by the prophets (Isa. 9:6–7; Jer. 23:5; Mic. 5:2). And the redemption of Israel is the prophets' great restoration hope (Isa. 40–66; Jer. 31; Ezek. 36–37), prayed for to this day in the petitions for the ingathering of the exiles, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the Branch of David. Paul's claim is simply that this whole age-old, daily-prayed hope has its Yes in the risen Jesus.

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead?

Paul turns, mid-speech, and asks a question — and note that the Greek is plural. Any of you. He is no longer speaking only to the king. He has turned to the whole hall: the tribunes, the leading men of Caesarea, the governor. He puts one question to a room full of pagans and a Jewish monarch, and then goes straight back to his story without waiting for a reply.

The question is not a debating trick. It is asking people to state their actual objection.

Because think about what is being claimed and where the difficulty really sits. If there is a God at all — a God who made the heavens and the earth out of nothing, who spoke light into existence, who assembled every living thing from dust — then reassembling one dead man is not the hard part. It is nowhere near the hard part. A God who can start life from nothing can certainly restart it.

So the resurrection is not, in fact, being rejected on the grounds of power. Nobody in that room believed in a God who could create the universe and would then find one grave beyond him. The resistance is somewhere else entirely.

Here is the test, and it is worth running slowly, because it applies as much in a modern sitting room as in a Caesarean audience hall. When someone says the resurrection is impossible, ask what would follow if it were true. Not whether it is likely — what would follow. Because if a dead man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then he is who he said he is, and the universe has an owner, and everyone in it has an appointment. Most of the case against the resurrection is not an argument about evidence. It is a preference about consequences, wearing an argument's clothes.

Paul knew that from the inside, which is why the very next sentence is about himself.

I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

He does not say he was indifferent, or uninformed, or had never looked into it. He says he was convinced — and that he believed opposing Jesus was a duty. He was not sinning against his conscience; his conscience was fully engaged, and it was pointing the wrong way.

That is a sobering thing to sit with. A man can be sincere, disciplined, devout, thoroughly persuaded, entirely at peace with himself — and be at war with God. Sincerity is not a defence. Paul's was total, and it made him more dangerous rather than less.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I not only locked up many of the saints in prison… but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them.

He is speaking to a king, and he tells him this.

Nothing compelled it. He is on trial; the charge is stirring up riots; his own criminal past is not in evidence and no prosecutor has raised it. Paul volunteers the worst thing about himself to the most important man who will ever hear him speak — and he does it in detail.

Take the detail, because each phrase costs him something.

Many of the saints. He calls his victims saints. The people he hunted are, he now knows, the holy ones of God, and he uses their proper title in the middle of his confession.

When they were put to death I cast my vote against them. The Greek is a voting idiom — literally, I cast down a pebble, the stone dropped into an urn to register a verdict. Whether Paul was formally a member of the Sanhedrin (which some argue would mean he had been married) or whether this is simply the language of registered approval, commentators differ and the text does not settle it. What the text does settle is the plural. When they were put to death. Stephen was not the only one. Paul has more than one execution on his conscience, and Luke has told us about exactly one of them.

I tried to make them blaspheme. The verb is imperfect — he kept trying, repeatedly, as a method. This is torture applied to force Christians to curse the name of Christ. It is worth knowing that this became the standard imperial test: some eighty years later a Roman governor in Bithynia would write to the emperor explaining that he released anyone who would curse Christ, since none of the real Christians could be made to do it. Paul used that technique against the church long before the empire adopted it.

In raging fury. Here Luke plants something the English cannot easily show. The word is emmainomenos, from mainomai — to rave, to be out of one's mind. Hold on to it, because in thirteen verses Festus is going to shout Paul, you are out of your mind, using that same root (v. 24). Paul has already answered him. The madness in this story was not the preaching of a risen Christ. It was a brilliant, devout, exactingly trained man in a raging fury, dragging women out of their houses in the name of God.

So why say any of it out loud, in a courtroom, to a king?

Because Paul is not building a character reference; he is building an argument, and his own biography is the evidence. Something turned that man into this one. No education did it, no disappointment did it, no gradual softening did it — three verses from now he will name what did.

And there is a pastoral turn here that a reader should not miss. A man who has genuinely received mercy loses the need to manage his own reputation. Paul can say the worst about himself calmly, in public, to power, without flinching or excusing — not because the sin was small, but because the pardon is settled. People who are still uncertain of their forgiveness cannot do this. They edit. The freedom to tell the truth about your own past is one of the quieter proofs that grace has actually landed.
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests.

The word for commission is epitrope — a delegated authority, a warrant. Paul is establishing that this was not a private vendetta. He was on official business, carrying the paperwork of the Jerusalem establishment, doing exactly what the men now prosecuting him had authorised him to do.

That is a barbed thing to say in front of a Roman governor. The prosecution's own institution issued the warrants.

At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun.

Two details in this telling, and both are chosen for the man in the chair. The first he had given the crowd too (22:6); the second is new.

At midday. Not dusk, not a bad night's sleep, not a lonely vigil. Noon, on a public road, in Syria, where the sun at that hour is punishing. This is the least atmospheric moment of the day — the hour when nothing looks mysterious and everything is flatly, mercilessly visible.

Brighter than the sun. Paul is standing under the fiercest natural light his world knew, and something outshone it. It is a small phrase and it makes a large claim: what stopped him was not a trick of heat or exhaustion, and it was not of this order of things at all.

He is arguing like a witness rather than a mystic. Ask the men who were with me; they saw the light too. Whatever else is in dispute, something objective happened on that road at noon in front of company.

This is the third time Luke has told this story — first as narrator (9:1–19), then in Paul's own words to a Jerusalem mob (22:3–21), and now to a king. The differences between the three tellings are real, and they have been worked through where they arise, at chapter 9 and chapter 22; there is no need to re-argue them here. What is worth noticing is why this version is shaped as it is. To a Jewish crowd Paul made Ananias the hinge, because a devout man of good reputation in Damascus was everything to that audience. To a king, Ananias disappears entirely, and the commission comes straight from the mouth of the risen Christ on the road.

Not because Ananias has been edited out of history, but because Paul is doing what every honest preacher does: telling the same true story to the person actually in front of him, and giving that person the part of it he most needs to hear. A king needs to know who gave the orders.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language…

Three things in this verse are unique to this telling, and every one of them is worth its weight.

We had all fallen. The relationship between this and the account at 9:7, where Paul's companions are standing, is a genuine question and it has been dealt with at chapter 9 — the short of it being that a party knocked flat by a light at noon does not stay flat, and Luke is not writing a police report. It is settled there; it does not need re-arguing here.

In the Hebrew language. This is the detail Paul saved for a Jewish king, and it is astonishing if you slow down over it. The risen and glorified Christ, enthroned at the right hand of God, blazing brighter than the Syrian noon — speaks Aramaic. The everyday language of Galilean villages and Jerusalem streets. He did not shed his humanity at the resurrection or exchange his mother tongue for the language of heaven. The man who is Lord of all still speaks like a man from Nazareth.

It is hard for you to kick against the goads.

A goad was a long pole tipped with iron, used to drive oxen. If the animal resented it and lashed backwards, its own kick drove the point deeper. The proverb was well known in the Greek world — it appears in Euripides and in Aeschylus — so the tribunes and the leading men of Caesarea, listening in, would have caught it instantly. The Lord speaks Aramaic to Saul and quotes a Greek proverb in the same breath, and both halves of the room can follow him.

But sit with what the proverb actually says about Saul, because it is the most personally revealing sentence in the chapter.

You cannot kick against a goad you have never felt. The image only works if something had already been prodding him — persistently, for some time — and he had been driving himself into it. The risen Christ tells Saul, in front of witnesses, that the persecution had been hurting the persecutor.

Scripture does not say what the goads were, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise. But Luke has been laying things in front of us for seven chapters and it is hard not to notice them: a face like an angel's in a courtroom; a dying man praying for his killers, out loud, while Saul held the coats; people who would not curse the name however hard they were pressed; and behind it all the uncomfortable possibility, for a man trained to read Moses and the prophets exactly, that these people might be right.

He would have called all of that noise. It was a goad.

And here is where it lands on the reader, because this is not only Saul's experience. There are people who have been arguing with something for years — a verse that will not leave, a memory of a Christian who was inexplicably kind, a suspicion at three in the morning that the case for meaninglessness is weaker than they say in daylight. It is very easy to treat that as an irritation to be managed and kicked at harder.

The Lord's word to Saul is that the kicking is what is doing the damage. The goad was never the injury. It was the mercy.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you, Lord? … I am Jesus whom you are persecuting.

Saul asks the shortest and most important question a human being can ask, and he gets a name in reply.

Not a title. Not a description of divine glory. A name belonging to a man from a village in Galilee whom Saul knew perfectly well to be dead — and whose followers he was at that moment travelling to arrest.

Whom you are persecuting. Present tense, and note the object. Not whose people. The Lord of glory says that to lay hands on a believer in Damascus is to lay hands on him. It is the seed of everything Paul would later write about the church as the body of Christ, and since it belongs to the road rather than to this hearing, it is worked out where Paul first told it (22:7). The point for Agrippa is simpler and harder: the man you all agree was executed is speaking, and he is taking the arrests personally.

But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose.

The words are Ezekiel's. Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you (Ezek. 2:1) — spoken to a man flat on his face before the glory of God, who is then sent to a rebellious people. Paul is being commissioned in the language of the prophets, and a king who knows his Scriptures would hear it.

Then the two words that define the rest of his life: a servant and witness.

The first is hyperetes — an assistant, a subordinate officer, a man under orders. He does not choose the course; he does what he is told.

The second is martys — a witness. A witness has no authority of his own and no freedom to improve the account. He reports what he saw. It is the plainest possible description of a preacher, and it is the reason Paul could say later that he had determined to know nothing among them except Christ crucified. He was not at liberty to be original.

And there is a phrase at the end that is easy to miss: to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you. The Damascus road was not the last of it. There would be more — the night vision at Corinth, the Lord standing by him in the barracks, the angel on the ship, and whatever it was he could not put into words (2 Cor. 12:2–4). Christ was not commissioning him from a distance and leaving him to it.

(On the much-debated question of when in this Damascus-road encounter Paul was actually born again — whether he is already regenerate as he answers 'Who are you, Lord?' — see the honest discussion at 22:10: the short of it is that Scripture does not pin the moment, the marks of a heart already being turned are plainly present, and the certain thing is not the when but the who — sovereign grace seized the persecutor.)

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you.

Read the promise carefully, because it is not the promise we would have written. The word is exairoumenos — rescuing, plucking out. Not protecting you from. Not keeping you clear of. Rescuing you out of, which presupposes being in.

And that is exactly how it went. He was stoned at Lystra and left for dead, flogged five times by his own people, beaten with rods three times, shipwrecked, imprisoned, and eventually executed. The Lord promised him rescue, and every single rescue happened, and not one of them was an exemption. Paul was delivered out of things, never spared them.

Then the commission itself, and it is the fullest statement of it anywhere in Scripture — five clauses, and every one of them deserves plain words.

To open their eyes. Not to inform people, but to make blind people see. The assumption underneath is that the human problem is not primarily a shortage of information. Paul had all the information and was blind.

To turn from darkness to light. A change of realm, not of opinion.

From the power of Satan to God. This is the clause modern readers skip, and it should not be skipped. The New Testament says people are not neutral: they are held. Not usually in anything dramatic — mostly in the ordinary machinery of self-interest, appetite, fear of what people think, and the settled conviction that one's life is one's own. It is a real dominion with a real ruler, and getting out of it is not a matter of trying harder.

That they may receive forgiveness of sins. Receive — the posture of someone with open hands, not someone settling an account.

And a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me. A place. An inheritance, a share, a seat at the table with the holy ones — and the ground of it is faith in Christ, stated at the end so nobody can mistake what the whole chain hangs on.

And notice where this language comes from. a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon — that is Isaiah, describing the task of the Servant of the LORD (Isa. 42:6–7). Christ takes the Servant's own commission and hands it to Saul of Tarsus. What the Messiah was sent to do, he now sends this man to do in his name.

Consider what the risen Christ says he is in the business of doing. He opens eyes that have been shut since birth. He fetches people out of the dark — not by improving them, but by moving them, out of one dominion and into another, against the will of the power that held them. He forgives, freely and finally, the sort of man who had been dragging his followers out of their homes. And then he gives that man a share in the inheritance of the saints, as though he had never done any of it. Not one clause of that is achievable from below. The whole chain, from the opened eye to the place at the table, is the work of the Lord Jesus Christ upon people who were doing nothing but resisting him, and there is no other explanation for a single Christian who has ever lived.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.

It is one of the great understatements in Scripture, and the understatement is the point.

Set the sentence against what it is summarising. Roughly twenty-five years. Three missionary journeys across Cyprus, Asia, Macedonia, and Greece. Churches planted in a dozen cities. Five floggings of thirty-nine lashes from his own people, three beatings with Roman rods, one stoning that left him for dead, three shipwrecks, a night and a day adrift, constant danger from rivers, bandits, his own countrymen, Gentiles, false brothers; hunger, thirst, cold, sleeplessness; and daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Cor. 11:23–28).

I was not disobedient. That is his own summary of it, offered to a king who asked what he had been doing.

There is no sense of achievement in it, and no self-pity either. Just a man reporting that he did as he was told.

But declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles.

Trace the geography and you are looking at the outline of the book. Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). Paul's career is the programme of Acts 1:8 walked out by one pair of feet.

That they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.

Here is the message, and it is worth noticing how ordinary it sounds and how carefully it is built. Repent — change your mind. Turn to God — change your direction. And then do things that match.

Now, this needs a guard, because it is the apostle of justification by faith saying that repentance must produce deeds, and someone will hear a contradiction. There is none. Paul is not saying the deeds earn the turning; he spent whole letters demolishing that. He is saying the deeds demonstrate it. By grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works — and then, in the very next breath, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand (Eph. 2:8–10). The works are not the root. They are the fruit, and a tree with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.

Which turns into a plain test, and it is more searching than a general resolution to do better. Repentance in the New Testament is specific. It has an object. So: name one. Not a category — a thing. A conversation you have been avoiding because you were in the wrong. Money that is not yours. A habit conducted privately. A person you have written off. What is the deed that would be in keeping with the repentance you would say you have?

If nothing comes to mind at all, that is worth sitting with rather than hurrying past.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God.

Paul puts the cause plainly: this — the Gentile mission, the opened eyes, the place among the sanctified given to outsiders by faith — is why they tried to kill him. Not the resurrection in the abstract. The resurrection with the door left open.

Then a phrase worth stopping over: the help that comes from God.

The word is epikouria, and it is rare — it appears only here in the New Testament. In ordinary Greek it carried a military flavour: the aid an ally brings, reinforcements arriving for a position under pressure. Paul does not say he has been resilient, or that he has coped, or that he has a strong constitution. He says help arrived from outside.

And to this day gathers up an extraordinary list. The basket over the Damascus wall. The plot at Jerusalem. The stoning at Lystra. The prison at Philippi. The riot at Ephesus. The ambush at Corinth. The mob in the temple court. The whipping post. The forty men and their oath. Every one of those should have ended the story, and Paul's account of why it did not is one word: help came.

That is a truer picture of the Christian life than the one we usually carry. Perseverance does not feel like strength of character from the inside. It feels like being kept — like arriving at the end of another week still believing, and being unable to identify a single heroic decision that accounts for it.

Testifying both to small and great.

He is standing in front of a king, a governor, the tribunes, and the aristocracy of a Roman capital, and he mentions the small first. That order is not accidental in a man who had said the same things to a jailer at midnight, to a slave girl in the street, and to a group of women at a riverside.

The gospel Paul preached to Agrippa is the gospel he preached to the man who guarded him. There was no upgraded version for the room with the tribunes in it.

Saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass.

And this is the hinge of his whole defence. Paul's claim is not that he has founded something. It is that he has not added a syllable. Everything he preaches, he insists, was already in the books Agrippa's own priests read out every Sabbath. The charge against him is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room, and his accusers are the ones who have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

And consider what it means that they were all speaking of him. Moses at the burning bush and the passover lamb; the prophet like Moses yet to be raised up; the seed of Abraham in whom the nations would be blessed; David's son on a throne that would not end; the child born in Bethlehem, too small a town to matter; the Servant with no beauty that we should desire him, despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own, silent before his shearers, numbered with the criminals, and afterward seeing the light of life and being satisfied.

Some thousand years of writing, by men who mostly never met each other, in Hebrew and Aramaic — and all of it converging on one week in Jerusalem and one man walking out of a tomb. The whole library was about him. Every promise God ever made has its Yes in Jesus Christ, and there has never been a word spoken from heaven that did not, in the end, point to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.

This is the summit of the speech, and Paul has built the whole thing to land here. Three claims, tightly packed, every one of them contested.

That the Christ must suffer. The must is doing enormous work. For most first-century Jewish expectation, a suffering Messiah was not merely unexpected — it came close to being a contradiction in terms. The Messiah was the one who ended suffering, not the one who absorbed it. Paul says the suffering was never an accident or a setback; it was the appointment. The Lord himself made the same point on the Emmaus road: Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26).

The first to rise from the dead. This needs a careful word, because it is easy to trip over. Others had been raised before — the widow's son, Jairus's daughter, Lazarus. But every one of them died again; they were returned to the life they had, and each of those graves was eventually reopened. Christ is the first to rise and stay risen — out the far side of death permanently, in a body that cannot die. That is why Paul elsewhere calls him the firstfruits (1 Cor. 15:20): not the only sheaf, but the first of a harvest, and the guarantee that the rest is coming.

He would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles. And here Paul says the thing that has been getting him beaten for twenty years, and says it to a king, in a room full of Romans, without softening it.

And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, ‘Paul, you are out of your mind.’

He shouts. The governor of Judea, presiding, loses his composure in public and interrupts a prisoner mid-sentence — and note precisely where. Not at the light for the Gentiles, which no Roman would object to. At the resurrection.

His diagnosis is almost affectionate: your great learning is driving you out of your mind — literally, the many books. Festus has decided that Paul is a scholar who has read himself into a delusion. It is the oldest way of not answering an argument: locate a cause for the belief and you need not examine the reasons for it. He is not saying Paul is wrong. He is saying Paul is unwell, which is easier.

What did Paul mean by 'proclaim light'? Not a vague glow of 'enlightenment,' but something concrete: God's saving rescue dawning on a world sunk in darkness. Paul is not coining an image; he is quoting Isaiah. The very phrase — light 'to our people and to the Gentiles' — is the Servant Songs' language: 'I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' (Isa. 49:6); 'a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners' (Isa. 42:6–7). In Isaiah, 'light' stands with three things — salvation, the opening of blind eyes, the freeing of prisoners. That is what the light is: God's saving deliverance, sight for the blind, rescue for those in the dark.

And we are not guessing — the lines converge. Paul had already applied that exact text to his mission: 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth' (Acts 13:47, quoting Isa. 49:6) — so 'light' means salvation reaching the nations. The immediate context defines it too: a few sentences earlier (26:18) his commission was 'to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness.' And the engine of the verse is that it is 'by being the first to rise from the dead' that Christ proclaims light — the resurrection itself is the sunrise, new-creation life breaking over the grave (Isa. 9:2; 60:1–3).

Where did Moses and the prophets say this? Paul does not list the texts, but the apostles preached from them: the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and the sufferer of Psalm 22 for the death; Psalm 16:8–11 (cf. 2:25–31; 13:35) and Isaiah 53:10–12 for the resurrection; and the promise to bless the nations through Abraham and to make the servant a light for the nations (Isa 49:6; cf. 13:47).

One more confirmation, and it is beautiful. Luke opened his Gospel with old Simeon lifting the infant Jesus and calling him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel' (Luke 2:32) — again Isaiah 49, again light for Gentiles and Israel. What Simeon sang at the cradle, Paul declares at the climax of the mission: the same Isaianic light, for the same two peoples. So the meaning is sure: Christ crucified and risen is God's promised light — salvation, sight, and life — now streaming to Jew and Gentile alike. (The 'sons of light / sons of darkness' image was current in Paul's Jewish world — the Dead Sea community used it freely — but the source he cites is Isaiah.) For everyone who has ever sat in a long inward darkness, this is the gospel: the Light has come, and his name is Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words.

Paul has been interrupted, publicly, by the most powerful man present, and told he is insane in front of the entire provincial establishment. Watch what he does with that.

He does not lose his temper, and he does not grovel. He addresses Festus by his correct title — most excellent, the formal style of address for a governor — and then flatly denies the charge. Courtesy and contradiction in the same breath. He gives the office its honour and gives the accusation nothing at all.

Then he picks his word with precision. The Greek is sophrosyne — soundness of mind, sober judgment, the settled self-possession the Greek moralists prized above almost everything. It is the exact antonym of mania, the word Festus has just thrown at him. Paul is not merely denying the charge; he is claiming the opposite virtue, in the vocabulary the room respects.

And the reader who has been paying attention already knows how this argument comes out, because Paul settled it fourteen verses earlier without anyone noticing. When he described himself hunting Christians in raging fury (v. 11), the word he used was built on that same root — mainomai. The madness in this story has already been located, and it was not on the Damascus road. It was the exactingly trained Pharisee dragging people out of their houses in the name of God.

For this has not been done in a corner.

A proverb, and a claim, and it is the backbone of Christian apologetics ever since.

The mystery religions of the ancient world did their business in corners — secret rites, private initiations, truths for insiders that could never be checked. Paul says his message is the opposite kind of thing. It concerns events that happened in public, in a known province, in a named city, under a Roman governor whose name is on record, in front of hostile witnesses who are still alive and could be called.

That is why he can say to Agrippa the king knows about these things and speak boldly. He is not appealing to a private experience the king has no way of assessing. He is appealing to recent, public, checkable history in the king's own territory.

Which is still the shape of the thing. Christianity does not ask anyone to accept a feeling that occurred to somebody in private. It stakes everything on a claim about a particular execution and a particular tomb, in a particular week, in a city you can still walk around. Paul was content to have that investigated. He was, in fact, asking for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.

Paul turns from the governor, who has just called him mad, and puts a direct question to the king — and then does not wait for the answer. He supplies it himself.

It is the boldest moment in the speech, and it is also a beautifully laid trap, though not a cruel one. Consider Agrippa's position. If he says yes, I believe the prophets, he has conceded the entire argument, because Paul has just spent twenty verses demonstrating that the prophets promised a suffering and rising Messiah who would bring light to the Gentiles. If he says no, he has publicly renounced the Scriptures in front of the Jewish subjects whose high priest he appoints, with Roman officers listening.

He can neither affirm nor deny. So he does the third thing.

In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?

The Greek here — en oligo — is genuinely ambiguous, and honesty requires saying so. It can mean in a little time, and it can mean with little effort or by a little argument. The King James took it as degree and gave us the famous rendering, almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian; most modern translations take it as time. The tone is not recoverable from the page. Read one way it is a courtroom deflection with a smile in it; read another it is the nearest a Herod ever came.

What is not ambiguous is the word he reaches for: Christian. It appears only three times in the New Testament — coined as a nickname at Antioch (11:26), used by Peter of those who suffer under it (1 Pet. 4:16), and here, on the lips of a king, almost certainly with an edge on it. Agrippa will not name the man; he names the party.

And whichever way the irony ran, the effect was the same. He changed the subject, and a few sentences later he stood up and left.

Whatever Agrippa's exact tone, the old rendering 'almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian' has fixed on a tragic spiritual place, and it is worth naming. To be almost persuaded — interested, impressed, moved, near the kingdom — is still to be on the wrong side of the line; almost saved is wholly lost. Many perish not as scoffers but as the 'almost': those who came close, admired the gospel, felt its pull, hesitated — and never crossed over. Mark Paul's reply (v. 29): he longs that Agrippa and all who hear would become 'such as I am' — not almost, but altogether — 'except for these chains.' Do not stop at almost.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.

Agrippa has just deflected him with a piece of wit, and everyone in the hall would have understood that as the end of the exchange. A king makes a joke; the room smiles; the awkward moment passes.

Paul does not let it pass. Whether short or long — he picks up the king's phrase and refuses the exit. Little or much, quickly or slowly, it does not matter to me; what I want is the thing itself.

And then he does something that should stop us. In a Roman audience hall, on trial, in front of a governor, a king, the tribunes and the leading men of the city, Paul prays out loud. I would to God is not a figure of speech; it is a wish addressed to God in the hearing of everyone present. He stops arguing and starts interceding, in public, for the man judging him.

That not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am.

Consider what he is offering, and from what position. He owns nothing. He has been in custody for over two years. He is going to be put on a ship to Nero. Everyone in that room outranks him, and every one of them will sleep tonight somewhere better than he will.

And he looks around it — the king in his state, Bernice in her jewels, the officers, the money, the governor — and what he feels is not envy. It is pity. He wishes every one of them had what he has.

That is either delusion or it is the most serious claim in the book. There is no third option. A man in irons pitying a king is either out of his mind, as Festus has just said, or he possesses something that makes a Herodian court look impoverished.

Except for these chains.

The kindest clause Paul ever spoke, and it does two things at once.

It tells you what he was actually asking for. Not sympathy. Not release. Not agreement in a debate. He wanted them to have Christ, and he was careful to specify that he was not wishing his suffering on them — only his Lord.

And it tells you the chains were on his mind. He is not posturing as a man above his circumstances. He knows exactly what he is wearing and mentions it lightly, without complaint, as the one part of his life he would not pass on.

Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them.

Nobody answers.

The most direct appeal in the New Testament, made by the finest preacher of the age, to a man who knew the Scriptures — and the response is that everyone stands up and the meeting ends. Not a refutation. Not an argument. An adjournment.

That is how most people decline Christ, then and now. Not with an objection, which at least takes the thing seriously, but by finding that the hour is late and there are other matters and the conversation has reached a natural close. Agrippa did not say no. He simply stood up, and the standing was the answer.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.

The verdict is delivered in the corridor, after the doors have closed, where it costs nothing and changes nothing.

That is the fifth time. Gallio at Corinth threw the case out (18:14–15). Claudius Lysias put it in writing that he found nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Festus told Agrippa the prosecution had brought no charge of the kind he expected (25:18), and then admitted to the assembled province that he had nothing to write (25:26–27). And now a Jewish king, a Roman governor, and the senior officers of the garrison agree among themselves that the prisoner has done nothing at all.

Luke has been laying these down for eight chapters without a word of comment. He does not need one. Christianity was investigated repeatedly by the authorities best placed to convict it, and the file kept coming back empty.

This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.

The last line of the chapter, and it is layered.
