This ship left Alexandria to carry Egyptian grain to Rome. That is what she was built for, that is what the owner invested in, that is why she was at sea in the wrong month, and that is the reason 276 people were aboard her at all. Every ounce of it is now at the bottom of a bay off Malta.

Some manuscripts read seventy-six. The number 276 is far better attested, and the shorter reading probably arose from a copyist’s confusion of Greek numerals. A large grain ship could easily carry that many.

The voyage failed completely, by every measure it was undertaken for. And it succeeded entirely, because the one cargo God cared about on that ship was a prisoner he had promised to get to Rome — and 275 people he had thrown in as a gift.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land.

Daylight at last, after fourteen nights — and they still do not know where they are. Not one man aboard, including a crew that had worked these waters for years, recognises the coastline in front of them. It is Malta, and they will not learn its name until they are ashore (28:1).

But they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore.

Note Luke's caution: if possible. Nobody is confident. They can see one feature that offers any hope at all — a bay with a beach rather than cliffs — and the plan is to drive the ship straight at it and hope.

So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach.

Three actions, and any sailor reading this will recognise every one.

They cast off the anchors and left them in the sea. Not weighed — cut. Four anchors and their cables abandoned on the bottom, because hauling them up would take an hour they do not have and weight they cannot carry. This is a one-way manoeuvre. The instant those cables part, there is no stopping and no second attempt.

Loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Ancient ships steered with two great oars, one each side of the stern. They had been lashed out of the way for a fortnight so the storm would not smash them. Now they are freed, because for the first time in two weeks the ship is going to be steered somewhere on purpose.

Hoisting the foresail to the wind. A small headsail, enough to give steerage way and drive her forward. They need speed to reach the beach and control to hold the line.

It is a good plan, executed correctly by professionals who have been awake for two weeks. Everything they can control, they control.

And in the next verse it goes wrong, through something no seamanship on earth could have prevented.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground.

Luke's phrase is a curious one — literally, they fell into a place of two seas. It describes a shoal or a spit of land with open water on both sides, the sort of hidden bar that produces a cross-current where two bodies of water meet. There is such a formation at the mouth of St Paul's Bay.

The point is that it was invisible. From a ship's deck at dawn, in surf, with the coastline unrecognised, there was no way to see it. Nothing in the crew's handling of the vessel was wrong. They simply hit something they could not have known was there.

Which is worth pausing on, because it is not how we prefer disasters to work. The wreck of this ship is not caused by the bad decision at Fair Havens — that produced the storm, and they survived the storm. The wreck is caused by an underwater ridge that nobody could see, three hundred yards from safety, at the end of a manoeuvre performed correctly.

The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf.

The two halves of the sentence are the two halves of their situation. Forward, the ship is jammed solid in the bar, going nowhere. Aft, she is being systematically demolished by the sea, plank by plank, with 276 people standing on her.

This is the worst moment of the entire voyage — worse than the northeaster, worse than the fourteen nights. The storm was survivable because the hull held. Now the hull is coming apart underneath them, in surf, off an unknown shore, and there is no boat, because they cut it away in the dark.

And notice that the angel's promise is at this moment exactly half fulfilled. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22). The ship is being destroyed in front of them, precisely as God said it would be. The destruction of the vessel is not the promise failing; it is the promise coming true, and the half they are watching is the half they were told to expect.

Which leaves them standing on a breaking wreck with only God's word for it that the other half will hold too. That is very often the exact position of faith: the painful part of the promise arriving on schedule, and nothing yet to show for the good part but the character of the one who said it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape.

A brutal verse, and it needs its context or it simply looks like cruelty.

Under Roman military discipline, a guard who let a prisoner escape was liable to suffer the penalty the prisoner would have suffered. Luke has already shown us this twice: Herod executed the sentries when Peter got out (12:19), and the Philippian jailer drew his sword on himself rather than face what was coming (16:27). These soldiers are not sadists. They are men doing arithmetic about their own necks, at the one moment when several condemned men are about to be in open water in the confusion of a wreck.

It is also a reminder of what Paul's fellow passengers were. Some of those prisoners may well have been bound for the arena. They have just survived fourteen days of storm on the promise of a God they do not know, and their reward at the water's edge is a drawn sword.

But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan.

Julius intervenes, and Luke tells us exactly why: he wanted Paul alive.

Not the prisoners. Paul. And because he wanted this one man to live, he vetoed the killing of every man in the group — so a shipload of anonymous convicts, whose names nobody recorded and whose crimes we will never know, walked out of the surf alive because of who they happened to be chained near.

That is the third time in this chapter that Paul's presence has saved people who had no idea it was doing so. The angel gave him the lives of all 275 others (v. 24). His warning about the sailors kept the crew aboard (v. 31). And now his value to a Roman officer turns aside the swords.

It is impossible to read that pattern and not see the shape of the gospel in it — not because Luke says so, but because the shape is unmistakable once you have seen it elsewhere. People with nothing to commend them, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. Abraham found it in Sodom: ten righteous men would have saved a whole city (Gen. 18:32). And at the centre of everything stands One who did not merely happen to be standing nearby, but who deliberately took the place of the condemned and let the sentence fall on himself instead.

The prisoners on that beach owed their lives to a man they had probably never spoken to. Every Christian alive owes rather more than that, to a Man who sought him out.

He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land.

And having saved their lives, the centurion organises the evacuation — swimmers first, so the strongest are ashore and able to help the rest. It is sensible, decent, competent leadership from a pagan officer, and it is the last thing he does in the book.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.

Look at how the promise of God is kept.

Not by a calmed sea. Not by an angel carrying them ashore, not by the waters parting, not by a single thing that anyone would call a miracle. Two hundred and seventy-six starving, exhausted, half-drowned people go over the side into cold surf at dawn and thrash their way to a beach, and the ones who cannot swim cling to broken bits of the ship that has just been destroyed under them.

The wreckage is the lifeboat. The very timbers of the disaster are what carry them in.

That is worth holding on to, because most Christians spend a good deal of energy waiting for God to keep his promises in a manner they would find impressive. He rarely does. He is far more likely to keep them by way of a plank — something splintered off the thing that fell apart, floating within reach at the moment you go into the water.

And so it was that all were brought safely to land.

Luke's last word on the voyage is the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is perfect.

Two hundred and seventy-six went aboard. Two hundred and seventy-six came ashore. The angel had said there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship, and the ship is matchwood in the bay behind them and not one human being is missing. Paul's own earlier assessment had feared the loss of lives; the word of God went further.

Notice also the verb Luke chooses at the very end. Brought safely — the word is built on the ordinary Greek root for save, and he has been sounding that note through the whole chapter: all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned (v. 20); unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved (v. 31); and now, at last, all were saved through to land. A reader who knows what that word carries in the rest of Acts is meant to feel the resonance, and Luke does not press it.

Everything the God of Israel said would happen has happened, in order, exactly. The storm came, as Paul warned. The ship was lost, as the angel said. Every soul survived, as the angel said. And the man God had promised to bring to Rome is sitting on a beach on Malta, soaked and shivering and some five hundred miles short of it — with the promise entirely intact.

He said not one of them would perish, and not one of them perished. That is simply what his word is like. It does not arrive tidily, or on the schedule anyone would have chosen, or in a form that would look well in a painting — but it arrives, in full, down to the last person on the roll, because the One who gave it does not deal in approximations and has never yet mislaid a single thing entrusted to him. Two hundred and seventy-six people stood dripping on a foreign shore that morning as living proof of it, and most of them had no idea whose word they had been carried in on.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The last leg of the journey, and almost all of it is carried by people who did not know whose errand they were running.

The fire (vv. 1–2). They learn the island's name only after they are ashore. Luke calls the Maltese barbaroi — not an insult, simply people who did not speak Greek; they spoke a Punic dialect and nobody could understand anybody. And they show unusual kindness, philanthropia: they build a fire in the rain for nearly three hundred soaked strangers who cannot thank them in any language they know.

The viper (vv. 3–6). Paul is gathering firewood — the apostle doing the servant's job, and Luke states it so plainly it is easy to miss. A snake fastens on his hand, and the islanders reason it out: escaped the sea, caught by Justice, therefore a murderer. Their theology is coherent and their arithmetic is exactly wrong; it is the mistake of Job's friends and of the disciples at the blind man. Then he shakes it into the fire, and on identical evidence they promote him from murderer to god. Both verdicts are worthless, and he takes no notice of either.

Publius (vv. 7–9). Luke calls him the chief man of the island, which Maltese inscriptions confirm was the actual title of the Roman administrator there. His father is ill with recurring fever and dysentery — Luke's medical vocabulary is precise, and a fever of just that kind is so characteristic of the island that it was later named Malta fever. Paul visits, prays, lays hands on him, heals him; and then the whole island comes.

The provisioning (vv. 10–13). They arrived having thrown everything they owned into the sea. They leave three months later with a fully stocked ship, aboard another Alexandrian grain freighter — this one carrying Castor and Pollux on the bow, so the apostle sails to Rome under the faces of two pagan gods and thinks nothing of it. Then a south wind, and two hundred miles in two days.

Rome (vv. 14–16). At Puteoli they find brothers — nobody sent them; the gospel had already travelled the trade routes ahead of the apostle. Then six words the whole book has been moving toward: and so we came to Rome, recorded flatly, because that is what happens to the things God has said. And on the Appian Way, Roman Christians who had never met him — some of them almost certainly among the twenty-six names in Romans 16 — walk out thirty and forty miles to stand at the roadside, and on seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it comes from a believer. A fire lit by islanders who worship other gods. Three days' hospitality from a Roman official. A winter's provisions loaded aboard by people who thought Paul was a deity. A ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux. A favourable wind. God furnishes the last stage of his apostle's journey almost entirely out of pagan hands, and not one of those hands knows what it is doing.

That is the same doctrine the storm chapter taught, arriving now in a gentler key. There God used a centurion's fear and a crew's seamanship; here he uses simple human decency. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes is not an abstraction in Acts — it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and drew a confident conclusion about his standing with God, and they were as wrong as it is possible to be — twice, in opposite directions, within one evening. Scripture is consistent about this: you cannot read a person's standing before God off the surface of their life. Job's friends could not, the disciples could not at the blind man (John 9:2–3), and neither can we, in a sickroom or anywhere else.

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15. Paul took courage, which means he needed to. God's provision for a discouraged apostle was not an angel — he had used angels earlier and would again — but a handful of ordinary Christians who walked two days out along a road to be standing there when he passed. The means God most often uses to keep his servants going is other believers turning up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Believers in Rome heard that a prisoner they had never met was on the road. They had one letter from him, written three years earlier. So they walked — thirty-three miles to Three Taverns, forty-three to the Forum of Appius — stood at the side of the Appian Way, and waited. They did not free him, feed him, or improve his legal position by a single clause. They just turned up. And the apostle to the Gentiles looked at them, thanked God, and found he could go on.

Now: Two things follow, and both cut. The first is that the strong Christian you know is more likely to need this than to say so. Paul had faced down a mob, survived a shipwreck and shaken off a snake, and he still arrived on that road with his courage low. The assumption that mature believers are past needing encouragement is one of the loneliest lies in the church. The second is that showing up almost never feels worth the trip. It accomplishes nothing you can point to, it costs a day you did not have, and you will usually never learn whether it mattered. Luke thought it mattered enough to record, in a book with no room to spare, in the sentence immediately before Paul walks into Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta.

They did not know where they were until somebody told them. Two hundred and seventy-six people stand dripping on a beach at dawn, and the first piece of information anyone acquires is the name of the place.

Malta is a small island about sixty miles south of Sicily, well off the route to Italy. They have been blown roughly five hundred miles in a fortnight.

The native people showed us unusual kindness.

Two words need explaining, and both repay it.

The native people. Luke's word is barbaroi, which came into English as barbarians and has picked up a sneer it does not carry here. To a Greek speaker it simply meant people who did not speak Greek — the word imitates the sound of unintelligible speech, bar-bar. The Maltese spoke a Punic dialect descended from Phoenician. Luke is not insulting them; he is telling you that nobody on that beach could understand the locals and the locals could not understand them.

Unusual kindness. The word is philanthropia — literally love of human beings, the root of our philanthropy. And Luke marks it as unusual, out of the ordinary, more than anyone had a right to expect.

Now put the scene together, because it is easy to read past it. Nearly three hundred strangers come out of the sea at dawn in a storm — soldiers, prisoners, sailors, a shipwrecked crew with nothing left, speaking a language nobody understands, on a small island in November. They are a burden of the first order. Every one of them will need feeding.

For they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold.

And what the islanders do is build a fire.

There is no sermon here, no miracle, no revelation. There is wet wood, and rain coming on, and people who did not have to bother going to the trouble of getting a blaze going for a crowd of foreigners who could not thank them in any language they knew.

Keep an eye on how God has been provisioning this journey, because it is nearly all like this. A centurion's professional courtesy at Sidon. A crew's seamanship in the gale. And now a bonfire on a beach, lit by people who had never heard the name of the God who sent them the guests. He does not appear to feel any need to use religious instruments. He simply uses what is there, and the people he uses generally never find out.
verseByVerse.note: Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect, not Greek — hence “native people.”

verseByVerse.quote: "When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, 'No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire…

Stop on that before the snake.

Paul is the senior figure in this company by any spiritual measure — an apostle of Jesus Christ, the man whose God has just brought 276 people through a fortnight of storm, the one person aboard whose word turned out to be worth anything. He is also, by now, an elderly man who has been beaten more times than he can count and has just swum ashore from a wreck.

And what he is doing is collecting firewood.

Not directing the collection of firewood. Not resting by the blaze while others fetch it. Luke says he gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, and Luke says it so plainly that it is possible to read the whole chapter without noticing.

That is the same man who wrote that Christ Jesus, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). He had learned it from someone.

A viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.

Exactly what happens when you throw a bundle of sticks on a fire: something cold-blooded that was sleeping in it wakes up.

A word on an old objection, since a thoughtful reader may meet it. There are no venomous snakes on Malta today, and sceptics have made something of that. It is not much of an argument. Two thousand years of dense settlement on a small island routinely wipes out snake populations, and the more telling detail is in the text itself: the islanders recognised the creature on sight and knew precisely what to expect from it. They were not guessing. They stood there waiting for a specific and familiar death.

No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.

They have a theology, and it is worth taking seriously because it is a good deal more common than its pagan dress suggests.

Justice is Dike, a Greek goddess — retribution personified, the power that makes sure the guilty do not get away with it. Their reasoning is tight: this man survived a shipwreck, which looked like a reprieve; now a viper has him; therefore the reprieve was an illusion and the debt has been collected. The universe is morally accountable and it has caught up with him.

Half of that is right, and it is the half we are least comfortable with. There is a moral order. Guilt is real, and it is not finally evaded.

What is wrong is the arithmetic — the assumption that you can read a person's standing with God off the surface of their circumstances. It is exactly the mistake Job's friends made across forty chapters. It is what the disciples assumed when they saw the blind man and asked whose sin had caused it (John 9:2). And it is alive in every sickroom where somebody wonders aloud what they did to deserve this.

The islanders' logic is coherent. Their conclusion is the precise opposite of the truth. The man with the snake on his hand is the one person on that beach that God had personally promised to bring safely to Rome.
verseByVerse.note: “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.

The understatement is magnificent, and it is Luke's, not Paul's. No drama, no speech, no gesture toward heaven. He shakes his hand over the flames and goes on with the evening.

They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead.

Luke, who was a doctor, gives the two things the islanders were watching for — local swelling or sudden collapse. They knew the symptoms. Everyone on that beach is now staring at one man's hand.

They changed their minds and said that he was a god.

And there is the whole fickleness of human judgment in a single sentence. Within the space of one evening, on exactly the same evidence, Paul goes from murderer to deity.

Nothing about him has altered. He has not spoken. He has not argued his case or defended his character. The crowd simply ran their theology forward, found the result unacceptable, and reversed it entirely — and their second verdict is as wrong as their first, and considerably more dangerous.

He had been through this before, at Lystra, where a healing brought out the priest of Zeus with oxen and garlands and Paul tore his clothes and ran into the crowd shouting that he was a man like them (14:14–15). Luke does not record a protest here, but there is no shrine on Malta and no cult of Paul in the record — only, in the next verse, a sick old man being visited and prayed for. He answered the compliment by behaving like a servant.

Which is worth turning on the reader, because most of us are governed by verdicts of this quality far more than we would like to admit. The people who decide you are wonderful and the people who decide you are worthless are frequently the same people, working from the same evidence, a fortnight apart. A man who needs the first verdict will be destroyed by the second. Paul appears to have taken no notice of either.

One word on snake-handling, since this passage has been put to a use it will not bear. There are churches that deliberately handle venomous snakes in worship, appealing to this episode and to Mark 16:18. It is worth saying plainly what is wrong with it. Paul did not seek the snake; he was collecting firewood, and it bit him. Every genuine instance of divine protection in Scripture comes upon a servant in the course of duty — never as a stunt performed to prove something. To pick up a viper on purpose is not faith; it is precisely what the Lord Jesus refused to do when he was invited to throw himself off the temple, and he answered it with a verse: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matt. 4:7). Protection is a promise to be received on the road, not a mechanism to be triggered.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius.

Luke's title for him is protos — literally the first — and it is one of those small details that quietly vouches for him. Inscriptions found on Malta, in both Greek and Latin, show that first man of the island was the actual formal title of the Roman administrator there. Luke did not guess it and did not generalise it. He used the local job title correctly, in the right place, decades before anyone could have checked him from a reference book.

Who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days.

Do the arithmetic on that hospitality. This is not a dinner party. Publius takes on the feeding and sheltering of the shipwreck company for three days — and even if it is only the officers and their charges rather than all 276, it is a serious act of generosity at the beginning of winter.

Once again the provision comes from someone with no interest in the God who is arranging it.

It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery.

Here Luke the physician shows his training. The Greek reads, literally, fevers and dysentery — the plural for fever being the standard medical idiom of the period, used by the Greek doctors, for a condition that comes in recurring bouts.

It is worth knowing that a recurrent fever of exactly this kind is endemic to Malta and was so well known there that when nineteenth-century physicians finally identified it — a bacterial infection carried in goat's milk — they named it Malta fever after the island. Luke describes, in correct medical language, a disease characteristic of the place he says he was in.

Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him.

Three verbs, and the order is the whole of it.

He visited. The apostle goes to the sickroom. Whatever else the miracle involves, it begins with a man walking down a corridor to sit with someone who is ill.

He prayed. Before he touched him. Paul does not treat the gift as something he carries in his pocket; he asks.

He laid his hands on him and healed him. Luke, who elsewhere is careful to say that it is the name of Jesus that heals (3:16; 4:10), here writes it plainly and briefly.

Does this mean healing ministries continue today? These healings confirmed Paul as an apostle (2 Cor 12:12), as the gospel came to a new people. Yet Paul himself left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Tim 5:23). Believers still pray for the sick, as James teaches (Jas 5:14–15), and God heals as he wills; but no one today holds the apostle’s gift.

There is something worth noticing about the order of this chapter. Paul has just been declared a god by the whole island, and the next thing he does is go and sit with one sick old man and pray for him. The healing does not follow the acclaim as a demonstration. It follows the acclaim as a correction of it.
verseByVerse.note: “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman official on Malta, found in inscriptions there. Luke, a doctor, names the illness precisely.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured.

The word spreads, and Malta comes to the door.

Luke's verb for what happens to them, etherapeuonto, is the one that gives us therapy; it is the ordinary word for being treated and made well, and Luke uses it throughout his Gospel for what Jesus did. It is in a tense that suggests this went on — not one occasion, but a stream of people over the weeks.

And here is a question the passage raises and does not answer, which is worth being honest about. Luke records no preaching on Malta. Three months on that island, and not one sermon in the text.

Two things should be said, and the second matters more than the first.

First, Luke plainly is not telling us everything. He is compressing three months into five verses, and it is inconceivable that Paul spent a winter among people who had just watched God heal their sick and said nothing whatever about him. The silence is Luke's, not Paul's.

Second, and more usefully: what Luke does record is a season in which the gospel travelled almost entirely by kindness received and kindness returned. A fire lit by strangers. A house opened for three days. A sick man prayed for. A queue of islanders healed. Provisions loaded aboard at the end.

Now, mercy shown to a body is not a substitute for telling people about Christ, and it must never be offered as one; a man can be cured of dysentery and go to hell. Paul knew that better than anyone and spent his life saying so. But mercy is not less than a sermon either, and it is very often the thing that gets a sermon listened to.

Here is the test, and it is a plain one. Most Christians will not preach a sermon this year. Every Christian will have a winter's worth of small chances of exactly the Maltese kind: the practical thing done for someone who cannot repay it, the visit made, the meal taken round, the help given to people whose language you do not really speak. Paul gathered sticks and sat with an old man with a fever. There is no record that he thought either activity was beneath his calling.

verseByVerse.quote: "They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed.

The company arrived on Malta having thrown literally everything they owned into the sea — cargo, tackle, gear, the last of the wheat. They leave three months later with a fully provisioned ship.

The honours may well have included gifts of money, though Luke does not say; what he does say is that the islanders supplied their needs. Every scrap of that provision came from people who worshipped other gods and had no notion that they were outfitting the apostle to the Gentiles for the last leg of his journey to Caesar.

After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead.

Another Alexandrian grain freighter — the same class of vessel that was smashed to matchwood in the bay three months earlier. They get on board anyway, which is its own quiet comment on how the promise of God is meant to be held: not by avoiding the kind of thing that went wrong last time.

And Luke names the figurehead, which he did not have to do.

The twin gods are Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, sons of Zeus in the old stories, and the patron deities of sailors. Their carved images rode on the bow, and Mediterranean seamen prayed to them for safe passage. Ancient ships were named for their figureheads, so this vessel was, in effect, called The Heavenly Twins.

So the apostle of the living God completes his journey to Rome aboard a ship dedicated to two pagan gods, under their painted faces, having been fed all winter by islanders who thought he was one himself.

Luke reports it with a completely straight face, and there is no anxiety in it anywhere — no suggestion that Paul should have sought a more suitable vessel, no hint that the figurehead compromised anything. The gods on the bow were nothing, and the God who governs the wind had already said where this ship was going.

That composure is worth learning from. There is a kind of Christian nervousness that needs the world to be scrubbed of every pagan trace before it can be used or enjoyed, and it is not the confidence of the New Testament. Paul, who wrote that an idol has no real existence (1 Cor. 8:4), sat under the twin gods all the way to Puteoli and thought nothing of it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus and protectors of sailors.

verseByVerse.quote: "Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium.

Read the geography and feel the pace change.

Syracuse is the great city of Sicily, three days' stop. Rhegium sits on the toe of Italy, at the Straits of Messina — and Luke's phrase we made a circuit probably describes tacking, working the ship up the coast against an unhelpful wind.

And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.

A south wind. After everything, a following breeze.

The distance from Rhegium to Puteoli is around two hundred miles, and they cover it in two days — a fast passage by any standard, the sort of run a master would remember. The contrast with the previous voyage is total and Luke does not point it out. Weeks of fighting a headwind, then a fortnight driven blind through a gale, then a wreck; and now, in the last stretch, the wind simply gets behind them and they fly.

Puteoli, on the Bay of Naples, was the principal port of Rome and the terminus of the Egyptian grain fleet. Ships of this class were famous there; the philosopher Seneca describes the crowds of Puteoli turning out to watch the Alexandrian corn ships come over the horizon under full topsail, because the whole city knew what they carried.

So the voyage ends the way it should have ended six months ago: an Alexandrian grain ship making a fast run into Puteoli with a south wind behind her.

Whatever is in her hold, what she is actually delivering is one prisoner, and neither the master nor the centurion nor the port has any idea that this is the only cargo the voyage was ever really for.

And there is one more thing worth noticing about this leg of the journey, now that the danger is past.

Nobody on that ship prayed for this wind, so far as Luke records. Nobody fasted for it or held a meeting about it. After six months in which every single thing had gone wrong, the weather simply turned helpful, and a company of exhausted men made good time up the Italian coast in early spring.

God had been just as much in charge of the northeaster.
verseByVerse.note: Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy; Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the grain ships.

verseByVerse.quote: "There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days.

Four words worth their weight: there we found brothers.

Nobody sent them. There is no record in Acts of a mission to Puteoli, no apostle assigned to the Bay of Naples, no church-planting strategy that took in the port towns of Campania. Paul arrives in Italy for the first time in his life and discovers that Christians are already there.

That is how the gospel had actually been moving all along, underneath the narrative Luke has been telling. Along the trade routes, in the luggage of merchants and sailors and slaves whose names nobody wrote down. Someone carried the message to this port, and Luke does not know who, and neither do we.

And they take the whole company in for a week — which means the centurion Julius agreed to it, one last courtesy from a man who has been quietly decent to Paul since Sidon.

And so we came to Rome.

There it is.

Six words, dropped in without ceremony, and the entire book has been travelling toward them. Luke does not build to it. There is no flourish, no paragraph of reflection — just a plain sentence of arrival tucked between a week's hospitality at Puteoli and the details of the final road.

Consider what stands behind those six words. A promise made in the dark of a Jerusalem barracks by the Lord himself: you must testify also in Rome (23:11). A conspiracy of forty men sworn to prevent it. Two years wasted in a cell at Caesarea under a governor angling for a bribe. A hearing before Festus, an appeal to Caesar, a hearing before Agrippa. A fortnight in a storm with the sun and stars blotted out. A shipwreck. A viper. A winter on Malta.

And Luke's whole account of the fulfilment is: and so we came to Rome.

Who founded the church in Rome? Not Paul, who wrote to it before he had visited (Rom 1:13; 15:22–24), and nothing in Scripture says Peter did. It most likely began with Jews and converts from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (2:10), and with believers who moved there. Here the Roman Christians come out to meet Paul.

That restraint is not coldness. It is a man who knows that the promise never needed decorating. God said Rome, and here is Rome, and the correct way to record it is flatly, because that is what happens to the things God has said.
verseByVerse.note: From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us.

These are Roman Christians who have heard that Paul's party is on the road, and they walk out to meet him.

The distances are worth having. The Forum of Appius is about forty-three miles from Rome; Three Taverns about thirty-three. On the Appian Way, on foot, that is two days out and two days back for the first group. They may have gone in two waves, or the nearer group may have set out later. Either way, ordinary believers with jobs and households took the best part of a week to go and stand at the roadside on the chance of meeting a prisoner.

And they had never met him.

Paul had written to this church perhaps three years earlier — the letter we call Romans, the most closely argued document in the New Testament, sent to a congregation he had never visited and had wanted to visit for years (Rom. 1:11–13; 15:23–24). The last chapter of that letter greets twenty-six people by name. Some of them, in all likelihood, were standing on that road.

On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage.

This is the tenderest sentence in the last quarter of Acts, and it should not be hurried.

Notice first what it admits. Took courage means he needed some. Paul — who faced down a mob from the barracks steps, who told a shipful of despairing men that not one of them would die, who has just walked away from a snakebite without comment — is, on the road into Rome, a man whose courage is running low.

Which is entirely understandable and almost never how we picture him. He is going to the capital as a prisoner to be tried before Nero. He is old, he has been at sea for months, he has lost everything he owned in the wreck, and the outcome is a matter of life and death.

And what God sends him is not an angel. He had angels earlier in the story, and they were exactly what was needed then. Here, on the Appian Way, the provision is a small crowd of Christians standing by the road because they wanted to see him.

Notice too what Paul does with them: he thanked God. He does not merely feel better. He looks straight past the people to the one who sent them and gives him the credit, and then his courage comes back.

There is a test in this, and it cuts two ways. If Paul needed this, the strong Christians around you need it, and they will not tell you so — the assumption that a mature believer is beyond encouragement is one of the loneliest lies in the church. And on the other side: the walk to the Forum of Appius accomplished nothing practical. Those men did not free him, feed him, or improve his legal position by a single clause. They simply showed up on a road, and the effect on the apostle to the Gentiles was that he thanked God and found he could go on.

Was Paul in prison? He was in military custody, chained to a single soldier, but allowed to live in his own rented quarters and to receive visitors freely (vv. 23, 30). He was a prisoner awaiting trial before Caesar, and the gospel still went out unhindered.

Almost nobody thinks turning up is worth the trip. Luke thought it was worth a verse.
verseByVerse.note: The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, roughly 40 and 30 miles from Rome. Paul was kept under house arrest, chained to a soldier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Acts ends not with a verdict but with a conversation, and then with an adverb.

The summons (vv. 17–20). Three days after arriving, Paul sends for the Jewish leaders — the synagogue first, as in every city for a quarter of a century, and this time in the capital of the empire. He plants himself inside the family before defending himself: brothers, our people, the customs of our fathers. His legal summary is scrupulously fair and leaves out the temple mob and the forty assassins. And then the most gracious sentence of his career: he appealed to Caesar, though I had no charge to bring against my nation — arriving at the one court with power to redress a quarter-century of wrong, and filing nothing. He lifts a chained wrist and says it is worn because of the hope of Israel.

The hearing (vv. 21–24). No letters have come from Judea — most likely the winter closed the shipping lanes behind him — so for the first time in years Paul faces a Jewish audience that has not been prepared against him. They know the sect is spoken against everywhere, which is true and which some of them may remember from Claudius's expulsion; and they ask to hear him anyway. On the appointed day he expounds from morning till evening, testifying and arguing, and the outcome is what it has been since Pentecost: some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved.

The prophet (vv. 25–27). Paul's parting word is Isaiah 6:9–10, the hardening text — the passage the New Testament reaches for more than any other to explain unbelief, quoted by Jesus and by all four evangelists. Note how he introduces it: the Holy Spirit was right in saying… through Isaiah, God speaking and a man genuinely writing, in one clause. The eyes are shut by those who own them, and God is sovereign over the outcome, and Scripture holds both without flattening either. And the passage does not end in judgment; it ends with a physician — and I would heal them.

The last word (vv. 28–31). Salvation has been sent to the Gentiles and they will listen — which is not the rejection of Israel, as the man who wrote Romans 11 to this very city is the last person who could mean. Then two years in rented lodgings, chained to a rotating guard, welcoming everybody who came, with the prison letters coming out of that room and the gospel reaching Caesar's own household. Luke gives no trial, no verdict, no execution. He ends his two volumes on a single adverb — akolytos, unhindered — because his subject was never Paul's biography but the journey of the word from Jerusalem to the end of the earth, and the word has arrived and cannot be stopped.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Book Has No Ending

The abrupt close of Acts is a decision, not an accident. Luke had written the death of Stephen and the death of James; he could have written the death of Paul. Instead he stops with his hero alive, chained, and preaching.

The reason is that Luke's subject was announced in his first chapter and it was never Paul: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). That programme is now complete. The word has travelled from an upper room in Jerusalem to rented lodgings in Rome, and it is being preached in the capital of the world without restriction. There is nothing left to report.

Hence the final word, akolytos — unhindered — the last word of the Greek text and Luke's verdict on everything that came before it. The Sanhedrin ordered the message silenced; it spread. Stephen was stoned; it spread. Herod killed James and jailed Peter; the door opened. It was flogged out of Philippi, mocked in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, tried in four courts, sworn against by forty men, driven into a fortnight's storm, wrecked on Malta, and bitten by a snake. At the end, the emperor's soldiers have the preacher chained by the wrist — and the word walks in and out of that room for two years and nobody can touch it.

Two guards keep this from becoming triumphalism. First, unhindered does not mean unopposed; every hindrance in the list was real and several were lethal, and Paul himself would die under Nero within a few years. Second, the man is still in chains as the book closes. Luke's claim is not that the church wins its comfort, but that the word of God cannot be stopped — which is a very different and much sturdier promise, and the only one he offers.

As for Paul himself: early tradition outside Scripture, and therefore to be held loosely, says he was released, travelled again — perhaps to Spain as he had hoped (Rom. 15:24) — was re-arrested and executed at Rome. The Pastoral Epistles read like letters from that later period. Luke declines to tell us, and his silence is the point.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last thing Luke shows us is a prisoner in a rented room, chained by the wrist to a soldier who changed shift every few hours, unable to leave the building. He could not travel to a single one of the churches he had planted. And out of that room, on the traditional reckoning, came Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon — letters that have reached further than all his journeys put together — while the guard rotation carried the gospel through the imperial barracks until there were believers in Caesar's own household.

Now: The circumstance that looks like the end of a person's usefulness is very often the beginning of the part that outlasts them. Illness that stops a working life. A redundancy. A move to somewhere with no ministry to speak of. Children, or care of a parent, that shrinks the world to a few rooms for a decade. Every one of those feels like being taken off the field, and every one of them puts you in a room with a small number of people who cannot easily get away from you. Paul's chain did not interrupt his ministry; it relocated it, narrowed it, and made it permanent. He did not know that at the time either. He simply welcomed whoever came through the door, every day, for two years — and that is the last thing the book of Acts records anybody doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, 'Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews.

Three days. He has just arrived in the capital of the world after a journey of six months that nearly killed him, he is under house arrest chained to a soldier, and he waits three days before convening a meeting.

And notice who he sends for first. Not the Roman church, though they had walked forty miles to meet him and he plainly loved them. The synagogue.

This is the pattern of his entire ministry, held to the very last scene of the book: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16) — the principle he had written to these very people. In Pisidian Antioch, Thessalonica, Corinth, Ephesus, he went to the synagogue first and was thrown out of it, city after city, year after year. It never once altered the order in which he knocked on doors.

There is a kind of faithfulness in that which is easy to miss. Paul had every reason to have given up on the synagogue as a matter of policy. He kept going, and he kept going because he loved them, and he had written to this city that he could wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers (Rom. 9:3).

Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.

Every word of that opening is chosen with care, and the care is pastoral rather than legal.

He calls them brothers. He speaks of our people and the customs of our fathers. Before he defends himself at all, he plants himself inside the family. Whatever these men have heard about the sect that is spoken against everywhere, the person in front of them is not an outsider making a case against them.

And then the summary, which is scrupulous. He does not say the Jews of Jerusalem tried to murder him, though they did. He does not mention the forty men and their oath. He uses a passive — I was delivered — and moves on.

When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.

The book has now recorded one official finding of no crime after another. Gallio threw the case out at Corinth. Claudius Lysias wrote it in a letter. Felix heard it and did nothing. Festus admitted he had nothing to write. Agrippa said the man could have been freed. And now Paul states the cumulative verdict to the Jewish leadership of Rome as simple fact, because by this point it is.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar.

Two things are being said, and the second is the one that matters.

First, the appeal was forced. Compelled is the word — he was left with no other route. Festus had proposed sending him back to Jerusalem for trial, which would have been a death sentence with extra steps, and the appeal was the only door left open.

Though I had no charge to bring against my nation.

And second — this. Read it slowly, because it is one of the most gracious sentences Paul ever spoke, and it costs him something to say it.

An appeal to Caesar was not a passive act. It put a case before the emperor's court, and it would have been entirely open to Paul to lay counter-charges: attempted murder, false witness, conspiracy, malicious prosecution by the leadership of his own people. He had ample evidence and he had suffered enormously. Any competent advocate would have advised it.

He declines. He tells the Jewish leaders of Rome, on his first day of business with them, that he has come to their city with no accusation against his nation.

Consider what he was declining to prosecute. A mob in the temple court that beat him and would have torn him apart. A high priest who ordered him struck in the face without a charge. Forty men under an oath to assassinate him. Two years of his life spent in a cell at Caesarea because a governor wanted a bribe. A campaign of hostility spanning a quarter of a century and half the empire.

And when he finally reaches the court with the power to do something about all of it, he says: no charge.

The man had written the reason to this city already. I am speaking the truth in Christ — I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit — that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Rom. 9:1–3).

That is not diplomacy. A man who could wish himself damned for their sake is not going to sue them.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in proportion to how justified you are. Paul had a genuine case. The wrongs were real, documented, and serious, and nobody would have blamed him for pressing them. He let it go — not by pretending it had not happened, not by minimising it, but by declining to use the leverage he actually had, because the people who had wronged him were the people he most wanted saved.

Most of us do not release grievances because we are still waiting to be told we were right. Paul was right, and everyone in the story knew he was right, and he came into Rome with nothing to file.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.' And they said to him, 'We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.

He says it with the chain on his wrist. There is a soldier attached to the other end of it, standing in the room while Paul talks.

The hope of Israel. He has used the phrase before, at every stage of this long legal ordeal — to the council (23:6), to Felix (24:15), to Agrippa (26:6–8) — and it has meant the same thing every time: the resurrection of the dead, and the coming of the Messiah in whom the promise to the fathers is kept. Paul's whole defence, from first to last, has been that he is not on trial for abandoning Israel's hope but for believing it has arrived.

And notice the logic of the sentence. He does not say despite the hope of Israel I am in chains, as though the two were in tension. He says because of it. The chain is not the price of a mistake or the interruption of his ministry. It is what holding Israel's own hope has cost him, and he lifts his wrist to make the point.

We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.

Their answer is unexpected, and honestly it is a little surprising. Nothing has arrived from Jerusalem — no formal notification, no warning, no character assassination in advance.

Why not? Luke does not say, and the honest commentators do not pretend to know. The most likely explanation is simply the sailing season: Paul left Caesarea in the autumn and the sea closed behind him, so no ship could have carried a dispatch ahead of him or after him through the winter. It is also possible that the Jerusalem leadership, having twice failed to get a conviction and once failed to get him killed, had concluded the case was not worth pursuing to Rome.

What it means practically is that for the first time in years Paul is speaking to a Jewish audience that has not been prepared against him. There is no riot waiting to happen in this room. Nobody here has been told what to think of him.

It is a small mercy and a real one, and it is the kind of thing that never looks like providence at the time — a winter storm closing the shipping lanes, and an old man in Rome getting a fair hearing because of it.
verseByVerse.note: “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.

An honest and rather appealing reply. They know nothing about Paul; they know something about the movement; and what they know is that it has a bad reputation in every city.

Which was true. Luke's own book is the evidence — riots at Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth, Ephesus, Jerusalem. Wherever the message went, trouble followed it. These men are not slandering the Way; they are reporting the state of its public reputation accurately.

The word they use is hairesis — a party or school of thought, the word from which we get heresy but without that weight yet; it is the same word used of the Pharisees and Sadducees as parties within Judaism (5:17; 15:5). At this stage the Christians are, to a Roman synagogue, one more faction inside the Jewish world, and a disreputable one.

There is also history in this room that Luke does not spell out. Around AD 49, the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome — and the Roman historian Suetonius, writing decades later, says the expulsion followed disturbances stirred up over one Chrestus, which is almost certainly a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Luke has already told us the consequence in passing: Aquila and Priscilla turning up in Corinth because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (18:2).

So when these leaders say the sect is spoken against everywhere, some of them may be remembering being put out of their homes over it. Their caution is earned.

And yet — we desire to hear from you what your views are. They have every reason to shut the conversation down, and instead they ask him to explain himself, and they set a date.

That is more than Paul got in most cities, and it is worth naming for what it is: a group of people with a bad impression, real grievances, and genuine reasons for suspicion, who nevertheless decide to hear the man out before deciding. It is not faith. It is only fairness. But Christianity has rarely asked for more than that as a starting point, and it does not often get it.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers.

They set a date, and when the day comes there are more of them than before. Word has gone round the synagogues of Rome, and the room is full.

From morning till evening he expounded to them.

Let that stand as it is written. Sunrise to sunset. A full day — eight, ten, twelve hours — of one man teaching the Scriptures to a room of people who had come to make up their minds about him.

Luke stacks up three verbs for what Paul did, and each says something different.

He expounded. The word means to set out, to lay open — the patient work of taking a text apart and showing what is inside it. This is exposition, not oratory.

Testifying. Bearing witness, the courtroom word. He is not offering an opinion; he is reporting what he has seen.

Trying to convince them. The verb is peitho, to persuade, and it is in a tense that means he kept at it. He is not content to state the case and leave the outcome to atmosphere. He argues, all day, because he wants these particular men to believe.

And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved.

And after all of that — the full day, the whole Old Testament, the finest mind in the early church working at the top of his powers on an audience that was genuinely willing to listen — the outcome is split.

That is worth sitting with, because it is the last word Acts has to say about how people respond to the gospel, and it declines to be tidy. Paul did everything right. The hearers came in good faith. And some believed and some did not.

Luke has been reporting this same division since Pentecost, and he reports it here without embarrassment and without explanation. The next thing Paul says will offer an explanation, and it will come from Isaiah.

Notice how the book ends: Paul 'testifying to the kingdom of God' — and the last verse says the same (v. 31). Acts opens with the risen Jesus 'speaking about the kingdom of God' (1:3) and closes with Paul preaching it in Rome — the whole church-age mission framed, start to finish, as kingdom-proclamation. (On what that means now, and the gracious difference between the Reformed 'already in the kingdom' reading and the dispensational instinct to reserve the kingdom for a future Israel, see 20:25 and 8:12.) The point here is simply that the kingdom was Paul's message to Jew and Roman alike, in this age, now.

And 'the Law of Moses and the Prophets' — does that leave out the Psalms, the wisdom books, the histories? It is standard shorthand for the whole Old Testament. The Jews divided their Scriptures in three — the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi'im), and the Writings (Ketuvim), together the Tanakh. Two things. First, 'the Prophets' is broader than we might guess: it includes not only Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest, but the great narrative books — Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings (the 'Former Prophets') — so much of the story already falls under that word. Second, 'the Law and the Prophets' was simply the everyday two-fold name for the entire Bible (Matt. 5:17; 22:40; Rom. 3:21).

The threefold shape was known in Paul's day too — the prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC) speaks three times of 'the Law and the Prophets and the others that followed' — and Luke elsewhere gives the fuller form on Jesus' own lips: 'everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms' (Luke 24:44), where 'the Psalms' stands for that third division.

So 'the Law and the Prophets' here means the whole Old Testament; and in practice Paul ranged across all of it — his sermon in Acts 13 reasons from the Psalms (Ps. 2, 16) as freely as from the Prophets (Isaiah, Habakkuk). The deeper wonder is Luke's constant point: all of it testifies to Jesus (Luke 24:27, 'beginning with Moses and all the Prophets... in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself'). Paul spent a whole day doing just that — showing the kingdom and the King hidden in plain sight on every page Israel already revered.

verseByVerse.quote: "And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: 'The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: "Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement.

The day ends without resolution. They are still arguing as they go out the door, and Paul lets them go with a single parting sentence — a quotation.

The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet.

Before the quotation itself, look at how Paul introduces it, because that clause is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament about what Scripture actually is.

The Holy Spirit was right in saying. The speaker is God. Not Isaiah wrote, not it says in the prophets — the Holy Spirit said this.

Through Isaiah the prophet. And yet it came through a man, in his own idiom, in the eighth century BC, out of his own vision in the temple.

Both at once, in one sentence, with no sense of strain. That is the doctrine of inspiration in the form Scripture usually gives it: God speaking, and a real human being genuinely writing. Peter puts it the same way — men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1:21).

And there is a third thing in the clause, easily passed over. To your fathers. The Spirit said it to Isaiah's generation eight hundred years earlier — and Paul applies it, without apology, to the men walking out of his lodging that evening. Scripture is not a record of what God once said to other people. It is God's address to whoever is in the room.

Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.

The quotation is Isaiah 6:9–10 — the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning, in the year King Uzziah died, when he saw the Lord high and lifted up and the seraphim covering their faces.

It is worth knowing what a heavy thing Paul has just picked up. This is the most-quoted Old Testament passage in the entire New Testament on the subject of unbelief. Jesus quoted it to explain why he taught in parables (Matt. 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10). John quoted it to explain why the miracles had not produced faith (John 12:40). Paul reaches for the same theme in Romans 11:8, from Deuteronomy and Isaiah 29. Every writer who has to account for the fact that Israel heard the Messiah and did not receive him goes to the same place — the words God gave a prophet on the day he called him.

Notice also that Paul does not soften it, and does not aim it at them personally as an accusation. He states it and leaves. The text does the work.

parallels.desc: keep on hearing, but do not understand

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed.

Look at the order, because Isaiah built it deliberately and it is a small piece of architecture.

Going in, the sequence runs heart → ears → eyes: the heart dulls first, then the hearing goes, then the eyes shut. Coming out — in the healing clause that follows — it runs the other way: eyes → ears → heart. Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn.

The way out is the way in, run backwards. Sight, then hearing, then a heart that understands, and then the turning. It is a description of how a person actually comes to faith, written in reverse as a description of how they avoid it.

Now the hard part, and it should not be dodged.

Their eyes they have closed. That is active. Nobody did it to them. In the Greek Paul is quoting, the shutting of the eyes is something the people do to themselves — the deliberate refusal to look at something they suspect they will have to act on.

And yet in Isaiah 6 the prophet is commissioned to produce this effect: make the heart of this people dull… lest they see with their eyes. God sends the message knowing, and in some sense intending, that it will harden.

Both are in the text and Scripture never resolves them into one. Paul himself wrestled with it for three whole chapters in the letter he had already sent to this city (Rom. 9–11), and his conclusion was not a formula but worship: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! (Rom. 11:33). What he refuses to do — and what we must refuse — is to let either side cancel the other. The hardened are genuinely responsible; they closed their own eyes. And God is genuinely sovereign over the outcome. A reader who has to flatten one of those to keep the other has stopped reading the Bible and started tidying it.

What must not happen is that this verse becomes a weapon. Paul quotes it in sorrow, about his own people, having just spent a full day trying to persuade them, having said he would be damned for them if it were possible.

And I would heal them.

And then the last clause, which changes the colour of everything before it.

The sentence does not end with judgment. It ends with a physician. The whole terrible mechanism of dulled hearts and stopped ears and shut eyes exists in the text as an explanation of what is being kept out — and what is being kept out is healing. God's own stated desire, at the end of the hardest passage in the prophets about unbelief, is I would heal them.

That is the God being refused. Not a God looking for a reason to condemn, casting about for an excuse. A God standing at the door of a nation with medicine in his hands, saying that if they would only look, and listen, and understand, and turn, he would heal them — and grieving that they have shut their eyes rather than let him. The tragedy of Israel in this verse is not that God was unwilling. He was never unwilling. He says so in the same breath in which he describes their refusal, and he has been saying it since Isaiah stood in the temple, and he is saying it still.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.

Paul's last recorded words to a Jewish audience in Acts, and they need to be handled with care, because they have been badly misused.

First, what the sentence says. This salvation of God — the same salvation, not a substitute or a second-best. It has been sent — a passive; God sent it, this is not Paul's decision or Paul's reprisal. And they will listen — a plain future, and a confident one.

Second, what it does not say. It does not say God has finished with Israel. It cannot, because the man speaking had already written, to this very city, the definitive answer to that question: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Rom. 11:1). Paul is himself the counter-example, and he says so. He goes on in that letter to speak of a remnant now, a hardening that is partial and temporary, and a future in which mercy comes round to Israel again (Rom. 11:5, 25–26).

And note what happened in the room that very day: some were convinced (v. 24). Even in this final scene, the response is divided, not uniform. Some Jews in Rome believed Paul that afternoon.

This is also the point in Acts where readers in our own congregations will differ, and the difference should be handled with respect rather than scored. Many dear brothers and sisters hold that God's promises to national Israel await a literal future fulfilment — and they hold it because they take the promises seriously and refuse to spiritualise them away, and that instinct deserves respect. Teachers who have shaped many of us have taught it warmly and carefully.

The Reformed reading emphasises rather that all God's promises find their Yes in Christ and that Jew and Gentile are made one new man in him (2 Cor. 1:20; Eph. 2:14–16) — and that is the more likely reading, because the New Testament itself declares the promises fulfilled in Christ and his one people. What both readings hold — and this is far more than what separates them — is that God has not finished with the Jewish people, that his covenant faithfulness does not fail, and that Romans 11 forbids any Gentile Christian from the smallest trace of superiority: do not be arrogant toward the branches (Rom. 11:18).
