A note on the missing verse 29. Readers following in an older Bible will find a verse 29 here — And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves — and will not find it in the ESV, which prints it only as a footnote. This is not something being removed from Scripture. It is the opposite: the earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have the sentence, and it appears to have been added later by a copyist, most likely to smooth the transition into v. 30. Modern translations set it in a footnote so the reader can see exactly what the evidence is. Nothing whatever hangs on it; the substance is already in v. 25, where they departed disagreeing among themselves.

It is worth knowing that this openness is a strength rather than a weakness — the manuscript record of the New Testament is so rich that we can see precisely where a later hand has smoothed a seam, and say so out loud in a footnote.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: “And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.”

parallels.desc: your saving power among all nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him.

Two years. Luke gives no verdict, no trial, no execution, no release — just two years, and then he stops writing.

Take the picture first, because it is a strange one. Paul is under military custody, chained by the wrist to a rotating guard, in rented lodgings he is paying for himself. He cannot go out. So everyone comes in.

Welcomed all who came to him. All. Jews and Gentiles, the curious and the convinced, householders and slaves — and, since the guard changed shift by shift, a steady procession of Praetorian soldiers who had no choice but to stand there and listen. Paul mentions the result in a letter written from this house: the gospel had become known throughout the whole imperial guard, and there are saints of Caesar's household (Phil. 1:13; 4:22).

And on the traditional view this is where the prison letters come from. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon — written in these two years, in this room, by a man chained to a soldier. The chain that stopped him travelling produced the documents that reached further than his travelling ever did.

Proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

Luke's last sentence, and every word of it is chosen.

Proclaiming the kingdom of God. The book opened with the risen Christ spending forty days speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3). It closes with his prisoner doing the same in Rome. The two ends of the book are tied.

With all boldness. Parresia — the frank, unguarded speech of a free man. It is the word the church prayed for when the authorities first told them to be quiet (4:29), and God gave it then and has not withdrawn it now.

Without hindrance. Akolytos. And this is the very last word of the Greek text of Acts — Luke ends his two-volume history on an adverb, and the adverb is unhinderedly.

Which raises the question every reader asks: why does it stop there? What happened to Paul?

The honest answer is that Luke does not tell us, and the reasons offered are worth weighing. Some think he wrote before the case was decided, which would explain the abruptness. Others note that a third volume may have been intended. But the strongest reason is simply that Luke has finished the story he set out to tell. His subject was never Paul's biography; it was announced in the first chapter — you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). The gospel has reached the capital of the world and is being preached there without restriction. That is the end of the story.

As for the man: early tradition, outside Scripture and therefore held loosely, says he was released, travelled again — possibly to Spain, as he had hoped (Rom. 15:24) — was re-arrested, and was executed at Rome under Nero. The Pastoral Epistles read as though they come from that later period, and 2 Timothy sounds very much like a man writing his last letter.

But Luke will not end there, and it is important to see that this is a decision rather than an accident. He could have written the death of Paul; he had written the death of Stephen and the death of James. He ends instead on an adverb about the word of God.

And consider what that word has come through to earn it.

It was ordered silenced by the Sanhedrin, and it spread. Its first preacher was stoned in the street, and it spread. Herod put James to the sword and Peter in prison, and the angel opened the door, and the word spread. It was flogged out of Philippi, shouted down in Thessalonica, laughed at in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, and dragged through four courts. Forty men swore an oath to stop it and failed. The sea rose against it for fourteen days and put it on a beach, alive. A snake fastened on it and it shook the snake into the fire. And here at the end, the emperor of the world has the preacher chained by the wrist in a rented room in his own capital — and the word of God walks in and out of that room, all day, every day, for two years, and no one on earth can lay a finger on it.

That is why the book has no ending. It is not a story that has finished; it is a story that is still running, and the last word Luke wrote is the reason. Unhindered.

And the last thing to say about the book of Acts is not about Luke, and not about Paul.

Thirty years before that rented room, a handful of frightened people stood on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching a man go up out of their sight. They had nothing — no standing, no money, no protection, no plan anyone would have funded. What they had was his word that they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth, and the promise of his Spirit, and the memory of an empty tomb.

And he did it. Not they — he. He poured out the Spirit at Pentecost and three thousand came in. He struck down his own worst enemy on the Damascus road and made him the apostle to the nations. He opened a businesswoman's heart at a riverside in Philippi and, some days later, shook the prison doors open. He stood beside his servant in a barracks cell in the dark and told him he would see Rome, and then he held a ship together for fourteen days to keep the appointment. Every mile of it was his doing, and every soul brought in was his.

The Lord Jesus Christ is building his church, exactly as he said he would, and the gates of hell have not prevailed and will not. He is doing it still, in places no apostle ever heard of, in languages Luke could not have pronounced, through people whose names will never be written down — and he will not stop until the last of them is home. The chain was on the apostle's wrist. It was never anywhere near the word of God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Luke ends with the gospel preached “without hindrance” at the heart of the empire.

parallels.desc: the word of God is not bound

28.title: Rome at Last
28.text: <sup>1</sup>After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. <sup>2</sup>The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. <sup>3</sup>When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <sup>4</sup>When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” <sup>5</sup>He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <sup>6</sup>They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <sup>7</sup>Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <sup>8</sup>It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <sup>9</sup>And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <sup>10</sup>They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. <sup>11</sup>After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. <sup>12</sup>Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. <sup>13</sup>And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <sup>14</sup>There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome. <sup>15</sup>And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. <sup>16</sup>And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. <sup>17</sup>After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <sup>18</sup>When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case. <sup>19</sup>But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—though I had no charge to bring against my nation. <sup>20</sup>For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” <sup>21</sup>And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. <sup>22</sup>But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.” <sup>23</sup>When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. <sup>24</sup>And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. <sup>25</sup>And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: <sup>26</sup>‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. <sup>27</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>28</sup>Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.” <sup>30</sup>He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, <sup>31</sup>proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
